title: Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis Reveals Differential Exon Usage and Virulence Gene Family Dynamics in Plasmodium falciparum during Severe Malaria
authors: Ansah, P. M., Dzadey, W. O., Martey, A., Abdullah, H., Awuku, W.
abstract: Malaria remains a leading cause of child mortality in developing countries, with roughly 610,000 deaths per year. While the disease is caused by five human Plasmodium species, Plasmodium falciparum (Pf ) causes the most severe form. Progression from uncomplicated to severe malaria is characterized by high proliferation of the parasite, severely affecting children under five years old. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression remain an active area of research. Many multicopy genes have been implicated in Pf virulence. Some of these genes are implicated in cytoadherence, host-cell invasion, immune evasion, sequestration of infected erythrocytes, and antigenic variation. We employed an integrative transcriptomic analysis in this study to elucidate the molecular underpinnings of severe malaria and gene expression patterns, virulence gene dynamics, and the potential contribution of alternative splicing. Results show an overexpression of protein synthesis and ribosomal genes associated with severe malaria. About 86% (n=1865) of all differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were downregulated in severe malaria, and 226 genes exhibited both differential expression and differential exon usage (DEU). Pf virulence genes and antigenic genes such as var (pfEMP1), stevor, surfin, rif (rifin), ptm-2TM, and msp were upregulated in severe malaria compared with uncomplicated malaria, except for rifin. In severe malaria, there was evidence of co-expression and regulation within multigene families, as well as DEU and alternative splicing in virulence genes and antimalarial resistance-related proteins. Pf does not employ a single mechanism for disease progression but suppresses and deregulates nonessential pathways, processes, and genes, which are upregulated virulence genes, DNA replication, mRNA transcription, and protein synthesis. Multicopy genes are co-expressed and regulated to meet the molecular needs of the parasite. The parasite employs alternative splicing and DEU mechanisms for immune invasion and evasion, host-parasite interaction, as well as antimalarial resistance.

title: Amino acid clustering and epistasis guide sequence-based prediction of phenotype modulation
authors: Hernandez Berthet, A. S., Sanchez, I. E., Noguera, M. E., Roman, E. A.
abstract: Protein sequences encode the molecular information necessary for their biological function. As functional adaptation often emerges from combined effects of multiple positions, understanding how sequence variation gives rise to functional differences remains a central challenge. Here, we developed an improved strategy to identify phenotype modulating positions and use them to predict phenotypes, by relating amino acid identity to experimentally measured quantitative properties across families. Using family-specific sequence-phenotype datasets, our results show that epistasis plays a crucial role in phenotype modulation. Position specific amino acid clustering further improved performance indicating that key functional information is often captured by broad physicochemical amino acid classes, with hydrophobicity playing a crucial role in phenotype modulation. Our identified phenotype modulating positions involve both proximal and distal sites relative to functional sites. While the former is captured by individual positions, the latter is captured when epistasis is taken into account. Comparison with experimentally identified positions showed partial recovery of known functionally relevant residues, while at the same time revealing candidate positions that may contribute to phenotypic variation. Taken together, these results suggest that quantitative phenotypes are often governed by a network of interacting amino acid residues and may be engineered by a limited amount of sequence modifications. This finding highlights the potential of our framework to deepen our understanding of protein function, evolution, and adaptation, providing new targets for the rational modulation and engineering of protein phenotypes.

title: Ok-k-mer: Selecting k-mer length ensembles for calculating genomic distance
abstract: Current methods for computing sequence similarity across large groups of genome sequences tend to do so at the level of k-mers since this is far more efficient than base-by-base alignment. While these methods use default k-mer lengths, recent work shows that the particular choice of k-mer length greatly affects accuracy, and that using multiple values of k can boost accuracy relative to the best single choice of k, particularly when the goal is to estimate genomic distances that reflect true phylogenetic relationships. Here, we introduce Ok-k-mer, a tool to systematically select weighted k-mer length ensembles for pairwise genomic distance estimation, thereby increasing the accuracy of those estimates. Given a phylogenetic tree, Ok-k-mer ranks genome pairs by Jaccard distance across a range of k and uses a progressive search to maximize the Spearman correlation, {rho}, between weighted-average k-mer ranks and branch distances. Across eight Genome Taxonomy Database datasets, Ok-k-mer ensembles improved correlation over standard default k-mer lengths. In the Chlamydiales taxonomy, a three-length ensemble k=(9,17,22) achieved a 23.9% relative improvement over the best single length (k=20) and a 36.7% improvement over a commonly used default of 31-mers. We demonstrate that Ok-k-mer k-mer length ensembles remain stable (i.e. lengths and weights change only moderately) under genome subsampling within a taxonomy but vary across datasets. Ok-k-mer can annotate all subtrees of a phylogeny, which reveals distinct patterns of ensembles reflecting potential differences in genome evolution. Ok-k-mer provides a framework for moving beyond a "one-k-fits-all" k-mer analysis, improving genomic distance estimation in the era of massive-scale genomics.

title: Population Genomics of the Bovine Sialic Acid Network Reveals Functional and Evolutionary Diversity Across European and South African Cattle Breeds
authors: Ogun, o. J., Aiyesa, L. V., Idowu, P. A. P., Becker, D. P., Galuska, S. P.
abstract: **Background:** Sialic acids, mainly N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) and N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), are terminal monosaccharides of glycans involved in numerous physiological processes, such as immune and neuronal function. Their biosynthesis, transport, transfer and turnover depend on a network of genes, but genetic studies in cattle have mostly addressed individual genes or genetic associations with milk oligosaccharide concentrations, leaving variation across this network largely uncharacterized. In bovine milk, sialylated glycans that depend on this network vary among animals and change rapidly during early lactation. We therefore characterized variation in 13 selected genes of the bovine sialic acid network using whole-genome sequence data from European and South African cattle. **Results:** We analyzed 346 animals from 12 European and 4 South African breeds. Of 9,724 variants in the 13 target genes, 8,675 were intronic and 62 were predicted to alter the amino acid sequence. Integration of SIFT predictions, Rate4Site conservation and protein context, with population representation as supporting evidence, identified 15 prioritized candidates, including 7 high-priority candidates in NEU3, ST8SIA2, ST8SIA4, CMAH and ST3GAL4. The most differentiated candidates were not among the 15 prioritized variants. NEU3 Y136H showed the largest regional contrast in allele frequency (0.83 in South African and 0.34 in European cattle), whereas several prioritized candidates were represented by a single allele in the South African cohort. Genome-wide principal component analysis of 950,219 linkage-disequilibrium-pruned SNPs separated South African from European cattle along the first component, which explained about 25% of the variance. None of the 220 analyzed common pathway SNPs exceeded the corresponding genome-wide differentiation thresholds at breed, country or regional level. Within the ascertained pathway SNPs, diversity was higher in South African breeds, and Tajima's D was shifted toward positive values in European breeds and centered near zero in South African breeds. **Conclusions:** This study provides a network-wide map of predicted protein-altering variation in the bovine sialic acid pathway and identifies 15 candidates for functional investigation, most of them rare. Because the most differentiated variants were not those with the strongest functional support, population contrasts, evolutionary conservation and protein context provide complementary evidence for selecting candidates. The analyzed common pathway SNPs did not show exceptional differentiation relative to the genome-wide background. The candidates provide specific targets for genotyping, enzyme-level testing and genotype-informed milk phenotyping.

title: Transcriptome profiling reveals gene regulatory network governing seed size in Brassica napus
authors: Zoclanclounon, Y. A. B., Siles, L., Woolfenden, H., Morris, R. J., Kurup, S.
abstract: Seed size is a critical trait influencing yield and quality in oilseed crops such as Brassica napus. Despite their economic importance, the genetic and molecular mechanisms regulating seed size remain unclear, particularly in polyploid species, such as B. napus. To deepen our understanding of seed size regulation, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis across four developmental stages (heart, torpedo, green, and mature) and three distinct seed organs: the seed coat, embryo, and endosperm. Differential expression analysis between B. napus var. Zhongshuang (ZS11) and B. napus cv. Ragged Jack (RJ) was performed to uncover regulatory networks involved in seed size control. Our results uncovered dynamic gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and pinpointed key regulators, including well-established factors like ABI5 and BRI1, as well as novel candidate genes such as KNAT5, ARF11, SUS2, UGT72B1, UGT89A2, and SBT1.7. The present research provides an understanding of the regulatory networks governing seed size in B. napus. These findings not only enhance our knowledge of seed biology but also offer valuable resources for future breeding strategies aimed at optimizing seed size and yield in polyploid oilseed crops.

title: Genomes of Solenogastres Shed Light on Ancestral Molluscan Biomineralization Genes
abstract: Aplacophora (Solenogastres + Caudofoveata) is a group of worm-like molluscs that lack a shell and instead are covered with aragonitic spines and scales called sclerites. Sclerites are also found along the girdle in chitons (Polyplacophora) and are a synapomorphy for Aculifera (Aplacophora + Polyplacophora), which is the sister taxon of all other shell-bearing molluscs (Conchifera). However, whether the same genetic mechanism underlies the process of biomineralization in aculiferans and conchiferans is unknown. To investigate evolution of genes involved in biomineralization across Mollusca, we re-sequenced the genomes of two species of Solenogastres,   Epimenia babai   and   Neomenia megatrapezata  , producing near-chromosome-level assemblies through PacBio HiFi and Hi-C scaffolding. Using a combination of orthology inference and similarity searches against a known SMP database we identified 1,244 putative SMP orthogroups across Mollusca, 292 of which were present in at least one solenogaster genome. SMPs undergoing significant expansion/contraction at key nodes were further investigated. Of these, 15 were found in at least one solenogaster genome and included families containing chitin-binding, von Willebrand factor A, and C-type lectin domains. Across Mollusca, Solenogastres showed the highest number of significant losses in all gene families, including the SMPs investigated. Targeted searches for structural, silk-like proteins in Aculifera show further reductions in Solenogastres (16-17) compared to caudofoveates (29) and chitons (46-80). Altogether, our results support a conserved but reduced biomineralization toolkit underlying sclerite formation in Solenogastres and identify candidate genes for further proteomic and functional study.

title: Contrasting within-donor gene covariation identifies disease-associated cells and genes in case-control single-cell studies
abstract: In case-control single-cell studies, disease often affects only a subset of cells of a given type within each patient. Comparing all cells from patients with all cells from control donors therefore dilutes disease signals, while donor variation and recorded or unrecorded batch effects can be confounded with disease status. We present IDC (Identification of Disease-associated Cells), which uses this cellular heterogeneity as signal. A mixture of affected and unaffected cells creates coordinated variation among disease-associated genes within each patient, whereas shifts shared by all cells of a donor leave this within-donor covariance unchanged. IDC therefore contrasts within-donor gene-gene covariance between patients and controls to learn disease-associated expression programs without batch labels, then applies positive-unlabeled learning to score each cell's disease-like state and estimate each donor's disease burden. IDC also computes, in closed form, gene contribution scores and leave-gene-out cell scores that exclude each tested gene, enabling within-donor differential expression testing and cross-donor meta-analysis without retraining. In simulations, IDC identified affected cells and estimated donor burden more accurately than deep generative and label-refinement methods, remained robust to strong unrecorded batch effects, and detected differentially expressed genes more sensitively than case-control pseudobulk methods while controlling false discoveries. In human pancreatic islets and prefrontal cortex, disease burden in held-out donors separated type 2 diabetes (T2D) from non-diabetic donors in beta cells, and late-stage Alzheimer's disease (AD) from non-AD donors in astrocytes and inhibitory neurons, while placing prediabetic and early-AD donors at intermediate levels. Genes with the highest IDC contribution scores were more strongly enriched for the KEGG T2D and AD pathways than case-control pseudobulk rankings, and within-donor testing revealed coordinated metabolic, cell-adhesion and synaptic changes along the inferred disease axis.

title: PyTorch Frustratometer: An Ultra-fast, Parallelized Tool for Proteome-Scale Local Energetic Frustration Analysis
authors: Draizen, E. J., Jaafari, H., Bueno, C., Llaberia, A., Clark, F., Galpern, E. A., Simonetti, F. L., Freiberger, M. I., Wolynes, P. G., Ferreiro, D. U., Parra, R. G.
abstract: Most natural protein sequences fold into well-defined three-dimensional structural ensembles, satisfying interactions that have been shaped over evolutionary timescales. The principle of minimal frustration states that most native interactions are energetically more favorable than alternative non-native ones, resulting in a funnel-shaped folding energy landscape. The FrustratometeR tool measures how the energetics of a residue or contact compares to decoys with different amino acid identities or configurations. Contacts are classified as minimally frustrated when these are more stable than random alternatives, highly frustrated when less stable, or neutral when energetically indistinguishable from them. Clusters of highly frustrated interactions are often evolutionarily conserved and are typically associated with functional regions. Therefore, identifying and quantifying local frustration can provide insights into both protein stability and function. Here we present a PyTorch reimplementation of FrustratometeR that accelerates conventional frustration calculations by 70-13,000x on a single GPU, depending on chosen frustration mode and protein size, with substantially larger gains for exhaustive mutational scanning, enabling proteome-scale local frustration analysis. We benchmark against the original algorithm on the CATH v4.4 S40 dataset and show near-identical results across all three frustration modes and mutational scanning. Source code is freely available at https://github.com/ParraLab-ESBG/pytorch-frustratometer.

title: Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
authors: Rao, P. V., Sommer, D., Davidson, D., Alberstein, R. G., Ludwiczak, J., Kleinhenz, J., Vani, B., Park, E., Lee, J. H., Izadi, S., Kiefer, J. R., Bonneau, R., Mahajan, S. P., Watkins, A. M., Dreyer, F. A.
abstract: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

title: HERACLES for fast and accurate likelihood-based reconstruction of massive lineages
abstract: CRISPR-based lineage recording technologies can trace the ancestry of hundreds of thousands of cells, yet reconstructing accurate phylogenies at this scale remains computationally challenging. Likelihood-based methods employ explicit evolutionary models of CRISPR editing that improve tree accuracy but require computationally expensive searches over tree topologies, whereas distance-based alternatives scale efficiently but rely on distances that may not faithfully represent the editing process, introducing biases whose magnitude and direction are unknown. Here, we introduce HERACLES, which optimizes cell coordinates in hyperbolic space under a quartet-based composite likelihood of CRISPR editing. By recovering local branching structures directly from embedded distances, HERACLES guides continuous optimization with an explicit evolutionary model without repeatedly constructing and evaluating complete phylogenies. Across simulated benchmarks, HERACLES improves reconstruction accuracy over existing methods and scales to lineages containing 150,000 cells in about four hours on a single GPU. On experimental KP-tracer and PEtracer datasets, HERACLES reconstructs phylogenies consistent with independent anatomical annotations and temporal lineage markers. Its flexible likelihood framework also accommodates different recording mechanisms: incorporating sequential editing improves reconstruction of simulated DNA Typewriter lineages. Together, these results establish continuous optimization of local evolutionary relationships as a scalable and flexible approach to probabilistic lineage reconstruction.

title: Systematic promoter perturbation reveals limitations of AlphaGenome gene expression predictions
authors: Sreenivasan, V. K. A., Aksu, E. D., Spielmann, M.
abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) models promise to facilitate the interpretation of noncoding variants by predicting their effects on gene regulation directly from genomic sequence. However, whether these models recapitulate fundamental principles of transcriptional biology remains unclear. Here, we tested whether AlphaGenome recognizes the expected consequences of promoter disruption on predicted gene expression. We systematically perturbed annotated promoter elements in silico for 2,111 promoter-gene pairs using dinucleotide shuffling, GC-adjusted random base substitution, and N-masking. We then compared AlphaGenome-predicted CAGE and RNA-sequencing signals across 20 tissues for reference and promoter-disrupted sequences. While CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions were strongly correlated for reference sequences, promoter disruption markedly reduced predicted CAGE activity, with N masking producing reductions of approximately three orders of magnitude. By contrast, the predicted RNA-sequencing signals were substantially less affected, resulting in an uncoupling of two molecular readouts of gene expression. Exon-level analyses showed that AlphaGenome predicted reduced RNA-sequencing signal when exonic sequences are within the disrupted region, but frequently failed to propagate this effect to downstream exons. This divergence between the CAGE and RNA-sequencing readouts was apparent from the second exon onward and was more pronounced in longer genes. Although alternative transcription initiation and shared downstream exons may explain individual cases, it is unlikely to account for the systematic discordance between CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions. These findings indicate that AlphaGenome can recognize the local loss of promoter activity without consistently capturing its consequences across the corresponding transcript. More broadly, our results show that predictions from individual S2F output tracks do not necessarily reflect a coherent model of transcription. Systematic biological benchmarking and experimental validation therefore remain essential before such predictions can be used to prioritize or classify noncoding variants in research or diagnostic settings.

title: Genome assembly and characterization of two Brazilian soybean cultivars contrasting for stink bug resistance
authors: Godoy Filho, M. A. d., Viana, J. P. G., Santos, L. B. d., Wei, W., Santos, M. d. F., Pinheiro, J. B.
abstract: Brazil's tropical soybean germplasm still has few genomic resources: only one assembly of a Brazilian cultivar is available at NCBI. Here we describe chromosome-level de novo assemblies of two contrasting cultivars: IAC-100, described as resistant to phytophagous stink bugs, and CD-215, susceptible. We sequenced high molecular weight DNA using 10x Genomics linked reads, assembled the reads with Supernova, anchored the assembly to the Williams 82 reference with RaGOO and corrected structural errors with REAPR. The assemblies span 1.057 and 1.061 Gb, with scaffold N50 values of 53.6 and 54.2 Mb (48.0 and 47.7 Mb excluding gaps), and recover more than 97% of conserved plant genes assessed by BUSCO. Homology-based projection of the reference protein-coding genes generated 46,774 and 46,620 gene models. Comparing the proteomes of the two cultivars, we identified 2,002 divergent isoforms in 1,427 loci, classified by sequence divergence, length variation, combined divergence and non-conserved homology. These data expand the genomic resources for tropical soybean germplasm, still underrepresented in public databases, and for studies of insect resistance.

title: Rapid environmental DNA detection with isothermal amplification methods: a comparison with the real-time quantitative PCR in the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita).
authors: Chieux, A., Guerrieri, A., Bellemain, E., Boyer, F., Merzi, T., Tablerlet, P., Iribar, A., Zinger, L., Bonin, A.
abstract: Species detection relying on environmental DNA (eDNA) traditionally relies on Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). This amplification technique takes in general a minimum of one hour and requires in most cases access to specialized laboratories and equipment. Isothermal amplification techniques, originating from clinical research, are emerging as rapid and field-deployable alternative methods. Yet, whether their sensitivity, specificity, and cost/time-efficiency are comparable to the traditional real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) remains to be assessed. In this work, we compare the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with qPCR to detect the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita) from aquatic filtrations. This objective was achieved in three steps. First, we developed LAMP and RPA primers specific to the target species based on its mitochondrial genome. Second, we amplified DNA extracts from E. calamita and from tissues of closely related species using real-time fluorescence detection with LAMP, RPA, and qPCR commercially available protocols to evaluate and compare the sensitivity and specificity of the three methods. Finally, we validated all protocols on eDNA extracts recovered from water samples from ponds surveyed by field scientists. We show that RPA had a sensitivity equivalent to that of the qPCR, while LAMP sensitivity was ten times lower. All our assays amplified the species DNA in eDNA samples where the species was observed by field scientists. Through this work, we thus propose a robust methodology for implementing isothermal amplification assays for eDNA applications and show that RPA is a good alternative to qPCR for detecting conservation-priority species (i.e. protected or invasive species) when time and lab facilities are constrained.

title: Uniformly re-analysed public omics data and graded meta-analyses of exercise responses in humans and rodents
abstract: Hundreds of omics studies have profiled molecular responses to exercise, but they differ in species, tissue, protocol, sampling time and analysis pipeline, so their results are hard to combine. This dataset places the public evidence on a common scale. We screened GEO, PRIDE and Metabolomics Workbench for exercise studies in humans, mice and rats, defined exercise-control contrasts from sample-level metadata and uniformly re-analysed 1,037 contrasts from 448 independent study clusters, covering 20 tissue classes and seven molecular data types. For every contrast, the dataset provides moderated standardized effect sizes for each gene, protein, miRNA or metabolite and, for expression data, pathways. For 88 analysis units defined by tissue, exercise paradigm and molecular layer, it provides random-effects meta-analyses of every feature measured in at least three independent studies, with heterogeneity statistics, evidence classes assigned by pre-specified criteria and replication tests in two held-out training atlases. Curation records, code and a static query website are included. The data support look-up of molecules, new meta-analyses and planning and benchmarking of exercise studies.

title: Integrating bacterial genomics and host transcriptomics links Burkholderia pseudomallei variation to melioidosis mortality and neutrophil responses
authors: Wongprommoon, A., Boonklang, P., Burnham, K. L., Chomkatekaew, C., Angchagun, K., Wongsuvan, G., Ngernseng, T., Limmathurotsakul, D., Boonchalermvichien, T., Coston, T. D., Phunpang, R., Yimthin, T., Rongkard, P., Lee, W., Kronsteiner, B., Knight, J., Corander, J., Peacock, S. J., Parkhill, J., Day, N. P. J., Dunachie, S. J., West, T. E., Chantratita, N., Thomson, N. R., Davenport, E. E., Chewapreecha, C.
abstract: Bacterial genetic variation contributes to the outcome of infection, but its relationship with host immune responses is rarely investigated in the same patients, limiting the biological interpretation of pathogen-associated disease severity. Here, we integrated pathogen genomics, clinical outcomes and host transcriptomics to investigate host-pathogen interactions in melioidosis, a frequently fatal infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. We analysed prospective clinical data from 2,142 patients, whole-genome sequences from 2,101 infecting isolates and 646 paired host blood transcriptomes across five cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. Infections were typically dominated by a single strain, with limited within-host diversification, supporting the use of an infecting isolate genome to investigate pathogen-associated clinical outcomes. Bacterial genome-wide association studies identified one locus associated with binary mortality at genome-wide significance. Incorporating patient age, sex, body mass index and Charlson Comorbidity Index increased this to four, while modelling time to death as a continuous phenotype identified seven loci. Integration with paired host transcriptomes linked mortality-associated bacterial genetic variation to imputed signatures of increased immature neutrophils and reduced neutrophil degranulation. An intergenic region upstream of the polyketide synthesis locus BPSS1006-BPSS1011 was additionally associated with downregulation of host genes involved in myeloid-cell signalling and cell proliferation pathways. These findings connect naturally occurring B. pseudomallei genomic variation associated with mortality to distinct host immune signatures, providing insight into pathogen-host interactions underlying severe melioidosis and a framework for investigating the contribution of pathogen genetic diversity to clinical outcomes.

title: Realism and resolution: How AI-predicted protein structures differ from experimental structures
authors: van der Kant, R., Delgado Blanco, J., Serrano, L., Schymkowitz, J., Rousseau, F.
abstract: Protein structure predictors can recover protein folds with remarkable accuracy, and their models are increasingly used as if they were experimental structures. Yet even for a confidently predicted fold, it remains difficult to judge how faithfully the model reproduces protein geometry. We introduce WhatRes, which assesses a structure from its coordinates on two complementary axes. Apparent resolution estimates the experimental resolution its local geometry most closely resembles. Realism measures how closely that geometry matches experimental structures at the same apparent resolution. Predicted models can score well on apparent resolution while showing systematically less variation in bond lengths and angles than is observed in high-resolution crystal structures. WhatRes reveals this over-idealisation even in high-confidence models.

title: BEHAV3D-Explorer enables natural language-assisted profiling of 3D cellular dynamics
authors: de Blank, S., Rios-Jimenez, E., Rubio-Munoz, A., Hoffman, O., Vervoort, B. M. T., Wezenaar, A. K. L., Mazalo, J. K., Molina-Moreno, M., Chang, H.-F., Wehrens, E. J., Rios, A. C., Alieva, M.
abstract: Obtaining quantitative measurements from live 3D microscopy remains difficult to implement across research settings, particularly without profound image-analysis expertise. We present BEHAV3D-Explorer, an interactive, user-friendly platform that uses natural-language guidance to help users select analysis strategies, tune parameters and configure workflows. BEHAV3D-Explorer enables time-resolved behavioral classification and integrates it with morphological, interaction and functional analyses, thereby connecting dynamic readouts to yield interpretable results across imaging applications.

title: scHiR learns joint cellular representations from paired single-cell transcriptome and 3D genome data
authors: Zhao, Y., Jia, P., Hill, M. C., Tang, L., Fang, Z., Zheng, R., Li, M.
abstract: Simultaneously sequenced scRNA-seq and scHi-C technologies provide matched measurements of gene expression and three-dimensional (3D) genome organization within individual cells, offering complementary insights into cellular state. However, integrative analysis remains challenging due to the heterogeneous structures and characteristics of these modalities. To realize the full potential of such data, we need effective computational methods to learn joint cellular representations. Here, we present scHiR, a framework based on a hyperspherical variational autoencoder (S-VAE) for learning co-embeddings from paired gene-expression profiles and chromatin contact maps. The framework facilitate downstream analyses such as cell clustering, fine-grained cell-state characterization, and developmental trajectory inference, while modality-specific decoders enable the signal recovery of input profiles. We evaluated scHiR across six paired datasets generated by HiRES, GAGE-seq, and LiMCA. scHiR captured cell-type-specific information and achieved improved clustering performance compared with representative single-omics methods. It was also capable of resolving fine-grained subclusters and revealed discordant and distinct cellular profiles. In developmental biological datasets, scHiR preserved trajectory-related structure and improved pseudotime in agreement with known developmental progression. Finally, scHiR generated reconstructed transcriptomic and chromatin contact profiles with reduced noise, enhanced cell-type-related signals, and improved recovery of held-out chromatin contacts. These results demonstrate that scHiR provides an effective method for learning joint cellular representations from paired scRNA-seq and scHi-C data.

title: π-SPECFormer: A Mass Spectrometry-based Foundation Model for Decoding the Dark Proteome
authors: Ling, T., Liu, T., Xu, F., Zhang, Y., Xia, J., Huang, X., Chen, S., Xie, L., Xu, R., Yang, T., Li, K., Wang, G., Liang, Z., Zhu, J., Li, S. Z., He, F., Wang, Y., Chang, C.
abstract: In mass-spectrometry-based proteomics, a substantial proportion of acquired spectra remain unidentified, concealing a vast reservoir of biological variations commonly termed the "dark proteome", potentially obscuring sequence mutations, non-canonical peptides and post-translational modifications. Existing deep-learning methods largely rely on supervised training with peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs), limiting their ability to learn from the much larger pool of unannotated spectra. Here we introduce {pi}-SPECFormer, a mass-spectrometry foundation model pre-trained on 291 million spectra through a two-stage framework that combines self-supervised and PSMs-guided representation learning. {pi}-SPECFormer transfers effectively to de novo peptide sequencing, spectrum clustering and modification detection, consistently outperforming task-specific baselines. When applied to proteomic profiles from 103 individuals with lung adenocarcinoma, the model identified nine high-confidence mutated peptides, including six that were absent from the reference databases. {pi}-SPECFormer thus enables unbiased decoding of molecular complexity beyond the boundaries of the canonical proteome.

title: LinearKnot: linear-time ensemble analysis of RNA density-2 pseudoknots under hierarchical folding
abstract: Motivation: A pseudoknot is an arrangement of crossing base pairs. Pseudoknots complicate structure prediction and calculations over possible structures (an ensemble). CParty sums structure weights for hierarchical pseudoknots that keep a supplied pseudoknot-free structure (scaffold). Its time is cubic in sequence length. Results: LinearKnot approximates CParty with beam pruning. It combines at most two partial structures in each step and keeps the highest-ranked candidates. At fixed beam width, hairpin length limit, and scaffold search limit, partition functions, minimum-free-energy (MFE) predictions, and representative {gamma}-centroid structures from base-pairing probabilities take linear time in sequence length. Loop profiles give probabilities for pairing and six unpaired loop types, including gaps between crossing stems (PseudoLoop). Window accessibility is the probability that a window is unpaired. For each RNA, we compared each base's distributions over pairing partners (including the unpaired state) and structural contexts with exact probabilities and averaged their total variation (TV) distances over bases unpaired in the scaffold. At width 200, the 90th percentiles of these RNA averages among 300-399-base RNAs were 0.0015 for pairing and 0.0017 for contexts. At width 100, LinearKnot completed partition functions for all 107 real RNAs through 29 kilobases. Under our settings, CParty completed RNAs up to about 1 kilobase and was faster on them. For the RNAcentral long non-coding RNA URS00023A4DB9 (29,106 nt), partition-function, pairing-probability, and MFE calculations at width 100 took about 7 minutes and 3.22 GiB. We compared free energy and pairing probabilities before and after each increase in beam width and local limits. These changes generally became smaller at larger widths. At width 200, the calculations for URS00023A4DB9 took about 20 minutes and 5.68 GiB. In rat telomerase RNA, a four-base window next to a pseudoknot was mostly unpaired as part of a PseudoLoop. A pseudoknot-free calculation with the same scaffold gave lower accessibility and placed the window mainly in a hairpin when unpaired. Availability and implementation: LinearKnot provides the linearknot command at https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearKnot. Experiment scripts and data are at https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearKnotExperiments.

title: TideCluster: clustering and classification of tandem repeats for comparative and pangenomic analysis
abstract: Satellite DNA, composed of tandem arrays of relatively short repeated units, is a ubiquitous component of plant and animal genomes. Despite its biological importance, systematic investigation of satellite DNA remains challenging, in part because integrated bioinformatic tools for structured comparative analyses across individual arrays, chromosomes, and genomes are lacking. Here, we present TideCluster, a reference-independent pipeline that converts fragmented tandem repeat detections into genome-wide, interpretable repeat family catalogs. Starting from a genome assembly, TideCluster consolidates detected regions into arrays, clusters arrays by sequence similarity, reconstructs representative monomer consensus sequences, estimates locus-specific periodicity, identifies higher-order repeats, and generates GFF3 annotations. In addition to predefined visualizations, including the chromosomal distributions of satellite repeat families, TideCluster produces information-rich outputs that can be adapted for user-specific downstream analyses. We demonstrate its capabilities using the well-characterized genome of Arabidopsis thaliana and a set of Solanum species with highly diverse satellite repeat complements that vary markedly in abundance and have monomer lengths ranging from a few base pairs to more than 20 kb.

title: Extracting and Updating Compact Colored k-mer Indexes
authors: Depuydt, L., Alanko, J. N., Marchet, C., Puglisi, S. J.
abstract: Colored k-mer indexes record, for every k-mer of a collection of genomes, the genomes or species that contain it, and underpin pseudoalignment and sequence search against large collections. Construction of such an index is expensive, yet the collection it represents is rarely final: genomes are retracted or found to be contaminated, users need an index of a single species or clade, and new genomes keep arriving. Rebuilding the index after every such change requires the original sequences and repeats the costly construction. We show that colored indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) can instead be updated efficiently in batches, without the original sequences, and with a result equivalent to the index built from scratch. Given an SBWT and any subset of its k-mers, we first extract the SBWT of this subset directly from the input, in one linear pass and without building a new index. Removing genomes, intersection and difference all reduce to this operation. We then carry the colors through every operation, by finding from the inputs alone where the color sets of the result change, so that removing or extracting genomes, as well as the union, intersection and difference of two colored indexes, each directly yield a complete colored index. In our experiments, editing paid off for large results: removing a genome from an index of 3,682 E. coli genomes took 54 seconds instead of 13 minutes for a rebuild, and adding one took about a minute. On AllTheBacteria, with 192 billion k-mers and 12,733 species, extracting M. tuberculosis, with 180,094 genomes, took less than four hours, and set operations then traced contamination of its color, some of which the next release of AllTheBacteria still contains. Our work turns large colored k-mer indexes from static snapshots of a collection into resources that can be maintained as the collection evolves. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LoreDepuydt/colored-sbwt-setops.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Personalised Gene Expression Prediction Improves Cell-Type-Specific Association Testing
authors: Styll, P., Di, Y., Cai, N.
abstract: Linking genetic variation to disease requires accurate prediction of its effects on gene expression in relevant cell types. Sequence-to-function models offer a way to predict these effects and, with training on personal genomes, have begun to capture inter-individual expression differences. However, effect sign accuracy remains limited, and predictive uncertainty is unquantified. Here we introduce ATTICUS, which combines personalised sequence representations with uncertainty-aware expression prediction. ATTICUS transfers regulatory information learned in bulk expression pretraining to cell-type-specific expression prediction without requiring genotypes paired with single-cell expression data. Across blood and brain cell types in OneK1K and ROSMAP, ATTICUS approximately doubles expression prediction correlations relative to scPrediXcan and substantially improves sign accuracy. Moreover, ATTICUS enables uncertainty-aware transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). Applied to systemic lupus erythematosus and Alzheimer's disease, ATTICUS identifies more associations, with greater cell-type specificity and stronger directional concordance, and reduced statistical inflation. Together, our results demonstrate that personalised training makes predictions more directionally consistent, and uncertainty propagation improves the calibration of TWAS and the prioritisation of disease genes. ATTICUS provides a framework for both, enabling the use of single-cell expression datasets without matched genotypes to inform uncertainty-aware TWAS, expanding their use in prioritising disease-associated genes and cell types.

title: A genomic prediction framework for growth traits in black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) breeding programmes
authors: Gowda, K. B., Massault, C., Jerry, D. R., Zenger, K. R.
abstract: Background Genomic prediction has been applied in livestock, plant and aquaculture species to accelerate genetic gain. However, its application and potential still remain unexplored in farmed black soldier fly (BSF), an emerging globally important insect production species. Due to the diversity of BSF feed sources, selection strategies need to be evaluated across various feedstocks and production environments to aid in building genomic selection into BSF breeding programmes. In this study, 2,083 BSF larvae from the base population were reared on three diets (SYK: Soy-okara, BSG: brewers' spent grain and FVW: fruit and vegetable waste), and 536 from the F7 population were reared on a chicken starter feed diet. Larvae were phenotyped for four growth traits (LBW, larval body weight; LL, larval length; LW, larval width; LSA, larval surface area) and genotyped across 4,680 SNPs. Genomic prediction was evaluated using seven methods under additive (A) and additive-dominance (AD) models, considering across- and within-diet effects, genotype by diet (G x D) interactions, differences amongst reference and test generations, and SNP densities. Results Performance varied across all scenarios, with LBW showing higher predictive ability (PA) among the growth traits. Accounting for dominance generally improved PA. Multivariate models accounting for G x D performed similarly to, or marginally better than, within-diet predictions. Cross-diet prediction was more variable and generally lower than within-diet prediction, showing reduced transferability across untested nutritional environments. Reducing the SNP density from 4,680 to 3,000 SNPs maintained comparable PA; however, PA decreased below 3,000 SNPs. Across multiple generations, predictive performance declined, resulting from reduced genetic connectivity and possible genotype-by-environment (G x E) interactions between the reference and testing populations. Conclusions Overall, these results provide an application-based framework for genomic prediction in BSF in semi- or commercial production settings. Results also highlight the importance of the genetic model, representative reference populations, and appropriate marker densities for genomic selection.

title: Leave-One-Out-Cross-Validation Based Machine Learning Algorithms for Efficient, Scalable, and Robust Prediction of Artemisinin Resistance in Plasmodium falciparum Kelch13 mutants.
authors: Das, R., Dutta, S., Bhattacharjee, S.
abstract: Emerging Plasmodium falciparum resistance to frontline artemisinin (ART) derivatives threatens global malaria control efforts. Current protocols assigning ART-sensitive (ART-S) or -resistant (ART-R) phenotypes to parasite strains with Kelch13 (K13) mutations remain time-intensive for real-time surveillance. Ring-survival assay (RSA), an ex vivo gold standard mandates laboratory-adaptation under culture conditions and frequently does not replicate clinical ART-responsiveness, thereby limiting its utility for rapidly triaging newly emerging K13 variants. In contrast, advent of artificial intelligence (AI)-derived models hold potential to screen >100 K13 variants within hours, enabling rapid near-real-time prediction of ART-S/R. Here, we engineered a panel of forty representative K13 variants by computing their relative deviations from wild-type K13 across ten physicochemical and structural descriptors, yielding a compact feature set which captures mutation-induced perturbations in folding, stability, and solvent exposure. These can be further utilized to train and validate AI classifier to predict resistance.

title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica) reveals extensive centromeric satellite arrays
authors: Torresen, O. K., Brysting, A. K., Danneels, B., Sandean, R., Kollias, S., Ferrari, G., Tooming-Klunderud, A., Yant, L., Jakobsen, K. S.
abstract: We present a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 322 Mb and 295 Mb, with 89.7% and 95.6% respectively, each scaffolded into 7 chromosomes. Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 97.8% in each haplotype), with 34,213 and 29,684 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. The chromosomes contain extensive centromeric satellite arrays that cover up to half of some chromosomes. Their precise functional boundaries remain undetermined.

title: GeneEmbedLLM: Harnessing Large Language Models for Gene Functional Embedding and Association Prediction
authors: zhang, z., yang, l., he, z., ding, j., Li, Y., Shen, R.
abstract: Effective and high-quality gene function representations are crucial for bioinformatics tasks. While biological knowledge about genes is inherently textual, encompassing functional descriptions and pathway annotations, current methods often rely on single-source, non-textual data, failing to capture the rich semantic information in multi-source gene annotations. In this paper, we propose GeneEmbedLLM, a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered framework for generating universal, semantically-aware gene embeddings. The proposed approach advances the gene representation learning through multi-source structured text integration from five authoritative databases and attribute-aware attention based on Longformer architecture and contrastive learning. Experimental results on diverse downstream tasks, ranging from molecular interactions and phenotypic dependencies to epigenetic regulation, confirm the validity and effectiveness of our proposed approach, where competitive performance is achieved across all evaluated benchmarks. We further validate the quality of the generated embeddings through comprehensive analyses, including embedding visualizations, intra-pathway similarity assessments, ablation study, and parameter analysis.

title: scPolyA enables efficient, interactive and agent-guided alternative polyadenylation analysis in single-cell and spatial transcriptomes
authors: Yang, J., Yang, H., Liu, L., Wen, J.
abstract: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) changes which regulatory sequences an RNA retains, creating a layer of cellular variation that gene-level expression profiles cannot resolve. Here we present scPolyA, a unified, AI-enabled framework that transforms conventional single-cell and spatial 3'-end transcriptomes into quantitative maps of RNA-end choice. scPolyA connects de novo poly(A)-site discovery to cell- and spot-resolved measurements of terminal-site usage, 3' untranslated region length and intronic polyadenylation, enabling differential APA analysis across cell states and tissue regions. Its integrated deep-learning module, DeepCPS, improves recognition of sparsely supported poly(A) sites and predicts cleavage positions at nucleotide resolution. An integrated graphical workspace brings parameter exploration, efficient rerunning and genome browsing together, while an APA-specialised AI agent translates natural-language research questions into executed analyses, verified outputs and evidence-guided interpretation. Across diverse single-cell protocols and spatial platforms, scPolyA achieves higher reference-atlas agreement than most evaluated de novo methods, while single-cell benchmarks demonstrate competitive runtime and memory use. Applied to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, scPolyA reveals recurrent 3' untranslated region shortening in tumour keratinocytes across all ten patients and corresponding patterns in tumour-enriched regions, with tissue-level contrasts shaped by cellular composition. scPolyA extends conventional transcriptomics from gene abundance to RNA-end regulation, linking transcript choices to cellular states and tissue organisation.

title: RabbitCD-HIT: Distributed High-Sensitivity Greedy Incremental Clustering for Billion-Scale Protein Sequences in Hours
authors: Gao, Y., Ma, G., Yin, Z., Yan, L., Yang, Y., Zhang, T., Zhao, T., Liu, Z., Duan, X., Niu, B., Schmibt, B., Liu, W.
abstract: We present RabbitCD-HIT, a scalable distributed high-sensitivity greedy incremental clustering tool for ultra-large protein sequence datasets. It fully exploits cluster resources to enable efficient billion-scale clustering. RabbitCD-HIT clustered the March 10, 2026 NCBI nr snapshot (1.02 billion sequences; 487 GB FASTA) at 90% identity within 5 hours on 64 nodes; the resulting representatives and cluster assignments are released as a public database resource. On a 256-core server, RabbitCD-HIT achieved a 2.1$times$--6.6$times$ speedup over CD-HIT with identical results under matched settings. Our approach addresses performance bottlenecks of traditional greedy incremental algorithms and provides an effective solution for large-scale protein sequence clustering.

title: Homology-aware average nucleotide identity estimation at scale with TurboANI
authors: Zhao, J., McDonald, D., Patel, L., Wang, C., Gonzalez, A., Knight, R.
abstract: Here we introduce TurboANI, a fast homology-aware average nucleotide identity (ANI) estimation algorithm that implements the seed-chain-quasi-alignment scheme using SIMD seeding, compact indexing, lightweight chaining, and cache-friendly bitset sliding minwise hashing, achieving up to ~40,000-fold speedup over the alignment-based ANI algorithm with near-perfect agreement. TurboANI is also >40-fold faster than the state-of-the-art FastANI and ten-fold faster than skani while maintaining better accuracy. In the sensitive mode, it has a ten-fold higher true-ANI recovery rate than skani.

title: Evaluation effects can rival reported concordance gains in cross-cancer survival prediction
abstract: Studies of cross-cancer learning for survival prediction from tumour omics have reported concordance gains of 0.020 and 0.045, but how such gains compare with evaluation effects remains unclear. We examined these effects across 13 TCGA cancers (5,761 patients, 1,526 disease-specific deaths), using five repeats of five-fold cross-validation and paired bootstrap intervals. When model selection did not use test data, our borrowing model gained 0.009 (95% interval 0.001 to 0.016) over its target-fitted reference when cancers received equal weight (post hoc). Random-effects pooling gave a gain of 0.002 (-0.002 to 0.006), with most weight assigned to cancers where the model made little use of the pretrained score. Choosing the fusion weight on test splits raised the apparent equal-weight gain to 0.017. We reimplemented a published method, VAECox, which showed no pretraining gain over random initialisation at the last or validation-selected training step. Choosing each network's best test step, as the published code does, raised concordance by 0.03 to 0.05 across the 13-cancer and ten-cancer overall-survival settings, but barely changed the difference between networks. In a constructed post hoc experiment, choosing the best test step only for the pretrained network changed the equal-weight mean difference from -0.004 to +0.045 (+0.035 to +0.054). Across seven multi-omics comparisons, estimates from single five-fold runs differed from their cancer's five-run mean by at least 0.02 in 11% to 42% of runs. Concordance was about 0.02 lower at held-out tissue source sites. Interpreting a reported gain therefore requires each model's selection rule, variation across repeated partitions, the weighting of cancers and the evaluation population.

title: The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier (Peron & Lesueur, 1822), genome reveals genomic and epigenomic signatures of shark evolution and demographic history
authors: Pearce, J. R., Doran, A., De Jong, E., Kwong, S., Jewell, O., D'Antonio, B., Fraser, M. W., Corrigan, S., Thomas, L., Edwards, R. J.
abstract: Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) represent one of the oldest extant vertebrate lineages, persisting for over 450 million years, yet genomic resources remain limited for many species despite widespread conservation concern. The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier (Peron & Lesueur, 1822), the sole surviving member of the family Galeocerdonidae, is a circumglobally cosmopolitan predator vital in ecosystem regulation but is experiencing population declines. Here, we generated the first chromosome-scale haplotype-phased reference genome for the tiger shark and integrated comparative and population genomics with methylomics to characterise its genome architecture and evolutionary history. This assembly presented the first evidence of male heterogamety in this species. Comparative analyses revealed lineage-specific transposable element expansions across the chondrichthyan class suggesting ongoing genome restructuring in Carcharhiniform sharks. We report the first hydroxymethylome in a chondrichthyan, higher than that of other vertebrates, hinting at novel DNA evolutionary and regulatory pathways in an early-diverging lineage of jawed vertebrates. We identified genomic signatures of prolonged population decline that correlated with historical climate fluctuations and have resulted in sustained low levels of genetic heterozygosity in this species. These findings offer new insights into shark and broader vertebrate genomic and epigenomic evolution while providing valuable resources for conservation genomics of one of the world's most widespread top-order predators in the face of accelerating environmental change.

title: MorphoANOVA: Dissecting Histology-Gene Expression Relationships in Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Chen, P.-W., Yan, G., Yu, S., Li, J. J.
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures the expression of hundreds to thousands of genes within tissue architecture, often accompanied by histology images. However, it remains challenging to systematically characterize which genes exhibit associations with tissue morphology, whether these associations vary spatially, and which genes show additional spatial expression patterns beyond those captured by morphology. Here we introduce MorphoANOVA, a gene-wise statistical framework for characterizing morphology--expression relationships across genes measured by ST. Using nested spatially varying coefficient models and sequential ANOVA, MorphoANOVA assesses slide-wide associations with an H&E-derived morphology feature, location-specific changes in these associations, and additional spatial variation after accounting for the selected feature. The resulting statistics enable gene prioritization and pathway enrichment analysis, while spatial component maps support the interpretation of individual genes. Simulations demonstrate MorphoANOVA's ability to distinguish the modeled components and recover their spatial patterns. Applications to human cortex and breast cancer identify biological programs associated with different morphology--expression patterns and reveal distinct relationships with cell composition. Across three HER2-positive breast cancer patients, invasive-cancer marker genes consistently exhibit stronger evidence of location-specific morphology associations. MorphoANOVA thus provides a framework for systematically interpreting spatial gene-expression patterns in relation to tissue morphology.

title: Mutation and Recombination Rates in Free-Ranging Polar Bears
authors: Desai, D., Rivkin, R. L., Newediuk, L., Northrup, J. M., Richardson, E. S., Garroway, C. J., Shafer, A. B.
abstract: Mutation rate () and recombination rate (r) are fundamental population-genetic parameters, yet demographic and conservation inference in polar bears (Ursus maritimus) has relied on values borrowed from humans and other mammals. Known values vary by an order of magnitude across mammals, and inaccuracies in these estimates propagate into downstream analyses, such as inferences of demographic history. To address this, we used high-coverage whole-genome resequencing of eight parent-offspring trios from the Western Hudson Bay subpopulation of polar bears. We identified 329 de novo mutations and estimated a pedigree-based germline mutation rate of 1.22 x 10?? per site per generation, which is within the mammalian range and close to values previously assumed for this species. Trio-based phasing yielded 522 crossovers across 16 meioses (32.6 per meiosis), and a pedigree-inferred recombination rate of 1.50 cM/Mb. From 44 unrelated individuals sampled from the same subpopulation, we inferred a demography-aware recombination map with a length-weighted genome-wide recombination rate of 3.03 cM/Mb (median 1.28 cM/Mb). We also identified 8,515 recombination hotspot regions covering 2.10% of the genome, accounting for 43.8% of total map length, a 20.9-fold concentration. Crossovers overlapped LD-defined hotspots 5.06-fold more often than expected by chance (p < 0.001). Nucleotide diversity was low and positively rank-correlated with recombination rate, consistent with linked selection. Genomic features explained only ~3% of recombination rate variation, with GC content and SINE abundance the only significant predictors. These species-specific parameters provide an empirical foundation for future demographic reconstruction and population projection in this vulnerable, ice-obligate species.

title: Bioinformatic pipeline for functional inference of Rickettsia akari hypothetical proteins reveals virulence-associated and effector candidates
authors: Kaliukanov, S., Csicsay, F., Skultety, L., Quevedo Diaz, M. A.
abstract: Background Rickettsia akari, the causative agent of rickettsialpox, is an obligate intracellular pathogen with a highly reduced genome encoding numerous hypothetical proteins (HPs) of unknown function. Many of these HPs are expressed during host-cell infection, yet their roles in bacterial physiology and potential contribution to virulence remain unclear. Methodology/Principal Findings We performed an integrative in silico characterization of 54 R. akari HPs previously identified by mass spectrometry in purified bacterial cells. Using a benchmarked computational workflow, we predicted their physicochemical properties, subcellular localization, putative secretion signals, protein folds, potential interaction partners, and evolutionary conservation. Most HPs were predicted to be thermostable. The majority of HPs were predicted to be cytoplasmic (37.00%) or membrane-associated (29.63%). Predicted features associated with the type IV secretion system were more frequent than those associated with type I secretion. Network and structural analyses identified candidate HPs with features consistent with potential roles in outer membrane assembly, host-cell interaction, and immune modulation, including predicted peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerases, oxidoreductases, methyltransferases, and putative E3 ubiquitin ligases. Several HPs were predicted to be antigenic and showed conservation across multiple rickettsial genomes. Molecular docking and normal mode analysis supported the plausibility of selected predicted protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions. Evolutionary analyses indicated predominant purifying selection among the analyzed HPs. A8GP20 showed elevated sequence divergence and warrants further investigation as a potential effector candidate. Conclusions/Significance Our findings prioritize A8GPG8, A8GP63, A8GNV4, A8GMM8, A8GM41, A8GMJ7, A8GMI5, A8GP20, A8GN23, A8GMB4, A8GM08, and A8GM39 as promising candidates for experimental validation of their predicted functions and potential roles in R. akari biology and pathogenicity. This work provides an integrative and reproducible bioinformatic framework to guide functional discovery in R. akari and related neglected intracellular pathogens, and identifies candidate proteins for future studies of rickettsial pathogenesis, antigen discovery, and therapeutic target development.

title: Segment-dependent phylogenetic resolution reveals geographic and host sampling gaps in Oropouche virus genomes
authors: Siam, R., Elbehery, A. H. A.
abstract: Background. Oropouche virus (OROV) has been reported in areas beyond its historical Amazonian range since 2023, accompanied by rapid growth in publicly available genomic data. However, the extent to which these data provide reliable phylogenetic and epidemiological resolution, and whether that resolution differs among genome segments, has not been systematically examined. Methods. Nucleotide sequences annotated under Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense were retrieved from NCBI Virus (accessed 13 May 2025) and filtered to retain records at least 70% of the reference length for each segment, yielding 898 S, 831 M, and 832 L sequences. Segments were aligned independently with MAFFT, and maximum-likelihood phylogenies were inferred with IQ-TREE using ModelFinder and ultrafast bootstrap approximation. Trees were annotated with collection date, country, and host in iTOL. Results. Phylogenetic resolution differed among segments. Contemporary Brazilian sequences formed a largely unresolved region in the S segment tree, whereas the M and L trees resolved recent clusters to differing degrees. Resolution did not track segment length: the M tree resolved contemporary structure more strongly than the longer L tree, and total tree length was approximately 3.5 times greater in the M tree despite near-identical taxon sampling. Sequences collected before 2010 were recovered in supported clusters in all three segment trees, although their configuration differed by segment. These sequences were also predominantly non-Brazilian and non-human, preventing collection date, geographic origin, and host from being separated as explanations for the observed clustering. The species-level query also retained three reassortant viruses, which may influence segment-specific topologies; sequences annotated to the United States were Iquitos virus rather than OROV. Two Italian sequences clustered with Cuban sequences across all three trees, concordant with published travel histories. Conclusions. Publicly available sequences contain phylogenetic structure that differs among the S, M, and L segment trees, but interpretation is constrained by uneven temporal, geographic, and host sampling and by the inclusion of reassortant species in a species-level dataset. The concentration of sequences from Brazil and human hosts, together with limited representation of non-human hosts, restricts inference about OROV diversity and ecology. Broader and more balanced genomic surveillance would improve the ability to resolve OROV evolutionary and transmission patterns.

title: Glycine-Proline driven flexibility and interface-dependent conservation of six-residue {Omega}-loops in protein complexes
authors: Tajane, S. V., Pohane, S., Dey, S.
abstract: {Omega}-loops are six- to sixteen-residue, non-regular structural motifs that occur in protein structures, connecting regular regions and forming a well-defined, ordered structural segment. They are functionally important because of their strategic location on the protein surface, where they are often associated with molecular recognition, ligand binding, and catalytic activity. Their non-regular nature enables them to adopt different conformations, which makes them important in protein dynamics and allosteric communication. In this work, we have curated six-residue {Omega}-loops from diverse protein-protein complexes of varying stability and found them to be abundant across all. We identified 1205 hydrogen-bonded and 6518 non-hydrogen-bonded {Omega}-loops, leading to an average of ~1.7 {Omega}-loops per structure. Glycine and proline were the most enriched residues in the loop, with proline preferentially positioned at the fourth position and glycine distributed across multiple positions, supporting their roles in chain reversal and conformational flexibility. Using ProteinMPNN-based sequence-design modelling and Rate4Site evolutionary-rate analysis, we show that {Omega}-loops occupy a relatively constrained sequence space, with interface loops in obligate homodimers and heterodimers more conserved than non-interface loops; the opposite trend was observed in transient and crystal dimers. Mapping known pathogenic and benign mutations onto the {Omega}-loop present in human proteins, together with a case study of the TEM1 {beta}-lactamase {Omega}-loop, further illustrates how small sequence changes within these loops can produce crucial structural and functional consequences, leading to altered enzyme activity and antibiotic resistance. Altogether, we report that {Omega}-loops are not merely connectors of secondary structure but are structurally constrained, evolutionarily significant elements that contribute to protein folding, stability and function.

title: Accelerating discovery and integration from RNA to Protein with R2T2P
authors: Albanese, R., Campbell, A. E., Bonfanti, M., Ali, A. S., James, C. T., Graziadei, A., Tasca, G., Riva, A., Krijgsveld, J., Jagannathan, S., Calviello, L.
abstract: Integrating transcriptomics and proteomics data remains an unmet challenge in the post-genomics era, discouraging researchers from pursuing integrative approaches to molecular biology research. Leveraging the power of translation profiling, we present RNA to Translation to Protein (R2T2P), a computational platform integrating genome-guided transcriptome assembly with identification of translation and proteins, including a tailored differential analysis framework and support for multiple reference transcriptomes. We applied R2T2P to investigate a cellular model of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD), where ectopic expression of the DUX4 retrogene in skeletal muscle triggers significant alterations in transcription and RNA metabolism. We uncovered hundreds of uncharacterized, highly overexpressed RNAs, including antisense and alternative transcripts, and quantified their contribution to translatome and proteome. Re-analysis of expression datasets from patient-derived myotubes and muscle biopsies validated this alternative transcriptome in FSHD patients, adding a reservoir of bona-fide novel molecular actors in a rare disease. Available at https://github.com/nfdata-omics/R2T2P/, R2T2P is a flexible and powerful workflow in modern integrative biology.

title: Pseudo-observations of longevity improve detection of resilience-associated genes in the Radiation Late Effects Cohort of rhesus macaques.
authors: Lawandos, J. H., Paukner, M., Schaaf, G. W., Olson, J. D., Raveendran, M., Harris, R. A., Rogers, J., Cline, J. M., Quillen, E. E.
abstract: Non-human primates are an ideal model for interrogating the genetic basis of human lifespan and resilience due to their long lifespan compared to other model organisms, development of similar age-related chronic conditions, and genetic similarity. However, like humans, statistical methods for modeling survival suffer from the challenges of dealing with non-proportionality of hazards, large numbers of living individuals that must be censored, and loss-to-follow-up over studies that may last a decade or more. Here we overcome these challenges through the use of pseudo-observations of Restricted Mean Survival Time as a measure of resilience to the acute challenge of radiation exposure and chronic challenges of aging and a Western-style diet in rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) from the Wake Forest Non-Human Primate Radiation Late Effects Cohort. Our whole-exome analysis used Genome-wide Efficient Mixed Model Association (GEMMA) to identify variants associated with longevity, and a subsequent Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) highlighted the cadherin and integrin signaling pathways as central to this resilience. As dysregulation of cell adhesion and extracellular matrix signaling is central to the development of fibrosis, we tested the functional relevance of these signals using a targeted Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) score-weighted Sequence Kernel Association Test-Optimal (SKAT-O) analysis of GSEA leading-edge genes from both the cadherin and integrin pathways. This linked variant burden in PCDHGA5, PCDHGA3, PCDHGB2, PCDHA11, and PSENEN to the severity of myocardial fibrosis, and in IBSP, PDGFD, and LAMC2 to the severity of pulmonary fibrosis observed at necropsy. Critically, we note that the genetic variants are not caused by the radiation but rather create an underlying risk for disease that is then exacerbated by the acute and persistent stressors challenging these animals' intrinsic resilience. The success of this method in identifying biologically relevant genetic variants underlying survival in animals undergoing a strong challenge to their resilience highlights not only the role of genes predisposing animals to fibrosis in lifespan, but the overall utility of pseudo-observations in overcoming the limitations of survival analyses in humans and other long-lived species.

title: PEEK: integrated primer design for silent-mutation and restriction-site engineering, validated in silico and by whole-plasmid sequencing
authors: Ghobadi, K., Kura, N., Warrington, J., Singh, N.
abstract: Motivation: Silent introduction of restriction sites, direct site insertion, and verification of the result are routine operations in molecular cloning, yet they are typically distributed across separate tools built on inconsistent thermodynamics. Primer design is itself mature and heavily validated; the gap is not accuracy in principle but integration, together with the absence of any explicit account of why one synonymous edit should be preferred over another. Because melting temperature (Tm) gates which primers a tool will accept, any unified tool must first be shown to compute Tm correctly against an external standard, and then shown to produce the edits it proposes. Results: PEEK, a web-based toolkit, unifies silent-mutation discovery, restriction-site insertion, and amplification and screening primer design built on a single thermodynamic model of primer melting temperature (Tm). PEEK's silent-mutation engine identifies the smallest set of synonymous changes required to form a restriction site at a specific position, and ranks the options by codon usage, local mRNA folding, and edit size. Predicted melting temperatures closely matched those of the NEB Q5 Tm Calculator across 17 primers of varying length and GC content (Pearson R^2 = 0.9995, mean absolute error 1.32 C) without any fitted correction, and annealing-temperature (Ta) recommendations exactly matched NEB's rules. In independent trials, a total of 15 silent-mutation designs were translationally silent and contained the intended restriction site. Experimental validation was performed by installing a KpnI site into a 9.9 kb lentiviral CAR plasmid using both a silent-mutation primer and an insertion primer. Whole-plasmid sequencing confirmed that each primer introduced exactly the designed changes, with no off-target differences across the construct and no change to the encoded protein. Availability and implementation: PEEK runs at https://peekbiology.com and requires no registration. Source code, documentation, and test data are available at https://github.com/nkura-arch/PEEK-Protein-Engineering Efficiency-Kit. Implemented in Python 3.11 with Flask, Biopython, and ViennaRNA. Contact: nathan.singh@wustl.edu

title: THiRST: Computer Vision Empowered Three-dimensional High-Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics Analytics
authors: Zhu, J., Wang, Y., Lu, Z., Qu, C., Zhu, Y., Yang, Y., Zhao, S., Yang, H., Huo, Y., Deng, R.
abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) preserves gene expression within tissue architecture but remains limited to individual two-dimensional (2D) sections, restricting analysis of continuous three-dimensional (3D) structures and cross-section consistency. We present THiRST, a computational framework for reconstructing multi-resolution 3D spatial transcriptomic representations from serial sections. THiRST combines coarse-to-fine morphology-guided registration, spatial matching of ST units, cross-section association of segmented structures, and integration of Visium V2 and high-definition ST. In serial kidney sections, patch-level refinement increased the same-cluster proportions of matched units at adjacent offsets from 63.8% and 65.6% to 70.7% and 70.0%, respectively, while improving expression concordance. The reconstructed correspondences enabled 3D glomerular and object-level expression analysis, with 54.1% of differential genes detected only in 3D. Cross-platform integration further aligned V2 and high-definition measurements in a shared expression space. THiRST demonstrates the feasibility of object-level 3D ST analysis from serial 2D sections and underscores the importance of accurate local registration.

title: Unveiling immune targets via TriStageHLA: high-throughput screening of peptide presentation, peptide-HLA binding, and immunogenicity
authors: LU, T., Wang, Z., Wang, Y., Li, Z., Chen, T., Cho, K., Yao, Z., Li, X., Wong, K.-C.
abstract: High-throughput screening of HLA class I epitopes underpins neoantigen vaccine design, T cell therapies, and pathogen immune monitoring, yet proteome-scale prioritization remains challenging under severe class imbalance. We present TriStageHLA, a compact three-stage framework that decomposes epitope discovery into peptide-only screening (PRE), allele-specific binding/presentation prediction (BIND), and immunogenicity prediction (IM). PRE performs early pruning via a LoRA-adapted ESM-2 classifier; BIND integrates quantitative binding affinity and eluted ligand data with a dual-branch architecture combining global cross-attention and local motif extraction; IM is fine-tuned on curated human T-cell assay data with a decoupled LoRA head. Trained on IEDB-derived datasets with per-allele balancing and allele-discordant supervision, TriStageHLA-BIND achieves AUROC of 96.2% and AUPRC of 95.2% on combined BA/EL evaluation, while TriStageHLA-IM reaches AUROC of 81.4% and AUPRC of 73.8% on held-out immunogenicity data, improving over the strongest immunogenicity baselines ImmuneApp (70.7% / 63.6%) and BigMHC-IM (60.1% / 51.5%). With substantially fewer trainable parameters than prior models, TriStageHLA enables efficient, calibrated epitope prioritization across binding, presentation, and immunogenicity. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/SkywalkerLuke/TriStageHLA.

title: MaaD-TAD: an all-atom model of the duplicated PRAMEF/HNRNPCL chromatin domain built from sequence homology
authors: Santos, J. R. L., MacIsaac, M., Moon, E. B., Befus, A. D., Marcet-Palacios, M.
abstract: In the nucleus, the placement of genes in the 3D fold of DNA affects how they function. Models of this fold use two kinds of data: contact maps constructed from Hi-C, and nucleosome maps showing where DNA is wound around nucleosomes. Over evolution, sections of the genome were copied, creating near-identical regions. Reads from these regions cannot be assigned to one copy and are discarded, leaving "void regions" in both maps. We tested MaaD-TAD, a pipeline that models topologically associating domains (TADs) at the atomic level, on the PRAMEF/HNRNPCL locus on human chromosome 1. This challenging locus spans 652 kb, with only 15% of its nucleosome positions known and most contact data missing. To test our hypothesis that copies with similar sequence lie close in space, i.e. homology as a surrogate for proximity, we constructed a map of sequence homology in place of Hi-C and used CSynth to fold it into a 3D path. We then lengthened the path to fit a chromatin fibre, and refined the model by adding cohesin complexes, which stabilize chromatin structure. Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex through which a loop of chromatin is threaded; the loop is commonly anchored by CTCF proteins bound on either leg. Using known databases, we placed CTCF sites in our model and joined three to their copies with cohesin rings; in each pair the sites face each other, as loop anchors do. The final model holds 3,359 nucleosomes and about 55 million atoms. Micro-C, an advanced, higher-resolution form of Hi-C, provided data on two other duplicated regions that support our hypothesis: matching copies touched 1.2 to 1.9 times more often than expected. Our approach provides a novel method to reconstruct DNA regions with absent contact data and, to our knowledge, the first all-atom model of a complete TAD.

title: MELD: Mutation Effect Learning through Differential embeddings
authors: Alajji, A., Jashil, R., Mall, R., Elshrif, M.
abstract: We introduce MELD (Mutation Effect Learning through Differential Embeddings), a compact model for predicting the functional consequences of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) by training directly on the wild-type (WT) versus mutant differential. Interpreting SNVs is central to clinical genomics, yet experimental characterization cannot scale to millions of observed variants.
