Leading sequence-to-function models (Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome) are trained on absolute genomic tracks and score variants post hoc through in-silico mutagenesis (ISM), so the WT-mutant difference never enters the training loss. MELD instead places the logit difference {Delta}z = zmut - zwt inside the supervised objective. It combines a shared CNN-Transformer encoder, a mutant-specific mutation-mask boost, multiscale mutation-centered pooling, and a learned adaptive amplification factor . On ClinVar (1.57M variants), MELD (1.9M parameters) reached an AUROC of 0.986 versus 0.800 for a same-data, same-backbone ISM baseline, with ablations confirming the contribution of each component. On a shared benchmark, it outperformed frozen foundation models with 3-1,300x more parameters (AUROC 0.967 vs. 0.924 for AlphaGenome and 0.936 for Nucleotide Transformer). With only 50, 000 training variants, it exceeded the ISM baseline trained on all 1.48M (AUROC 0.903 vs. 0.796) variants. On BRCA1 saturation genome editing, frozen MELD achieved a Spearman {rho} of 0.42, above Borzoi (0.40), and ClinVar transfer raised it to 0.45. These results demonstrate that direct differential supervision is a compact, data-efficient alternative to post-hoc ISM scoring with substantially larger pretrained models.

title: AOPTK: Open-Source Software for AI-Assisted Toxicological Literature Analysis
authors: Durnik, R., Bajard, L. M., Blaha, L., Babica, P., Sovadinova, I., Hecht, H.
abstract: Motivation: Toxicologists today face a challenge: although vast amounts of data describing how chemicals affect human health are available across scientific publications and regulatory reports, much of this information remains underutilized because extracting and interpreting evidence across thousands of studies is impractical to perform manually. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs), provide new opportunities to automate toxicological literature analysis. Results: Herein, we present the Adverse Outcome Pathway Toolkit (AOPTK), an open-source Python package for AI-enhanced analysis of toxicological and biomedical literature. AOPTK supports (i) automated literature retrieval from databases such as PubMed Central and Europe PMC, (ii) direct processing of full-text articles in PDF format, and (iii) LLM-assisted analysis tools to identify chemicals and extract their relationships to biological effects under user-defined conditions. We demonstrate its utilities through a case-study identifying potential non-genotoxic carcinogens based on their ability to inhibit gap junction intercellular communication (GJIC). The LLM-enhanced analysis achieves 81% agreement with an expert-curated inhibitor list and 95% accuracy in predicting inhibition versus no inhibition when analysing the same subset of 86 publications. Automated retrieval and analysis of 1 124 publications from PubMed Central further demonstrated the feasibility of applying AOPTK to large-scale literature analyses. Availability: The package is developed open source on GitHub, disseminated through PyPI and Bioconda and releases are archived on Zenodo. Individual tools are available in the Galaxy platform for accessible data analysis with user-friendly, findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) and end-to-end workflows provided via WorkflowHub. The tools are available on usegalaxy.eu and usegalaxy.cz and are developed open source on GitHub.

title: mFrag: Integrating External DNA Methylation References Improves Lung Cancer Early Detection by Fragmentomics
authors: Cui, S., Swarup, N., He, Q., Hsu, W., Wong, D., Zheng, Y., Scharpf, R. B., Sun, W.
abstract: Fragmentomics analyzes features of circulating cell-free DNA fragments (e.g., fragment length or end motifs) derived from whole-genome sequencing of liquid biopsy samples (blood or other body fluids), enabling non-invasive early cancer detection. Here we present mFrag, a framework that integrates external methylation reference atlases with fragmentomic features for lung cancer detection. mFrag comprises two complementary methods: mFrag-Weight, which uses DNA methylation information to weight fragmentomic features, and mFrag-Net, which integrates fragmentomic features and external DNA methylation data through neural networks. We average the output probabilities of the two methods to obtain a final prediction score. The mFrag model was trained using 287 individuals at risk for lung cancer. In an independent case-control testing set comprising 385 non-cancer controls and 46 cancers (28 stage I, 12 stage II, and 6 stage III or IV), mFrag outperforms a DELFI-style fragmentomic approach, improving PR-AUC from 0.455 to 0.720 and sensitivity at 99% specificity from 0.043 to 0.478, with ROC-AUC from 0.871 to 0.908. For stage I lung cancer, mFrag raises PR-AUC from 0.314 to 0.558 and ROC-AUC from 0.855 to 0.894. Applied to end 4-mer motif features, mFrag likewise improved over an unweighted baseline, with gains contributed by both mFrag-Weight and mFrag-Net. In summary, mFrag improves the accuracy of fragmentomics-based lung cancer detection through integrating external DNA methylation data and the complementarity of its two component models, without incurring any additional data-generating cost.

title: Community benchmarking of generative models for privacy-preserving synthetic bulk RNA-seq data generation
abstract:
Background
                      The synthesis of anonymized data derived from real-world cohorts offers a promising strategy for regulatory-compliant and privacy-preserving biological data sharing, potentially facilitating model development that can improve predictive performance. However, the extent to which generative models can preserve biological signals while remaining resilient to adversarial privacy attacks in high-dimensional omics contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, the CAMDA 2025 Health Privacy Challenge launched a community-driven effort to evaluate synthetic and privacy-preserving data generation for bulk RNA-seq cohorts. 
                  
                     Results
                      Building on this initiative, we systematically benchmark 11 generative methods across two cancer cohorts (~ 1,000 and ~ 5,000 patients) over 978 landmark genes. Methods are evaluated across distributional fidelity, downstream utility, biological plausibility and empirical privacy risk, with emphasis on trade-offs between vulnerability to membership inference attacks and other evaluation dimensions. Expressive deep generative models achieve strong predictive utility and differential expression recovery, but are often more vulnerable to membership inference risk under the evaluated threat model. Differentially private methods improve resistance to attacks at the cost of reduced utility, while simpler statistical approaches offer competitive utility with moderate privacy risk and fast training. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Synthetic bulk RNA-seq quality is inherently multi-dimensional and shaped by trade-offs between utility, biological preservation and privacy. Our results indicate that model architecture drives distinct trade-offs across these axes, suggesting that model choice should align with dataset characteristics, intended downstream use and privacy requirements. Privacy risk should also be assessed using multiple complementary attack methods and, where possible, mitigated through formal differential privacy protection.

title: PGCopilot: an AI‐assisted research agent for plant functional genomics
authors:
Chenyu He, 
Lin Liu, 
Zhenglin Du, 
Yu Xiu, 
Jianbo Xie
abstract:
System architecture of PGCopilot. The system architecture comprises four layers: (1) data sources, including locally built resources (Botanical Knowledge Base using ChromaDB and Qwen3‐embedding; Multi‐Database Resources with 1.83 M records across seven plant species) and runtime‐accessed external resources (PubMed via NCBI E‐utilities); (2) an MCP Tool Layer with 31 specialized tools built on the FastMCP framework, including locally developed tools implemented with FastMCP and the official STRING MCP service; (3) PGCopilot Core integrating prompt governance, LLM reasoning engine (DeepSeek‐V3.2), and evidence integration modules; and (4) a Query & Response Interface providing entity grounding, ID mapping, multi‐database retrieval, and conflict reporting.







Summary

The exponential expansion of multi‐omic data presents a major bottleneck for researchers seeking to derive biological insights from heterogeneous genomic resources. Although large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction with scientific knowledge, general‐purpose LLMs are not designed to reason over plant‐specific biological issues and frequently produce hallucinated or oversimplified outputs.
We developed PGCopilot, an AI‐assisted research agent tailored for plant functional genomics. It integrated task planning, identifier disambiguation, and tool orchestration to actively retrieve and synthesize evidence across heterogeneous biological databases using the Model Context Protocol. Built on a knowledge base of 1.83 million records, together with online access to PubMed titles and available abstracts covering over 33 million indexed articles and STRING protein–protein interaction data, it could plan retrieval strategies and integrate evidence into grounded responses, reducing unsupported outputs and addressing data fragmentation and identifier discrepancies.
In expert‐guided benchmarking, PGCopilot achieved higher performance than the evaluated baseline LLMs, demonstrating advantages in task relevance, evidence integration, hallucination control, and research utility, and providing more verifiable citations and explicit reporting of cross‐database inconsistencies. As an autonomous agent supporting multiturn tool interaction, it streamlined cross‐database evidence integration from labor‐intensive search‐and‐retrieval to automated analysis‐and‐synthesis.
This approach streamlines cross‐database navigation and evidence integration, allowing researchers to focus more on hypothesis formulation, experimental design, and critical interpretation of comprehensive evidence.

title: C2H2 zinc‐finger transcription factor FveJAG cooperates with SIMPLE LEAF1 to regulate compound leaf morphogenesis in strawberry
authors:
Zhenying Zhu, 
Mengting Pi, 
Zeying Huang, 
Jianglan Zhu, 
Wanglong Zhao, 
Shaoqiang Hu, 
Ruhan Zhong, 
Chunying Kang
abstract:
Proposed model for the regulatory network of FveJAG governing leaf shape in woodland strawberry.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Leaves play a vital role in photosynthesis, respiration, and transpiration, significantly impacting a plant's adaptability and crop yield. Strawberry plants develop trifoliate compound leaves, the molecular regulatory pathways of which are not well-understood.
Here, we identified a woodland strawberry ( Fragaria vesca ) mutant, designated  simple leaf 2  ( sl2 ), which exhibits the complete suppression of the two lateral leaflets. The causal gene encodes a C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor that is homologous to JAGGED and is named  FveJAG . A point mutation located within the intron triggers alternative splicing and generates a premature stop codon.
The prior key transcriptional regulator of leaflet initiation, SIMPLE LEAF1 (SL1), directly targets the promoter of  FveJAG  to activate its transcription. The synergistic interaction between  sl1  and  sl2  indicates that  SL1  and  FveJAG  function within the same regulatory pathway. Genetic and expression analyses suggest that  FveJAG  also acts downstream of  FveMYB117a  during leaflet initiation.
Taken together, our results uncover a direct SL1 target gene and elucidate a complex regulatory network involving  SL1 ,  FveJAG , and  FveMYB117a  in strawberry compound leaf morphogenesis, offering further mechanistic insights into the genetic regulation of leaf complexity.

title: Auxin-dependent miR167-ARF6/8.1-SAURs module coordinates local growth to shape floret diversification in Asteraceae
abstract: Abstract The corolla is a primary determinant of floral architecture and reproductive success. However, the processes that translate localized growth patterns into species-specific morphologies remain unclear. The complex inflorescences (capitula) of Asteraceae consist of different types of flowers. In  Chrysanthemum × morifolium , anemone-type varieties represent a distinct floral form characterized by dramatically elongated corolla tubes in bisexual disc florets. Using the anemone-type chrysanthemum, characterized by dramatically elongated disc florets, we demonstrate that sustained corolla formation depends on localized auxin enrichment. Two auxin response factors,  CmARF6  and  CmARF8.1 , have been identified as positive regulators of this process. These ARFs are post-transcriptionally regulated by miR167 in a dose-dependent manner, establishing a regulatory module that directly activates the auxin-biosynthesis gene  CmYUC2  and auxin-transport gene  CmPILS1 . Concurrently,  CmARF6  and  CmARF8.1  stimulate localized tissue proliferation by activating  CmSAUR64 and CmSAUR76 . Comparative analyses across diverse Asteraceae species suggest that auxin-associated regulatory mechanisms may contribute to region-specific corolla growth. Our findings demonstrate that auxin regulation contributes to region-specific corolla growth in the bisexual disc florets of chrysanthemum, providing a framework for investigating related morphological variation in other Asteraceae species.

title: A SNP in the MdWRKY11 promoter controls the segregation of Glomerella leaf blotch susceptibility in apple
abstract: Abstract  Glomerella  leaf blotch (GLB), a severe fungal disease caused by  Colletotrichum gloeosporioides , threatens the apple ( Malus domestica  Borkh.) industry worldwide. The susceptibility of apple to GLB is controlled by a single dominant locus. Although several markers for GLB susceptibility have been developed, the causal genes and their functional variations have not been explored. In this study, we used MapQTL and fine mapping to identify SNP544 C/G in the  MdWRKY11  promoter as the major factor underlying the variation in GLB susceptibility in apple. The SNP544 G allele generates a W-box motif that is directly bound by MdWRKY29 and activates  MdWRKY11  expression during  C .  gloeosporioides  infection. In turn, MdWRKY11 binds to the  MdDMR6.1  promoter and activates its expression, leading to salicylic acid degradation and leaf necrosis. The  MdWRKY11  SNP544 G allele was strongly associated with GLB susceptibility, with a prediction accuracy of 96.2% in 767  Malus  accessions. In addition to SNP544, we identified nine allelic variations in  MdWRKY11  across 29  Malus  accessions, with a combined prediction accuracy for GLB susceptibility of 99.6%. These findings shed light on the genetic control of GLB susceptibility in apple and provide an efficient molecular marker for breeding GLB-resistant cultivars.

title: The effect of a reduction in population size on mean fitness and inbreeding depression
abstract: Abstract A sudden reduction in population size increases the rate of genetic drift, reducing variability and increasing the mean level of homozygosity. The resulting increase in exposure of strongly deleterious, recessive or partially recessive alleles to selection against homozygotes may lead to their being purged from the population, potentially allowing mean fitness to increase after an initial decline, and accelerating the decline in inbreeding depression associated with reduced variability. However, detailed population genetic theory on the effects of population bottlenecks on mean fitness and inbreeding depression remains limited. We develop a theoretical framework for small, randomly mating populations founded from a large population at mutation–selection–drift equilibrium, using both simulations and approximate analytical results. These provide quantitative predictions for the dynamics of the population’s mean fitness and level of inbreeding depression following a bottleneck. In particular, we derive an approximate expression for the time needed for mean fitness to recover after an initial decline; such a recovery requires selection to be sufficiently strong relative to drift, and mutations to be sufficiently recessive. In contrast, weakly deleterious mutations cause reductions in mean fitness and inbreeding depression that are similar in size to those predicted from increases in homozygosity for neutral alleles, over the relatively short timescales considered here.

title: SPACE-Tag Enables High-Throughput Spatial Chromatin Profiling With CUT&Tag
authors: Yan, C., He, R., Fernandez, S., Pleska, M., Maniatis, S., Raimondi, I., Vickovic, S.
abstract: Spatial epigenomics maps chromatin states within intact tissues, yet current methods remain limited by accessibility and scale. We developed SPACE-Tag, a spatial CUT&Tag framework that converts epigenetic marks-associated DNA into polyadenylated RNA through T7 based linear amplification, enabling direct integration with standard spatial transcriptomic workflows. Applied to the mouse brain, SPACETag resolved activating and repressive chromatin landscapes, recovered region-specific gene regulatory programs across anatomical domains, and showed strong correlation with existing bulk and single cell reference data. We generated an integrated multimodal atlas of the aging mouse brain, profiling five histone modifications and the transcriptome in parallel across the adult lifespan to establish the largest spatial multimodal dataset to date. This analysis uncovered sharp regional divergence with aging in the brain: fiber tracts showed widespread transcriptional downregulation, often without nearby chromatin state transitions, whereas the isocortex showed coordinated chromatin transcriptome changes, including an H3K4me1 peak module that increased with age, was enriched at super-enhancers and linked to upregulation of neuronal plasticity regulators. These findings highlight the power of multimodal and high throughput spatial genomics in uncovering the divergent regulatory logic that governs tissue-specific vulnerability and resilience in the aging brain.

title: CADE: a reference-free workflow for coefficient-sensitivity analysis in bulk transcriptomic differential expression
abstract:
Background
                      Bulk differential-expression (DE) coefficients can change when disease alters cell-type abundance, but matched single-cell references are often unavailable in small or rare-disease studies. Existing marker-covariate adjustments can produce an adjusted DE table, yet they do not directly report which gene-level coefficients are stable, attenuated, amplified or representation-sensitive after composition adjustment. Coefficient-sensitivity analysis deliberately asks a narrower question than deconvolution: for each gene, how much does the reported group effect change once marker-derived composition weights are added to the model, in which direction does it change, and is that change stable to marker choice and to the coordinate representation of the weights? The output is a per-gene ranking of coefficient stability, not an estimate of cell-type fractions. 
                  
                     Results
                      We developed CADE (Composition-Aware Differential Expression), an R workflow that estimates marker-derived relative composition weights, fits paired unadjusted and composition-adjusted limma models, and computes a per-gene Composition Confounding Index (CCI). CADE reports signed coefficient-change labels, marker-dropout bootstrap rank stability (repeatedly omitting markers and re-ranking genes, to show which rankings persist), label-permutation calibration, denominator-threshold diagnostics, stabilised-denominator output and isometric log-ratio coordinate-sensitivity analysis. Genes whose classification depends on the coordinate representation of the composition weights are explicitly identified. In the controlled synthetic composition-bias benchmark, CADE preserved recovery of cell-intrinsic DE genes under composition bias, including AUROC 0.996 at 100% synthetic bias versus 0.902 for unadjusted limma. Marker-derived weights recovered PBMC ground-truth relative composition with mean r = 0.993, and a macrophage activation syndrome pseudobulk evaluation against scRNA-seq-derived composition showed mean r = 0.779, with all seven mappings that had a usable scRNA-seq reference showing p < 0.001 (of eight preset categories; Neutrophils had no reference in this ground truth). In familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis PBMCs (GSE26050; n = 11 versus 33 controls), CADE illustrated the separation of low-CCI from model-sensitive coefficients within a targeted immune, iron and ferroptosis panel. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      CADE provides a reference-free, reproducible workflow for characterising how sensitive bulk transcriptomic DE coefficients are to marker-derived composition adjustment. It reports coefficient stability and does not estimate absolute cell fractions. The FHL analysis is used as a small-cohort worked example, and disease-specific findings remain hypothesis-generating.

title: Altered plastidial fatty‐acid condensation is associated with changes in membrane composition and postembryonic leaf development in Arabidopsis
authors:
Evan R. Angelos, 
Amirreza R. Bagh‐abrishami, 
María Fernanda Gómez‐Méndez, 
Katharina Gutbrod, 
Andrea A. Zanini, 
De Fan, 
Hee‐Seung Choi, 
Liping Zeng, 
Jiaxuan Cheng, 
Bailong Zhang, 
Meng Chen, 
Tessa M. Burch‐Smith, 
Peter Dörmann, 
Katayoon Dehesh
abstract:
Significance Statement 
 Membrane lipid composition is fundamental to organelle structure and environmental adaptation, yet how plastidial fatty-acid metabolism influences developmental plasticity remains poorly understood. Here we find that sustained elevation of the plastidial fatty-acid enzyme KASII disrupts chloroplast architecture, light-responsive growth, and postembryonic leaf development, and supports a link between plastidial fatty-acid metabolism and developmental responses to light and gibberellin availability.
 
 How organelle metabolism relates to whole-plant development remains a fundamental question in plant biology. Our study shows that perturbations of plastid fatty-acid metabolism are not developmentally equivalent: Sustained elevation of KASII, unlike SSI2, is associated with striking changes in postembryonic development and environmental responsiveness. This specificity identifies KASII-associated fatty-acid metabolism as a distinct metabolic state linked to developmental plasticity rather than a general consequence of altered fatty-acid metabolism. These findings extend the biological significance of plastid fatty-acid metabolism beyond lipid production and provide a foundation for understanding how specific organelle metabolic states are associated with plant development and environmental responses. 
 
 SUMMARY 
 Membrane lipid composition is fundamental to organelle structure and environmental adaptation, yet how plastidial fatty acid metabolism influences developmental plasticity remains poorly understood. We examined the effects of sustained elevation of the plastidial fatty-acid enzymes KASII (β-ketoacyl-ACP synthase II) and SSI2 (Δ9 stearoyl-ACP desaturase 2) in  Arabidopsis thaliana  using lipidomic, ultrastructural, cellular, molecular, and physiological analyses. KASII overexpressing plants (KASIIox), but not SSI2 overexpressing plants (SSI2ox), increased carbon 18-containing lipid species and exhibited reduced plastidial galactolipids together with increased extraplastidial phospholipids. KASIIox plants displayed enlarged chloroplasts with disrupted thylakoid organization, impaired palisade differentiation, altered mesophyll patterning, and reduced seed coat mucilage. Under low light, KASIIox plants failed to exhibit the characteristic petiole elongation observed in control and SSI2ox plants, accompanied by altered phyB and PIF4 protein abundance. Exogenous gibberellin intensified, whereas inhibition of gibberellin biosynthesis partially alleviated KASIIox leaf and cellular phenotypes. Together, these findings associate sustained KASII elevation with changes in membrane lipid composition, chloroplast architecture, light-responsive growth, and postembryonic leaf development, supporting a link between plastidial fatty-acid metabolism and developmental responses to light and gibberellin availability.

title: Discovery and Deployment of Herbicide Tolerance in Domesticated Pennycress (Thlaspi arvense L.) to Enable Modern Agronomic Integration
authors:
John M. Howard, 
Mason Tuite, 
Tyler Mueth, 
Maria Celeste Varela, 
Martina Lazzaro, 
Lucas Lieber, 
Shengjun Liu, 
Krishan M. Rai, 
Ratan Chopra
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
 Modern agronomic systems for large-scale oilseed production rely heavily on chemical weed control, presenting a barrier to the adoption of newly domesticated crops that lack herbicide tolerance. Pennycress ( Thlaspi arvense  L.), a domesticated winter oilseed developed to increase land productivity and support sustainable biofuel production, is highly sensitive to commonly used herbicides targeting acetolactate synthase (ALS) and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPPD). Here, we report complementary strategies for identifying and deploying herbicide-tolerant alleles in pennycress. ALS inhibitor tolerance was identified through Ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-derived chemical mutagenesis, whereas HPPD inhibitor tolerance was explored using a microbial-based rational enzyme design platform as proof of concept. Selected alleles were introduced into advanced germplasm via homology-directed repair (HDR) and evaluated across developmental stages. Plants carrying the P187S mutation in the ALS gene exhibited robust tolerance at both seedling and rosette stages without detectable penalties to growth or seed yield. In contrast, the G419A allele in the HPPD gene conferred tolerance to residual herbicide activity when overexpressed but showed limited efficacy when expressed from its native locus, indicating context-dependent functionality. Collectively, this study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating herbicide tolerance into a newly domesticated oilseed crop and highlights the utility of combining mutagenesis-based discovery, rational enzyme engineering, and precision genome editing to support agronomic compatibility and crop deployment.

title: PhYAB4 directly activates PhAGL6‐2 to regulate lip‐related organ curvature morphology in Paphiopedilum henryanum
authors:
Yuying Yin, 
Yan Li, 
Jingjue Zeng, 
Lin Li, 
Kunlin Wu, 
Xiaomei Deng, 
Huacai Zhuang, 
Chao Feng, 
Ming Kang, 
Songjun Zeng, 
Lin Fang
abstract:
PhYAB4–PhAGL6-2 regulatory module controls lip-related organ curvature in  Paphiopedilum henryanum .
 
 
 Summary 
 
The orchid lip is a highly specialized floral organ that contributes to floral architecture and pollinator interaction. However, the developmental and molecular mechanisms underlying lip-related organ curvature in  Paphiopedilum  remain poorly understood.
Using  Paphiopedilum henryanum  and its Type A peloric mutant, we found that visible divergence between wild-type petals and mutant lip-like petals begins at Stage 4. Curvature was associated with adaxial–abaxial epidermal cell number imbalance in the distal region, whereas average epidermal cell area remained largely unchanged.
Transcriptome and expression analyses identified  PhAGL6-2  as a lip-associated  AGL6  homolog enriched in lips and lip-like petals during Stages 4–5.  PhAGL6-2  was preferentially expressed on the abaxial side, particularly in regions associated with curvature. Virus-induced gene silencing-mediated silencing of  PhAGL6-2  in  Dendrobium  Chao Praya Smile and  P. henryanum  affected perianth organ curvature, suggesting a broader role in floral organ morphogenesis.
The YABBY transcription factor PhYAB4 directly bound the AGTGTG motif in the  PhAGL6-2  promoter and activated its transcription. Silencing  PhYAB4  reduced  PhAGL6-2  expression and caused stronger floral curvature, lip outgrowths, and partial disruption of floral symmetry. These findings identify a PhYAB4– PhAGL6-2  pathway associated with epidermal cell number imbalance and lip-related organ curvature.

title: Banana fruit with nutritionally significant concentrations of iron and zinc: results from the field evaluation of genetically modified bananas (Musa spp.) in Australia
authors:
Tal Cooper, 
Bulukani Mlalazi, 
Harjeet Khanna, 
Jennifer Kleidon, 
Phuong Hoang, 
Jeff Daniells, 
Wilberforce Tushemereirwe, 
Jesse Beasley, 
Alexander Johnson, 
Robert Harding, 
James L. Dale, 
Jean‐Yves Paul
abstract:
Iron and zinc distribution in wild-type and transgenic Cavendish banana ( Musa  spp.) lines.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Iron deficiency remains a major public health problem in East Africa, where banana is a staple food for > 30 million people. This study investigated whether genetic modification could produce banana fruit containing nutritionally significant concentrations of iron while maintaining agronomic performance under field conditions.
Six transgenes associated with iron homeostasis were expressed singly or in combination in Cavendish and Lady Finger bananas. In total, 450 genetically modified plants were field evaluated in Australia and fruit mineral concentrations assessed in the first planting crop.
Elevated fruit iron and zinc concentrations, reaching 45.5 and 51.9 mg kg −1  dry weight, respectively, were associated with increased nicotianamine (NA) accumulation following expression of  OsNAS . Iron concentrations sufficient to meet 50% of the estimated average requirement for children were achieved in 28 lines, with elevated NA suggesting improved iron bioavailability. Increased mineral accumulation negatively correlated with yield; however, this effect was partly mitigated by co-expression of  OsVIT1 .
Early indicators of yield penalty included low corm iron, high leaf zinc concentrations and reduced photosynthetic efficiency. These findings demonstrate the potential of using genetic modification for the mineral biofortification of bananas in East Africa while highlighting factors that may assist in the early identification of high-performing biofortified lines.

title: Antagonistic second-messenger signalling coordinates  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  surface colonization and virulence

title: Somatic Structural Variant Discovery from Tumor Specific Strings Computed Against a Draft Composite Germline Reference
authors: Monti, D. C., Ciccolella, S., Cozzi, D., Della Vedova, G., Bonizzoni, P., Denti, L., Hormozdiari, F.
abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) are among the most clinically relevant genomic alterations in cancer. However, their accurate detection remains challenging due to complex genomic rearrangements, repetitive genomic regions, difficulties in distinguishing somatic variants from germline variation and sequencing artifacts, and limited sequencing support for low-frequency events. Existing mapping-based somatic SV callers are susceptible to alignment ambiguities in repetitive regions and near complex SV breakpoints, while approaches relying on comparisons of independently generated tumor and normal variant callsets may propagate errors from both callsets. Building on the concept of specific strings, previously applied to germline SV discovery, we introduce VESPA-SS, a novel approach for detecting somatic SVs from paired tumor-normal long-read whole-genome sequencing data. VESPA-SS directly extracts somatic SV signals using specific strings computed from tumor reads against a Draft Composite Germline Reference, without requiring initial read mapping or a high-quality germline assembly. These signals are subsequently clustered and refined through consensus sequence generation and alignment-based procedures to identify somatic SVs. Evaluation on real PacBio HiFi datasets demonstrates that VESPA-SS outperforms state-of-the-art somatic SV callers, achieving F1 scores exceeding 0.92 and 0.90 on the well-characterized HG008 and COLO829 cancer cell lines, respectively, compared with the highest F1 scores of 0.86 and 0.85 achieved by the evaluated methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of specific string based signal extraction for accurate somatic SV discovery and establish a new computational paradigm for identifying complex genomic alterations in cancer. VESPA-SS is freely available at https://github.com/dcmonti/VESPA.

title: scCircaSim: A Circadian Simulator for Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Li, C., Zhang, L., Zhang, Q., Zhao, L., Song, X., Tian, Y., Tang, G., Zhou, H., Wang, Z., Sun, P.
abstract: Motivation: Simulated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets that capture circadian dynamics while providing known ground truth remain scarce, limiting systematic evaluation of circadian analysis methods. Results: We developed scCircaSim to generate circadian single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data from a single-time-point reference. The framework combines phase progression with reference-derived network propagation of anchor gene rhythms and incorporates neighborhood effects for spatial simulation. Outputs retain reference heterogeneity and provide known cell or spot phases, rhythmicity labels, and gene-level mesor, amplitude, and phase values. Validation showed retention of reference structure and recovery of specified temporal patterns. Benchmarks of four cell phase inference methods and three rhythmic gene analysis methods revealed differences in phase accuracy, rhythmicity detection, and parameter recovery. scCircaSim supports reproducible method evaluation and preliminary experimental planning. Availability and Implementation: scCircaSim is implemented in R and available at https://github.com/Liwei-DynamicsLab/scCircaSim.

title: Integrative Multiomics Analysis of the Angiogenesis-EMT Interface in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
authors: Das, S., Natarajan, E., Singh, R., Shaikh, R.
abstract: Angiogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) are key hallmarks that contribute to the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), but whether the two programs vary simultaneously across tumors and how much of this reflects tumor composition remain unclear. We scored predefined, non-overlapping 20-gene angiogenesis and EMT signatures with a rank-based method in 342 primary oral cavity tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA-OSCC). The two programs were strongly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.809, P = 2.7 x 10^-80), and 2,396 bridge genes were associated with both programs across the transcriptome. The bridge genes were enriched in pathways associated with focal adhesion and extracellular matrix-receptor interaction. In the cellular case, fibroblast and endothelial marker scores were prominent and correlated with the program scores. The coupling was attenuated but remained positive after joint adjustment for tumor purity and stromal and immune scores (partial rho = 0.406) and with an epithelial-restricted EMT score (rho = 0.710). Further correlation was performed with a partial EMT (pEMT), which shows a significant positive correlation (rho = 0.59) and an inverse correlation with tumor purity (rho = -0.70). 146 final gene candidates were found using multi-omic evidence and candidate-level testing on the external cohort GSE30784; after adjusting for inferred cell fractions, 101 of these candidates supported the dual program. For thorough characterization, three candidates with an emphasis on OSMR, MICAL2, and LHFPL2 were chosen. Additional CPTAC data were used to confirm protein-level support, which was strongest for MICAL2. No significant connection was seen between the Interface score and overall survival (hazard ratio per 1-SD increase, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.78-1.08). These results describe a coordinated angiogenesis-EMT transcriptional state in OSCC that is attenuated but retained after accounting for tumor composition, and nominate candidate genes for experimental study.

title: Genome-wide Analysis of the VQ Gene Family and Expression Profiling in Sorghum bicolor
authors: Wang, F., Zhang, W., Zhang, F., Wu, L., Wang, M., Wang, Q.
abstract: Soil salinization severely restricts agricultural productivity, making the stress-tolerant sorghum an ideal model for studying crop adaptation. VQ motif-containing proteins are plant-specific transcriptional co-regulators vital for stress responses, yet their roles in sorghum remain underexplored. Here, we identified 35 VQ genes in sorghum, classifying them into seven subfamilies. Evolutionary analysis indicated that the family's expansion was primarily driven by segmental duplication. Notably, synteny analysis revealed a lack of collinearity between sorghum and Arabidopsis VQ genes, suggesting significant functional divergence during monocot evolution. Expression profiling showed distinct patterns among VQ members, with SbVQ34, SbVQ39 adn SbVQ40 significantly upregulated under salt stress. Furthermore, protein-protein interaction analysis highlighted SbVQ39 as a potential key regulator in sorghum salt tolerance. This study provides novel insights into sorghum's salinity tolerance mechanisms and establishes a foundation for utilizing VQ genes in breeding salt-tolerant crops.

title: spearfish: ultrafast Δ-mapping of long reads to redundant transcriptomes
authors: Abdelgawad, H., Martayan, I., MARCHET, C., Patro, R.
abstract: In a transcriptome, isoforms share most of their sequence, and gene families add further near-copies. Yet most long-read mappers treat each isoform as a separate target and repeat seeding, chaining and alignment for each. We introduce spearfish, a long-read mapper built for this redundancy. Its delta mapping ({Delta}-mapping) computes each target's alignment-score difference from the best candidate. It skips sequence that all candidates share, which cannot change the difference, and aligns where they differ once per distinct sequence rather than once per target. Seeds come from locally consistent parsing (LCP), so every isoform that contains an exon receives the same seeds in its interior. Collapsing them gives a core graph, a de Bruijn-like graph whose size is bounded by the distinct exonic sequence plus a small term per splice junction, independent of the number of isoforms. Over this graph, spearfish computes the exact colinear chaining score of every candidate transcript, sharing dynamic-programming state among transcripts via a procedure which we prove is equivalent to chaining on each transcript separately. Across RNA-seq experiments, using 32 threads, spearfish maps reads 26-83x faster than minimap2 in at most a seventh of the memory, and 2.6-11.3x faster than lr-kallisto's pseudoalignment. On simulated reads it ranks the true transcript first more often than minimap2 on HiFi reads and within 0.5 percentage points of it on ONT reads at 95% accuracy. When using spearfish's {Delta}-mapping with oarfish for abundance estimation, the abundance estimates match or improve on those that make use of minimap2's alignments on both simulated reads (especially when they are untrimmed) and on seven SG-NEx runs with spike-ins, and quantification is 3.0-8.8x faster than lr-kallisto in going from reads to abundances.

title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
authors: Libiseller-Egger, J., Gotsmy, M., Guillen-Gosalbez, G., Zanghellini, J.
abstract: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.

title: Disparities in avian genomic resources highlight gaps across the Global South
authors: K. L., V., Arvind, C., Goyal, N., Warudkar, A., Reddy, S., Robin, V. V.
abstract: Avian genomes have proliferated rapidly in recent years while expanding our knowledge of genomic evolution. However, evaluating bird sampling across the tree of life and across their distributions is necessary to assess their contributions to global bird diversity and diversification patterns. We evaluated all available avian genome assemblies across geography, taxonomy, conservation status, and time. The 1,712 species with at least one genome assembly represent only ~15% of recognized avian diversity. Although all orders were represented, 24 bird families (all restricted to the Global South) lacked any genome assembly, and only ~37% (N= 2,397) of recognized genera had genomic representation. Nearly 78% of the most evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered (EDGE) lineages lacked a genome. Genomic resources are concentrated in temperate regions of the Global North, whereas species-rich tropical regions in Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia remain severely underrepresented relative to their diversity. Even after accounting for conservation status, evolutionary distinctiveness, and ecology, Global South species had roughly fourfold lower odds of having a genome than Global North species. Notably, the post-2021 surge in genome sequencing has counter-intuitively widened this gap. Together, our results highlight persistent gaps in genomic resources across the Global South and the need to collectively address these global knowledge gaps via collaborative efforts.

title: Hierarchical Temporal Transformer for Cancer Grade Prediction and Cross-Cancer Transfer Learning from Pathology Reports
authors: Brimo, n., Anand, R., Sabath, A., Harb, H., Serdaroglu, D. C.
abstract: Background: Language models for cancer reports usually read one document at a time and are tested on tumour types seen in training. Continuous-time sequence models address the first gap, but whether they use visit timing, not just order, is seldom tested. Methods: We developed the Hierarchical Temporal Transformer (HTT), which encodes reports with adapted BiomedBERT and reads the sequence with a cancer-type-conditioned temporal transformer. We evaluated it against best-possible AUROC ceilings on two synthetic benchmarks, one with the label stated in the text and one recoverable only from tumour sizes and visit intervals (ten seeds). Diagnostics led to an interval-aware time code (HTT-IA). On 4,786 TCGA pathology reports in 14 types, three types were withheld, and a text-only HTT was compared with a survival model. Results: On the phrase benchmark HTT reached AUROC 0.931 +/- 0.012 against 0.913 +/- 0.007 for a last-report baseline (+0.018, 95% CI -0.009 to +0.050); dates cannot raise the ceiling there. On the growth benchmark the initial time code scored 0.790, equal to a no-time model (0.787), whereas HTT-IA reached 0.843 (+0.053, 0.026 to 0.082) against ceilings of 0.894 without and 0.979 with dates. On unseen tumour types HTT reached 0.925 +/- 0.007, equal to in-distribution performance and to a single-report baseline. Text-only macro C-index was 0.592 (CALM 0.626-0.652). Conclusion: Cross-type transfer is carried by the pre-trained encoder. Visit timing is used only when the data make it identifiable and the time code is on a clinical scale. Ceilings, order-only ablations and re-dating probes are inexpensive checks for such models.

title: Structural Variant Aware Identity-by-Descent Detection on Pangenome Graphs
authors: Islam, U. I., Marsico, F., Garrison, E., Boucher, C.
abstract: Identity-by-descent (IBD) detection identifies genomic segments inherited from a common ancestor, and supports studies of relatedness, demographic history, and disease mapping. Existing methods primarily use linear genome representations and do not identify structural variants (SVs) shared within IBD segments. Pangenome graphs encode SVs and store each haplotype as a path through the graph. We present GIBD (Graph Identity-by-Descent), which detects IBD segments in the Graph Burrows-Wheeler Transform (GBWT) of a pangenome graph and annotates each detected segment with the SVs it carries. GIBD enumerates the pairwise-maximal exact matches between all pairs of haplotype paths in a single traversal of the GBWT, and visits each shared subpath once. On graphs of bounded degree, the traversal takes time linear in the number of nodes on the haplotype paths and the number of matches it enumerates. On a standard IBD benchmark, the power and accuracy of GIBD are within 0.009 and 0.001 of hap-ibd, a widely used linear method. Compared with impop_k, a pangenome-based IBD method, GIBD detects more 2-4 cM segments and runs in 33 seconds instead of 9.6 hours. In simulations of 1,000 haplotypes built from assemblies of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC), the insertion, deletion, and inversion labels of GIBD have a precision of 1.000, with and without assembly error. In a real four-generation family, GIBD identifies the inherited allele on parent-offspring segments at all 3,235 SVs on chromosome 20 where the parent is heterozygous, and reports no IBD between unrelated members. It also tracks a disease-associated 900-kb inversion at 17q21.31 across three generations and correctly labels all segments that share it. GIBD makes SVs visible in IBD detection from pangenome graphs.

title: Hub labeling makes exact distance calculation practical for large human pangenome graphs
authors: Truong, Z., Novak, A., Paten, B.
abstract: Pangenome graphs are now a standard reference representation, and tools built on them depend on fast minimum-distance queries between graph positions, for example, when clustering seed matches during read alignment. The baseline distance index, previously used by the vg toolkit, answers such queries based on a decomposition of the graph into nested subgraphs called "snarls". Within each snarl, the index uses a dense all-pairs distance matrix. Because such a matrix is quadratic in a snarl's number of children, the large, complex snarls that often occur in many pangenome graphs dominate the overall index size. This means whole-genome graphs can be impractical to index. To mitigate this, the baseline distance index does not fully index the largest snarls, and thus cannot itself answer certain queries involving them. We replace the dense matrix with a hub labeling for snarls above a size limit. Because hub labeling and associated methods are defined for directed graphs, we introduce a directed representation of a snarl's bidirected internal "net graph", whose shortest path lengths are the net graph's minimum walk lengths. Hub labels are built using pruned landmark labeling, ordered by a contraction hierarchy. On four human chromosome pangenomes, our hub-labeling-based distance index indexes every snarl in 0.9 GB to 3.0 GB at a snarl limit of 500, an estimated 28x to 119x less space than dense distance matrices would need for those snarls with more than 500 children, and supports the 3-18.6% of node-to-node queries that the previous index cannot answer by itself. On the queries both indexes can answer, query time distributions broadly overlap. We explore the snarl limit parameter space and are able to build indexes under 50 GB for four human whole-genome pangenomes in under 6 hours, where we estimate dense matrices could have required multiple terabytes.

title: Generative 3D Spatial Reconstruction of Cellular Organization from Single Cell Expression
authors: Azim, E., Alif, M. N., Hwang, T. H., Zheng, H., Zhang, W. i.
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles cellular states at scale but removes their three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization. Reconstructing this organization requires recovering not only individual cell positions but also the physical size, geometry, and neighborhoods of an entire tissue. Existing methods either map cells onto measured spatial references or reconstruct two-dimensional sections independently, leaving the joint reconstruction of a new 3D specimen unresolved. Moreover, predicting the average plausible position of each cell can reduce per-cell error while compressing tissue geometry. We introduce ORBIS, a generative framework that jointly reconstructs whole 3D specimens from single-cell gene expression without requiring a spatial reference at inference. ORBIS learns spatial organization through flow matching in a shared physical coordinate frame, using training views sampled from sparse serial sections, tissue blocks, and whole specimens. At inference, a shared spatial state is iteratively updated through dynamically regrouped windows, enabling the generation of millions of cell positions without independently reconstructing and stitching tissue regions. We evaluate physical size, cell-population shape, per-cell placement, and neighborhood organization separately to distinguish accurate tissue geometry from low per-cell error. Across eight held-out specimens spanning whole mouse brains, thick brain blocks, and Drosophila embryos, ORBIS achieves lower cell-population shape error than all five evaluated baselines on every test and reconstructs specimens containing up to 3.7 million cells. On a single GPU, ORBIS samples million-cell brains in 0.9-2.8 minutes, approximately 38 times faster than the sampler of LUNA-3D, our 3D extension of the state-of-the-art generative spatial reconstruction method LUNA. On two held-out brain tests, sampling reduces size error by 3.3-fold and shape error by 1.8-fold compared with a single-call variant. On an independent dissociated single-cell brain atlas, ORBIS returns on average 37.9% of each region's cells to their dissection region across 23 regions, compared with 28.5% for LUNA-3D.

title: Label-free flow operators and stability operators from single-cell time courses: what local dynamical operators can and cannot identify
authors: Redd, D. M., Green, S. G., Terooatea, T. W.
abstract: Local Jacobians of single-cell dynamics are used to locate unstable cells along trajectories, but what they identify from measured data has rarely been tested against independent truth. We present scJDO2, which separates two per-cell operators by the time information they require: a score operator, the Hessian of a score-matched log density, available from any snapshot; and a flow operator, the Jacobian of a drift fitted to a measured velocity, here estimated label-free from a sampled time course by entropic optimal transport. Both are summarized in a shared operator space of magnitude-free descriptors, with the invariance of each stated, and evaluated with pre-registered tests. On synthetic data calibrated to six real datasets, the flow operator from the time course alone separated fate-bifurcation cells from committed cells on held-out seeds (AUC 0.89-1.00) with a-priori settings; tuning on development seeds overfit. On LARRY lineage-traced hematopoiesis, its fitted drift predicted the clonal displacement of barcoded cells beyond population movement (Spearman 0.56, permutation p < 0.001; 0.50 after removing the mean shift) and a held-out sampling day better than mean-displacement and no-movement baselines (energy distance 0.69, 95 % CI 0.66-0.73, vs 0.87 and 0.88); lineage thus validates the velocity, not {lambda}. Mini-batch transport reproduced dense transport (velocity cosine 0.9998) and scaled to all 130,887 cells (transport 5 min and 2.5 GB; drift fit and Jacobians 21 min and 1.3 GB). On an independent simulator it detected two of three bifurcations and two of three cycles and never reported instability on linear trajectories. Several readings failed. Neither operator recovers the values of the true Jacobian; the flow operators leading eigenvalue ranks branching cells empirically. The flow operator depends on the transport metric and inverts on Factor Analysis. Operator archetypes isolated bifurcation cells but did not outperform expression clustering and were unstable across fit seeds. The score operator did not predict CRISPRi knockdown responses or sister-cell fate coherence. A confirmatory test of transition timing could not be constructed, and diffusion is not identifiable at typical sampling intervals. The released software reports these diagnostics.

title: Toward space-optimal approximate colored indexes at scale
authors: Okcu, T., Alkan, C., Limasset, A.
abstract: Searching current petabase-scale sequence repositories requires indexes that combine compact storage with high query throughput. Although exact colored indexes retain complete sequence information, their construction and storage costs can become substantial for highly diverse collections. Indexes based on approximate membership query (AMQ) filters offer a compact alternative with fast construction and queries. Being hash-based, these indexes support different seeding schemes without structural changes, while sampling can reduce storage requirements, construction time and query time by an order of magnitude. Within the AMQ framework, querying many independent filters causes scattered memory accesses, reducing throughput. This motivates interleaved filters, which address this weakness by storing filter slots contiguously by position, enabling cache-friendly access and simultaneous membership queries. However, existing implementations face a trade-off between guaranteed construction and space-efficiency. Here, we introduce a new indexing framework based on interleaved ZOR filters, fingerprint-based structures with guaranteed construction that require only approximately 1% more space than the theoretical minimum for AMQ. To exploit redundancy between genomes, we introduce a color-preserving merging mechanism that extends fingerprints with membership bits, allowing multiple genomes to share a filter while retaining their individual identities. Together with a lightweight, sketch-based layout planner, this mechanism yields a compact index structure that accommodates collections with widely varying genome sizes and degrees of similarity. Our third contribution extends the AMQ framework beyond contiguous -mers through a low-density minimizer scheme alongside efficient implementations of sensitive seeds, including gapped -mers and randstrobes. We implement these methods in Zindex, a parallel, SIMD-accelerated Rust index that scales to millions of genomes while supporting diverse seeding and sampling schemes. Zindex indexes the latest RefSeq release of 564,401 assembled genomes in under 22 hours, producing a 289.5 GB index. It further scales to all 2,763,297 genomes of AllTheBacteria, producing a 406.3 GB index in four days with a peak memory footprint of 43.8 GB. Availability. Zindex is available at https://github.com/Malfoy/Zindex

title: Somatic structural variation discovery on cancer pangenome graphs
authors: Kara, M., Ashyralyyev, A., Alkan, C.
abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) drive tumorigenesis across most cancers, yet low variant allele frequencies in subclonal populations often necessitate multi-sample sequencing per patient. Existing somatic SV callers rely on whole-genome read alignments against a single linear reference, incurring high computational costs and reference bias. We present JANUS, which discovers somatic SVs directly within a personal pangenome, a colored de Bruijn-like graph of locally consistent parsing (LCP) cores built from matched normal and tumor PacBio HiFi reads. JANUS identifies candidate SV sites traversed exclusively by tumor reads without prior alignment, mapping only short read snippets surrounding each site. Across five tumor-normal pairs in the CASTLE panel, JANUS leads the 18-caller consensus with a mean F1 score of 0.887 (next-best caller: 0.858), widening its lead under low-signal regimes (0.489 versus 0.362 at 5x; 0.683 versus 0.520 at 20% purity). End to end, JANUS analyzes a tumor-normal pair in ~11 minutes on average with 16 threads, which is ~24x faster than read alignment alone on the same machine. In a 20-tumor patient simulation, joint graph calling outperforms independent pairwise runs in speed and accuracy, particularly at low depth. By processing multi-sample cohorts jointly and maintaining sensitivity at low coverage and purity, JANUS provides an efficient, reference-unbiased framework for cancer genomics. JANUS is available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/janus.

title: Contrasting Range and Demographic Histories in two Palearctic Dragonfly Species (Odonata: Anisoptera)
authors: Goodman, A. M., Tolman, E., Kohli, M.
abstract: Climatic suitability is often used to infer historical range changes, yet whether suitable area predicts effective population size remains unexplored. We investigated this relationship in two Palearctic dragonflies with contrasting ecologies: Somatochlora arctica, a widespread peatland specialist, and S. meridionalis, a southern European species associated with shaded streams. We combined demographic reconstructions from individual reference genomes using the pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC), maximum entropy (MaxEnt) species distribution models projected across six paleoclimatic intervals spanning approximately 3.3 million years, and ancestral state reconstructions of peatland specialization. Predicted suitable area was consistently greater for S. arctica, reaching its greatest extent during the Last Glacial Maximum. However, its inferred effective population size was smaller than that of S. meridionalis for most of the last ~275,000 years. Ancestral reconstructions placed the most probable gain of peatland specialization in the S. arctica lineage (Clade I) during the late Miocene, with a median age of 9.4 million years, predating the modeled climatic intervals. These findings indicate a decoupling of climatic suitability and demographic history. Patchy breeding habitat, population structure, and the isolated Scottish origin of the sampled S. arctica may contribute to this mismatch. Combining genomic, ecological, and phylogenetic approaches provides complementary insights into historical biogeography and highlights the limitations of interpreting suitable climate as available breeding habitat or using individual genomes to characterize species-wide demographic histories.

title: Isoform diversity as a complementary dimension of gene expression
authors: Shanas, S., Lubaton, E., Jermans, S., Mikl, M.
abstract: Most human genes produce multiple mRNA isoforms through alternative splicing and alternative transcription start and end sites. Isoforms of the same gene can differ in function, and their relative abundance varies between tissues and conditions. However, gene expression analysis is often restricted to the gene level, masking its diversification into mRNA and protein isoforms with potentially distinct functionality. Here we show, using an adaptation of Shannon evenness applied to 4,814 GTEx samples from 25 tissues, that isoform diversity constitutes a distinct dimension of gene expression, complementary to gene-level abundance and whole transcriptome diversity. Isoform diversity separated tissues based on non-differentially expressed genes and changed with age in a gene- and tissue-specific manner, most strongly in the brain and often without changes in overall gene expression levels. During neuronal differentiation, it increased most notably in RNA processing and splicing genes. Our results suggest that isoform diversity represents an independent dimension of gene expression and may help explain functional differences between tissues and cell states that are not captured by analyzing expression levels alone.

title: Multimodal cellular context enables molecular phenotyping from single-molecule trajectories
authors: Redchuk, T., Rehm, L., Sui, Y., Mäkelä, J.
abstract: Single-molecule tracking (SMT) provides direct measurements of molecular dynamics in living cells, but motion alone rarely specifies the underlying biological process, without accounting for the cellular environment in which that motion occurs. Here, we present MIST (Multimodal Interpretation of Single-molecule Trajectories), a framework that brings the paradigm of image-based profiling to single molecules by integrating trajectory dynamics, emitter properties and cellular context into a common, reusable phenotype space. Using a reference panel of nine proteins in live Escherichia coli, we show that multimodal context more than doubled protein-specific information relative to trajectory features alone, a gap that learned trajectory representations did not close. MIST allowed de novo identification of shared transcription-translation phenotype at the nucleoid periphery. A fixed reference space detected effects of previously uncharacterized MukB ATPase mutations without retraining. MIST provides an interpretable and extensible framework for comparing proteins, mutants and conditions within a common space of molecular phenotypes.

title: Plumage diversity without differential expression of pigmentation genes in a rapid avian radiation
authors: Recuerda, M., Repenning, M., Toomey, M. B., Kraemer, S., Rosoni, J. R. R., Silveira, L. F., Kopuchian, C., Campagna, L.
abstract: Uncovering the molecular basis of reproductive traits is key to understanding species divergence. Capuchino Seedeaters ( Sporophila ), a radiation of genetically similar birds differing mainly in male reproductive plumage color, can be leveraged to study how such traits evolve. Outlier scans identified candidate pigmentation variants primarily in noncoding sequence, implying regulatory changes. However, RNA-seq of growing feather follicles generally did not show differential expression of pigmentation genes among different colors, with only ASIP downregulated in crown feathers. Gene expression patterns instead varied by body region. The largest difference between dimorphic sexes was the upregulation of the carotenoid-degrading gene BCO2 in males, accompanied by lower carotenoid content in male feathers. An improved genome annotation assigned 9.5% of candidate variants into coding and untranslated sequence. This suggests species-diagnostic variants lie within transcribed sequence and could act post-transcriptionally, rather than through transcript abundance, leading to a revised hypothesis for plumage divergence in this radiation.

title: scCont: Interpretable Contrastive Learning for Functional Characterization of Cellular State Transitions
authors: Kewalramani, N., Wuchty, S., Crovella, M., Paul, I., Emili, A.
abstract: Timecourse single-cell RNA (scRNA) datasets have become indispensable biological tools for studying and uncovering the underlying regulatory processes driving continuous cell-state transitions such as the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. However, these highly fluid, non-linear gene program dynamics remain difficult to disentangle. While deep neural network models can effectively map complex topologies, they are biological black boxes, lacking the gene-level interpretability required by experimental practitioners. Here, we introduce scCont, a fully unsupervised contrastive learning framework for extracting interpretable functional transition units from scRNA-seq data. Rather than relying on explicit temporal labels or clustering priors, scCont uses an unsupervised k-nearest neighbors approach to project local transcriptomic neighborhoods into a low-dimensional embedding. During post-training analysis, scCont employs Shapley network attribution to determine gene-latent relationships, mapping latent dimensions directly into functional gene programs. We quantitatively and qualitatively validate this representation by demonstrating that scCont captures biologically interpretable dynamics more effectively than baseline methods such as LDVAE. Evaluated across 13 diverse EMT timecourse datasets and four simulated datasets, scCont exposes interpretable functional dynamics and effectively maps context-dependent functional groups, helping to bridge the gap between deep learning representation and translational biological utility. scCont is an open source software available on GitHub (https://github.com/nramani611/scCont).

title: How mutation rate evolves: Gene expression shapes genome-wide mutation rates in Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans
authors: Phillips, D. P., Kriaucionis, S., Sarkies, P.
abstract: Mutation rates vary across the genome, linked to biochemical properties of local DNA sequences. However, mutation rate variation also associates with functional genomic features, raising the possibility that intragenomic mutation rate variation is shaped by adaptive evolution. In particular, recent studies in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana suggested that highly conserved genes under strong purifying selection also have reduced de novo mutation rates, suggesting that natural selection may have acted to reduce mutation rate specifically at important genes. However, whether this is true for wider taxa, including animals, remains unknown. Here we repurposed published mutation accumulation datasets from Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans to investigate the determinants of de novo single nucleotide variant (DNV) rates genome-wide under minimal selection. Loci under stronger purifying selection accumulated fewer mutations, including intronic and synonymous mutations. Various sequence-specific (i.e. GC content) and regulatory features (e.g. chromatin modifications) were strongly correlated with mutation rate, but gene expression best explained the depletion of mutations within strongly conserved loci, even after accounting for correlations amongst variables. Using excision repair (XR)-sequencing data we determined that higher levels of transcription- coupled repair (TCR) were associated with reduced mutation rates, strongly suggesting that TCR lowers mutation rate of highly conserved genes. Furthermore, by comparing orthologs between C. elegans and its close relative Pristionchus pacificus, we found that altered gene expression across evolutionary time correlated with altered mutation rate. These findings support a model whereby developmental transcription modulates local mutation rates through TCR. A corollary is that adaptive mutation bias may emerge indirectly, downstream of gene regulation evolution, providing a mechanistic framework that reconciles non-random local mutation rate variation with established evolutionary theory.

title: Rapid, accurate, and memory-frugal sub-gene-level quantification of probe-based, multiplexed single-cell data
authors: He, D., Gao, Y., Patro, R.
abstract: Probe-based, multiplexed single-cell assays enable accurate transcriptome profiling while processing multiple samples in parallel. Their predefined probe sequences and additional sample barcodes introduce computational requirements that differ from those of poly(A)-based assays, for which many existing single-cell quantification tools were developed. We extend simpleaf to enable efficient demultiplexing and quantification of probe-based single-cell libraries. A new, cache-friendly dictionary specializes lookup to small probe references, while a shared thread budget balances parallel decompression and mapping. We extend RAD and downstream tools with reusable sample-scoped correction plans and external-memory collation of hierarchically barcoded data, retaining probe identities through quantification to enable rapid mapping and quantification with a small working memory budget. Across five 10x Genomics Flex datasets comprising 44 samples, simpleaf had the shortest runtime and lowest peak memory use of the three tools on every library, while producing gene-expression estimates, cell clusters, and marker genes concordant with cyto and Cell Ranger. Compared with cyto, simpleaf was on average 2 times faster and used approximately one-thirteenth as much memory. simpleaf also exports probe-level quantification results, allowing a range of analyses at sub-gene resolution. Here, we show that individual probe counts reveal expression changes obscured by gene-level aggregation, identify the transcript groups contributing to gene-level changes, and provide insight into splicing dynamics across cell types. These results demonstrate the computational and biological value of retaining probe-level information in multiplexed singlecell analysis.

title: QRAFT: Scaling coalescent-based species tree inference to one million taxa
authors: Rahman, A., Saha, A., Bayzid, M. S.
abstract: Species tree inference from multi-locus data under the multispecies coalescent has not kept pace with phylogenomic datasets that now span hundreds of thousands of species. We present QRAFT, a statistically consistent method for estimating species trees by maximizing quartet support on phylogenomic datasets at unprecedented scales. For n taxa and k gene trees, QRAFT achieves near-linear running time of O(kn log^2 n) when its recursion is balanced, which is within a polylogarithmic factor of the O(kn) time required simply to read the input. It also achieves asymptotically optimal O(kn) memory, so its memory requirements grow only linearly with the input size. QRAFT infers a million-taxon species tree from 1,000 genes in just three hours using only 298 GB of RAM, 64 CPU threads, and no GPUs. We estimate that the same analysis with ASTRAL-MP, a scalable parallel implementation of the widely used method ASTRAL, would take about 36 years (>100,000 times longer) and require prohibitive amounts of memory, far beyond practical computational limits. QRAFT maintains accuracy comparable to, and in many cases better than, leading species tree estimation methods. Notably, QRAFT reconstructed a microbial tree of life comprising 199,330 genomes in just a few hours using modest CPU resources. Thus, QRAFT brings highly accurate statistically consistent coalescent-based species tree inference to the unprecedented million-taxon regime and enables phylogenomic analyses towards the scale of the tree of life. QRAFT is publicly available at https://github.com/risenfromashes/qraft.

title: Measuring American black bear genetic load in fixed structural variants and runs of homozygosity
authors: Azimi Chetabi, F., Shafer, A. B., Puckett, E. E., Northrup, J. M.
abstract: Populations living in geographically isolated regions are expected to have reduced gene flow, increased genetic drift, and elevated levels of inbreeding, influencing both genetic load and possibly the distribution of structural variants. The American black bear (Ursus americanus) is widely found across Ontario, Canada, where populations inhabit diverse landscapes ranging from relatively intact contiguous forested landscapes to isolated regions such as the Saugeen Peninsula. Here, we investigated the population genomic history across five Ontario black bear populations using a combination of short-read (SR) and long-read (LR) sequencing data. We compared population genetic metrics including nucleotide diversity ({pi}), Tajimas D, runs of homozygosity (ROH), and genome-wide structural variants (SVs) to assess population health and identify signatures of isolation. Our results showed that the isolated Saugeen Peninsula population is genetically distinct and exhibited reduced nucleotide diversity, greater ROH and SV abundance compared with mainland populations. The population also showed elevated genetic load in all genomic features, suggesting increased exposure of deleterious variation that are expressed in ROH and population specific SVs. We further discuss the integration of ROH, SVs and genetic load in conservation assessments.

title: Growing a Root from Its Genome : Emergent Tissue Layers and Zones in a GPU-Native Simulation of the Arabidopsis Root Tip
authors: Auger, E., Gandecki, M., Heng, F.-X.
abstract: Models of the Arabidopsis root tip usually take its cell identities as given. Here we grow a root tip from a single genome. In a two-dimensional median section, every cell reads the same network of 62 genes (26 core genes from an earlier, unpublished model of callus and 36 added for the root) and starts with the same expression; the only spatial cues are the polarity of auxin transport, auxin from the shoot and the free surface. Identities and zones are never given to the simulation; they are read from gene expression. Cells are polygons of a shared mesh, relaxed towards mechanical equilibrium under turgor at every step. In 48 simulated hours, a tip-shaped template grows into a root of 3 000-4 500 cells with epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle and stele in order along most of its length, SHORT-ROOT and SCARECROW in the endodermis, an auxin maximum, a quiescent centre and a cap at its tip, and meristem, elongation and mature zones. A WOX5 gate built from published interactions and one hypothesis keeps a quiescent centre to 48 h in 17 of 20 simulated roots that were not used for tuning (85%; Wilson 95% interval 64-95%; criteria fixed before the run), against 9 of 20 roots used for tuning, before the gate. The niche is not maintained beyond 48 h: grown on to 73 h, only 6 of these 20 roots still have a quiescent centre (30%; 15-52%). All pre-registered criteria hold in only 1 of 20 roots, because the quiescent centre is too wide at 0 h; without that count, 12 of 20. The meristem is too long, and cortical cells made after the start of growth elongate only three- to four-fold instead of eightto thirty-fold, a limit set in large part by the numerical growth scheme. Mutants are a major weakness: several look like their published phenotype, but an exploratory re-run of a mutant benchmark fixed in advance for our first model passes one of nine predictions. Nor does the root regenerate: cut near its tip, it re-forms an auxin maximum and a columella but no quiescent centre. On a first, simpler model and without any polarity cue, a mass of identical cells still sorts into concentric layers and, when PIN carriers follow the auxin flux, concentrates auxin into a few foci, but forms no stem-cell niche: the genome lacks a lateral inhibition between foci. We state the limitations and the next stages.

title: QUANTA: A quantum annealing framework for species tree estimation using weighted quartet amalgamation
authors: Kumar Mondal, N., Bayzid, M. S.
abstract: Reconstructing species trees from genome-scale data is challenging due to pervasive gene tree discordance. Maximizing quartet consistency is a widely used approach for species tree inference from multi-locus data. Quartet amalgamation approaches, such as Quartet Fiduccia-Mattheyse (QFM) and Quartet MaxCut (QMC) families, have emerged as highly accurate quartet-based species tree inference techniques, but their reliance on computationally expensive classical bipartitioning heuristics, such as Fiduccia-Mattheyses (FM) and MaxCut, limits their scalability. Here, we introduce QUANTA, a quantum annealing-based quartet amalgamation method that, to our knowledge, represents the first quantum formulation of quartet-based approaches and the first species tree estimation method for multi-locus data that runs on real quantum hardware. At the core of QUANTA is a novel, general formulation of weighted quartet bipartitioning as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem that enables quantum annealing to replace the classical bipartitioning strategies underlying the QFM and QMC families of methods. We prove that our formulation uses the minimum possible number of qubits to represent bipartitions and that its energy function correctly orders satisfied, deferred, and violated quartets for any positive penalty weights. We implemented QUANTA on real D-Wave quantum annealing hardware, and evaluated it on a wide range of simulated and biological datasets. QUANTA achieves accuracy comparable to the state-of-the-art methods, including ASTRAL and wQFM, under challenging evolutionary conditions. We also reanalyzed several biological datasets, including the avian phylogenomic dataset comprising 14,446 genes across 48 genomes, on which QUANTA reconstructed a species tree with a higher quartet score than wQFM. Remarkably, despite running on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, QUANTA's bipartition technique achieved 4100x speedup over the FM bipartitioning technique in wQFM on bipartition containing 90-200 taxa, while maintaining comparable tree accuracy. By establishing a theoretically grounded, hardware-independent quantum optimization framework for weighted quartet amalgamation, QUANTA opens a new direction for quantum-assisted phylogenomics and provides a foundation for increasingly scalable and accurate species tree estimation as quantum computing hardware advances. QUANTA is publicly available at https://github.com/QuitttCat/QUANTA-Phylogenomics.

title: Towards a foundation model for raw nanopore signal through discrete tokenization
abstract: Nanopore sequencing reads nucleic acids as changes in ionic current that carry information beyond the base sequence. Self-supervised pretrained models have advanced genomic sequence modeling and single-cell analysis, but remain underexplored for raw nanopore signals, which are continuous and lack a native token vocabulary. Here we present Brieno, an approach combining reconstruction-based tokenization through residual vector quantization with a Transformer for contextual representation learning. We pretrain the Transformer using masked-token prediction on raw nanopore signals from 118 million reads. With frozen or fine-tuned features, the model identifies species without requiring reference genomes. It complements Dorado by accurately classifying reads left unclassified in native-barcode demultiplexing, approaches Dorado's basecalling performance across six genomes, and exceeds Dorado's specialized 5-methylcytosine model as well as a dedicated 6-methyladenine caller. Brieno also supports accurate CpG methylation detection with limited labeled data. Across tasks, pretrained contextual representations improve downstream performance over non-pretrained baselines and generalize across sequencing runs. Together, these findings support self-supervised pretraining as a basis for transferable representations of raw nanopore signals.

title: Residual barcode-like sequences and barcode-associated artifacts after Dorado and Barbell preprocessing of metagenomic reads
authors: Dinse, T., Englaender, V. R., Metz, S., Schrezenmeier, H., Messerer, D. A. C.
