title: Harnessing catalytic knowledge to guide enzyme discovery and evolution with AlphaEnzyme
abstract: Retrieving an enzyme for a target reaction provides a starting point for evolution, but predicting how to improve it remains difficult. This requires connecting evolutionary information with the structural and chemical context of catalysis. Here we present AlphaEnzyme, an enzyme foundation model built on a structure-grounded representation of an enzyme paired with its reaction, from which catalytic compatibility, kinetics and mutational response are read out together. On a time-separated benchmark, AlphaEnzyme achieves a top-1 catalyst retrieval success rate of 30.1%, against 17.2% for the strongest baseline. Michaelis constant predictions achieve the highest rank correlations among the compared methods, reaching 0.64 for enzymes sharing at most 40% identity with the kinetic training set. The model also enriches high-fitness TrpB variants at a budget of 16 candidates without target-specific fitness training. In prospective transaminase engineering, several prioritized variants exceed the parent, with the best design yielding a 30.4-fold increase in product signal in a lysate-based assay while retaining (R)-selectivity. Together, AlphaEnzyme provides a common molecular basis for selecting starting enzymes and prioritizing sequence changes for their improvement.

title: RPI-Zero: Zero-shot RNA-Protein Interaction Prediction
authors: Eren, K., Esendemir, E. I., Shukueian Tabrizi, S., Hashemi Aghdam, H., Cicek, A. E.
abstract: In vivo protein-RNA interactions are mapped almost exclusively by CLIP-seq, which profiles one protein in one cell type per experiment and needs a specific antibody; only about 10% of the roughly 2,000 human RNA-binding proteins have been assayed, and the Protein Data Bank holds around 5,000 protein-RNA complexes, a quarter of them ribosomes. Sequence-based prediction could extend coverage to unprofiled, newly discovered, or designed molecules, but existing predictors are not built for that case. One family trains a separate model per protein and cannot move beyond proteins with CLIP data; the other scores pairs but targets a single RNA class. Most are evaluated with random splits and randomly paired negatives that leave near-identical sequences on both sides of the split, and many require structure or read only short windows, discarding the context around a binding site. Their accuracy falls sharply when whole molecules are held out. We address this with two contributions. First, a strict benchmark of 2.1 million examples built from 11.6 million peaks of CLIP experiments targeting 209 proteins, taken from four public databases, in which each RNA is a spliced transcript with nucleotide-level labels, and sequence-similarity clusters are assigned whole to training, validation, and test sets, giving separate slices for unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. Negatives are matched to positives in length and in the number of other proteins binding the transcript, removing the shortcut by which a model predicts binding from how popular a transcript is without reading the protein. Second, RPI-Zero, a sequence-only model that reads any full-length protein and RNA jointly in up to 4,096 tokens, so the RNA representation is conditioned on the protein, and describes every protein as a mixture of shared motif prototypes, placing unseen proteins in the same terms as training ones. One model covers all proteins and RNA classes, uses no structure, and needs no interaction data for a new molecule. Compared with five state-of-the-art methods, it achieves the highest score in eight different metrics on unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. The model and data are available at https://github.com/ciceklab/RPI-Zero and https://zenodo.org/records/23748141, respectively.

title: Earl Grey ParTEA: scalable, consistent transposable element annotation from pangenomes to deep phylogenetic scopes
authors: Baril, T. J., Feurtey, A., Croll, D.
abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in D. miranda. The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.

title: Quantitative Spatial Analysis of Matrix Remodelling in Wounds Using Digital Pathology and Fractal Analysis
authors: Zhang, X., Arani, A. R., Herrera, J., Marienko, N., Robinson, C., Kurinna, S.
abstract: Wound healing involves spatially heterogeneous changes in matrix composition and organisation that can be difficult to capture using qualitative histological assessment alone. We developed a reproducible digital pathology workflow to quantify matrix features in cutaneous wound sections, compare them with unwounded skin, and derive an exploratory Histological Wound Index (HWI). Four normal-skin and six wound sections were analysed using QuPath, ImageJ/FracLac and Python. Approximately 500 x 500 micrometer regions of interest (ROI) were assigned to normal skin, wound centre, proximal edge or distant edge. Collagen, mucin and necrotic tissue coverage were quantified using image classifiers and analysed with linear mixed-effects models. Collagen architecture was assessed from collagen-selective binary masks using fractal dimension and lacunarity. Collagen coverage, fractal dimension, mucin coverage, necrosis and lacunarity were z-standardised and integrated into the HWI. Unwounded skin showed high collagen coverage and fractal dimension, with low lacunarity, mucin and necrosis. In contrast, wound-centre tissue showed low collagen coverage and fractal dimension together with higher mucin and necrosis. Distant-edge regions retained comparatively normal-like characteristics, whereas proximal-edge regions showed intermediate values. HWI was highest in normal skin and lowest in the wound centre. A descriptive matched-ROI comparison of two wound sections reproduced this regional ordering when all component measures were derived from identical ROI boundaries. This workflow provides a reproducible framework for quantifying regional ECM features and collagen-mask architecture in wound histology. The HWI is an exploratory histological summary requiring validation in larger longitudinal datasets.

title: MorphoProt: RNA-Conditioned Integration of Multiscale Histology for Spatial Protein Inference
authors: Xu, L., Zheng, L., Zhan, Y., Zhang, Y., Zhang, K.
abstract: Spatially resolved protein abundance reveals cellular states and tissue organization that RNA expression cannot fully capture, yet direct spatial protein profiling remains costly and limited in coverage. Histology images routinely accompany spatial transcriptomics and offer complementary morphological information for protein inference. Here, we introduce MorphoProt, a multimodal framework that jointly predicts spatial protein abundance from RNA expression, multiscale histology and tissue neighborhoods. MorphoProt uses RNA-guided cross-attention over five histological fields of view, so that the morphological context read for each spot is conditioned on its molecular state. The fused representation is refined by gated aggregation of RNA-derived information from physical and transcriptomic neighborhoods before joint protein prediction. On held-out sections of human tonsil, mouse spleen and human liver, MorphoProt achieves mean proteinwise Spearman correlations of 0.652, 0.604 and 0.372, outperforming matched RNA-only and graph-based baselines and the histology-based HIPI and multimodal SPRINT baselines in all three tissues. Combining fields of view, rather than any single one, carries the histology gain: in spleen and liver, the multiscale model outperforms every single-field model, and its learned scale preference separates white-pulp from red-pulp compartments. Predicted proteins preserve protein-defined tissue domains and their marker identity, and recover pathologist-annotated germinal centers as accurately as measured proteins.

title: Highly prevalent cargo genes of F plasmids harbored in pathogenic Escherichia coli
authors: Guirao-Rico, S., Flament-Simon, S. C., Madrid, C., Balsalobre, C., Huttener, M., Blanco, J. E., Blanco, J., Rozas, J., Juarez, A.
abstract: Analysis of prevalent orthogroups (OGs) in a collection of F plasmids from extraintestinal Escherichia coli ST131 isolates has led to the identification of two groups of previously uncharacterized cargo genes that may be widely distributed among F plasmids of pathogenic E. coli. Group 1 comprises four OGs whose encoded proteins are predicted to be involved in transport-related functions. The corresponding genes cluster with other genes associated with metabolism and are highly prevalent in extraintestinal ST131 isolates. Group 2 comprises several OGs whose encoded proteins currently have unknown functions. These OGs are present in a large proportion of F plasmids from both intestinal and extraintestinal E. coli isolates. The corresponding genes cluster within an F-plasmid region that also contains genes involved in DNA metabolism, suggesting that the proteins encoded by these newly identified OGs may likewise contribute to F-plasmid DNA biology. Characterizing the functions of these newly identified proteins may improve our understanding of the contribution of F plasmid to E. coli virulence and reveal novel targets for antimicrobial intervention, either by limiting F-plasmid dissemination among multidrug-resistant (MDR) E. coli strains or by directly targeting plasmid-carrying bacteria.

title: NanoPAMDA enables rapid PAM characterization of metagenome-derived Cas9 effectors
authors: Genel, I., Suren, C., Kurt, I. C.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 660,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in E. coli. Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.

title: Improving phosphoproteomic kinase activity inference by contextual refinement of Kinase Library relationships
abstract: Kinase activity inference from phosphoproteomic data relies on kinase-specific substrate sets defined by kinase-substrate relationship (KSR) priors. Kinase Library (KL) expands candidate substrate coverage using experimentally derived kinase specificity profiles, but its predictions reflect sequence compatibility rather than established intracellular regulation. We benchmarked KL-expanded KSR priors using 222 perturbation phosphoproteomic samples covering 396 annotated activation or inhibition events across 78 kinases. Broad KL expansion increased the number of scoreable kinases from 108 to 391, but reduced perturbed-kinase discrimination, directional accuracy and ranking performance. Higher error rates occurred among kinases with limited curated substrate support, while broad expansion also increased redundancy among inferred activity profiles. To improve the reliability of motif-derived relationships, we constrained KL-derived KSRs using predicted protein co-localization and protein-association evidence. Protein-association filtering consistently improved inference performance, reduced activity redundancy and provided a more favorable accuracy-coverage balance than co-localization filtering. The selected protein-association-filtered prior retained activity estimates for 308 kinases with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) above 0.75 and extended inference to 200 kinases not scoreable using curated KSRs, which were significantly enriched for dark kinases. These newly scoreable kinases showed structured activity patterns across perturbation contexts and interpretable signaling associations. Our results show that protein-association evidence can refine motif-derived KSR priors while preserving broad kinome coverage, providing a practical framework for more reliable phosphoproteomic kinase activity inference.

title: FeatureMAP enables network-guided interpretation of untargeted metabolomics
authors: Wang, Y., Zhang, F., Peng, G., Qiu, L., Zeng, L., Liu, Y., Kinchagawat, J., Yang, X., Liu, C., Johnson, C., Su, Q., Wang, C., Shen, X.
abstract: Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics generates thousands of features, but incomplete metabolite annotation and reliance on predefined pathways limit their biological interpretation. Here we present FeatureMAP, an LC-MS feature-centric computational framework that integrates multi-evidence metabolite annotation, network-guided refinement, metabolic module discovery, and structured large language model-based functional interpretation. Across ten public datasets, FeatureMAP improved MS1-based metabolite candidate prioritization while reducing annotation redundancy. In semi-synthetic benchmarks, FeatureMAP recovered coordinated metabolic perturbations, achieving 92% recovery of a simulated perturbation, and distinguished concurrent metabolic processes. Controlled benchmarks further evaluated functional interpretation under competing metabolite-level signals. Based on FeatureMAP, we additionally developed PhenoMAP, a phenotype-aware knowledge graph comprising 12,929 dysregulated metabolic modules from 501 human metabolomics studies spanning 326 phenotypes. Module-level comparisons revealed reproducible metabolic similarities across independent studies and biologically supported relationships among phenotypes. Application to Alzheimer's disease cerebrospinal fluid and cellular datasets identified convergent membrane-lipid alterations and implicated galactose-linked glycosphingolipid remodeling. Together, FeatureMAP and PhenoMAP enable network-grounded interpretation of incompletely annotated LC-MS metabolomics data and systematic investigation of metabolic dysregulation across biological conditions.

title: Multi-objective domain adaptation for pan-cancer transfer of pharmacogenomic drug response to patient tumours
abstract: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between preclinical models and patient samples. However, alignment without explicit biological constraints can produce unreliable representations when cancer lineage structure and clinically relevant patient heterogeneity are not preserved. Here, we introduce MODAE+, a pan-cancer multi-objective deep learning domain adaptation framework that jointly balances domain alignment, deconfounding, drug-response prediction, survival prediction, and cancer-lineage classification across 9,696 TCGA tumours, 1,293 CCLE cancer cell lines, and CTRP sensitivity profiles for 544 compounds in 738 matched cell lines. This multi-objective design improved cross-domain alignment while preserving cancer-lineage organization and patient heterogeneity. For drugs shared between the pharmacogenomic screen and TCGA treatment records, MODAE+ predicted sensitivity was significantly associated with overall survival among patients who received each drug in 46.3% of evaluated cancer-drug pairs by log-rank testing and 41.5% by multivariable Cox analysis. Biological validation across four curated drug-gene resources identified significant expression differences exceeding 1.5-fold for 34.9-64.4% of drugs in pan-cancer analyses, based on the lowest-p-value annotated gene per drug. Drug-class-specific patterns involved intended molecular targets for targeted therapies and predominantly transport, metabolism, detoxification and resistance-related genes for classical chemotherapies. As an additional validation, we derived pretreatment responder-nonresponder gene-expression signatures from 13 external breast cancer datasets and evaluated their concordance with MODAE+ predictions across 69 signature-drug comparisons in TCGA patients treated with paclitaxel or doxorubicin. Consensus signature scores showed Spearman correlations of 0.791 with predicted paclitaxel sensitivity and 0.724 with predicted doxorubicin sensitivity, averaging 0.758 across the two drugs. Together, these complementary analyses provide supporting evidence for the clinical relevance and biological consistency of MODAE+ predictions, suggesting their potential to identify drug-sensitive tumour subgroups and generate hypotheses about mechanisms of drug resistance.

title: TRACE: a framework for traceable biomedical resource construction demonstrated through single-cell glaucoma data
authors: Liang, X., Jayakumar, R., Strbenac, D., Torkel, M., Bian, B., Lee, E., Gu, J., Phan, V. T. N., Crowston, J., Yang, J. Y. H., Shim, H.
abstract: The growing availability of public omics datasets presents opportunities for biomedical research, yet constructing research question-driven resources from distributed studies remains challenging due to heterogeneous data, incomplete metadata and limited documentation of curation decisions. Here, we present TRACE (Traceable Resource Assembly and Curation Ecosystem), a general framework that links systematic knowledge discovery, data curation and resource delivery while preserving provenance throughout resource construction. We demonstrate TRACE through TRACE-scGlaucoma, a curated single-cell transcriptomics resource for glaucoma and optic nerve biology. Systematic screening identified 57 eligible studies, of which 42 provided accessible datasets comprising approximately 3.3 million cells. The resource provides harmonised metadata, standardised cell-type annotations and reusable expression objects while retaining original study information and curation provenance. We demonstrate its analytical utility through cellular enrichment of glaucoma GWAS-associated genes, comparing candidate drug-repurposing signals across distinct biological contexts and assessment of cell-type annotation reliability. TRACE provides a systematic and traceable approach to transforming fragmented public datasets into reusable biomedical resources, supporting reproducible analyses and future extensions across disease areas and data modalities.

title: WheatPanRef: a unified linear pan-reference genome for wheat genomics
authors: Niu, J., Zhao, P., Du, W., Zhang, X., He, H., Appels, R., Zhao, J., Ma, S., Chen, T., Haberer, G., Spannagl, M., Cao, Z., Zhang, Y., Miao, L., Chen, S., Zhang, B., Wu, W., Wang, L., Li, G., Wu, J., Wang, Z., Chen, Y., Jiao, C., Zhang, X., Pozniak, C. J., Krattinger, S. G., Choulet, F., Ling, H., Jia, J., Wang, D., Yan, W., Hu, Z., Xin, M., Peng, H., Ni, Z., Grewal, S., Alaux, M., Varshney, R. K., Guo, W., Deng, X. W., Sun, Q.
abstract: Linear reference genomes provide coordinates for read mapping, variant discovery and multi-omics data integration, yet assembly-specific coordinate systems limit data reuse, particularly in the large, repetitive and polyploid wheat genome. Here, we present WheatPanRef, a scalable linear pan-reference and coordinate framework that integrates wheat sequence diversity within a stable coordinate system. We reconciled independent Chinese Spring assemblies by resolving structural and sequences discrepancies to constructed a 14.50-Gb consensus sequences CS-NP. Using CS-NP as backbone, we incorporated 4.37 Gb of non-redundant non-CS sequences from 37 diverse wheat accessions, generating WheatPanRef (18.87 Gb). WheatPanRef improves read-alignment performance and captures putative wild-relative introgressions and sequences absent or unanchored in conventional references. Bidirectional coordinate-translation system enables accurate projection between WheatPanRef and individual assemblies without remapping, facilitating genomic resource integration and reuse. WheatPanRef provides a common sequence and coordinate foundation for population-scale wheat genomics, with potential utility for genomic resource integration in other complex crops.

title: memVar: an integrated resource for interpreting human membrane protein variation in molecular and disease contexts
authors: Xu, Y., HUANG, S., Zhao, J., Sun, J.
abstract: Interpreting membrane protein variation requires connecting clinical evidence to the membrane environments and molecular interactions that govern protein functions. Here, we introduce memVar (https://memvar.sunnylab.org), an integrated database of 10,906,688unique single-nucleotide variants from ClinVar, COSMIC, and gnomAD across 7,732 human membrane-associated proteins. memVar reconciles genomic, transcript, and protein coordinates to link variants with membrane topology, bilayer depth, lipid contacts, functional sites, partner-specific interaction interfaces, and variant-effect predictions, alongside disease, tissue-expression and regulatory annotations. Coordinated sequence, structure and variant views retain source provenance and distinguish clinical assertions, experimental observations, and computational predictions. Our analysis reveals that pathogenic/likely pathogenic missense substitutions are enriched in transmembrane segments and predicted protein-protein interaction sites relative to benign/likely benign substitutions, with pooled odds ratios of 2.47 and 6.67, respectively. IntAct-derived interaction loss or decrease was experimentally recorded for 57.9% of pathogenic/likely pathogenic substitutions versus 7.4% of benign/likely benign substitutions. CFTR examples contextualize the established G551D gating defect and prioritize W202R, a variant of uncertain significance, for tests of protein maturation, surface abundance and channel activity. By connecting variant records to specific molecular questions, memVar potentially supports mechanism-oriented investigation and prioritization of functional experiments.

title: TIGRdisco: a tool for the discovery of TIGR arrays and TIGR-associated Tas proteins from nucleotide sequences
authors: Gu, S., Gong, Z., Mortimer, J.
abstract: Tandem Interspaced Guide RNA (TIGR)-TIGR-associated protein (Tas) systems mediate DNA targeting through a hypercompact Tas effector, guided by dual spacers within a tigRNA that is processed from TIGR arrays. TIGR-Tas loci are composed of a Tas coding sequence associated with TIGR arrays of short units in either dual-repeat or stem-loop architecture. Unlike CRISPR (Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) arrays that comprise units of direct repeats interspersed with unique spacers, units within the two distinct TIGR architectures only conform through extremely short box motifs, complicating detection. Here, we present TIGRdisco, an integrated tool capable of discovering both the Tas protein and its associated TIGR arrays directly from unannotated nucleotide sequences. TIGRdisco implements independent engines to detect the two array architectures through a motif-agnostic approach. We benchmarked TIGRdisco against a reference dataset of TIGR-Tas loci, recovering more than 80% of array units within its search window. Furthermore, TIGRdisco recovered arrays for loci within entire clades of Tas where associated arrays were unannotated in the reference. We found that these arrays largely contain non-canonical box motifs or unit lengths. Lastly, as a case study, we utilized TIGRdisco and successfully uncovered TIGR-Tas loci across metagenomic and genomic datasets.

title: Benchmarking Statistical Methods for Differential Composition Analysis in Population-Scale Single-Cell Data
authors: Wu, W., He, M., Hu, Y., Su, C.
abstract: Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data capture cellular composition across cohorts ranging from several dozen to thousands of individuals, enabling the detection of cell-type composition differences between conditions. These differences reveal cellular shifts in disease pathogenesis and suggest potential targets for therapeutic intervention. However, differential composition analysis in scRNA-seq data is challenged by the unique features of cell count data, such as compositionality, prevalence of zeros, overdispersion, and confounding by technical and biological covariates. While this analysis is routinely performed, no study has yet systematically evaluated existing methods. Here, we benchmarked 12 methods for differential composition analysis using three population-scale scRNA-seq datasets with diverse and representative characteristics. Analyses of real data revealed low agreement across methods, while permutations and simulations based on the real data demonstrated excessive false discoveries for most methods. Overall, LOCOM emerged as the top-performing method that controls the false discovery rate while maintaining good statistical power, followed by ANCOM-BC and linear regression with centered-log-ratio transformation. Integrating evidence from real-data analyses and data-informed permutation and simulation experiments, we provide practical guidance tailored to common real-world challenges in differential composition analysis.

title: Mapping the regulatory wiring of endothelial cell differentiation reveals a critical role for Hippo mechanosignaling
authors: Nguyen, T. C., King, H. D., Amgalan, D., Pushkarev, O., Mo, Y. A., Munger, C. J., McCreery, C., Gupta, R., Zeng, T., Zhou, R., Conley, S. D., Batta, S. P. R., Sheth, M. U., Mattei, E., Masaltseva, A., Kang, H. Y., Ma, X. R., Tran, N., Gaskell, L., Shoresh, N., Orlova, V., Kundaje, A., Sumanas, S., Ang, L. T., Loh, K. M., Engreitz, J. M.
abstract: At each step of development, stem cells encounter a branching decision to differentiate into one type of cell or another. This decision is executed through the action of competing gene programs that specify different cellular identities. Consequently, creating a comprehensive map of the gene programs that drive each branching step of human cell differentiation remains a long-sought goal of developmental and stem cell biology. Here, we introduce a framework combining genome-wide CRISPR screens, single-cell readouts, and gene program inference to systematically discover and characterize regulators of cell differentiation. This framework includes a method for CRISPR perturbations paired with single-cell RNA-seq called circular capture Perturb-seq (CC-Perturb-seq), which improves gRNA detection from split-pool combinatorial indexing protocols and enables perturbing many candidate regulators to map their effects on gene programs. We applied this framework to map how human pluripotent stem cells differentiate into arterial endothelial cells (ECs), and identified 174 regulators that promote or inhibit EC differentiation. By tracking gene programs across three stages of differentiation, we resolved when and how regulators divert cells toward alternative fates. This map revealed an unexpected requirement for the Hippo mechanosignaling pathway in EC specification. During lateral mesoderm differentiation, Hippo mechanosignaling was required to activate ETV2, the master transcriptional regulator of endothelial identity. Inhibiting Hippo blocked ETV2 even in the presence of VEGF and diverted progenitors to a mesenchymal fate in vitro. Likewise, Hippo signaling was required for maximal etv2 expression in developing zebrafish embryos. Conversely, pharmacologically activating the Hippo pathway increased the purity of both arterial and venous EC differentiation in vitro. Our framework thus identifies novel regulators of endothelial cell differentiation, improves stem-cell differentiation protocols via manipulation of mechanosignaling, and provides a generalizable platform for mapping the regulatory wiring of human development.

title: Epigenetic reprogramming by promoter hypomethylation is linked to aberrant gene expression and transcriptomic plasticity in colorectal cancer
authors: Nunes, L., Eilertsen, I. A., Pinto, R., Vedeld, H. M., Bolstad, I. M., Saeed, U., Sjo, O. H., Yaqub, S., Nesbakken, A., Kryeziu, K., Lind, G. E., Lothe, R. A., Sveen, A.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) has high phenotypic plasticity, but regulatory mechanisms of aberrant cell states are not well described. We investigated DNA methylation-based regulation of cancer cell-intrinsic transcriptomic heterogeneity in 1,183 multiregional primary tumor samples, liver metastases and tumor organoids. Most genes with strong methylation-transcriptomic association reflected canonical promoter hypermethylation and expression repression related to the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). However, promoter hypomethylation and overexpression of APOLD1 and ELF5 identified two largely non-overlapping subgroups of canonical CIMP-negative CRCs enriched with stem-like and transit-amplifying cell states. APOLD1 tumors were further highly proliferative while ELF5 tumors were slow-cycling and associated with good survival in early-stage disease. Target genes showed patient-specific expression changes in matched primary-metastasis samples, and ELF5 aberrant metastases showed ex vivo sensitivity to putative targeting of stem cells by PI3K/mTOR inhibition, fetal de-differentiation and transition into non-canonical intestinal states. This implicates focal promoter hypomethylation in phenotypic plasticity in CRC metastasis.

title: Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning: A Stability-Constrained Framework for Molecularly Enhanced Survival Prediction in Lung Adenocarcinoma
authors: Shringarpure, P., Divakar, S., Khobragade, S.
abstract: Accurate survival prediction in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains challenging because high-dimensional molecular data can introduce overfitting and unstable feature selection. We developed Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning (CAISL), a framework that integrates a sparse molecular risk correction with a clinical baseline to improve prognostic discrimination while constraining model complexity and prediction variability. CAISL was evaluated using The Cancer Genome Atlas LUAD cohort comprising 470 patients and 119 observed deaths. Performance was compared with clinical Cox, molecular-only, and unanchored multimodal models using five independently seeded, event-stratified five-fold cross-validation runs. CAISL achieved a mean concordance index (C-index) of 0.7246, compared with 0.6970 for clinical Cox, yielding an absolute improvement of 0.0276 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [CI], 0.005 to 0.050). Time-dependent discrimination was higher at three years (AUC, 0.742 vs. 0.712) and five years (AUC, 0.721 vs. 0.691), while the integrated Brier score was lower for CAISL than for clinical Cox (0.164 vs. 0.181). Ablation analysis identified clinical anchoring as the component associated with the largest reduction in discrimination when removed. Stability analysis showed a mean pairwise Jaccard similarity of 0.46 between selected feature sets and a mean Spearman correlation of 0.86 between molecular correction scores. These findings support the potential of clinically anchored, stability-constrained molecular learning to improve internal survival-risk prediction in LUAD. Independent-cohort validation is needed to establish generalizability.

title: A protein language model for domain, functional site, and variant effect prediction
authors: Wang, P., Ahsan, M. U., Chen, T., Wang, K.
abstract: Protein sequence databases are growing far faster than experimentally curated annotations, limiting functional interpretation of newly identified proteins and coding variants. We developed PALM, a protein annotation language model that jointly predicts domain and functional-site occurrence, while preserving overlapping and nested annotations through a soft-target objective. PALM integrates ESM2 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), learned layer aggregation, and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) encoder. PALM was trained on ~15 million InterPro-annotated UniRef50 sequences spanning 17,951 domain and 1,383 site classes. Across 2.3 million held-out proteins, PALM achieved domain- and site-occurrence F1 scores of 0.941 and 0.877, respectively, and retained substantial performance in proteins with <20% sequence identity to the training and validation data. PALM also substantially outperformed ESM3 annotation baseline. Without training on variant-pathogenicity labels, PALM embedding disruption distinguished 151,823 ClinVar missense variants more accurately than ESM2 embedding disruption (AUROC 0.835 versus 0.710), and combining PALM embedding disruption with the ESM2 likelihood-ratio signal reached an AUROC of 0.877. The same combined zero-shot score outperformed AlphaMissense on a benchmark dataset on 128,161 missense variants, that were derived from literature but not present in ClinVar database. At the protein level, PALM embeddings showed stronger CATH-Gene3D superfamily organization than frozen ESM2 and ESM3 embeddings, and improved prediction of experimental activation and repression effects when combined with ESM2. In a downstream case study, we demonstrated the ability to use PALM-derived embedding as proxy of deep mutational scanning (DMS), showcasing the broad application of PALM. Together, PALM converts curated residue-level knowledge into transferable and mechanistically interpretable representations that connect protein sequence, function, and variant consequence.

title: Reconstruction of Cellular Trajectories with Biologically Interpretable States
authors: Wang, Y., Rattray, M., Barber, D.
abstract: Elucidating the trajectories of cellular evolution provides biologists with deeper insights into biological systems and disease progression, ultimately facilitating more informed discovery of mechanisms and therapeutic design. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is widely used to study cellular evolution. However, it faces two primary limitations. First, because the process destroys cells during gene-expression measurement, it is impossible to track the gene-expression profile of the same cell throughout the entire trajectory. Second, because scRNA-seq captures cells at discrete time points, it provides only static snapshots rather than continuous trajectories, limiting its ability to resolve the full dynamics of cellular transitions. Consequently, various computational approaches have been developed to address these challenges. However, existing models fail to capture the hidden state of each cell, which is essential for reconstructing gene expression at unobserved time points. As the gene expression profiles depend on the cell state, and may vary according to time, we propose a Latent Cell-State Model, where we approximate cell state transition as a Markov chain and obtain the gene expression of each cell at unobserved timepoints depending on the cell state, time, and a latent variable that represents the high-dimensional gene expression profile of a cell. Our model is able to infer biologically meaningful cell states and generate high-quality gene expression profiles at unobserved timepoints, showing potential for accurate trajectory reconstruction.

title: FoldAbS: Repurposing the Protein Folding Model as a Foundation Encoder for Antibody Screening
authors: Wu, J., Wu, F., Zhu, X., Huang, D., Cheng, K., Ma, J., Feng, F., Yao, J.
abstract: Therapeutic antibody screening requires prioritizing antibody candidates across specificity, affinity, and developability. Current pipelines typically silo these objectives and underuse structural information that governs antibody-antigen recognition. To address these inefficacies, we introduce FoldAbS, a unified supervised screening framework that reconceptualizes protein folding models as frozen foundation encoders, exploiting their internal representations to capture rich sequence, geometric, and interaction dynamics well beyond basic structure prediction. By coupling the folding model with lightweight, task-specific heads, FoldAbS seamlessly evaluates all three therapeutic criteria within a single architecture. Instantiating this framework with the open-source Protenix model (FoldAbS-Px) yields consistent improvements over baseline approaches, achieving significant performance gains of up to 13.1%, 9.2%, and 6.2% in specificity, affinity, and developability, respectively. Collectively, these results reposition protein folding models from structure predictors and confidence scorers into reusable foundation encoders for comprehensive and supervised antibody screening. Our code is available at https://github.com/nohandsomewujun/FoldAbS.

title: PartiDesign: A structure-sequence co-design paradigm for practical all-to-all biomolecules design
authors: Jin, Z., Zhang, X., Kang, Y., Hou, T.
abstract: Engineering interactions among biomolecules offers a route to creating new biological functions. Although unified models have advanced biomolecular structure prediction and design, efficient and controllable generation across molecular modalities remains challenging. A key challenge is to couple three-dimensional structure generation with sequence or chemical-identity design across chemically diverse systems. Here, we introduce PartiDesign, a unified structure-sequence co-design model that extends the partially latent framework of La-Proteina to proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules. PartiDesign jointly generates molecular structures and their corresponding sequences or chemical identities, while providing fine-grained control over secondary structure, chemical bonding and amino acid preferences. Across diverse benchmarks for the de novo design of proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules against specified targets, PartiDesign achieved the highest estimated successful-design throughput among the evaluated methods on most benchmarks under the adopted compute-budget protocols. Its configurable constraints further support cyclic peptide and antibody design, allowing generation to be tailored to specific structural and chemical requirements. PartiDesign was developed using 128 Huawei Ascend 910B accelerators, each with 64 GB of memory. The source code is available at https://github.com/MegaGatlingPea/PartiDesign-official, and a freely accessible web server at https://cadd.zju.edu.cn/partidesign/ enables users to generate binding partners without programming expertise. Together, these capabilities provide a versatile and accessible framework for all-to-all biomolecular design, with applications in molecular engineering and drug discovery.

title: Genome evolution and glycosyltransferase diversification shape asperosaponin biosynthesis in Dipsacus asperoides
authors: Yang, R., Fu, C., Zhao, X., Zhao, Y., Huang, W., Li, M., Xiang, G., Xiong, J., Wang, Y., Chen, G., Liu, Q., Yang, S., Zhang, G., He, S., Liang, Y.
abstract: Deciphering the genomic and enzymatic features associated with high-abundance specialized metabolism is important for understanding and engineering bioactive natural product biosynthesis. Asperosaponin , a hederagenin-based saponin, accumulates at exceptionally high levels in Dipsacus asperoides roots and is by far the predominant triterpenoid saponin. Here, by integrating a chromosome-level genome assembly with comparative genomics, transcriptomics, metabolite profiling, and biochemical characterization, we reconstructed a major biosynthetic route to asperosaponin and identified diversification of triterpenoid-associated gene families. Functional analyses revealed an ordered glycosylation sequence in which DaUGT73GZ2 preferentially accepts C-3-glycosylated substrates retaining a free C-28 carboxyl group, thereby establishing a C-3-before-C-28 glycosylation order during asperosaponin biosynthesis. Phylogenetic and biochemical analyses further uncovered functional differentiation among UGT85CA enzymes involved in C-3 arabinosylation, while genomic and expression analyses revealed lineage-specific patterns of pathway gene duplication and transcriptional regulation. Together, these findings identify genomic, enzymatic, and transcriptional features associated with the distinctive, high-abundance triterpenoid saponin profile of D. asperoides roots and provide a framework for understanding and engineering triterpenoid saponin biosynthesis.

title: Salinity adaptation in date palm (Phoenix dactylifera): evidence for selective sweeps at Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) genes
authors: Muchina, P., Younuskunju, S., Ahmed, A. A., Mohamoud, Y. A., Malek, J. A.
abstract: The date palm is a high salinity tolerant fruit tree grown mainly in the region spanning from North Africa to parts of South Asia. Climate change models of this region indicate the possibility of increasing salinity in the future. The Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) pathway is crucial for salinity tolerance in plants, serving as a primary defense mechanism by facilitating sodium exclusion. To better understand date palms' salt tolerance, we analyzed variation in SOS pathway genes in a set of 197 date palm genomes collected from across the range of cultivation. Here, we show evidence for selective sweeps in multiple SOS pathway genes. A single major pdSOS1 haplotype is at very high frequency in Eastern and Western subpopulations, with a minor, likely ancestral haplotype still present in both geographical locations. Allele-specific gene expression analysis showed differences in salt-treated roots between swept and ancestral haplotypes. Interestingly, sequence-based analysis of the pdSOS1 haplotype suggested a second, much earlier introgression event between P. theophrasti and date palm, though direction is unclear. This event happened before both the selective sweep and the previously reported recent introgression to date palm. We identified a MITE transposable element inserted into a pdSOS1 intron on the swept haplotype, and a similar insertion was found in an intron of the SOS2 paralog pdCIPK8. Both insertions are unique to date palm among Phoenix species. The pdCIPK8 haplotype containing the MITE is also at high frequency in both populations. Further analysis showed evidence for a selective sweep spanning the pdSOS3 region in the western population that shares similarity to an Eastern haplotype spanning the promoter region only. Slower extended haplotype homozygosity decay surrounding the genes in the western population suggests that the swept haplotype originated in the East and spread to the West in all cases. Altogether, our data provide evidence of selective sweeps in the date palm SOS pathway and may go to explaining how this species has developed such high salinity tolerance.

title: OncoSpot enables benchmarking of cancer spatial transcriptomics methods across tumor evolutionary modes
authors: Bhattarai, P., Yuan, W., Zhou, X. M., Mallory, X.
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is increasingly used to map clonal architecture within tumors, yet methods for analyzing cancer ST data are difficult to evaluate because real tumors lack ground truth for copy-number alterations (CNAs), subclonal identity, and malignant cell fraction. Existing ST simulators model normal tissue and do not represent tumor evolution, CNA-driven expression, or the spatial organization of malignant subclones. We present OncoSpot, a cancer-aware simulator of Visium-like spot-based ST data. OncoSpot combines a spatial evolutionary scaffold from DEMON, CNAs generated along the resulting clonal phylogeny with CNAsim, cancer-type-specific malignant transcriptional programs, and spatially clustered nonmalignant cell types, and aggregates cells into spots with known malignant fraction, subclone, and copy-number profiles. We demonstrate OncoSpot on high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, which represent three distinct modes of tumor evolution. Simulated subclones were spatially clustered and showed stronger phylogeny-space concordance than those generated by scCube under matched subclone populations. Benchmarking CopyKAT, CancerFinder, Clonalscope, and RCTD revealed cancer-dependent performance: Clonalscope recovered copy-number signals more accurately in ovarian and colorectal cancer, whereas CopyKAT performed better in hepatocellular carcinoma, reflecting both the assumptions of each method and the copy-number landscapes of the three cancers. OncoSpot's ground truth also exposed a failure mode in Clonalscope's malignant spot identification, in which tumor and normal labels were inverted, and allowed us to trace its cause. These method-dependent behaviors would be difficult to detect in real data. OncoSpot provides a framework for benchmarking CNA inference, subclone detection, malignant spot identification, and normal spot deconvolution, and its modular design and guidelines allow extension to additional cancer types. OncoSpot is freely available at https://github.com/compbio-mallory/OncoSpot.

title: A comparative transcriptomic framework across kidney organoid, assembloid, and transplantation models
authors: Glibetic, N., Lee, K. C. Y., Barnhill, J., Ortega, M. A.
abstract: Human kidney organoids recapitulate key aspects of renal development and have emerged as valuable platforms for disease modeling, nephrotoxicity screening, and therapeutic development. The field now includes a wide range of emerging protocols with distinct cellular compositions and maturation states, which complicates systematic comparison and model selection. Here, we integrated single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomes from 11 studies spanning kidney organoid and assembloids, both in vitro and following transplantation, benchmarked against fetal and adult kidney references. Transcriptional maturation toward adult identity is compartment specific and does not correlate with protocol complexity. Assembloid protocols show the most adult-like podocyte and distal nephron signatures, transplantation is associated with enhanced tubular oxidative metabolic features, only protocols incorporating ureteric progenitors reliably generate collecting-duct lineages, and no protocol achieves mature adult proximal tubule identity. Annotating against either fetal or adult kidney reference alone leads to misassignment, because early fetal nephron epithelium transcriptionally resembles injury-dedifferentiated adult proximal tubule cells. Assembloid and transplantation models share elevated mechanosensing pathway expression independently of vascularization. Together, these findings provide a framework for kidney organoid model selection.

title: Genome-wide chromatin accessibility during early embryogenesis in a generalist cichlid fish
authors: Midhukrishna,, Smith, A. M., Joyce, D., Di-Palma, F., Haerty, W., Mehta, T. K.
abstract: Background Lake Malawi's haplochromine cichlids are one of the most rapid and species-rich vertebrate adaptive radiations known, generating hundreds of species within < 1 million years, yet how regulatory regions shape their embryonic development remains poorly understood. Astatotilapia calliptera, a generalist riverine lineage and proxy for the ancestral stock that seeded this radiation, offers a developmental chromatin baseline against which regulatory divergence in specialised lineages can be compared. Results We generated genome-wide ATAC-seq profiles of A. calliptera embryos across three developmental stages (3, 7 and 12 days post-fertilisation, dpf), identifying 550,876-701,889 accessible chromatin peaks per stage. Accessible chromatin was enriched at gene promoters and at both highly conserved and accelerated conserved noncoding elements at every stage. The functional repertoire of accessible-promoter genes shifted across development, from early patterning at 3 dpf to the broadest regulatory repertoire at 7 dpf, and an increasingly neural- and locomotory-behaviour-enriched repertoire by 12 dpf, coinciding with post-hatching motor maturation. Differential accessibility showed that chromatin opening, rather than closing, dominates the earliest transitions (3 vs 7 and 3 vs 12 dpf), driven mostly by general metabolic genes, whereas the smaller, later 7 vs 12 dpf transition combined targeted gains at tissue-remodelling and apoptosis genes with losses at genes governing early neural and retinal patterning; almost all of these losses (96%) were at promoters that had opened between 3 and 7 dpf, indicating transient rather than sustained opening. Transcription factor (TF) footprinting identified stage-specific regulatory activity among developmentally important TFs, while the broader TF-promoter network remained topologically stable across all three stages, built around conserved hub regulators of core neural and sensory patterning genes e.g., SOX2, FOXG1, PTF1A, SOX10. This suggests that wiring is established early and largely maintained, following the hourglass model, with developmental progression driven by changes in activity of this conserved programme. Conclusions Together, these findings establish the first embryonic epigenomic resource for A. calliptera, revealing a developmental chromatin landscape of broad early opening and progressive functional specialisation, and providing a comparative framework for understanding how regulatory evolution has shaped Lake Malawi cichlid diversification.

title: TriTower-m6Am: A triple-tower heterogeneous deep learning architecture integrating semantic, sequential, and structural information for mRNA N6,2′-O-dimethyladenosine site prediction
abstract:
by Kaifeng Xiong, Jianhua Jia 
Background  N 6 ,2′-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) is a cap-proximal mRNA modification deposited by PCIF1 (phosphorylated C-terminal domain (CTD)-interacting factor 1) at the first transcribed nucleotide of eukaryotic mRNAs. Knowing where m6Am sites sit would help explain how cells tune mRNA stability and translation, but current predictors typically depend on a single representation and do not jointly model multiple views of the same RNA sequence.  Results  We present TriTower-m6Am, combining semantic (RNA-FM, a pretrained RNA foundation model, with BellPooling), sequential (One-Hot BiLSTM, bidirectional long short-term memory), and structural (RGCN, a relational graph convolutional network, over the 41-nt window) representations of each RNA window. On an independent test set of 640 sequences, TriTower-m6Am reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.776 and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.425, against DTC-m6Am’s AUC = 0.765 and MCC = 0.411, using 4.4 times fewer trainable parameters; at every matched specificity between 0.40 and 0.70 it recovers 1–7 more true sites out of 320 than DTC-m6Am. The AUC-weighted voting keeps every tower’s contribution readable for any individual prediction. Analyses of the graph tower delimit its benefit to the relational aggregation of local backbone adjacency over sequence-derived node features: the edge-type ablation, the node-feature ablation, and a structure-permutation control agree that the specific RNAfold-predicted fold carries no attributable signal, and a probing analysis shows that per-base base-pairing status is largely recoverable from the sequence-derived RNA-FM embeddings (AUC = 0.72 vs. 0.65 from the raw sequence), so the fold annotation is substantially redundant with the semantic representation the ensemble already receives.  Conclusions  Combining semantic, sequential, and structural views of the same RNA sequence improves m6Am prediction beyond any single representation, and the ensemble’s voting weights make each prediction auditable without a post-hoc explainer. Whether the triple-tower pattern transfers to other RNA modification prediction tasks remains to be tested in future work.

title: A computational framework to model cartilage degeneration induced by mechanoinflammation and cytokine-driven inflammation in post-traumatic osteoarthritis
abstract:
by Moustafa Hamada, Atte S. A. Eskelinen, Joonas P. Kosonen, Sanna Hakonen, Cristina Florea, Alan J. Grodzinsky, Rami K. Korhonen, Petri Tanska 

Knee joint injury is a major risk factor for post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA), often associated with early cartilage degeneration. Mechanical overloading and cytokine-driven inflammation are key drivers of this process, yet the underlying mechanisms and their distinct temporal and spatial contributions to cartilage degradation remain unclear. Here, we present a mechanobiological finite element framework that simulates cartilage degradation through cell-mediated proteolytic activity triggered by injurious loading-driven mechanoinflammation and cytokine-driven inflammation. The model reproduces experimentally observed depth-dependent loss of collagen and aggrecan, with mechanoinflammation inducing a transient response and cytokine-driven inflammation sustaining prolonged matrix degradation. Sensitivity analysis further shows that mechanoinflammation-driven degradation is governed mainly by protease production per cell, whereas cytokine-driven degradation is more sensitive to the rate of cellular stimulation. Together, this framework provides a mechanistic basis to study proteolytic cartilage degeneration and supports future  in silico  evaluation of therapeutic strategies aimed at mitigating cartilage degradation in PTOA.

title: Ten simple rules for a successful global health roundtable
abstract:
by Maria Gabriela Uribe Guajardo, Amanda Rush, Michelle Cunich, Kathleen Cravero, Carmen Huckel Schneider 

Qualitative approaches play a critical role in global health research by capturing the social, political, and contextual dimensions that shape health outcomes. While interviews and focus groups are widely used, these methods are often time‑limited and project‑specific. Global health roundtables offer a complementary approach, providing a flexible and long-term platform for engaging diverse stakeholders—including researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and community representatives—in collective dialogue, knowledge exchange, and collaboration. When designed well, roundtables can support co‑production of knowledge, address complex system‑level challenges, and generate insights with relevance beyond a single event. Despite their growing use, practical guidance on how to design and run roundtables specifically for global health remains limited. In this article, we present ten simple rules for organising successful global health roundtables, drawing on existing literature, practice‑based experience, and examples from different geopolitical and health‑system contexts. The rules address key stages of the roundtable lifecycle, including topic selection, objective setting, inclusive participation, management of power dynamics, optimisation of engagement and commitment, ethical recognition of contributions, and translation of dialogue into meaningful outputs and sustained collaboration. Together, these rules provide an accessible framework to support researchers, practitioners, and policy actors in using roundtables as ethical, inclusive, and impactful tools for global health research, policy development, and practice.

title: Membrane tension and cell–nucleus mechanical coupling regulate confined cell migration
abstract:
by David Hernandez-Aristizabal, Anotida Madzvamuse, Rachele Allena 

Cell migration is a fundamental physiological process essential from embryogenesis to cancer metastasis. It is primarily governed by the coupled mechanics of the plasma membrane (PM) and the nucleus, together with cytoskeletal dynamics. Being the largest and stiffest organelle, the nucleus is considered a rate-limiting factor in confined migration. However, nuclear positioning varies across cell types and migration modes, and the forces orchestrating its mechanical coupling with the PM are not completely understood. In recent decades, mathematical modelling has gained relevance to support cell migration research, yet models face the fundamental challenge of balancing mechanistic detail with computational efficiency. Here, we develop a dimensionless, biophysically grounded model based on geometric surface partial differential equations (GS-PDEs) for cell migration. This approach benefits from dimensional reduction—the PM and the nuclear envelope (NE) are modelled as energetic geometric membranes—and is solved using the evolving surface finite element method (ESFEM), balancing mechanistic detail with computational feasibility. The model reproduces experimentally observed migration patterns: exhaustion of lipid reservoirs and nuclear–lamina unfolding limit PM and NE surface area, blocking cell passage through constrictions; nuclear velocity peaks upon pore exit; and nuclear movement alternates between pulling and pushing regimes. Moreover, the modelling approach makes key predictions: the velocity peak upon nuclear pore exit is driven by the release of the curvature-elastic energy stored as membrane tension at the NE rear, and PM–NE mechanical coupling can hinder cell translocation, since part of the locomotion energy is invested in nuclear positioning. The model quantifies forces that are not easily experimentally accessible, including membrane tension, bending energy, osmotic pressure, PM–NE elasticity, and contact forces, offering an interpretable platform to test and propose mechanistic hypotheses on confined cell migration.

title: Social manipulations trigger shifts in group-level dominance patterns
abstract:
by Annemarie van der Marel, Xavier Francis, Claire L. O’Connell, Cesar O. Estien, Chelsea Carminito, V. Darby Moore, Elizabeth A. Hobson 

Within dominance hierarchies, individuals often direct aggression based on their own rank and the rank of others. When many group members make the same rank-informed aggression decisions, a broader group-level “dominance pattern” can emerge which further structures aggression within the framework of the dominance hierarchy. However, whether groups can change their group-level dominance patterns over time, and what factors might drive these changes, are not well understood. We investigated aggression dynamics by experimentally manipulating captive groups of monk parakeets ( Myiopsitta monachus ) using targeted rank-based removals and reintroductions of group members to induce social instability. Dominance patterns often shifted after experimental perturbations but remained stable in their absence. The rank of the perturbed individual affected both individual aggression decisions and the shifts in dominance patterns observed. In particular, reintroductions of top-ranked birds led to marked changes in aggression and shifts in dominance patterns. Understanding the factors that shape these dynamics can help explain how animal societies respond to social disturbance.

title: Genome-wide scan for transmission ratio distortion in trios from the Norwegian MoBa cohort rules out moderate distortion at common variants
abstract: Transmission ratio distortion has been demonstrated in model organisms but is understudied in humans. We conduct single- and multi-locus transmission disequilibrium tests to detect transmission ratio distortion in up to 43,829 parent–offspring trios from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study. We find little evidence for moderate to high levels of transmission ratio distortion at common variants. However, our multi-locus analyses implicate genes involved in meiosis, fertility, and prenatal development.

title: Two nearly complete genomes reveal the molecular mechanism underlying the significant fruit quality differences caused by bud sport between yellow and white‐fleshed loquat (Eriobotrya japonica L.)
authors:
Ke Zhao, 
Jinquan Chao, 
Yangang Pei, 
Tao Lang, 
Guoliang Jiang, 
Shuxia Sun, 
Hongjiang Xie, 
Jing Li, 
Meiyan Tu, 
Dong Chen, 
Mingchun Liu, 
Ronggao Gong, 
Haiyan Song
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Bud sport is a common and stable somatic variation in perennial fruit trees. Loquat ( Eriobotrya japonica  L.) is an evergreen fruit tree that can be categorized into yellow-fleshed and white-fleshed types based on the flesh color. To uncover the genetic basis, we herein assembled two nearly complete genomes for a yellow-fleshed ‘Dongting’ loquat (TBY) and its white-fleshed bud sport (TBW). The final sizes of assemblies were 773.29 Mb and 728.86 Mb with contig N50 of 31.87 Mb and 28.63 Mb for TBY and TBW, respectively. Comparative genomics analysis indicated that the heterozygosity ratio of TBY was nearly two-fold higher than that of TBW (0.53% vs. 0.27%). Integrated multi-omics and molecular marker detection results revealed that homozygosity of the  EjPSY2A 
 
    d 
 / EjPSY2A 
 
    d 
  allele is the cause of the change in flesh color from yellow to white in TBY. Additionally,  EjSUSs  ( −1 ,  −2 ,  −3 ,  −12 ) and  EjSPS3  might be the key genes responsible for the significant accumulation of hexoses and sucrose, respectively, in the flesh of TBY and TBW. Furthermore, high expression of  EjC4H8  and  Ej4CLs  ( −7 ,  −10 ,  −20 ) in TBY might lead to the accumulation of more lignin in its flesh. Taken together, these findings provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanism differences between yellow- and white-fleshed loquat and highlight the significance of bud sport as a valuable approach for generating novel germplasm resources in fruit trees.

title: Arabidopsis thaliana BOLA proteins, new actors in plant growth and iron homeostasis
authors:
Maël Taupin‐Broggini, 
Anaïs Rodriguez‐Euzet, 
Brigitte Touraine, 
Nathalie Berger, 
Julie Bals, 
Daniel Marino, 
Christian Dubos, 
Florence Vignols
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 The universal iron–sulfur (Fe-S) clusters embedded in proteins support numerous fundamental biological processes. However, many proteins involved in Fe-S assembly machineries remain poorly characterized in plants. Here, we revealed that  BOLA1  and  BOLA4,  two members of the BOLA family previously described as Fe-S assembly factors in various organisms, are critical growth regulators that play a role in Fe homeostasis in  Arabidopsis thaliana . Expression analyses showed that  BOLA1  and  BOLA4  are ubiquitously expressed across most Arabidopsis tissues. Using protoplast transfection assays, we also demonstrated that both BOLA-GFP fusion proteins localize to chloroplasts and mitochondria. Mutant analyses revealed that while single  bola1  or  bola4  knock-out mutants are phenotypically indistinguishable from the wild type, double  bola1 bola4  mutants display severe growth defects, including early growth arrest of the primary root. Notably, this phenotype was rescued by grafting a wild-type root system onto the  bola1 bola4  aerial part. Fe quantification, Perls staining, and RT-qPCR analyses further demonstrated that  bola1 bola4  double mutants exhibit altered Fe distribution and Fe-homeostasis-related gene expression. Overall, our findings show that  BOLA1  and  BOLA4  act redundantly to maintain primary root growth and rosette development and are essential players in Fe signaling and partitioning in Arabidopsis.

title: Population genomics of heterosporous lycophytes: allopatric speciation and historical persistence through paleoclimatic fluctuations
authors:
TongXin Ye, 
Ran Wei, 
JiGao Yu, 
NingXin Wang, 
SiQi Liang, 
XianChun Zhang
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Speciation is the fundamental process driving the origin of earth biodiversity. While speciation mechanisms have been revealed in many plant taxa, the evolutionary dynamics of heterosporous lycophytes remain largely unexplored. Here, we used the  Selaginella sanguinolenta  group, comprising seven montane species in eastern Asia, as a model system. We generated a high-quality, chromosome-level reference genome for  S .  aitchisonii , conducted whole-genome resequencing of 191 individuals across 49 populations, and integrated population genomic, phylogenomic, morphological, and ecological analyses. Our results revealed that strong geographic isolation, driven by Miocene paleogeographic events, led to high genetic differentiation and restricted interspecific gene flow. The unique combination of heterospory and independent gametophyte generations might exacerbate extreme inbreeding, further impeding the ability of these lineages to surmount geographical barriers. Ecological niche divergence indicated that these species experience heterogeneous selection pressures; moreover, evidence of selective sweeps, leaf arrangement variation, and functional gene divergence indicates that natural selection gives rise to new species with environmentally adaptive traits. Demographic reconstructions revealed a shared trajectory of expansion followed by contraction into bottlenecks from the late Miocene to the Pliocene. Montane refugia likely played a role in species persistence, preserving genetic diversity for the postglacial expansions observed in four species since the Last Interglacial. We conclude that the  S. sanguinolenta  group underwent allopatric speciation since the Miocene and successfully persisted through severe Quaternary climatic fluctuations, which provides novel insights based on population genomic analysis into the evolution of early-diverging vascular plants.

title: Duality of root‐dominated net soil organic carbon gain and mycelium‐mediated carbon loss in hyper‐arid afforestation
authors:
Xinping Dong, 
Yanju Gao, 
Akash Tariq, 
Xiaozhen Pu, 
Corina Graciano, 
Zhihao Zhang, 
Jordi Sardans, 
Josep Peñuelas, 
Weiqi Wang, 
Fanjiang Zeng
abstract:
Soil organic carbon (SOC) pool dynamics during hyper‐arid afforestation by root pathway and mycelium pathway.







Summary

Afforestation regulates soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration via plant‐ and microbial‐derived carbon (C) inputs, but root‐ and mycelium‐derived C inputs differ in quantity, turnover, and stabilization mechanisms, and these differences may shift as stands develop. However, how root vs mycelium pathways drive SOC dynamics across a dryland afforestation chronosequence remains unclear.
Using the ingrowth‐core method along a dryland afforestation chronosequence (young forests, middle‐aged forests, and mature forests), we quantified the contributions of root and mycelium pathways to SOC.
The root pathway promoted SOC accumulation via particulate organic C and mineral‐associated organic C inputs, contributing to 77.19–85.05% of the SOC changes. By contrast, the mycelium pathway induced net SOC loss via particulate organic C depletion, contributing to 14.95–22.81% of the SOC changes. SOC concentrations peaked in middle‐aged forests, whereas relative SOC stability peaked in young forests.
This study provides the first quantitative assessment of the distinct contributions of root and mycelium pathways to SOC accumulation and stabilization during dryland afforestation, advancing understanding of their roles in regulating SOC dynamics. As climate change intensifies land‐use pressure, management strategies should integrate stage‐specific root and mycelial traits to enhance SOC sequestration in arid forests.

title: OsERF27‐OsPLT4 regulatory module and ROS equilibrium control temporospatial rice crown root patterning
authors:
Khrang Khrang Khunggur Mushahary, 
Pragya Yadav, 
Komal Verma,

Shri Ram Yadav
abstract:
Schematic representation of the auxin- OsERF27-OsPLT4-ROS  module in regulating outgrowth and emergence of the  p CRP of the P 0  in rice.
 
 
 Summary 
 
In rice ( Oryza sativa ), the root architecture is heavily shaped by shoot-borne crown roots that arise from the phytomers at the stem base. Each phytomer typically generates two spatially distinct crown root populations – lower/proximal and upper/distal crown roots – that also emerge temporally, with the proximal roots forming first. The mechanisms that coordinate this temporospatial patterning, however, remain poorly understood.
Here, we identify an AP2/ERF gene  OsERF27  which is differentially expressed between proximal and distal crown root primordia and is specifically required for the timely development of proximal roots. We further show that  OsPLT4  functions downstream of  OsERF27 , defining an  OsERF27-OsPLT4  regulatory module that drives the outgrowth and emergence of proximal crown roots.
Interestingly, we uncover a requirement for reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis in crown root development: Loss-of-function mutants display disturbed ROS accumulation pattern and sensitized root formation to ROS perturbation, indicating that this module promotes root emergence by spatially maintaining optimal redox balance.
Together, our findings reveal a multi-layered regulatory network that integrates genetic elements with positional cues with redox control to pattern distinct crown root populations. Our study highlights how localized developmental programmes scale to shape root system architecture for tuning plant form and function in grasses.

abstract: Cover Legend  The liverwort  Marchantia polymorpha  reproduces asexually through clonal propagules called gemmae. The image depicts a gemma deficient in microRNA production due to mutations in Mp DCL1a , a key enzyme in miRNA biogenesis; reduced MpmiR166a levels disrupt auxin homeostasis and release the repression of MpC3HDZ, leading to the formation of supernumerary meristems and papillae (pink), precursors of gemmae (blue) and ectopic gemmae (yellow), that emerge from the epidermal surface. title: Oviposition fluid protein NlOFP1 in the brown planthopper suppresses rice plant defenses
authors:
Qingkai Feng, 
Jiale Shen, 
Ying Tian, 
Yanyan Yang, 
Jichong Zhuo, 
Jianping Chen, 
Junmin Li, 
Haijian Huang, 
Chuan‐Xi Zhang, 
Jia‐Bao Lu
abstract:
NlOFP1 is an oviposition fluid protein deposited into rice tissue during oviposition that helps eggs resist desiccation and suppresses plant defense.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Insect oviposition fluid plays a role in the early recognition of plants and the initiation of plant defense responses. However, the characterization of oviposition fluid proteins and their relationship with plant defenses remains poorly understood.
The oviposition fluid protein NlOFP1 in the brown planthopper ( Nilaparvata lugens ) is synthesized in the ovarian follicular cells and can be deposited into rice tissue. Functional studies reveal that NlOFP1 helps eggs resist desiccation stress. Furthermore, it can suppress plant defenses.  NlOFP1 -silencing leads to decreased honeydew secretion, fecundity, and egg hatching rate. Orthologs of NlOFP1 in other planthopper species exhibit highly conserved functions.
Transgenic rice overexpressing NlOFP1 showed reduced lignin and salicylic acid, increased cellulose, and downregulated resistance genes, indicating weakened defense responses of plants. This phenotype effectively compensated for the adaptive loss caused by  NlOFP1  silencing in the brown planthopper.
NlOFP1 interacted with the photosynthetic electron transport chain component OsFeS. This interaction partially impaired the import of OsFeS into the chloroplasts and might lead to a decline in plant resistance. Our study reveals that NlOFP1 acts as an effector against plant defense responses and provides insights into pest reproduction and host defense evasion.

title: Local auxin biosynthesis links cell wall remodeling to lateral root emergence
authors:
Lei Li, 
Xinfang Zhu, 
Zhaojun Ding, 
Cuiling Li, 
Xiangpei Kong
abstract: Auxin promotes lateral root emergence by remodeling surrounding root tissues. Cell wall modifications, including altered lignin deposition, are associated with successful root emergence, revealing a mechanism by which plants establish branched root systems to sustain growth and survival.

title: ZmSGT1‐mediated competitive protection of ZmBBI1 enhances maize resistance to Rhizoctonia solani
authors:
Yuanyuan Sun, 
Le Wang, 
Xiaofei He, 
Bingding Zhu, 
Zhijin Ma, 
Kun Wan, 
Ning Li
abstract:
In maize, the Bowman-Birk protease inhibitor ZmBBI1 confers resistance against sheath blight but is suppressed by the  Rhizoctonia solani  effector Rs03254. The immune co-chaperone ZmSGT1 competitively displaces Rs03254 to recover ZmBBI1-mediated defense responses. This three-component conflict supplies candidate genes for breeding disease-resistant maize varieties.

  
 ABSTRACT 
 Banded leaf and sheath blight (BLSB), incited by the necrotrophic basidiomycete  Rhizoctonia solani , is a devastating soil-borne disease that severely constrains global maize ( Zea mays ) production. Bowman–Birk inhibitors (BBIs) constitute a critical class of protease inhibitors in plant innate immunity; yet, their biological functions and upstream regulatory circuits in maize defense against necrotrophic pathogens remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we show that  ZmBBI1 , a BBI family member transcriptionally upregulated upon  R. solani  infection, positively modulates BLSB resistance. Its defense activity is strictly dependent on trypsin-inhibitory function, mediated by the evolutionarily conserved Thr52 and Arg53 residues in its canonical reactive loop. We identify Rs03254, a secreted virulence effector from  R. solani , that directly engages ZmBBI1 and biochemically inactivates its protease-inhibitory activity to promote fungal colonization. We further demonstrate that the conserved immune co-chaperone ZmSGT1 physically interacts with ZmBBI1 and is genetically required for its full defense function. Mechanistically, ZmSGT1 competes with Rs03254 for binding to ZmBBI1, displacing the pathogen effector and restoring ZmBBI1's trypsin-inhibitory activity. Our work defines a tripartite molecular arms race module in the maize– R. solani  pathosystem and uncovers a noncanonical role for SGT1 as a molecular bodyguard that protects host defense factors from effector-mediated suppression, providing actionable targets for engineering durable BLSB resistance in maize.

title: SlMED2 regulates locule number through the SlTPL−SlKNU floral meristem module
authors:
Sufu Gan, 
Yong Kang, 
Can Luo, 
Ying Li,

Jianghua Cai, 
Leilei Zhou, 
Mondher Bouzayen, 
Baowen Huang,
