Zhengguo Li
abstract: The Mediator complex subunit SlMED2 controls carpel number in tomato through promoter-proximal and long-range genomic interactions with the  SlTPL–SlKNU  floral meristem module, which represses  SlWUS  and  SlCLV3 , resulting in termination of stem cell activity.

title: Temporal control of root system architecture under osmotic stress: ABA–SnRK2 signaling and adaptive plasticity
authors:
Yupeng Zhang, 
Ruirui Xu, 
Yue Wang, 
Chengchao Zheng, 
Guodong Yang, 
Shizhong Zhang
abstract:
Roots adjust their growth under osmotic stress, but how this changes over time is poorly understood. This review proposes a temporal coding system: different SnRK2 kinases act at different timescales, and a balance point indicates whether roots prioritize rapid defense or long-term adaptation, guiding stress-tolerant crop design.
 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Drought and salt stress impose osmotic and ionic challenges on plant roots, with drought reducing soil water potential and salt imposing additional ionic toxicity beyond osmotic stress, driving the plastic remodeling of root system architecture (RSA). Abscisic acid (ABA) is a central hormone regulating root adaptability, and its signaling coordinates adaptive responses of roots across multiple time scales through the SNF1-related protein kinase 2 (SnRK2) family kinases. This review systematically summarizes the temporal coding mechanisms of the ABA–SnRK2 signaling network underlying root adaptation to osmotic stress. We propose that plant roots achieve a dynamic balance between short-term defense and long-term adaptation through the coordinated activities of different SnRK2 subgroups along the temporal axis. This proposed “balance point” of temporal coding is shaped by multiple temporal readouts. We also review how crosstalk between ABA and other hormones such as auxin fine-tunes root plasticity. Based on this framework, we propose a “balance point engineering” strategy that provides a theoretical blueprint for designing stress-tolerant crops with tunable durations of stress responses.

title: Apoplastic sugars regulate stomatal opening and closure through integrated osmotic and metabolic mechanisms
abstract: Abstract The role of sucrose in stomatal regulation has been debated for more than a century, yet its underlying mechanism remains incompletely understood. Recent evidence indicates that apoplastic sucrose acts as a mesophyll-derived signal promoting stomatal opening in  Arabidopsis , yet whether this mechanism operates in other species and under fluctuating environmental conditions, how sugars contribute to stomatal closure, and to what extent these responses depend on sucrose uptake and metabolism within guard cells (GCs) remain unresolved. Here, we carried out stomatal, metabolomics, and modeling analyses in leaves, the leaf apoplast, and GCs from tobacco wild-type and antisense lines for the GC SUCROSE TRANSPORTER 1 (Nt SUT1 ). Daily variation in stomatal conductance ( g  s ) was associated with the accumulation of sugars and organic acids in the apoplast. Stomatal opening and closure were associated with low and high concentrations of apoplastic sucrose over the diel course, respectively. Sugar feeding accelerated stomatal opening and closure in dark and light-adapted leaves, respectively, both in a concentration-dependent manner. Nt SUT1  displayed alterations in apoplast and GC metabolite profiles, which resulted in lower  g  s  and impaired sucrose-induced stomatal closure, compared with tobacco wild-type. Our findings suggest that apoplastic sugars and organic acids are associated with diurnal  g  s  dynamics and that sugars can accelerate both stomatal opening and closure through an osmotic mechanism in the apoplast, and are also dependent on sucrose import and degradation within GCs. These results extend current models of stomatal regulation by demonstrating that sugars regulate both stomatal opening and closure through integrated osmotic and metabolic mechanisms.

title: The MaPUB23-mediated degradation of the MaHSFB1-MaHDA2 counteracts high temperature-inhibited chlorophyll degradation in banana
abstract: Abstract Banana fruits ripening at or above 30 °C soften but retain a green peel. Elucidating the mechanism underlying this high temperature-induced repression of chlorophyll catabolism would help to improve the marketability of bananas. Toward this end, we compared banana fruits ripened at 20 °C and 30 °C using transcriptome analysis, revealing several E3 ubiquitin ligases repressed in green fruits ripened at 30 °C. Among them, only the U-box type E3 ligase MaPUB23 promoted chlorophyll degradation when transiently overexpressed in tobacco leaves. MaPUB23 interacted with and targeted MaHSFB1 and MaHDA2 for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. MaHSFB1 specifically interacted with and recruited MaHDA2 to the promoters of chlorophyll catabolic genes (CCGs), transcriptionally repressed these genes via decreased histone acetylation, and inhibited chlorophyll degradation. However, high temperature attenuated the MaPUB23-mediated degradation of MaHSFB1 and MaHDA2, which enhanced the MaHSFB1–MaHDA2-mediated repression of  CCGs . These results suggest that high temperature attenuates the MaPUB23-mediated proteasomal degradation of MaHSFB1–MaHDA2, leading to green ripening in banana fruit. This study thus illustrates a novel, dynamic regulatory module controlling the high temperature-induced repression of chlorophyll catabolism in banana fruits. Elucidating this mechanism provides a theoretical basis for strategies to manage temperature-induced fruit quality deterioration.

title: Comparative transcriptomics reveals a novel variant of an energy signaling regulator for lateral branch domestication in cucumber
abstract: Abstract Genetic alleles derived from wild resources are of great importance for crop breeding and improvement; however, connecting the dots between the functional variants and genetic traits is a significant challenge due to the need for precise, diverse, and large-scale phenotyping. Differential transcripts, which carry genetic variants or alternative splicing (AS) sites, may exhibit altered gene expression and protein coding, therefore influence phenotypes, showing their potential for high-throughput identification of functional genes. In this study, full-length transcripts were assembled and analyzed from eight developmental stage tissues of wild and cultivated cucumbers, utilizing PacBio Iso-seq and Illumina RNA-seq. We identified 6,980 genes underwent AS in cucumber. Approximately 66% of AS events were cultivar-specific, and genetic variants significantly increased around these divergent AS events. Based on the transcript structure of genes and variant annotation, we focused on  cis -acting genetic variants that may affect gene function, in which a 21-bp insertion in the 5' untranslated region (UTR) of  SnRK-Activating Kinase1  ( CsSnAK1 ), an energy signaling regulator, was demonstrated to inhibit lateral branch development in cultivated cucumber by promoting  CsSnAK1  mRNA abundance. Our work provides a straightforward yet reliable approach for integrating transcript structure and variant annotation to identify novel functional alleles in domestication traits.

title: Phosphorylation Alters the Condensation State of the Potato Transcription Factor bZIP18 to Enhance Plant Immunity
abstract: Abstract Biomolecular condensates formed by transcription factors (TFs) via liquid-liquid phase separation enable precise spatiotemporal control of eukaryotic gene expression. Although phosphorylation is a well-established regulator of TF activity, its capacity to remodel condensate organization and transcriptional function in plant immunity remains largely undefined. Here, we report that pathogen-induced phosphorylation converts a pre-existing TF condensate into a dynamic transcriptional hub to enhance the immune response in potato. Upon infection by the oomycete pathogen  Phytophthora infestans , the mitogen-activated protein kinase StMPK9 phosphorylates the TF StbZIP18 at the conserved residue threonine 337. This modification triggers rapid changes in the nuclear StbZIP18 condensates, transforming pre-existing condensates into numerous smaller assemblies. The phospho-null StbZIP18 T337A  mutant maintains its presence in low-activity condensates and compromises immunity, whereas the phospho-mimetic variant StbZIP18 T337E  constitutively forms active condensates and enhances resistance. The gene encoding the TF StMYB44 was identified as the direct downstream gene target of StbZIP18. TurboID-based proximity labeling revealed that both wild-type StbZIP18 and StbZIP18 T337E , but not the phospho-null variant StbZIP18 T337A , selectively interact with the transcriptional cofactor StMBF1c to form transcriptional activation hubs that drive defense gene expression, including  StMYB44 . Together, our findings establish that phosphorylation-directed condensate reprogramming operates as a tunable phase-separation switch, converting a low-activity assembly into a transcriptional amplifier. This study unveils a biophysical mechanism for signal amplification in plant immunity and provides insight into how post-translational modifications modulate transcriptional condensate function.

title: Telomere-to-telomere assemblies of Glycine soja and Glycine max uncover novel genomic features of soybean
abstract: Abstract Achieving complete, gap-free genome assemblies remains a central challenge in genomics, particularly for repeat-rich plant genomes. Although several telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assemblies have been reported for soybean, highly repetitive genomic regions and the mitochondrial genome remain insufficiently resolved. Here, we assembled gap-free T2T nuclear genomes together with complete mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes for the wild soybean ( Glycine soja ) SoyW02 and the cultivated soybean ( Glycine max ) Zhonghuang 13. These assemblies substantially improved the resolution of repetitive genomic regions and enabled biological insights that were previously inaccessible. Comparative analyses uncovered a conserved subtelomeric exchange hub and refined the landscape of soybean satellite repeats, including pericentromere-enriched and chromosome-specific satellites. We further developed a  de novo  pipeline for identifying tandem duplication gene clusters, enabling systematic analyses of transcriptional and protein sequence divergence, and experimentally demonstrating expression and functional diversification between two duplicated oxidosqualene cyclases. Together, these assemblies establish a foundation for investigating the evolution and functional organization of repetitive genomic regions and will facilitate future soybean functional genomics and molecular breeding.

title: Plant Single-Cell Metabolomics and Metabolite Imaging: Current Advances and Future Directions
abstract: Abstract Plants are multicellular systems composed of highly specialized cell types, whose distinct transcriptomes, proteomes, and metabolomes collectively shape growth, development, defense, and environmental adaptation. While single-cell transcriptomics has transformed our understanding of plant cellular heterogeneity, metabolites provide a direct and integrative readout of cellular biochemical activity and physiological state and can offer valuable insights into phenotype. They provide essential information that gene expression alone does not capture. Recent advances in mass spectrometry-based single-cell metabolomics (scMet) have enabled direct measurement of metabolic variation across individual cells and subcellular domains. In parallel, mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) has emerged as a powerful approach for mapping the spatial organization of metabolites within intact plant organs, offering new opportunities to connect chemical diversity with anatomy, cell identity, and biological functions. This review summarizes current technologies for plant single-cell sampling, scMet, and MSI for spatial metabolomics. It further highlights emerging efforts to illuminate the plant’s cellular and spatial dark metabolome through spectral libraries, computational metabolomics, and AI-assisted annotation. A long-term objective is to build quantitative, spatially resolved, and biologically interpretable plant signaling and metabolic networks at single-cell resolution.

title: Precision recreation and multiplex stacking of disease-resistance alleles in tomato using optimized prime editing
abstract: Abstract Prime editing enables precise modification of plant genomes and provides a means to recreate beneficial alleles underlying agronomically important traits. However, efficient and multiplexable prime editing systems remain limited in dicot crops. Here, we developed optimized prime editing systems for tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) and applied them to engineer and stack disease-resistance alleles. Using three tomato prime editors, TomPE2, TomPE6c, and TomPE7, we recreated a naturally occurring resistance-associated deletion identified in pepper by precisely deleting two leucine residues from the CYSTM-domain proteins SlBs5 and SlBs5L. The resulting tomato lines exhibited enhanced resistance to Xanthomonas, demonstrating that a resistance allele can be functionally recreated across related crop species. In parallel, introduction of premature stop codons into the susceptibility gene SlDMR6 conferred resistance to both Xanthomonas and Pseudomonas syringae. Transcriptome profiling revealed distinct defense states: Slbs5/Slbs5L plants predominantly exhibited enhanced pathogen-induced defense responses, whereas Sldmr6 plants showed elevated basal defense. Comparison of prime editor architectures and culture temperatures revealed differences in editing activity and precision, with TomPE6c producing the highest proportion of precise edits. We further developed a modular multiplex prime editing system capable of simultaneously modifying multiple loci, enabling resistance alleles and regulatory variants to be combined within a single generation. The engineered alleles were stably inherited, and resistance phenotypes were maintained under elevated temperature conditions. Together, these results establish prime editing as an effective platform for precise recreation, engineering, and multiplex stacking of disease-resistance alleles and provide a framework for accelerating resistance breeding in crops.

title: Distinct Splicing Complexes Formed by RS2Z32 Isoforms Modulate Alternative Splicing and Flowering
abstract: Abstract Serine/arginine (SR) splicing factors can alter downstream precursor messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) splicing patterns and influence gene expression. However, the influences of different isoforms generated by alternative splicing of SR proteins themselves on the transcription and splicing of downstream target genes in plants remain to be elucidated. Here, we demonstrate that the interaction between arginine/serine-rich zinc knuckle-containing protein 32 (RS2Z32) splicing isoforms and the  Arabidopsis thaliana  ortholog of human splicing factor SC35 (SC35) leads to the formation of distinct complexes, through which the recognition of splice sites within intron 3 of the transcription factor  circadian clock associated 1  ( CCA1 ) gene is regulated, ultimately resulting in an altered ratio of the  CCA1  splice variants. Competitive binding of CCA1α and CCA1β to the  flowering locus  C ( FLC ) gene promoter can either promote or inhibit  FLC  transcription and flowering. This study elucidates the molecular mechanism by which RS2Z32 regulates  FLC  expression independently of its canonical splicing function, enhancing our understanding of transcriptional regulation mediated by splicing factors in plants.

title: Stable and selective C(sp3)–H halogenation over COF-modified β-Fe2O3 photoanodes
abstract: Abstract Photoelectrocatalytic synthesis provides a sustainable route to high-value organic chemicals, yet achieving high selectivity while maintaining long-term stability remains challenging because of limited interfacial reactant availability and competing radical-mediated reaction pathways. Here, we develop a COF-modified photoanode by integrating a functionalized covalent organic framework (COF) onto  β -Fe 2 O 3  to regulate aqueous C( sp  3 )–H halogenation. Using cyclohexane chlorination as a model reaction, the COF-modified  β -Fe 2 O 3  photoanode achieves a monochlorination selectivity of up to 96.8% under AM 1.5 G illumination (100 mW cm −2 ), far exceeding the 53.9% obtained over bare  β -Fe 2 O 3 . Under one-sun illumination, the photoanode delivers a photocurrent density of 2.8 mA cm −2  and remains stable for 300 h, retaining approximately 95% chlorocyclohexane selectivity at the end of the test. Even under 13-sun illumination, the photocurrent density reaches approximately 35 mA cm −2 , with a chlorocyclohexane selectivity of 91.9% after 100 h. The COF-modified photoanode also shows enhanced monobromination and monoiodination selectivities, demonstrating the generality of this approach.

title: Quantum predator-prey cycles in dissipative Rydberg array
abstract: Abstract The predator-prey cycle is a paradigmatic example of self-organized population oscillations in far-from-equilibrium systems, yet testing its underlying mechanism in natural ecosystems is often precluded by uncontrollable microscopic parameters. Here, we propose a quantum analogue of predator-prey dynamics using a tunable two-dimensional Rydberg atom array. Through mean-field analysis and large-scale numerical simulations based on the open-system discrete truncated Wigner approximation, we demonstrate stable predator-prey cycles of Rydberg excitations on microsecond timescales. We show that nonperturbative quantum coherence drives spontaneous time-translation symmetry breaking, leading to globally synchronized oscillations under short-range interactions. Even under desynchronization caused by quantum jumps, locally synchronized predator-prey cycles persist, with amplitude scaling inversely with the square root of the system size. Our work extends the study of predator-prey models to the quantum realm and advances quantum simulation strategies that leverage engineered many-body nonequilibrium effects.

title: Self-evolving Embodied AI
abstract: Abstract Embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) is an intelligent system formed by agents and their environment through active perception, embodied cognition, and action interaction. Existing embodied AI remains confined to human-crafted setting, in which agents are trained on given memories and construct models for given tasks, enabling fixed physical embodiments to interact with relatively static environments. Such methods fail in in-the-wild setting characterized by variable physical embodiments and dynamic open environments. This paper introduces self-evolving embodied AI, a new paradigm in which agents operate based on their changing physical embodiment and environment through five software-level components, namely memory self-updating, task self-switching, environment self-prediction, embodiment self-adaptation, and model self-evolution, together with a hardware-level component for physical embodiment evolution, aiming to achieve continually adaptive intelligence through software-hardware co-evolution. Specifically, we present the definition, framework, components, mechanisms, roadmap, and evaluation indicators of self-evolving embodied AI, systematically review state-of-the-art works for realized components, discuss practical applications, and point out future research directions. We believe that self-evolving embodied AI enables agents to autonomously learn and interact with environments in a human-like manner and provides a new perspective toward general artificial intelligence.

title: The series of genetic codes that preceded our own
abstract: Abstract We produce a working hypothesis for the steps by which the canonical genetic code might have been constructed. We assume amino acids were added in the order inferred from their enrichment or depletion in ancestrally reconstructed sequences dating back to the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA) relative to that in ancient but post-LUCA controls. To convert this ordering into a time series of 64-codon genetic codes, we followed the “2-1-3 rule” that information appeared first at the middle codon position, then mostly at the first before the third, with purine vs pyrimidine distinctions tending to precede distinctions between purines or between pyrimidines. Two notable deviations from the 2-1-3 rule suggest an ancestral promiscuity between valine/isoleucine/methionine, and between alanine/threonine, to produce “statistical proteins.” The same promiscuities enable amino acids to be added in order of appearance at successive nodes in the cladograms of Class I and Class II aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase catalytic domains. Trifonov's previous amino acid ordering did not produce this consilience, with both a worse fit to the 2-1-3 rule, and discordance of synthetase trees with the order. More support for late resolution of hydrophobic promiscuity comes from post-LUCA differentiation between the synthetases of valine and isoleucine, in a manner dependent on 2 conserved tryptophans. The observed promiscuous activities of synthetases, and deep mutational scanning data on which amino acid substitutions are best tolerated, also align well with our reconstructed time series of genetic codes. As a working hypothesis, this series can guide research on random peptides, urzymes, and substitution models.

title: scPhyloGRN: gene regulatory network inference guided by lineage topology in single-cell developmental data
abstract: Abstract  Motivation Gene regulatory network (GRN) inference from single-cell transcriptomes is complicated by expression patterns associated with both cell state and shared ancestry. Cellular phylogenies provide developmental context, but incorporating relationships among individual cells into gene-level regulatory inference remains challenging. Results We present scPhyloGRN, a supervised framework that integrates single-cell gene expression with cellular phylogeny to prioritize directed transcription factor (TF)–target candidates within the observed gene set. The framework maps cell ancestry to gene associations that guide graph construction, attention in a dual-stream encoder, and lineage-consistency regularization. We evaluated scPhyloGRN against ten methods across 17 dataset–reference settings spanning four mouse embryos and one  Caenorhabditis elegans  dataset. scPhyloGRN showed an overall advantage in regulatory edge prioritization, supported by additional evaluations using shared candidate spaces. Removing lineage information reduced AUPRC in the ablation analyses, while branch-level and regulator-level analyses showed improved ranking and recovery of reference-supported regulatory candidates. Availability and implementation Source code and analysis workflows are available at  https://github.com/Maria0852/scPhyloGRN , with a versioned archive at  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22793831 .

title: Au Quantum Dots Anchored Y‐MOF Enabling Directional Interfacial Charge Transfer for Synergistic Redox Photocatalysis
authors:
Hui Yang, 
Dong Xu, 
Xue Lu, 
Yinbao Wu, 
Feng Tang, 
Linfu Xie, 
Saisai Yuan, 
Xiaozhi Wang, 
Qitao Zhang, 
Bin Xu
abstract:
Metal‑support interaction and directional interfacial charge transfer in Au QDs-anchored Y-MOF synergistically greatly boost redox photocatalysis for hydrogen evolution and acetaldehyde removal.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 The synergistic photocatalytic production of hydrogen coupled with pollutant degradation offers a transformative pathway toward sustainable energy and environmental remediation. Here, a novel bifunctional photocatalyst was prepared by anchoring Au quantum dots (QDs) onto a pyrene-derived yttrium-based metal-organic framework (Au/YT) using a one-pot solvothermal approach. Notably, the optimized 2.0%Au/YT demonstrated an outstanding photocatalytic redox activity for H 2  production and toxic acetaldehyde (CH 3 CHO) removal simultaneously under visible light irradiation, surpassed 15.94- and 19.86-times higher than that of original H 4 TBAPy counterpart. Comprehensive optical and electrochemical analyzes indicated that Au QDs significantly expand the light absorption range while also successfully speeding up the separation of photogenerated carriers. Meanwhile, the intrinsic multilayered structure of Y-MOFs further synergizes with the anchored Au-QD sites to establish metal–support interactions and augment charge transport dynamics, leading to a remarkable improvement in collaborative photocatalytic efficiency. Additionally, in situ XPS tests and DFT calculations substantiated a robust electronic interplay at the Au/YT interface, which effectually orchestrates directed interfacial charge migration and optimizes the adsorption/activation energy of reactant molecules. This work pioneers the development of dual-functional rare earth-based MOFs photocatalysts and furnishes fundamental insights into the rational design of synergistic redox photocatalysis systems tailored for clean solar energy production and environmental stewardship.

title: Weak‑Solvation‑Mediated Localized High‑Concentration Electrolyte for Sodium Metal Batteries
authors:
Hongxu Qu, 
Huihua Li, 
Jingxuan Wang, 
Mingxing Zhang, 
Yang Wang, 
Yuhang Meng, 
Sailei Shao, 
Stefano Passerini, 
Huang Zhang
abstract:
A weak‑solvation strategy using MTBE as a fluorine‑free diluent constructs a localized high‑concentration structure, promoting FSI −  coordination and forming an inorganic‑rich SEI. This enables stable cycling with high‑loading cathodes and pouch cells, offering a sustainable, PFAS‑free electrolyte for sodium metal batteries.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Sodium metal batteries offer high energy density and material sustainability, yet their practical viability is severely compromised by the intrinsic instability of sodium metal anodes. Herein, we report a localized high‑concentration structure formed in a moderate‑solvating electrolyte by introducing methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE) as a fluorine‑free, weakly coordinating diluent in tetrahydrofuran (THF)/NaFSI electrolyte. MTBE displaces free THF molecules, promotes FSI −  incorporation into the inner solvation sheath, and transforms the solvation structure from solvent‑separated ion pairs to contact ion pairs and aggregates. This diluent‑participated solvation, with its weak interaction with Na + , accelerates desolvation kinetics and forms a robust, anion‑derived inorganic‑rich interphase that suppresses parasitic reactions, dendrites, and corrosion. The optimal electrolyte enables Na||Na 4 Fe 3 (PO 4 ) 2 P 2 O 7  cells to deliver 74.3 mAh g −1  at 5.0 A g −1  and remarkable cycling stability with a high-loading cathode (12 mg cm −2 ) over 600 cycles. A pouch cell sustains 300 cycles with a capacity of 92.4 mAh g −1  at 0.1 A g −1 . This work demonstrates a sustainable, polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)‑free electrolyte design based on weak solvation engineering, offering a practical route toward stable and fast‑charging sodium metal batteries with enhanced cathode compatibility.

title: Strain‐Enhanced Ultrastretchable Semiconducting Polymer Fibers for Organic Electrochemical Transistors
authors:
Zixu Chang, 
Ziao Xu, 
Qi Tang, 
Mingjuan Du, 
Faqiang Wang, 
Jiexun Zhu, 
Jianyong Yu, 
Bin Ding, 
Zhaoling Li
abstract:
The continuous fabrication of stretchable polymer semiconductor p(g2T-T) fibers is realized via wet-spinning. The p(g2T-T) semiconductor fibers possess an efficient strain energy dissipation mechanism and unique strain-enhanced electrical performance. They can be stretched to over 250% strain and exhibit an ultrahigh normalized transconductance of 276.4 S cm −1  when used in stretchable organic electrochemical transistors, far exceeding thin-film polymer semiconductors.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Wearable electronics and soft bioelectronics require stretchable devices with steady performance under deformation. However, the balance between electrical performance and stretchability remains a critical obstacle, and most approaches sacrifice charge transport mobility to achieve stretchability. Herein, we present a material design concept that utilizes a wet-spinning strategy to fabricate highly stretchable semiconducting polymer fibers, enabling high-performance organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) with stable or even enhanced charge transport mobility under large strains. The polymer chains are ordered within the fibers under the shear effects of the spinning fluid and can reorient during stretching to dissipate strain energy, further forming a more compact and ordered molecular arrangement. As a result, the fabricated semiconductor fiber can be stretched to over 250% strain and exhibit an ultrahigh normalized transconductance of 276.4 S cm −1 , far exceeding thin-film polymer semiconductors. More importantly, the fiber OECTs possess unique strain-enhanced electrical performance, with substantially improved charge carrier mobility after strain-induced ordered arrangement of molecular chains. The skin-like fully stretchable OECTs have been successfully applied for recording electrocardiogram signals. This work provides more possibilities for the further development of stretchable semiconducting polymer materials with high electrical performance.

title: Gd‐Mediated Spin‐State Modulation of Co Sites Enhances Oxygen Electrocatalysis in Zn‐Air Battery
authors:
Yijie Shen, 
Yu Zhu, 
Tianrui Zhao, 
Yiwen An, 
Xuan Wang, 
Meng Li, 
Dongmei Sun, 
Linda Zhang, 
Hao Li, 
Yawen Tang, 
Gengtao Fu
abstract:
The Gd-mediated spin-state modulation strategy was proposed to enhance electrocatalytic performance of Co sites towards oxygen reduction reaction. The Gd incorporation modulates the local electronic structure of Co centers by inducing pronounced spin splitting and orbital-selective spin polarization, which optimizes the adsorption of oxygen-containing intermediates and shifts the rate-determining step from *O protonation to *OH desorption, leading to excellent performance.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Co-based catalysts are promising alternatives to precious-metal catalysts towards oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), yet the limited electronic flexibility of Co sites constrains the adsorption and conversion of oxygen-containing intermediates. Herein, we propose a Gd-mediated spin-state modulation strategy to enhance electrocatalytic ORR performance of Co sites. The incorporation of Gd into Co sites is realized by zeolitic imidazolate framework-8, forming a Gd-modified Co─N─C catalyst (GdCo/NC). The resulting GdCo/NC exhibits a higher half-wave potential of 0.861 V in alkaline media than that of Co/NC (0.824 V) and commercial Pt/C (0.843 V). The rechargeable Zn-air battery assembled with GdCo/NC demonstrates great practical performance, delivering a high peak power density of 170.8 mW cm −2  and a large specific capacity of 733 mAh g −1 , outperforming that of Pt/C + RuO 2  benchmark. Theoretical calculations reveal that Gd incorporation modulates the local electronic structure of Co centers by inducing pronounced spin splitting and orbital-selective spin polarization, which shifts the dominant spin polarization from d z2  orbital to d yz  orbital and lifts the degeneracy of d xz  and d yz  orbitals. Such spin-dependent electronic reconstruction optimizes the adsorption of oxygen-containing intermediates and shifts the rate-determining step from *O protonation to *OH desorption, thus leading to excellent ORR performance.

title: A Single‐Capillary Open Microfluidic Probe for Robust and Versatile Spatial Multi‐Omics Using Ambient Mass Spectrometry Imaging
authors:
Xiangyu Zhu, 
Yunkai Li, 
Jianing Wang, 
Chengyi Xie, 
Lei Guo, 
Yanyan Chen, 
Thomas Ka‐Yam Lam, 
Shao‐Wen Shi, 
Kun Wang, 
Baoliang Chen, 
Zongwei Cai
abstract:
This study reports a knot-shaped single-capillary open microfluidic probe (Knot-probe) for robust and versatile spatial omics, enabling ambient mass spectrometry imaging with high spatial resolution, throughput, and structure-resolved capability. Knot-probe mitigates the trade-off between analytical performance and operational robustness, providing an accessible route to spatial lipidomics, metabolomics, isomer-resolved lipid imaging, and native mass spectrometry imaging of proteins and proteoforms.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 High-resolution spatial mapping of tissue molecular architecture—from metabolites and lipid isomers to native proteins—remains a central challenge for ambient mass spectrometry imaging (MSI). Existing methods typically rely on multi-capillary, alignment-sensitive liquid-extraction probes, compromising robustness and compatibility with structure-resolved spatial omics. We mitigate this trade-off by introducing a monolithic, knot-shaped open microfluidic probe (Knot-probe) fabricated from a single capillary. Knot-probe achieves 40 µm scan-direction spatial resolution and acquisition throughput up to 0.16 mm s −1 , yet can be fabricated in ∼30 min with standard laboratory tools and operated reliably for over one month. Without sacrificing conventional spatial lipidomics and metabolomics, Knot-probe enables structure-resolved spatial omics, delivering high-resolution imaging of phosphatidylcholine  sn -positional isomers via tandem MS and, in a pneumatically-assisted variant, native MSI of proteins and proteoforms with higher throughput and enhanced sensitivity than with probes lacking pneumatic assistance. These capabilities arise from the integrated knot geometry, which ensures a stable micro-liquid junction for localized extraction with a minimized sampling footprint and efficient mass transfer, while eliminating intricate probe alignment for robust operation. Readily integrated with standard electrospray ionization MS, Knot-probe bridges conventional ambient MSI and emerging structural spatial omics, offering a broadly accessible approach across diverse biological and chemical applications.

title: Mechanically‐Gated Stochastic Resonance for All‐Optical Acoustic Sensing in Noisy Environments
authors:
Xuyu Zhang, 
Minzheng Sun, 
Cunzheng Fan, 
Shuolong Zhu, 
Qilin Hong, 
Pan Xu, 
Min Zhu, 
Zhengliang Hu, 
Yongchao Zou, 
Qizhen Sun
abstract:
A mechanically‐gated stochastic resonance (MGSR) sensing system is demonstrated, wherein stochastic resonance is enabled by an all‐optical bistable fiber Bragg grating feedback loop and gated by mechanical resonance. Under ambient noise, the system generates bistable outputs satisfying the Kramers escape‐rate condition, yielding signal‐to‐noise ratio (SNR) gain for weak acoustic signals. This all‐optical, real‐time approach offers frequency‐selective, noise‐robust, electromagnetic‐interference‐immune detection.








ABSTRACT
Weak signal detection in harsh and noisy environments remains a critical challenge across diverse fields. Stochastic resonance (SR) offers a counterintuitive strategy by exploiting noise to enhance, rather than suppress, weak signals, yet its practical deployment is severely limited by poor frequency selectivity, inadequate adaptability to fluctuating noise levels, and reliance on offline post‐processing. Here we report the discovery and experimental demonstration of mechanically‐gated stochastic resonance (MGSR), a novel physical mechanism that couples stochastic resonance with intrinsic mechanical resonance. By using mechanical resonance to actively modulate the bistable potential, MGSR achieves targeted frequency‐line selection, robust adaptation to variable noise conditions, and markedly improved signal‐to‐noise ratio (SNR) gain for weak signal detection. We further realize a real‐time, electromagnetic‐interference‐immune all‐optical bistable system through a fiber Bragg grating feedback mechanism, enabling hardware‐level MGSR free of computational latency. In tests conducted under realistic ocean ambient noise, our system attains a substantial SNR gain of 19.26 dB at the designed frequency, representing a clear advance for hardware‐based stochastic resonance acoustic sensors. This work deepens the understanding of SR, establishes a robust all‐optical architecture, and opens a scalable pathway toward high‐performance, noise‐resilient acoustic and vibration sensing for environmental monitoring, structural health diagnosis, and underwater safety.

title: Surface‐State‐Driven Selectivity of Electrocatalytic Glucose Oxidation: Metallic Au, Au─OH, and CuO
authors:
Myeonghwan Oh, 
Hoeun Seong, 
Ga Eun Jo, 
Jiyoung Hwang, 
Yurim Sohn, 
Kyoungsuk Jin, 
Jong Hyeok Park, 
Wooyul Kim, 
Seok Ki Kim, 
Dong Ki Lee
abstract:
In the electrochemical oxidation of glucose, whether the pyranose ring opens upon adsorption decides the reaction pathway: ring opening on metallic Au yields gluconic acid, gluconolactone formation on Au─OH leads to glucaric acid, and C─C cleavage on CuO gives formic acid. Surface state thus governs product selectivity.








ABSTRACT
The electrochemical glucose oxidation reaction (GLUOR) offers a sustainable route for biomass valorization, yet its reaction mechanisms and the factors governing product selectivity remain poorly understood. Herein, we present a comprehensive mechanistic investigation of GLUOR on Au and CuO catalysts. Au catalysts preserve the C6 carbon backbone while exhibiting surface‐state‐dependent oxidation of terminal functional groups of glucose (GLU), whereas CuO catalysts preferentially promote C─C bond cleavage reactions. Theoretical investigation reveals that C─C bond cleavage is energetically unfavorable on Au surfaces, in either the metallic or the hydroxylated state, but it is thermodynamically preferred on CuO surfaces. Furthermore, we provide spectroscopic and computational evidence that pyranose glucose undergoes ring opening on metallic Au surfaces, while ring‐retained pathways dominate on Au─OH and CuO surfaces, leading to gluconolactone formation and C─C bond cleavage, respectively. These findings provide a fundamental framework for interpreting product selectivity in glucose oxidation and offer mechanistic insights applicable to a broad range of biomass valorization processes.

title: CKMT1 Counteracts VDAC1 Oligomerization‐Induced Neuronal Pyroptosis Through Steric Hindrance in Ischemic Stroke
authors:
Xiaoyu Wang, 
Sai Shi, 
Jianghui Wu, 
Jingge Zhang, 
Shuqin Li, 
Yuyan Hu, 
Haifeng Yin, 
Chenguang Zhao, 
Dong Ma, 
Xiaohui Xian, 
Lizhe Liu, 
Ling Zhao, 
Xiyun Liu, 
Zhikai Yu, 
Lihua Dong, 
Wenbin Li, 
Lingyan Zhang, 
Min Zhang
abstract:
CKMT1 inhibits VDAC1 oligomerization via a dual‐region mechanism: its NTD interacts with the VDAC1 C‐terminal domain, while residues 1–39 sterically hinder dimerization, thereby reducing mtDNA leakage and AIM2 inflammasome activation, suppressing neuronal pyroptosis and protecting against cerebral ischemic injury. 








ABSTRACT
Ischemic stroke is one of the leading causes of death and disability worldwide; yet effective therapeutic options remain limited. Cytosolic leakage of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a critical driver of ischemic brain injury. Voltage‐dependent anion channel 1 (VDAC1), embedded in the mitochondrial outer membrane, promotes mtDNA leakage through oligomerization. However, the regulatory mechanisms underlying VDAC1 oligomerization in ischemic stroke remain poorly understood. This study demonstrates that ischemic stroke promotes VDAC1 oligomerization, leading to mtDNA leakage, activating the absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2) inflammasome, and subsequent neuronal pyroptosis. Pharmacological inhibition of VDAC1 oligomerization using VBIT‐4 effectively disrupts this cascade. Creatine kinase mitochondrial 1 (CKMT1) is identified as a novel endogenous inhibitor of VDAC1 oligomerization. CKMT1 inhibits VDAC1 oligomerization through a dual‐region synergistic mechanism. Specifically, the N‐terminal domain of CKMT1 (residues R75 and E121) forms a stable interface with the C‐terminal domain of VDAC1 (residues R218 and E189), whereas the CKMT1 signal peptide (residues 1–39) sterically hinders VDAC1 dimerization, thereby blocking oligomerization. Moreover, neuronal overexpression of CKMT1 significantly attenuates neuronal apoptosis, whereas CKMT1 knockdown aggravates neuronal injury. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CKMT1 protects against cerebral ischemic injury by suppressing the VDAC1–mtDNA–AIM2 axis and identify CKMT1 as a novel therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

title: Bacterial Geosmin Biosynthesis is Compartmentalized Inside a Two‐Component Protein Shell
authors:
Asif Fazal, 
Cassandra A. Dutcher, 
Michael P. Andreas, 
Tobias W. Giessen
abstract:
This study reports the discovery that geosmin biosynthesis is compartmentalized inside a two-component protein shell in many bacteria. Sequestration of geosmin synthase inside a Family 2B encapsulin nanocompartment improves geosmin yield and increases enzyme stability as compared to the free enzyme.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Terpenoids are ubiquitous, structurally diverse natural products found across the three domains of life. One of the most commonly observed and well-studied terpenoids is the volatile, petrichoric compound geosmin, responsible for the earthy smell of soil to which humans are receptive down to a few parts per trillion. Bioinformatic analysis of bacterial geosmin synthase (GeoA)-encoding gene clusters reveals that many are colocalized with genes encoding Family 2B encapsulin shell proteins. Here, we focus on the encapsulin-encoding geosmin gene cluster of the model myxobacterium  Myxococcus xanthus  and show that the two shell proteins form a two-component Family 2B encapsulin with GeoA as the internalized cargo. Structural analysis highlights that the shell contains characteristic, external cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) binding-fold domains (CBDs), and that mixed shells can adopt a previously unobserved closed two-fold pore conformation. We show that GeoA cargo loading is mediated by repeating, short cargo loading peptides (CLPs), and that GeoA encapsulation provides benefits for enzyme activity and stability. This work expands the short list of Family 2B encapsulins known to be involved in specialized metabolite biosynthesis, and provides insights into a putative mode of cargo protein regulation via pore state modulation.

title: Epigenetic Activation of ANGPTL4 Drives EBV‐Negative Gastric Cancer via Neutrophil Recruitment and NET Release via Stabilizing ANXA5
authors:
Dandan Li, 
Xinqi Li, 
Xiangyin Luo, 
Jiayi Wang, 
Yiwei Zha, 
Zeng Zhou, 
Yanyan Chen, 
Qi Wang, 
Lingyun Xia, 
Weidong Leng, 
Shanshan Qin
abstract:
ANGPTL4 exhibits distinct promoter methylation patterns and expression profiles in EBV‐positive versus EBV‐negative gastric cancer. Secreted C‐terminal ANGPTL4 (cANGPTL4) acts as the dominant functional isoform driving GC proliferation, EMT, and neutrophil infiltration. cANGPTL4 promotes neutrophil recruitment via NF‐κB/CXCL8 axis. cANGPTL4 drives GC progression by inducing NETs release via directly stabilizing ANXA5.








ABSTRACT
EBV‐positive (EBVaGC) and EBV‐negative (EBVnGC) gastric cancers exhibit distinct clinical outcomes, prognostic features, and immune infiltration landscapes; however, the molecular mechanisms driving these subtype differences, as well as the subtype‐specific epigenetic regulation and biological functions of ANGPTL4 within the immune microenvironment, remain unclear. Here, through integrated analysis of multi‐omics data, we discovered that EBV infection induces marked hypermethylation at the ANGPTL4 promoter, leading to transcriptional silencing of ANGPTL4 in EBVaGC. Conversely, hypomethylation‐mediated ANGPTL4 overexpression is clinically associated with poor prognosis and distant metastasis in EBVnGC. Mechanistically, the C‐terminal secreted form (cANGPTL4) promotes GC progression by enhancing proliferation, epithelial‐mesenchymal transition (EMT), and neutrophil recruitment. Clinically, ANGPTL4 expression is positively correlated with neutrophil infiltration and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) levels in GC. Spatial transcriptomics and immunohistochemistry (IHC) analyses confirmed the spatial colocalization of ANGPTL4 with tumor‐infiltrating neutrophils. cANGPTL4 mediates tumor‐associated neutrophil (TAN) recruitment via the NF‐κB/CXCL8 axis and directly binds and stabilizes neutrophil‐derived ANXA5 to facilitate NET release, thereby driving GC progression. In conclusion, ANGPTL4 represents a potential intervention target for EBVnGC. Targeting ANGPTL4 may exert dual anti‐tumor effects by directly suppressing GC proliferation, EMT, and metastasis, and by remodeling the immunosuppressive microenvironment via attenuating TANs infiltration and NET release.

title: Electrocatalytic Urea Synthesis From CO2 and N2/NO3−: Bridging Catalyst Activity, C–N Coupling Kinetics, and Industrial Applicability
authors:
Fulin Dong, 
Ruihan Zhang, 
Huiyu Lou, 
Tianshi Gao, 
Guangjin Zhang, 
Menglei Yuan
abstract:
This review compares NO 3 
 −  + CO 2  and N 2  + CO 2  electrocatalytic urea synthesis in feedstock properties, catalyst design, C–N coupling mechanisms, performance optimization, and engineering applicability. The two systems correspond to a near-term deployable route and a long-term green synthesis goal, respectively.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Electrocatalytic urea synthesis enables the co-conversion of CO 2  and N 2 /NO 3 
 −  under ambient conditions and offers a sustainable alternative to conventional energy-intensive processes. This review systematically summarizes the NO 3 
 −  + CO 2  and N 2  + CO 2  systems in terms of feedstock properties, catalyst design, reaction mechanisms, performance optimization, and engineering applications. The NO 3 
 −  + CO 2  system, benefiting from facile NO 3 
 −  activation and high aqueous accessibility, has achieved significant improvements in efficiency and selectivity through rate matching and side-reaction suppression, with performance approaching practical viability. The N 2  + CO 2  system, though more sustainable in feedstock, remains constrained by the high N≡N bond energy and low solubility, with current research focusing on N 2  activation and intermediate regulation, while performance still lags considerably. The two systems differ markedly in nitrogen activation pathways and regulatory mechanisms, corresponding to distinct developmental stages and application potentials. Finally, challenges and future directions are outlined in terms of catalyst design, mechanistic studies, reactor engineering, and standardized evaluation, providing guidance for the construction of efficient systems and their scale-up applications.

title: Surface Coordination‐Dependent Oxygen Evolution Pathways in Rutile IrO2
authors:
Gahee Noh, 
Seong‐Sik Kim, 
Hyungwoo Lee, 
Jaejin Hwang, 
Michael Patton, 
Owen Ericksen, 
Tae Gyu Yun, 
Seung‐Hyun Heo, 
Suho Lee, 
Yurim Hong, 
In Su Lee, 
Daesu Lee, 
Chang‐Beom Eom, 
Jaekwang Lee, 
Minseok Choi, 
Sung‐Yoon Chung, 
Si‐Young Choi
abstract:
Epitaxial rutile IrO 2  surfaces with crystallographically distinct orientations reveal a strong dependence of oxygen evolution reactivity on surface atomic coordination. The (110) and (101) surfaces exhibit O-rich electronic character and an energetic preference for the quadruple oxygen coupling mechanism (QOCM), whereas the (001) surface shows more Ir-centered character and favors an adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM)-like pathway.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Rutile iridium dioxide (IrO 2 ) is renowned as an effective catalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), yet how its atomic structure governs orientation-dependent activity remains unclear. Here, we investigate epitaxial rutile IrO 2  thin films with crystallographically well-defined (110), (101), and (001) orientations and show that their OER activity follows the order: (110) > (101) > (001). Atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) analysis identifies distinct surface terminations and Ir-O coordination motifs that differ from commonly assumed idealized surface models. Experimentally informed electronic-structure calculations reveal that the (110) and (101) surfaces exhibit enhanced O 2 p  states near the Fermi level, favoring oxygen-involved charge transfer, whereas the (001) surface shows a more Ir-centered electronic character. Reaction-barrier calculations further indicate an energetic preference for the quadruple oxygen coupling mechanism (QOCM) on the (110) and (101) surfaces, whereas the (001) surface is more consistent with an Ir-centered adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM)-like pathway. These results establish surface coordination as a key descriptor linking atomic termination, electronic structure, reaction pathway, and OER activity, providing a basis for designing high-performance IrO 2  catalysts through surface-structure engineering.

title: Piezoelectric Amino Acid Salts with Halogen‐Based Coformers Produce Exceptional Force‐Generated Voltage Output
authors:
Krishna Hari, 
Shubham Vishnoi, 
Sarah Guerin
abstract:
Amino acid-based multicomponent crystals have emerged as high-performance, environmentally sustainable piezoelectrics. In this work, the correlation of crystal packing, molecular polarization, and electromechanical response is uncovered through integrated experimental and computational approaches. Notably, the high output voltage from L-histidinium trifluoroacetate highlights the potential of these molecularly engineered organic crystals for next-generation energy harvesting technologies.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Hierarchical self-assemblies of bio-inspired materials combine structural tunability with biocompatibility and environmental sustainability for multifunctional applications. Within this area of applied research, minimalistic building units such as amino acids and their derivatives have evolved as next-generation piezoelectric materials. Their tendency towards chiral nature, polar molecular structure, asymmetric crystal packing, and designability enable efficient linear voltage generation under mechanical stress, yet their technological translation is at formative stages. Amino acid-based multicomponent crystals ( MCC s) are an emerging class of sustainable piezoelectrics, which benefit from an integrated experimental-theoretical approach for commercial advancement. In this work, the piezoelectric properties of nine non-centrosymmetric amino acid salt crystals were confirmed experimentally using both piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) and  quasi -static piezoelectric measurements ( d 33 
  = 7.8 pC/N) and calculated using density functional theory (DFT), with a maximum predicted longitudinal piezoelectric coefficient of 7.5 pC/N. A large open-circuit voltage of 12.9 V was obtained for polycrystalline L-histidinium trifluoroacetate under direct ambient mechanical stimuli, exceeding the open-circuit voltage of ~6 V of a commercial ceramic disc. The close agreement between measured and computed electromechanical properties allows for correlations to be drawn between the  MCC  molecular structures and their macroscopic properties, facilitating the rational design of sustainable organic piezoelectrics.

title: Amyloid‐Guided Assembly of Magnetically Recyclable Enzymatic Nanofibers Toward Sustainable Biocatalysis
authors:
Shuangping Liu, 
Qilin Yang, 
Qian Zhang, 
Tiantian Liu, 
Xiao Han, 
Jian Mao
abstract:
A hierarchical strategy integrates linker engineering, amyloid-guided self-assembly, and magnetic immobilization to construct recyclable DPAO4-DMAO7 enzymatic nanofibers. The resulting magnetic composites enable biogenic amine conversion in complex food matrices and simulated wastewater, while rapid magnetic separation supports repeated reuse. The work demonstrates a coordinated route from molecular design to recyclable catalytic materials.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 The rational construction of recyclable protein-based catalytic materials requires connecting molecular enzyme design with higher-order supramolecular organization and functional recovery interfaces. This study establishes a hierarchical design strategy that integrates fusion-enzyme engineering, amyloid-guided self-assembly, and magnetic immobilization. The primary amine oxidase DPAO4 and the flavin-containing amine oxidase DMAO7 were joined through flexible or rigid linkers, and the rigid (EAAAK) 3  variant provided broad substrate coverage, greater tolerance to process-relevant stresses, and lower interdomain fluctuations in molecular dynamics simulations. N-terminal Sup35 1-61  or Ure2 1-80  domains promoted the formation of ThT-responsive fibrillar assembly, and the resulting enzymatic nanofibers were coupled to amino-functionalized Fe 3 O 4 @SiO 2 -NH 2  nanoparticles. The composites enabled magnetic separation within 30 s, catalyzed the degradation of eight biogenic amines under acidic, thermal, saline, and ethanol-containing conditions, and retained an average of 53.2% of their initial activity after four recovery cycles. As proof-of-concept evaluation in complex matrices, selected systems removed up to 70.6% of total biogenic amines from fermented beverages and 69.7% from soy sauce. The distinct responses of the Sup35- and Ure2-based composites suggest an association between assembly-domain identity and catalytic performance in complex matrices. This work demonstrates a hierarchical design approach for recyclable protein-based catalytic materials and sustainable biocatalysis.

title: Deep Learning for AD Risk Screening and Progression Prediction
authors:
Bin Lu, 
Yan‐Rong Chen, 
Rui‐Xian Li, 
Ming‐Kai Zhang, 
Shao‐Zhen Yan, 
Guan‐Qun Chen, 
Jing‐Hua Wang, 
Wen‐Hui Chai, 
Francisco Xavier Castellanos, 
Paul M. Thompson, 
Jie Lu, 
Ying Han, 
Chao‐Gan Yan
abstract:
A pretrained MRI‐based deep learning model generalizes from Western cohorts to an independent Chinese cohort, detects Alzheimer's disease with high sensitivity, and identifies elevated AD risk years before diagnosis. Its risk scores align with cognition and plasma biomarkers, and individualized brain risk maps uncover clinically distinct subtypes, highlighting structural MRI as a scalable route to early detection and risk stratification.








ABSTRACT
The rise of Alzheimer's disease (AD) immunotherapies underscores the need for accessible, time‐efficient biomarkers for early diagnosis. MRI‐based deep learning shows promise in this regard, yet few models have undergone comprehensive clinical validation. Using the SILCODE cohort (722 Chinese participants, 1,105 scans), we test the transportability of our classifier (pretrained on Western samples) to an independent Chinese cohort without retraining. The associations between risk scores and disease progression, cognitive performance, and plasma biomarkers are examined. In addition, an interpretable framework is developed to generate individualized brain risk maps and identify subtypes. The model classifies AD with an AUC of 0.913 and 95.2% sensitivity, identifying 90.5% of high‐risk individuals 2–3 years before clinical diagnosis. Risk scores correlate significantly with cognitive and plasma indices, particularly p‐tau 217. Brain risk maps reveal AD subtypes, including a subgroup with rapid cognitive decline. These findings establish a population‐robust, clinically relevant MRI‐based model for early AD detection and risk stratification.

title: Blocking Honeybee Preference for Neonicotinoids by Interfering With Dopamine Signaling
authors:
Jing Li, 
Yuan Ge, 
Wangjiang Feng, 
David C. Lyon, 
Pingli Dai, 
Yong‐Jun Liu
abstract:
Honeybees ( Apis mellifera ) paradoxically prefer nectar containing the harmful neonicotinoid thiamethoxam. This preference is associated with transient brain dopamine elevation during proboscis extension reflex (PER) responses and active feeding, and is reduced by the dopamine receptor antagonist fluphenazine. These findings provide a basis for future strategies to reduce honeybee attraction to neonicotinoid-laden nectar, thereby helping preserve pollination services.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Honeybees ( Apis mellifera ) prefer nectar containing neonicotinoids despite severe exposure risk leading to colony collapse. The neural mechanisms underlying this preference behavior remain unknown, impeding the development of effective blocking strategies. Neonicotinoids act as acetylcholine receptor agonists, and dopamine is a vital neuromodulator in addictive behavior. We hypothesize that neonicotinoids could activate brain dopamine signaling in honeybees, reinforcing their feeding behavior. Here, we show that thiamethoxam-laden food is preferred over uncontaminated options, and that prolonged consumption is associated with transient, state-dependent increases in brain dopamine concentrations. Introducing the dopamine receptor antagonist, fluphenazine, reduces thiamethoxam preference. Our study first reveals a key dopamine-associated mechanism underlying neonicotinoid-induced preference behavior in honeybees and provides a potential basis for future strategies to reduce honeybee attraction to insecticide-containing food source through modulation of the preference-related dopamine pathway, thereby helping to preserve honeybee pollination services.

title: Molecular MRI Reveals Macrophage‐Enriched Peritumoral Immune Remodeling After Incomplete Ablation in Liver Cancer
authors:
Yubei He, 
Han Xu, 
Julian M. M. Rogasch, 
Nikolaus Berndt, 
Jing Guo, 
Eyk Schellenberger, 
Akvile Häckel, 
Luisa Heidemann, 
Friederike Hesse, 
Yu Liu, 
Justus Ramtke, 
Nicola Beindorff, 
Frank Hofheinz, 
Avan Kader, 
Michael Mülleder, 
Kathrin Textoris‐Taube, 
Bernd Hamm, 
Dominik N. Müller, 
Robin Schmidt, 
Ralf Hauptmann, 
Heike Traub, 
Mathias Schannor, 
Lynn Jeanette Savic
abstract:
Incomplete microwave ablation (iMWA) induced a spatially organized, macrophage-rich immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) in orthotopic VX2 liver tumors. Molecular MRI enhanced with europium-doped very small superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (Eu-VSOP) noninvasively visualized this remodeling, showing preferential nanoparticle enrichment in macrophage-rich, CD206-associated peritumoral regions. This approach may provide a translational imaging strategy to complement conventional assessment by identifying biologically adverse post-ablation microenvironments and informing risk stratification following incomplete liver tumor ablation.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Incomplete image-guided ablation can promote local tumor progression by reshaping the residual tumor microenvironment toward immunosuppression, yet noninvasive biomarkers of this process remain limited. Here, a translational multiparametric PET/MRI strategy was developed to monitor macrophage-associated microenvironmental remodeling after incomplete microwave ablation (iMWA) in orthotopic VX2 liver tumors. Twenty-four tumor-bearing rabbits were assigned to untreated control, early post-iMWA (short-term), or late post-iMWA (long-term) groups and underwent clinical 3 T PET/MRI, including diffusion-weighted imaging, dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, [ 1 
 8 F]FDG PET, and T2-weighted MRI before and after administration of Eu-VSOP. Eu-VSOP-enhanced MRI revealed a hypointense peritumoral rim after iMWA, with the largest rim-to-liver signal decrease and rim thickness observed in the long-term group. Prussian blue staining and LA-ICP-ToF-MS demonstrated preferential iron and europium enrichment in macrophage-rich, CD206-associated peritumoral regions. Histology and proteomics further demonstrated increased CD206 and MMP-9 expression, extracellular matrix remodeling, immunosuppressive myeloid-associated changes, and metabolic reprogramming in viable residual tumors, accompanied by altered [ 1 
 8 F]FDG uptake. Together, these findings indicate that incomplete ablation induces a temporally evolving, macrophage-rich immunosuppressive peritumoral niche and support the potential of Eu-VSOP-enhanced multiparametric PET/MRI for noninvasive monitoring of post-ablation microenvironmental remodeling.

title: The Novel Viral Non‐Coding RNA LMP2A‐IT1 Promotes the Lytic Replication of EBV
authors:
Zheng‐Zhou Lu, 
Jun‐Fei Wu, 
Nannan Zhu, 
Ming‐Hui Yang, 
Le‐Le Zhang, 
Yuan‐Tao Liu, 
Wei‐Jun Chen, 
Jin‐Kun Tang, 
Jia‐Wei Ge, 
Chao‐Bo Lei, 
Tao Zhang, 
Yu Wang, 
Chao‐Yun Huang, 
Qian Zhong, 
Mu‐Sheng Zeng, 
Yan Li
abstract:
Decades after its discovery, EBV's genome still harbours unannotated “dark matter”. LMP2A‐IT1, a novel EBV‐encoded transcript identified in this work, is strongly upregulated during lytic replication and promotes BZLF1 expression, likely through activation of inflammatory responses, thereby enhancing viral propagation in a self‐reinforcing positive feedback loop.








ABSTRACT
The Epstein‐Barr virus (EBV) is recognized as the first human tumor virus and etiologically linked to a spectrum of malignancies and autoimmune diseases. EBV lytic replication contributes substantially to pathogenesis, but the viral components that enable efficient replication within host cells remain incompletely understood. Here, we identified a previously unknown EBV non‐coding RNA (ncRNA) from glycoRNA samples and designated it LMP2A‐IT1. This viral ncRNA was consistently detected across multiple EBV‐infected cell lines, in exosomes, and in EBV‐positive nasopharyngeal carcinoma tissues, exhibiting a predominantly cytoplasmic distribution. Functional analyses reveal that the induction of LMP2A‐IT1 during EBV lytic replication actively drives the lytic cycle, resulting in a self‐amplifying positive feedback loop. Mechanistically, LMP2A‐IT1 appears to activate an inflammatory response, which subsequently upregulates BZLF1, a master regulator of the EBV lytic cascade, to facilitate lytic progression. Together, our findings suggest that LMP2A‐IT1 represents a previously unrecognized viral factor that EBV deploys to achieve robust replication. To our best knowledge, this is the first report of a viral RNA harboring glycosylation modifications, thereby expanding the glycoRNA landscape. Moreover, this study offers new mechanistic insights into EBV replication as well as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for EBV‐associated diseases.

title: Formation‐Stage Interfacial Regulation of δ‐MnO2 Enables Stable and Reversible Aqueous Zn‐Ion Storage
authors:
Fanghua Liang, 
Ling Wang, 
Junpeng Xiong, 
Chunqing Niu, 
Atsuya Kawai, 
Wei Zhang, 
Chunhong Zhu, 
Azeem Ullah, 
Mayakrishnan Gopiraman, 
Mingzheng Ge, 
Ick Soo Kim
abstract:
Precursor-embedded Fe regulates the nucleation and growth of δ-MnO 2 , enabling a more accessible and stable Zn-storage interface with accelerated kinetics and suppressed Mn dissolution, while preserving the intrinsic Mn redox chemistry.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Layered δ-MnO 2  is a promising cathode for aqueous zinc-ion batteries, yet its practical application remains hindered by the coupled challenges of sluggish Zn 2+  storage kinetics and persistent Mn dissolution. Here, we develop a precursor-embedded Fe interfacial regulation strategy to modulate the nucleation and growth of δ-MnO 2  on porous carbon nanofibers (δ-MnO 2 @Fe-PCNFs). Rather than being dominated by homogeneous bulk substitution, the introduced Fe is predominantly present as low-content, highly dispersed surface-/interface-associated species established during δ-MnO 2  formation, where it regulates the local Mn─O environment and consequently modulates nanosheet growth and the accessibility of the reaction interface. The Fe-regulated δ-MnO 2  framework exhibits improved kinetic accessibility and suppresses Mn dissolution without altering its intrinsic Mn-based redox chemistry. Consequently, the δ-MnO 2 @Fe-PCNFs electrode delivers an initial capacity of 409.29 mAh g −1  at 0.2 A g −1  and excellent long‑term cycling stability, maintaining a capacity of 243.64 mAh g −1  at 1 A g −1  after 1000 cycles and excellent capacity retention of 81.1% after 3000 cycles at 5 A g −1 . This work highlights formation-stage interfacial regulation as an effective strategy to couple reaction accessibility with structural durability in Mn-based aqueous zinc-ion battery cathodes.

title: Zr Incorporation Into Lithium Nickel Oxides: Bulk or Surface Substitution?
authors:
Lars Winkler, 
Geon‐Tae Park, 
Liang‐Yin Kuo, 
Martin Ihrig, 
Konstantin Köster, 
Johan E. ten Elshof, 
Mark Huijben, 
Myoung‐Chan Kim, 
Min‐Gyu Seo, 
Yang‐Kook Sun, 
Payam Kaghazchi
abstract:
Mechanism of Zr incorporation into lithium nickel oxide (LNO) cathodes is studied from atomistic to macroscale. Zr doping enhances cyclability of Li-ion batteries with LNO via bulk, interface, and grain boundary optimization leading to structural integrity at atomistic- and micro-scale of secondary particle aggregates. However, excess Zr doping leads to insulating impurity phases limiting initial capacity.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 High-capacity lithium nickel oxides (LNO) are promising cathode active materials for next-generation batteries. However, their practical application is limited by poor cycling stability. Doping the LNO cathode with high-valence elements is an effective strategy to enhance structural stability. In this study, we investigate the mechanism of Zr 4+  incorporation into LNO using experimental and theoretical techniques. Our findings reveal that under oxygen-rich conditions, Zr-doped LNO can be realized as a single phase, but most Zr cations localize at the surface of primary particles. In contrast, under oxygen-deficient or non-equilibrium conditions a secondary layered Li 1-x Ni 1+x O 2  phase, characterized by Ni migration into the Li layers (cation ordering), is stabilized coexisting with Zr-doped LNO. This promotes elongation of primary particles at the aggregation surface. The Zr enrichment at the microparticle surface, Zr-induced cation-ordered superstructure, and the formation of elongated grains enhance the chemical stability as well as the structural integrity at atomistic- and micro-scale of the LNO cathode, improving its cycling performance. However, only 1–3% Zr is necessary to maintain the initial capacity and enhance cyclability through surface coating and low bulk doping with Zr. With increasing Zr concentration, an electronically insulating impurity (Li 2 ZrO 3 ) forms, leading to a decrease in the initial capacity.

title: Engineered Chiral Probiotics Ameliorate MASH via Gut–Liver Axis
authors:
Jing Chen, 
Shen Zhang, 
Yuli Zhu, 
Da Zhou, 
Chunya Ji, 
Mingrui Zhu, 
Sirui Wang, 
Yuting Shen, 
Jifeng Yu, 
Heng Zhang, 
Yan Fang, 
Huixiong Xu, 
Haohao Yin
abstract:
A chiral gold nanozyme was coated onto the gut commensal bacterium  Faecalibacterium duncaniae (F. duncaniae)  to create an engineered probiotic. In mouse models of MASH, this orally administered living therapeutic protected the bacterium against oxidative stress, enhanced its gut colonization, reversed steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis, and improved dysbiosis, metabolic disturbances, and cognitive impairment. 

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 The global epidemic of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is escalating without effective therapies. This study identified a significant depletion of the gut commensal bacterium  Faecalibacterium duncaniae  ( F. duncaniae ) as a core feature of MASH. To overcome the poor colonization by traditional probiotics in inflammatory environments, we engineered a living microbial therapeutic by incorporating chiral gold nanozymes onto  F. duncaniae . We discovered that biological performance is enantiomer-dependent: the right-handed nanozyme (D-Au) serves as a superior ROS-scavenging shield, protecting the probiotic from oxidative assault and enhancing its colonization in the inflamed gut. In mouse models of MASH, this engineered probiotic (F@D-Au) reversed disease progression, ameliorating steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis. It further restored systemic homeostasis, rectifying dysbiosis, metabolic disturbances, and—notably—MASH-associated cognitive impairment. Metabolomic analyses revealed that this multi-organ benefit was linked to the restoration of key microbial metabolites, including kynurenic acid and linoleic acid. Our work establishes a new class of chirality-enhanced living therapeutics that precisely remodel the gut–liver axis, offering a transformative strategy for treating MASH and its complications.

title: Wearable E‐Textiles for Cardiovascular Monitoring: Materials, Devices, and Integrated Systems
authors:
Bangul Khan, 
Mahmoud Tavakoli, 
Norbert Radacsi, 
Bee Luan KHOO
abstract:
The graphical abstract highlights the role of conductive materials and textile fabrication techniques in enabling smart textiles for cardiovascular applications. It showcases textile‐based ECG monitoring, pulse sensing, hemodynamic monitoring, and cardiovascular tissue engineering, while emphasizing the challenges and design considerations that govern device performance, wearability, and clinical translation toward personalized healthcare.








ABSTRACT
Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, highlighting the need for continuous, non‐invasive, and reliable physiological monitoring beyond conventional clinical assessments. Smart textiles have emerged as a promising platform for personalized cardiovascular healthcare by combining wearability, mechanical comfort, and seamless integration into everyday garments. This review examines recent advances in conductive materials, textile manufacturing technologies, and system‐level device integration for cardiovascular sensing applications. Metallic fibers, carbon nanomaterials, and conducting polymers are evaluated for electrical conductivity, stretchability, mechanical durability, and wash stability. Furthermore, textile fabrication approaches, including weaving, knitting, embroidery, printing, and electrospinning, are analyzed for their ability to translate material properties into scalable, manufacturable sensing architectures. Recent developments in textile‐integrated electrocardiography, pulse‐wave, blood pressure, and hemodynamic monitoring demonstrate performance approaching clinical standards, with high signal fidelity and strong agreement with conventional medical devices. Key challenges related to long‐term stability, power autonomy, signal reliability, and large‐scale manufacturing are discussed alongside emerging solutions, including MXene‐based electrodes, self‐powered sensing systems, and edge artificial intelligence. Finally, future perspectives are outlined for developing clinically validated, scalable, and intelligent smart textile platforms that enable continuous cardiovascular monitoring and next‐generation personalized healthcare.

title: Single‐Step Electrochemical Aptasensor for Melatonin Detection in Unprocessed Plasma
authors:
Hamed Shieh, 
Arash Khorrami Jahromi, 
Fernando Gonzales‐Aste, 
Sajad Shiekh, 
Roozbeh Siavash Moakhar, 
Sahar Sadat Mahshid, 
Sara Mahshid
abstract:
Melatonin is a well-known biomarker with significant potential for clinical use in diagnosing circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs) and monitoring patients with documented circadian clock disruption. An electrochemical aptamer-based biosensor (E-aptasensor), employing an optimized population of melatonin aptamers, has been proposed as a solution for the one-step, reagentless detection of melatonin within physiological levels.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Melatonin is a clinically relevant biomarker for diagnosing circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs) and monitoring circadian disruption associated with cancer, metabolic and cardiovascular disease, and psychiatric disorders. This work reports the implementation of an electrochemical aptamer-based biosensor (E-aptasensor) for direct reagentless detection of melatonin within physiological levels. The E-aptasensor employs an optimized surface population of the aptamers in a conformational change-based assay to detect melatonin over a broad dynamic range, including the picomolar physiological range. The behavior of the aptameric assay was validated both in bulk solution and in silico using fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) and molecular docking (MD). The E-aptasensor achieves sensitive and selective melatonin detection, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.75 pM and strong specificity against a panel of relevant interferents. Fitting the electrochemical responses to the Hill–Langmuir (HL) binding model yielded an apparent electrochemical dissociation constant (K d, app ) of 37 pM. Notably, the E-aptasensor showed promising performance in unextracted human plasma, avoiding the extraction step typically required for immunoassays. These features support future development of rapid melatonin profiling for CRSD diagnosis and monitoring, as well as future point-of-care implementation. The single-step E-aptasensor offers a promising, faster, and simpler complement to gold-standard techniques.

title: Cross-cancer knowledge transfer for lymph node metastasis prediction: Applicability of an axillary lymph node-based deep learning model
authors: Kang, J., Kang, J. W., Kwon, L. M., Cho, B.-J., Kim, B. J.
abstract: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920-0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875-0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672-0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment.

title: A Bias Correction Method for Substructure Estimation with Small Reference Sample Sizes
authors: Tifour, S., Price, A., Marker, K., Hendricks, A.
abstract: Reference data are important for accurate estimation of population substructure, yet sufficiently large reference samples are often unavailable for some populations. This limitation is especially important for methods that estimate population substructure from genetic summary data using reference allele frequencies derived from reference samples, such as Summix2. Here, we systematically evaluated how reference sample size for five continental reference groups [African (AFR), East Asian (EAS), European (EUR), Indigenous American (IAM), and South Asian (SAS)] affects Summix2 substructure estimates in simulated Latino-like, African American-like, and Peruvian-like populations, as well as real African American genetic data. We show that small reference sample sizes introduce systematic bias in substructure proportion estimates. We identified a sample size threshold of 150 individuals per reference group for accurate estimates with a mean estimation error below 0.05. We also developed two bias corrections: a simple inverse sample size correction and a flexible power-law correction. The power-law correction provided the greatest reduction in mean estimation error when all reference groups had small reference sample sizes, whereas the simple inverse sample size correction performed better when a single reference group had a small reference sample size. These findings provide practical guidance and bias adjustments for reliable population substructure estimation from genetic summary data, particularly when reference populations have small sample sizes.

title: Error-Controlled Discovery of Protein Interactions via Conformal Calibration
authors: Yang, Y., Li, D., Ding, D., Shi, L., Zhou, H., Lu, Y. Y.
abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are powerful predictors of protein interactions, but strong benchmark performance does not ensure reliable discoveries. We introduce PPI-Caliper, a model-agnostic framework that adapts conformal calibration to select interactions at user-specified false discovery rate (FDR) levels using held-out labels without retraining the predictor. Across five species, two PLM-based predictors, and two human training-data versions for each predictor, PPI-Caliper keeps empirical FDR at or below the target level under in-distribution calibration. Under distribution shift, transferred thresholds tend to become conservative when predictive performance improves, but can fail to control FDR when performance deteriorates. PPI-Caliper connects pre-trained interaction scores to explicit error targets and demonstrates why reliable biological discovery requires evaluating calibration alongside predictive accuracy.

title: Unified cell segmentation for spatial transcriptomics via transcript reassignment
authors: Zhang, J., Cheng, X., Wang, J., Chen, W., Chen, H.
abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression as individually localized molecules on imaging-based platforms or as counts in subcellular bins on sequencing-based platforms, and both must be assigned to cells before cell-level analysis. Existing segmentation methods focus on delineating cell boundaries, yet transcripts that diffuse beyond their cell of origin, fall where cells overlap, or lie in bins that cells only partially cover are still misassigned. Here we present Tracel, a two-stage optimal transport framework that assigns spatial observations to cells under the guidance of a matched single-cell RNA-sequencing reference. Tracel first aligns reference cells to spatial cells to estimate the expected expression profile at each cell location, and then maps transcripts to cells against these profiles. The same formulation assigns transcripts from imaging-based platforms (e.g., Xenium, CosMx) and bin counts from sequencing-based platforms (e.g., Visium HD). Across five human datasets spanning three platforms and three tissues, Tracel improves the separation of cell types over existing methods, assigning cell-type markers to their correct cells, retaining more cell-intrinsic transcripts and reducing contamination from neighboring cells.
