Tracel also preserves variation within cell types, yielding more accurate differential expression across spatial locations, and its expression profiles attribute ligand-receptor interactions to the correct cell-type pairs in cell-cell communication analysis. Tracel can enter the segmentation workflow at different stages, either refining an existing segmentation or segmenting cells starting from nucleus segmentation.

title: brisc: a multithreaded CPU toolkit for single-cell analysis
authors: Arbabi, K., Luquez, T., Jeeson, J., Lam, M., Heydari, H., Bader, G. D., Menon, V., Wainberg, M.
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing datasets have grown from tens of thousands of cells to tens of millions. At this scale, standard toolkits like Scanpy and Seurat need hours per analysis, hindering iterative exploration. We present brisc, the first end-to-end multithreaded CPU toolkit for single-cell analysis, spanning dimensionality reduction, integration, label transfer, clustering, embedding, differential expression and plotting. Unlike GPU-based counterparts, brisc strictly guarantees reproducibility: identical results between runs, regardless of thread count. Algorithmic innovations include a blocked inverted-file-index-based nearest-neighbors algorithm that makes 81-98% fewer errors than Scanpy and Seurat. On a 192-CPU node, brisc ran a standard workflow on 10 million cells in 3 minutes, 116x faster than Scanpy at under half its peak memory usage and 236x faster than Seurat with BPCells. On 96 CPUs, it matched the speed of rapids-singlecell on four H100 GPUs. brisc enables near-real-time, reproducible analysis of tens of millions of cells without specialized hardware.

title: CARTnet: Template-guided B-cell Epitope Prediction with Contact-aware Attention
authors: Roy, R. S., Abeer, A. N. M. N., Yoon, B.-J., Qian, X.
abstract: B-cell epitope prediction remains challenging due to the limited availability of experimentally characterized data and the incomplete understanding of antibody-antigen recognition. Here, we present CARTnet, a novel contact-aware deep learning framework that integrates multimodal features and template-derived epitope information. CARTnet demonstrated superior performance when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods across most evaluation metrics on both the internal and external test datasets. In particular, CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.243 on the internal test set, compared with 0.220 for DiscoTope-3, 0.140 for BepiPred-2, and 0.198 for BepiPred-3. This improvement was also observed on the external test set, where CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.267, compared with 0.192, 0.111, and 0.215 for DiscoTope-3, BepiPred-2, and BepiPred-3, respectively, supporting its generalizability. CARTnet also supports template-guided prediction, in which limited prior epitope information can improve the identification of additional epitope residues; a single template residue increased the AUPRC of the template-based variant from 0.225 to 0.403 on the internal test set. Furthermore, we demonstrated that epitope information from closely related viruses can be transferred across the genus Alphavirus to improve epitope prediction accuracy. These results establish CARTnet as an accurate framework for both de novo and template-guided B-cell epitope prediction.

title: Representation-aware calibration enables statistically reliable protein structure search
authors: Shi, L., Zhou, H., Yang, Y., Lu, Y.
abstract: Searching large databases of predicted protein structures can reveal remote homologs, but reliable discovery requires accurate significance estimates. We show that native E-values reported by protein structure search tools such as Foldseek and Reseek can be unreliable, leading to false discoveries or missed homologs. To address this problem, we introduce Struct-Caliper, which provides reliable query-specific p-values for protein structure search. The method uses representation-aware query randomization to generate background queries and compares observed alignment scores with the highest scores from randomized searches of the same database. In simulations, SG p-values generally kept reported false positive at or below the chosen cutoff under the evaluated randomization procedures. In searches of 15,177 ASTRAL40 structures, SG p-values increased Foldseek homolog recovery by 18.2% with slightly fewer false discoveries compared with native E-values at a cutoff of 0.01. For Reseek, false discoveries even decreased by 99.5%. Across 73 queries searched against more than two million AlphaFoldDB structures, SG p-values increased the mean recovery of DALI-supported matches by 23.5% at the same cutoff. These results show that Struct-Caliper can improve the reliability of structure searches and help prioritize discoveries for further biological analysis.

title: Comparative Transcriptomic Analysis of Gene Expression Patterns in Neutrophils from Rheumatoid Arthritis and COVID-19
abstract: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder characterised by chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation, and neutrophils play a key role in its progression. COVID-19 also involves neutrophil hyperactivation that contributes to severe immune responses. Emerging evidence links COVID-19 to increased incidence or exacerbation of RA, potentially through overlapping immune mechanisms. Objective: To compare neutrophil transcriptomic profiles in RA and COVID-19 and identify shared immune pathways and disease-specific features. Methods: Publicly available neutrophil RNA-seq count data from the Gene Expression Omnibus were analysed: RA versus healthy controls (GSE116899) and COVID-19 versus healthy controls (GSE212041). A second COVID-19 comparison (severe versus convalescent) was assembled from GSE272381 and GSE227116. Differential expression was analysed with DESeq2, pathway enrichment with fgsea (Hallmark gene sets) and topGO (Gene Ontology biological process and molecular function). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were compared between diseases by direction of change. Results: In RA neutrophils, 11,355 DEGs were identified, of which 90 had an absolute log2 fold change of at least 2 with p<0.05 (70 upregulated, 20 downregulated). Twenty-four Hallmark gene sets were positively enriched at adjusted p<0.05, led by interferon alpha and interferon gamma responses, and Gene Ontology analysis highlighted type I interferon, antiviral and double-stranded RNA terms. In COVID-19 neutrophils, 420 DEGs were identified (37 upregulated, 383 downregulated), and no Hallmark gene set reached adjusted p<0.05. Of the 90 RA DEGs, 46 changed in the same direction in COVID-19 without reaching significance, and 27 changed significantly in the opposite direction, including CAMK1G, SIGLEC1, OAS1 and OAS3. In the second COVID-19 comparison, several of these genes, including OAS1, OAS3 and SIGLEC1, changed in the same direction as in RA. Conclusions: RA neutrophils show a transcriptional programme enriched for interferon and antiviral-response pathways. Part of the RA signature is shared with COVID-19 neutrophils, while a subset of genes diverges, and this divergence depended on the COVID-19 comparison used. These findings are hypothesis-generating and provide candidate genes for experimental validation.

title: Long read sequencing reveals changes in measured isoform structure and abundance due to RNA processing
abstract: Oxford Nanopore Technology enables direct RNA sequencing without reverse transcription (RT) and cDNA sequencing without PCR amplification, allowing investigation of how RNA preparation protocols bias sequencing data. PCR amplification is known to introduce biases related to expression levels, transcript lengths, and GC content. However, biases introduced by RT have been described more recently and their quantification remains more elusive. Using seven cell line datasets from SG-NEx, we compared nanopore sequencing of direct RNA, direct cDNA, and PCR-amplified cDNA. We identified hundreds of differentially expressed genes and isoforms between protocols, indicating significant changes in observed expression. Differentially expressed isoforms displayed expected amplification biases, and further we observed decreased PCR counts associated with higher m6A methylation levels on native RNA. We also found differential transcript usage in hundreds of genes across cell lines, showing substantial changes in measured isoform proportions between protocols. Analysis of structural differences between isoforms that switch dominance revealed that while some events involve simple RNA fragmentation, most involve complex structural differences including novel junctions (e.g. exon skipping, intron retention). Compared to non-DTU genes, inserted introns (exitrons) were significantly more common after RT and amplification. Furthermore, visualisation of raw coverage data proved crucial for qualitative validation of experimental findings.

title: CloneVI: A deep generative model for deciphering the relationships between cell state and mitochondrial genotype
authors: Hibi, T., Kojima, Y., Hayashi, S., Hisose, H., Mizukoshi, C., Shimamura, T.
abstract: Cellular diversity arises from both genetic lineages and non-genetic regulation of cell states, and knowing which cell states are tied to lineages is central to understanding how clones shape disease. Single-cell multi-omics technologies measure mitochondrial DNA mutations together with gene expression or chromatin accessibility in the same cells, but clones are usually inferred from mutations alone, making such clones difficult to identify. We developed CloneVI, a deep generative model that infers clonal structure from a latent cell state derived from gene expression or chromatin accessibility. It estimates the clonal probability of each cell from this cell state, together with the allele frequency of each clone by reconstructing the observed mutation counts. In simulated data, CloneVI recovered the ground-truth clonal structure in both single-clone and mixed-clone cell populations. In clonal hematopoiesis single-cell RNA-seq data with enriched mitochondrial transcripts, the inferred clones were associated with specific mitochondrial DNA mutations, and some of them showed high expression of a T-cell receptor variable-region gene. In chronic lymphocytic leukemia mitochondrial single-cell ATAC-seq data, CloneVI separated populations with different heteroplasmy levels and identified increased PAX9 accessibility. In a multi-donor ovarian tumor cohort, CloneVI captured mutant-cell populations enriched in particular cell states, and a differential test weighted by the clonal probability revealed the transcription factor activity of the cell state in which the mutant cells concentrated. CloneVI thus identifies populations defined by mitochondrial DNA mutations and associated with cell states in single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data. CloneVI is available at https://github.com/TaichiHIBI/cloneVI.

title: gcat, its_a_scam: modular tools for single cell data processing and per-cellquality control
authors: Prabakar, R. K., Meyer, H. V.
abstract: Motivation: The era of designing bioinformatic pipelines using open source tools is giving way to monolithic, and often proprietary, tools designed for end-to-end analysis, especially in the context of single cell data. While these tools are convenient for going from sequencing data to an almost complete data analysis "in a few clicks", they can strongly limit data use beyond standard analyses Results: We developed Gene and Chromosome Analysis Toolkit (gcat) and It's a scam To Sell Another Single Cell Analysis Method (its_a_scam) for modular processing and quality control of single cell genomic data, freeing users from their reliance on proprietary tools. gcat is a C++ library for parsing genomic data and working with it over genomic coordinates. its_a_scam is built on top of gcat and provides a suite of tools for a wide range of single cell data processing and quality control. its_a_scam can be used in conjunction with commonly used open source tools for scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq count matrix generation, and for performing per-cell quality control directly from alignment files. These alignment-level per-cell metrics can be used for quality control of each cell or to understand celltype differences post-clustering or post-annotation. Using a peripheral blood mononuclear cell Multiome dataset, we show that the count matrices generated with the aid of its_a_scam are highly concordant with those generated by proprietary pipelines. The alignment metrics further demonstrate celltype differences in aligned genomic regions, metagene profiles, and genebody coverage. The modular nature of its_a_scam allows users to integrate it into their existing pipelines, while also enabling analysis beyond current pipelines. Availability: gcat (distributed as gcatlib) and its_a_scam are open source and available at https://github.com/rishvanth-kp/gcatlib and https://github.com/rishvanth-kp/its_a_scam. Detailed documentation is available at https://gcatlib.readthedocs.io/ and https://its-a-scam.readthedocs.io.

title: Evaluating the Identifiability of Temporal Delay and Response Attenuation in Endometrial Decidualization
authors: Krikun, E., Fahmy, W., Alkhateeb, A.
abstract: Endometriosis is associated with impaired endometrial decidualization, yet conventional differential expres-sion analyses cannot readily distinguish delayed transcriptional activation from reduced response amplitude.These mechanisms may produce similar expression differences at individual time points while implying distinct biological interpretations. Establishing when they can be distinguished is therefore a computational identifiability problem.We implement an identifiability-aware analysis of temporal displacement and amplitude attenuation in longitudinal transcriptomic responses. The approach combines reference trajectories, constrained amplitude-only and amplitude-plus-delay models, analytical examples of observational equivalence, and simulation-based assessments of mechanism distinguishability. Held-out time-point evaluation and culture-level sensitivity analyses examine the stability of model-dependent conclusions.In GSE246591, a candidate-delay-dependent dynamic-range filter excluded 30.9 - 38.3% of initially dynamic features under a hypothetical 24-hour shift across four endometrial stromal cultures. A two-component diagnostic separating retained dynamic range from affine shape similarity revealed that small projection residuals can arise from either loss of observable dynamics or similarity of response shapes. These findings demonstrate why a single separation statistic may be insufficient for interpreting temporal identifiability.Complementary independent in vivo analyses provided biological context. In GSE51981, an endometrial progesterone-response-associated transcriptional score was reduced in endometriosis samples (phase-model estimate 0.155, 95% CI 0.222 to 0.088). GSE6364 showed a directionally consistent but statistically inconclusive difference (0.033, 95% CI 0.068 to 0.002). Neither observation independently establishes a temporal delay.Together, these results support selection-aware evaluation of temporal transcriptomic responses, distin-guishing structural ambiguity and loss of dynamic signal from evidence of a biological timing change.

title: Autonomous generalizability auditing of scientific foundation models
authors: Ektefaie, Y., Jain, S., Sabeti, P.
abstract: Determining where scientific foundation models generalize beyond their development data is essential for reliable use, but aggregate benchmarks obscure performance limits and rigorous audits are difficult to conduct routinely. Here, we introduce AutoSPECTRA, a coding-agent protocol for systematic generalizability auditing. To inform its design, we reviewed 38 studies across five biological domains and evaluated coding agents, which generated hypotheses and empirical analyses but applied inconsistent standards for judging evidence. We then structured AutoSPECTRA around measurable generalization axes, prespecified analyses, controlled comparisons and independent confirmation. Across four biological foundation models, audits linked performance to protein sequence composition and relatedness to pretraining data (ESMFold2), representation of perturbations in training (STATE), effective spatial resolution (CONCH), and residue-level genomic, evolutionary and structural context (AlphaMissense). Agents also evaluated alternative explanations and rejected unsupported hypotheses. AutoSPECTRA provides a systematic approach to discovering and testing the limits of scientific foundation models.

title: A Distinct Mode of Chromosome-End Genome Instability Revealed by Circulome Characterization and Analyses
authors: Roy, G., Lei, Z., McCoy, M., Al Sardar, A., Shay, J., Scacheri, P., Lotan, Y., Levene, S. D., Fire, A., Shoura, M.
abstract: Genome instability is a central hallmark of cancer and it is characterized largely from sequence: mutation, copy-number change and rearrangement scored against a linear reference. The genome has additional degrees of freedom, such as the physical form (topology) of the DNA itself. A specific mode of localized genome dynamics changes both dimensions (sequence and topology) at once: defined chromosomal regions are also represented as extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA). The biogenesis of eccDNA is a feature of many cancers, supplying the tumor with genetic elements that can participate in phenotypic selection, and supplying the observer with a window into the genomic instability landscape. Genome-wide maps of where these circles arise have not been available at scale or at high resolution. Building such maps requires physical selection of circular species, because most sequenced reads from unselected DNA derive from unrearranged sequence, conflating the signal from dynamic rearrangements with that from bulk chromosomal DNA. Here we combine biophysical and biochemical isolation of circular DNA with next-generation sequencing, applying it to a panel of cancer cell lines and to patient tumors, with non-cancerous cells and adjacent normal tissues as controls. The resulting genome-wide maps of the circular-element repertoire, the Circulome, reveal a consistent and previously unreported enrichment of these elements at particular chromosome ends. The circles map to regions extending well past the telomeres, reaching varying distances up to tens of megabases inward. This activity is accompanied by corroborating rearrangements within the linear genome, consistent with regions of chromosomal instability. Together these features define a spatially localized mode of instability in cancer, which we term Erosion at Distal Genomic Ends (EDGE). We formulate a classification problem to discriminate bladder tumor from matched normal tissue, finding that the EDGE signal outperforms the mean of all interior chromosomal regions, for each chromosome. These findings define a distinct spatial signature of cancer chromosome instability detectable through Circulome analysis, and connect early models of region-specific instability to the human cancer genome.

title: Neural RNA splicing models rely on reading frame information unavailable to the splicing machinery
authors: Gupta, K., Wang, B., Sharp, P. A., Burge, C. B., Solar-Lezama, A.
abstract: Deep neural networks can accurately predict RNA splice sites from genomic sequence, but whether they do so by simulating the natural splicing process is unclear. We evaluate this question by examining mutations that should not have a strong effect on splicing, but are correlated with it in the human genome. We focus specifically on mutations that affect frame alignment because this is known to be relevant to machinery that operates spatially and temporally separately from the splicing machinery. We find that predictions made by commonly-used neural tools are impacted far more by deletions or mutations that alter translational reading frame, producing in-frame stop codons, than by those that preserve reading frame. This dependence on reading frame causes these models to systematically miss many poison exons, a clinically relevant category of exons where reading frame is disrupted. This dependence is much weaker in "grey-box" models that build in splicing-specific structure. Our results imply that widely-used black-box models of splicing rely on information that is not accessible to the RNA splicing machinery. Code is available at https://github.com/kavigupta/frame-alignment-checks.

title: Where single-cell foundation models help: a benchmark of annotation, perturbation and regulatory inference against simple baselines
abstract: Single-cell foundation models (FMs) are proposed as general tools for cell-type annotation, in silico perturbation and gene-regulatory-network (GRN) inference. To identify where they add value, we benchmarked five FMs (scGPT, Geneformer V1 and V2, Nicheformer, scFoundation), CellOracle, supervised perturbation models including STATE, and task-matched simple baselines on the same data, from K562 Perturb-seq screens and primary cells to healthy-donor and isogenic leukodystrophy brain organoids, a public organoid CRISPR screen and lung cancer biopsies. FMs were most useful when labels had to be transferred across species: from human to mouse lung, Nicheformer reached 0.98 accuracy and Geneformer V2 and scFoundation about 0.90, against 0.68 for the best baseline. Zero-shot in silico perturbations captured the direction of real responses in K562, with up to 75% of perturbations shifted in the expected direction (scFoundation, p < 1e-8), and Geneformer V2 networks recovered patient-level tumour differential expression better than co-expression (fold enrichment 2.9 versus 2.0). Within a species, FM embeddings annotated cells as accurately as principal components. In organoids, predicted knockout effects were largely explained by where the target is expressed, and an expression-matched control test isolated the gene-specific part, 12 to 35% of the effects. Isogenic Canavan and Krabbe organoids and 4H patient organoids, with one library per line and time point, did not yet separate methods from differences between clones and donors, which defines the replication needed for future validation. Fine-tuning changed classification accuracy but not knockout rankings. We release the benchmark, baselines, pipeline checks and the isogenic reference task as the fmaudit package, so that new models can be evaluated on the tasks where FMs already help.

title: NORMA 3.0: aesthetic and group-aware visualization and analysis of annotated biological networks
authors: Baltoumas, F., Karatzas, E., Koutrouli, M., Galaras, A., Aplakidou, E., Chasapi, I. N., Chasapi, M. N., Lazanas, P., Lamari, E., Przulj, N., Georgakopoulos-Soares, I., Pavlopoulos, G. A.
abstract: Summary: Interpreting a biological network often rests on the relationship between its connectivity and the functional groups annotated on it, such as pathways, complexes, or enriched terms. For example, whether a group forms a cohesive module, how groups overlap, and which proteins connect them. These relationships are often hard to assess visually when groups are numerous or overlap, and most tools represent membership only by node color. NORMA 3.0 is a complete client-side rewrite of its predecessors, delineating and laying out groups with convex hulls, bubble sets, or fog clouds. Multi-group nodes are rendered as pies and directed, and parallel edges retain their evidence channels. Eighteen 2D and nine 3D layouts are scored by silhouette width, outline intrusion and overlap, and benchmarked for group separation and run time. The implementation also includes edge bundling, network importers for six databases, 21 topological measures, group-level and enrichment statistics, comparison of up to ten networks, export of high-resolution images, and an Application Programming Interface. Availability and implementation: NORMA 3.0 is freely available at https://normaviz.org. The source code is available at https://github.com/PavlopoulosLab/NORMA.

title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
authors: Narayan, V., Merritt, B., Choudhery, S., Jimenez, D., Ta, S., Berman, D. S., Ratcliff, J., Gallagher, M. E.
abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

title: Missing by design: why genomic metadata must be captured at submission, not recovered from the literature
authors: Lee, S., Lodha, D., Alvarez-Jarreta, J.
abstract: Plant and metazoan genome assemblies are being deposited in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC) archives at an accelerating rate, but the biological context needed to interpret them, such as ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure, is often missing from the record: these attributes are optional in most submission checklists and, when supplied, are entered as free text. We describe the gap in three layers. Ploidy varies within a species and cannot be inferred from taxonomy; chromosome-naming conventions differ between assemblies of the same crop; and that inconsistency is concentrated in species named by subgenome and is not associated with the size of the research community, which points to the lack of a shared convention. As a case study, we built a pipeline that recovers these attributes from the publications linked to an assembly. On a benchmark of 82 assemblies, its current version reported one wrong ploidy, and across 1,059 plant assemblies an earlier, less strict version found the ploidy in a publication for about half; for nearly a third, it found a publication but no statement of ploidy in it. Recovery from the literature can annotate assemblies already deposited but cannot stop new ones from arriving incomplete. We therefore propose that ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure be captured at submission as mandatory, controlled-vocabulary attributes, building on existing INSDC and Genomic Standards Consortium checklists.

title: Marker-specific pixel attribution for single-cell protein quantification with PixAQ
authors: Zha, Y., Liang, C., Lin, Y., Li, G., Zhang, C., Huang, Z., Wang, Z., Zhang, L., Tong, M., Jiang, W., Xiao, X., Yu, R.
abstract: Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) typically quantifies all markers within the same cell mask, although their signals have distinct spatial distributions. This quantification method may omit relevant signals or include signals from neighboring cells. We present PixAQ, which improves single-cell protein quantification in IMC through marker-specific probabilistic pixel attribution. PixAQ combines spatial proximity with anchor-group intensity models to assign pixel-marker observations among neighboring cells and an explicit residual component. Original intensities are averaged over marker-specific supports. Across three cohorts (680 regions), comparisons in 366 patients showed improved agreement with predefined population-marker relationships, with cohort-median patient-paired gains of 1.99 to 4.83 percentage points in expected-marker share over shared-mask quantification. Ablation analyses showed that both spatial and intensity evidence contributed to these gains. Conventional and high-resolution IMC images linked supports to visible local and intracellular signal structures. PixAQ improves single-cell protein quantification by determining which local signals contribute to each marker measurement without changing cell segmentation.

title: Optimiser Repairs for Living-Cell Self-Driving Laboratories: Performance and Redundancy under Experimental Constraints
authors: Brimo, n., Zhang, H., Serdaroglu, D. C.
abstract: Living-cell self-driving laboratories must optimise experiments despite delayed readouts, changing responses and limited sample availability. In simulations, we evaluate when optimiser repairs improve closed-loop performance and when platform constraints make them redundant, separating consumption of a sample from permanent loss of the ability to repeat its condition. We prove that exclusions and confirmation requests produce exactly the baseline trajectory when they act only on conditions already forbidden by the platform, share the same posterior and selection procedure, and release infeasible requested slots. This result covers the evaluated pending-exclusion, previous-batch and confirmation rules under permanent condition retirement; it does not cover arbitrary selection interventions. We then conduct 33,900 simulated policy runs with 200-300 paired campaign seeds per setting. A public PBMC reference supports characterisation of the target-label readout, while condition-response landscapes remain synthetic. Across 27 landscape, assay-size and kernel settings, previous-batch exclusion changes final normalised performance by -0.004 to +0.283, with positive differences surviving Holm adjustment in 13 settings. Effects are small on the rugged landscape. Permanent retirement can be harmful under noisy rugged responses. All three subsumed interventions reproduce every saved baseline event on 200 of 200 paired seeds. These results establish the importance of explicit availability constraints and evaluation across experimental regimes when assessing optimiser repairs.

title: Sourmash accurately profiles strains from long-read metagenomes preserving gene content
authors: Angevin, L., Lipovac, J., Peterlongo, P., Roux, E., Vicedomini, R.
abstract: Background. Metagenomic strain-level profiling remains challenging because closely related bacterial strains often share more than 99% average nucleotide identity (ANI). However, they can differ substantially in gene content and functional potential. Sourmash uses k-mer sketches with FracMinHash to compare sequencing reads against reference databases, which makes it an interesting approach for strain-level profiling. Because it compares sketches rather than full alignments, it enables fast searches against large reference databases. However, its ability to recover biologically relevant strains and preserve community gene content has not been specifically assessed. Here, we evaluated the performance of sourmash for strain-level identification abundance, functional gene content recovery, and abundance estimations using five mock communities of increasing complexity with known composition. Results. We first assessed whether nucleotide similarity reflects functional similarity between strains. Gene content similarity was generally consistent with ANI but revealed important divergences between closely related strains. For example, Escherichia coli strains sharing more than 98% ANI showed gene content similarities ranging from 20% to 57%, highlighting that nucleotide similarity alone is insufficient to assess functional proximity and consequently the accuracy of strain identification. Above sufficient genome coverage, sourmash identified strains either exactly or with closely related strains sharing highly conserved gene content. These closely related strains provided a biologically relevant representation of the expected functional potential of the mock communities. Gene content recovery was highly accurate, with F1 scores ranging from 0.942 to 0.998 across the five mock communities. Genome abundances estimated against sourmash-identified genomes closely matched the expected community composition: Pearson correlation coefficients ranged from 0.823 to 1 at strain level and from 0.978 to 1 at species level. Conclusions. Our results show that sourmash provides a biologically relevant approach for strain-level characterisation in microbial ecosystems. Even when the exact strain could not be identified, closely related strains retained most of the expected gene content and abundance estimations were accurate, supporting the use of sourmash for downstream functional profiling or metabolic network reconstruction.

title: SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming): a simulation-informed Nextflow pipeline for cross-study harmonisation of 16S rRNA metabarcoding datasets
authors: Terrey, D., Huber, P., Pereira, E., Pelayo, M. C., Ferguson, R. M. W., Dumbrell, A. J., Sweet, M., Bani, A., Metz, S.
abstract: Global syntheses of 16S rRNA metabarcoding data rely on combining datasets, yet amplicon sequence variants generated with different primer pairs can rarely be compared directly. Existing approaches correct batch effects statistically or aggregate taxonomically; none first establishes whether the sequences are positionally comparable. We present SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming), a Nextflow pipeline that maps every studys variants onto a 16S rRNA full-length reference alignment, determines the largest window shared across studies, and tests by simulation whether trimming to that window degrades community structure before any data are merged. Applied to thirteen marine studies sequenced with three primer sets, twelve converged on a consensus window with a median trimmed read length of 249 bp (9,582 alignment columns). Degradation tests across twelve studies and six taxonomic ranks (72 study-rank combinations) returned 31 passes, 38 cautions and three confirmed failures. Eleven studies (682 samples after filtering) were harmonised (trimmed to the window and merged), collapsing 20,891 primer-specific variants into 12,667 MetaASVs, trimmed sequences deduplicated across studies. Harmonisation preserved community structure at family level (Mantel r = 1.00; Procrustes m{superscript 2} < 0.001) without adding between-study variance (|{Delta}R{superscript 2}| < 0.001). Alpha diversity, including observed richness, was recovered across all levels (intraclass correlations 0.93-1.00), whereas sequence-level congruence was moderate (Procrustes m{superscript 2} = 0.52), as expected where between-study similarity at sequence level exists only after harmonisation. The harmonised output supports synthesis from aggregated ranks down to exact sequences. By establishing positional comparability before merging, SeCAT opens the archive of primer-fragmented 16S rRNA surveys to sequence-level synthesis.

title: Uncovering cross-signal interactions in single-cell and spatial omics
authors: Sasson, J., Niasoff, B., Karin, J., Ezraty, Y., Nitzan, M.
abstract: Individual cells simultaneously encode multiple biological signals in their gene expression profiles, including spatial position, circadian phase, and disease state. These signals can be entangled in complex ways, including circadian patterns that vary along disease progression and cell cycle dynamics that shift along developmental trajectories. While methods to disentangle such signals have been recently developed, characterizing the interaction itself between multicellular signals along with its effects on tissue function, localizing cellular subpopulations which exhibit signal interactions, and identifying potential candidate genes which drive such interactions, all remain major challenges. We present CRISP which characterizes signal interactions in single-cell gene expression data based on the correspondence between the multiple, probabilistic signal-specific projections of the data. Across simulations with tunable couplings and four single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets, CRISP recovers diverse biological signal interactions and localizes them to informative cellular subpopulations and groups of associated genes; CRISP distinguishes healthy from fibrotic liver samples and localizes the loss of zonation-position coupling to individual fibrotic hepatocytes, resolves the asymmetric coupling of TGF-{beta} response, EMT, and cell-cycle phase to specific cell subpopulations, and flags transcriptionally delayed hepatocytes in Plasmodium liver infection. Beyond quantifying and localizing signal interactions, CRISP can refine existing labels, uncover continuous cellular transitions and reveal condition-associated genes.

title: KDRD: assessing discovery replicability based on summary association statistics from a single study
authors: Jiao, Z., Zhang, Y., Kang, J., Ma, L., Yang, Y., Zhao, W., Feng, J., Lai, Y.
abstract: Replicability is essential for reliable discoveries in large-scale association studies. However, conventional replicability assessments typically require independent datasets or repeated data splitting, which may be constrained by data availability, computational burden and reduced sample sizes. Here, we developed Kernel Density-based Replicability of Discovery (KDRD), a statistical framework for estimating the expected replicability of statistically significant associations using summary statistics from a single study. Combining Gaussian kernel representations of observed association statistics with a theoretical null component, KDRD estimates replicability between independent studies under comparable conditions and enables sample size calculations beyond those currently available. In random subsampling simulations involving proteomics-based association analyses of 45 brain-related traits in the UK Biobank, KDRD showed a close agreement with the Dice Similarity Coefficients (DSCs). When KDRD was applied to the full available data,33 of the 45 traits showed at least moderate replicability, including 19 with high replicability. In matched-sample comparisons, proteomic associations showed higher KDRD estimates than pQTL associations across all 45 traits, whereas metabolomic associations showed higher estimates than proteomic associations for 33 traits. Higher protein missingness, proportions below the limit of detection, proportions of low-abundance proteins and assay variability were associated with lower KDRD estimates. KDRD-based sample size calculations suggested that approximately 200,000 and 500,000 participants would be needed for all 45 traits to achieve moderate and high replicability, respectively. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that KDRD provides a practical framework for quantitative replicability assessment and sample size calculations.

title: Comparative molecular analysis of histopathologic subtypes reveals shared epithelial remodeling yet distinct fibroblast programs in scleroderma lung disease
authors: Yang, M. M., Auyeung, V. C., Kim, S. M. C., Flynn, E., Naikawadi, R. P., Bazarov, A. V., Lea, A., Deiter, F., Neely, J., Kukreja, J., Matthay, M. A., Jones, K. D., Greenland, J. R., Sirota, M., Wolters, P. J.
abstract: Rationale: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) drives mortality in systemic sclerosis (SSc), with a subset developing progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) resembling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Despite recognition of two distinct histopathologic patterns, the cellular basis of nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) and usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) remains poorly understood. Objectives: To define shared and distinct cellular and molecular features of SSc-NSIP and SSc-UIP compared to IPF. Methods: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were performed on explanted lungs from patients with SSc-NSIP (n=6), SSc-UIP (n=6), or IPF (n=6), and control donors (n=12) with immunohistochemistry and western blot validation. Main Results: Across 120,254 nuclei from 35 cell types, there was striking similarity across fibrotic subgroups in epithelial, endothelial, and immune compartments, including alveolar type 1 cell loss, pathologic alveolar type 2 (AT2) gene expression, and expansion of COL15A1 endothelial cells and profibrotic macrophages. Diseased AT2s showed activation of the p53/DNA damage pathway. Aberrant basaloid (AB) cells were present in both SSc-ILD subtypes and transcriptionally similar to IPF ABs. They consistently neighbored profibrotic CTHRC1 fibroblasts, even in SSc-NSIP, despite lacking fibroblast foci. Fibroblast heterogeneity differentiated the histopathologic subtypes. Inflammatory fibroblasts were enriched in SSc-NSIP and CTHRC1 fibroblasts in UIP. AB-to-pathologic fibroblast crosstalk was defined by profibrotic signaling, with amplified TGF-{beta} signaling in UIP. Conclusions: Convergent epithelial remodeling is a hallmark of PPF in SSc-ILD and IPF. Fibroblast heterogeneity characterized by altered TGF-beta signaling distinguishes SSc-NSIP from SSc-UIP and IPF. Accelerated aging, DNA damage, and p53-dependent senescence pathways may represent shared drivers of PPF.

title: Leveraging short and long-read sequencing to comprehensively characterize alternatively polyadenylated and alternatively spliced transcripts
authors: Gupta, M., Pasipamire, L., Peart, N., Li, J., Lockett, D., Todd, I., Rajakumar, H., Masamha, C. P.
abstract: Pre-mRNA processing through alternative splicing and alternative polyadenylation generates diverse transcripts from the same gene. Alternative splicing involves use of different exons and specific 3'Untranslated regions (3'UTRs). When limited to the same terminal exon, 3'end formation through alternative polyadenylation gives rise to transcripts containing 3'UTRs of different sizes which affect their subcellular localization, stability, and translatability. The full repertoire of transcripts arising from alternative pre-mRNA processing under different biological and disease states remains unknown. Using the blood cancer, mantle cell lymphoma's (MCL) as our experimental model we found that two genes, SOX11 and ATM, that contribute to the disease pathology, express transcripts that have short 3'UTRs. Apart from select transcripts, our analysis of short-read sequencing data did not uncover widespread global shortening of 3'UTRs in MCL. However, we discovered that both the canonical and non-canonical polyadenylation signals (PASs), were used for 3'end formation. We experimentally verified the PASs used by specific transcripts. Combining short-read and long-read sequencing data enabled us to characterize, classify and identify alternatively splicing in MCL. We identified splice variants for several genes including PTEN, EZH2 and validated the expression of GLS1 at the protein level and by using GLS1 inhibitors. Collectively, our approach provide insights into how to identify alternatively spliced and alternatively polyadenylated transcripts.

title: TensorPLS: an R package for exploring molecular and temporal patterns in longitudinal omics data using PLS-DA
authors: Giordano, A., Conesa, A., Balzano Nogueira, L.
abstract: Longitudinal omics datasets combine high-dimensional repeated measurements with missing observations, complicating supervised modelling and temporal interpretation. We present TensorPLS, an R package integrating missing-data handling, matrix-based partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), structured variable importance, subject-level nested cross-validation and downstream functional enrichment. Data are represented as subjects x features x time tensors. Missing values are handled by Tucker3 reconstruction or feature-time mean imputation, after which tensors are unfolded along the subject mode for PLS-DA. Cumulative variable importance in projection (VIP) scores are mapped to feature-time coordinates and summarised across time and cumulative PLS models. During nested cross-validation, imputation, component tuning, VIP-based feature selection and refitting are performed within training partitions. Full-cohort models are fitted separately for descriptive interpretation. We evaluated TensorPLS on two public longitudinal transcriptomic datasets using five-by-five nested cross-validation. In GSE68310 (109 subjects), Tucker3 reconstruction yielded Q2Y = 0.670, AUROC 0.971 and balanced accuracy 0.931. In GSE182616 (66 subjects), feature-time mean imputation yielded Q2Y = 0.294, AUROC 0.827 and balanced accuracy 0.756. Predictive metrics were calculated from pooled outer held-out predictions. TensorPLS supports predictive assessment, functional enrichment of selected genes and temporal interpretation of model-assigned feature importance.

title: Unprecedented urban freshwater microviral survey highlights shift from sewage to river water communities
authors: Langlais, A., Dumont, C., Mougin, J., Guerin-Rechdaoui, S., Roose-Amsaleg, C., Enault, F., Quaiser, A.
abstract: Microviruses are abundant yet still poorly resolved components of virosphere, particularly across urban freshwater continua. Here, we investigated complete microvirus genomes recovered from sewage water (SW), treated wastewater (TW), and river water (RW) along an urban SW TW RW continuum, providing an extensive genomic dataset of 18,449 complete genomes grouped into 825 genera. This catalog enabled a high-resolution assessment of microvirus diversity, taxonomy, and ecological distribution across anthropized aquatic compartments. All currently described microvirus orders were detected, with Gokushovirales dominating the dataset and Betagokushoviridae emerging as the most prevalent family in TW and RW samples. In contrast, Alpavirales were enriched in SW but strongly depleted after treatment, consistent with their association with gut-related bacterial hosts. Alpha- and beta-diversity analyses showed that water type was the main driver of microvirus community structure, whereas seasonal effects were weak and not robust under the hydrological conditions of the sampling year. Wastewater treatment plants thus acted as strong biological filters, reshaping viral assemblages and selecting compartment-specific microvirus populations. Finally, the pronounced and reproducible shifts observed across the continuum suggest that selected microvirus groups may serve as promising bioindicators of anthropogenic influence in freshwater systems.

title: De novo genome assembly of the floating-hook moss Warnstorfia fluitans
authors: Nguyen, M.-P., Galarza, J. A., Koskimäki, J. J., Mian, A. H., Podolich, O., Ahonen, S. H. K., Pirttilä, A. M., Lehosmaa, K.
abstract: The floating-hook moss Warnstorfia fluitans is a natural species dominant in subarctic and Arctic aquatic ecosystems. It is adapted to cold, acidic, and nutrient-deficient environments and possesses great potential for bioremediation by removing contaminants from polluted water in cold climate conditions. Here, we present the first de novo genome assembly of W. fluitans generated from pooled male and female gametophytes. The assembly is 725.04 Mb, has a N50 of 193.5 kb, a BUSCO completeness of 97.6% against the Viridiplantae lineage and 82% against the Embryophyta lineage. The whole assembly has Merqury quality value of 37 and Merqury completeness of 92%. A total of 30421 protein coding genes were predicted, with 78.62% completeness by compleasm and 87% OMArk completeness against the Embryophyta lineage. Repetitive sequences comprise 56.16% of the genome. We also present here the two complete circular chloroplast genomes and a linear mitochondrial genome of W. fluitans. This genomic resource will facilitate studies of ecological adaptation and a wide range of biological and evolutionary studies in bryophytes.

title: PLATE: a global atlas of food metaplasmidomes
authors: Aslan, M. U., Kayacan, R. A., Sögütdelen, S. A., Sagıroglu, O., Arıkan, M.
abstract: Plasmids play a central role in the acquisition and spread of genes underlying important traits in food-associated microorganisms. Although shotgun metagenomics has greatly expanded opportunities to study food microbiomes, their plasmid diversity remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we present the Plasmid Atlas of Food Ecosystems (PLATE), a curated global resource of food metaplasmidomes. Built from 4,690 food metagenomes spanning 55 countries and 17 categories, PLATE comprises a broad catalog (bPLATE) of 3,904,895 putative plasmid contigs (PPCs) and a refined catalog (rPLATE) of 213,474 PPCs, corresponding to 181,871 unique sequences. Both catalogs are complemented by curated sample metadata, host predictions, taxonomic assignments, and functional annotations covering antimicrobial resistance (AMR), protein families and KEGG orthologs, CRISPR-Cas systems, carbohydrate-active enzymes, and bioactive peptides. We demonstrate PLATE's utility through a case study of AMR genes detected on PPCs from food microbiomes. PLATE is freely accessible and enables users to interactively search for and download sequences, annotations, and associated metadata. By organizing plasmid-associated sequence diversity and functional potential across food ecosystems, PLATE provides a foundation for analyses of food metaplasmidomes.

title: HiFiTaxa: a reproducible analysis pipeline for full length 16S rRNA gene and ITS amplicon sequencing from PacBio reads
authors: N. Garritano, A., Modolon, F., Warren, C. R.
abstract: Long-read amplicon sequencing profiles communities at high resolution, but taxonomic accuracy depends on the reference, classifier and the parameters used. Here, we present HiFiTaxa, a reproducible, single command Nextflow pipeline for PacBio HiFi 16S rRNA gene and fungal ITS amplicons. It builds versioned references from current GTDB and UNITE releases and supports Bayesian lowest common ancestor (BLCA) and naive Bayes (NB) classifiers and the read level profilers Emu (16S rRNA gene) and EMITS (ITS). We benchmarked them on mock communities and on holdouts with 10% of GTDB or UNITE databases sequences withheld. On the 16S rRNA gene mock of 20 species, BLCA detected all 20 species and reported two false positives, NB detected 17 and reported none, and Emu detected all 20 and reported eight. In the GTDB holdout, for taxa represented in the reference, BLCA reached 80.0% species level accuracy against 48.1% for the exact matching species step of NB. However, NB produced fewer incorrect assignments for taxa absent from the reference. On fungal ITS, BLCA had slightly higher holdout accuracy at species level(54.7%) against 52.2% for NB. NB was more conservative for novel taxa, and EMITS detected the most mock species. HiFiTaxa therefore offers a single reproducible workflow that uses current GTDB and UNITE releases and enables users to choose between different classifier algorithms depending on their needs.

title: Discovering Prognostic Risk Strata and Heterogeneous Progression Routes from Cross-Sectional Survival Data
authors: Alzaid, E., Wright, G., Minhas, F.
abstract: Inferring how individual patients progress towards higher disease risk typically requires longitudinal observations, which are often unavailable. Population-level analyses of cross-sectional data can identify differences between risk groups but may obscure heterogeneous progression patterns across individual patients. In this work, we introduce GOTSurv, a framework for patient-specific progression modelling. Using cross-sectional survival data, it first learns to rank patients by survival risk and automatically stratify them into prognostic risk groups without requiring predefined risk cut-offs. It then uses unbalanced optimal transport to infer patient-specific changes in the magnitude and direction of features associated with transitions towards higher-risk strata. We evaluated GOTSurv across ten TCGA cancer cohorts using two modalities: gene expression (n=4,767) and whole-slide image representations (n=4,655), with external validation in two independent cohorts. Compared with established survival models, GOTSurv generally achieved stronger prognostic stratification without requiring predefined risk cut-offs, while retaining competitive survival-ranking accuracy. More importantly, GOTSurv enabled the discovery of individualised progression trajectories associated with increasing risk, revealing distinct progression patterns even among patients within the same risk stratum. Overall, GOTSurv provides a novel framework for inferring heterogeneous, patient-specific progression patterns from cross-sectional survival data, enabling the identification of distinct pathways associated with increasing disease risk and informing the development of personalised therapeutic strategies. The code for GOTSurv is available at https://github.com/EtharZaid/GOTSurv/.

title: Chromosome folding encodes mechanisms of cohesion maintenance
authors: Yan, X., Tortora, M. M. C., Goloborodko, A., Fudenberg, G.
abstract: After DNA replication, sister chromatids are physically linked by the cohesin complex. These cohesin linkages must be maintained for many hours for faithful chromosome segregation and DNA repair. Cohesin interacts with multiple rapidly exchanging cofactors, including SORORIN, which is often described as a molecular lock for cohesin on chromatin. How such transient SORORIN binding can protect cohesin over much longer timescales remains mechanistically unclear. Furthermore, how loop-extruding cohesins interact with and influence the positioning of sister-linking cohesins remains largely unknown. Here we show that changes in sister chromatid folding over time and after perturbations encode distinct signatures of the underlying mechanisms of cohesion maintenance. By integrating biochemical kinetics with polymer modeling, we infer cohesin turnover, motion, and encounter rules from these folding signatures. Repeated transient sequestration by SORORIN enables long-lasting protection yet acts as a quantitative modulator, rather than a binary switch for cohesion maintenance. Prolonging cohesin residence time by WAPL depletion exposes additional mechanisms shaping sister chromatid conformation, including pushing of sister-linking cohesins and diffusion of loop-extruding cohesins. Together, these results reveal how transient cofactor interactions regulate long-lived cohesin maintenance and establish sister chromosome organization as a quantitative readout of otherwise hidden molecular mechanisms.

title: Generalizable virtual staining from histopathology to spatial proteomics across biological scales
authors: Liu, Y., Falik, O., Zhong, Z., Yu, L., Luo, R., Jin, C., Chen, H., Mayer, A. T., Trevino, A. E., Chou, P., Dai, Y., Wu, Z.
abstract: Large histology archives capture morphological correlates of molecular tissue states but lack direct spatial protein measurements. In this study, we show that routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology can provide a queryable, morphology-based representation of spatial protein expression that remains informative from pixels to patients. To achieve this, we developed QUEST, a model framework that represents protein markers as semantic queries for flexible multiplex immunofluorescence (MIF) prediction. Trained on a heterogeneous atlas of paired H&E and MIF images comprising over 10,000 tissue regions, QUEST captured morphological patterns associated with protein markers and reconstructed their expression intensities across diverse tissue types and cohorts. Its utility extended beyond image reconstruction and preserved biologically meaningful information across multiple scales: virtual staining preserved protein marker expression at the cellular and tissue scales, supported cell phenotyping, cellular neighborhood analysis, and characterization of spatial tissue organization, retained clinically relevant signals for patient stratification, and enabled H&E-based queries to retrieve MIF references with similar molecular profiles. These findings position virtual staining not simply as image generation but as a flexible interface between routine histology and spatial proteomics, expanding the analytical value of existing H&E archives.

title: Four genome assemblies of new wild Gossypium hirsutum accessions from the Yucatan Peninsula, the center of domestication
authors: Grover, C. E., Arick, M. A., Ning, W., Bridgeland, A. H., Yu, J. Z., Simpson, S. A., Wood, M., Youngblood, R. C., Hulse-Kemp, A. M., Wendel, J. F., Peterson, D. G., Udall, J. A.
abstract: Gossypium hirsutum is a leading source of natural cotton fiber, accounting for most of the market share. While domestication and improvement have led to significant gains in fiber quantity and quality, the narrow germplasm base of modern cultivars creates vulnerabilities, including to emerging pests. Wild populations provide a reservoir for genetic diversity that may be valuable in identifying and transferring resistance or stress-adaptation alleles to modern breeding lines. Here we report four new genome assemblies of G. hirsutum representing distinct populations from its center of diversity in Yucatan, Mexico. These chromosome-level assemblies are highly contiguous and structurally similar to existing G. hirsutum genomes; however, comparative analyses highlight their distinctiveness, suggesting they form a valuable reservoir of untapped diversity. Preliminary analyses of nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptor genes underscore this variation, suggesting presence-absence variation may exist among populations. These findings demonstrate the potential of these new genomic resources for discovery of novel disease resistance alleles and, generally, for expanding the narrow germplasm base of the modern cotton cultivars.

title: Disentangling Context-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Progression Signatures through an Explainable AI Framework
authors: Li, A. W., Qiu, W., Arian, C., Young, J. E., Lee, S.-I.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology.

title: NBDC Data Tools: Building Analysis-ready Datasets From ABCD and HBCD Releases in R and Python
authors: Zhang, L., Das, B., Celhay, O., Smith, C. J., Ziemer, L. R., Dale, A. M., Linkersdörfer, J.
abstract: act The NIH Brain Development Cohorts (NBDC) Data Hub provides access to large-scale longitudinal datasets, including the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study(R) and the HEALthy Brain and Child Development (HBCD) Study. The studies release their tabulated data as hundreds of tables with tens of thousands of variables. Turning these files into a dataset for a particular analysis poses substantial informatics challenges, especially when data preparation and analysis workflows must be reproducible and reusable for new releases. We therefore developed NBDC Data Tools, a suite of open-source packages for preparing NBDC data in local or other approved computing environments. NBDCtools is the core R package for dataset construction and processing. The Python package nbdctools either calls the R workflow or assembles datasets natively in Python, and the R package NBDCtoolsData provides the release metadata support for both NBDCtools and nbdctools. Users define a dataset in code by naming the study, the release, and the variables or tables they need. The software then uses the standardized metadata released by the studies to locate the relevant files, join tables on the participant and session identifiers, convert data types, attach labels, and optionally recode non-response codes as missing values. Because the dataset definition is a short script that runs on the original release files, it can be rerun, shared with collaborators, and reported in publications. NBDC Data Tools complements the web-based data platforms of the NBDC Data Hub by providing a reproducible, scriptable path from approved data access to analysis-ready data for statistical analysis.

title: AlphaFold 3 Prediction Accuracy and Reliability across RNA Structures and Protein-RNA Interfaces
authors: Tennie, I. K., Uhl, M., Franke, J. K. H., Backofen, R., Runge, F.
abstract: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) models RNA and protein-RNA complexes, but when its predictions and confidence metrics can be trusted is unclear. We evaluated AF3 on more than 1,300 protein-RNA complexes and about 270 RNA-only systems, and compared post-cutoff RNAs with pre-cutoff candidates selected by sequence and fold similarity. On structurally novel RNAs, AF3 largely preserves the protein fold, while RNA-fold and interface accuracy drop sharply with little change in predicted RNA confidence score. Input ablations show that protein alignments and templates from RNA-bound proteins govern complex assembly, whereas RNA alignments matter most for single-chain and long RNAs. The most frequent failed interface retains protein-side contacts but places an often-misfolded RNA in the wrong pose. RNA interface confidence only partly distinguishes this error from correct placements. Against CLIP-seq, SELEX and RNAcompete motifs, AF3 usually places the protein against the experimentally observed motif-bearing RNA segment, even where the interface fails, but often not in the native pose. In protein-RNA complexes released in 2026, a score combining AF3 confidence with RNA familiarity and template use ranked RNA chains with accurate folds and correctly placed interfaces better than AF3's ranking score.

title: Genome-scale metabolic models reveal phylogenetic conservation of amino acid fermentation-linked metabolic traits in soil bacteria
authors: Song, Y. C., Ayala-Ortiz, C. O., Stratton, K. G., Chakrawal, A., Graham, E. B.
abstract: Soil microorganisms drive biogeochemical cycling of carbon, nitrogen, and other elements, but the partitioning of metabolic fluxes among taxa remains poorly understood, limiting our ability to link community composition to ecosystem function. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) offer a mechanistic framework to connect taxa and their metabolic pathways to these fluxes. However, heterogeneity of soil communities has hampered recovery of high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), constraining application of flux balance analysis (FBA) to soil metagenomes and skewing available GEMs towards cultured model organisms. This gap limits our understanding of soil microbial physiology and responses to disturbance. Here, we present a collection of GEMs for 550 MAGs (497 bacterial, 53 archaeal) recovered from 94 soil samples across the continental United States. As an example application, we used FBA to estimate uptake and secretion of 44 commonly exchanged metabolites and tested whether these fluxes are phylogenetically conserved. While the overall bacterial phylogenetic signal was weak (median r = 0.029), eight metabolites showed significant conservation: amino acids (L-methionine, L-leucine, L-isoleucine), fermentation intermediates (pyruvate, acetaldehyde, ethanol), and amino acid degradation by-products NH and CO2. Most bacterial MAGs were predicted to import branched-chain amino acids, and a subset also secreted pyruvate and ethanol, identifying candidate cross-feeding interactions. Thus, fermentation-linked traits may be phylogenetically conserved and predictable from community composition, whereas most other metabolites showed no detectable signal. Ultimately, this resource enables genome-resolved prediction of soil microbial metabolisms, from cross-feeding and carbon-use efficiency to community responses to disturbance, providing a mechanistic bridge between microbial taxonomy and ecosystem-scale biogeochemistry.

title: Spectral Adaptive Repositioning for Flow-Based Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling
authors: Verma, S., Wang, M., Kadadi, S. D., Lanman, N. A., Mohammadi, S., Grama, A.
abstract: Predicting transcriptome-wide cellular responses to genetic and biomolecular perturbations is central to functional genomics and therapeutic target discovery. Existing methods assign gene positional encodings derived from arbitrary orderings or static co-expression masks built from unperturbed cells, and cannot capture the functional rewiring induced by perturbations. We present SPEAR, a generative framework built on two complementary positional mechanisms. Spectral positional encoding grounds each gene's position in the geometry of the co-expression network via continuous coordinates derived from the graph Laplacian. Adaptive repositioning then derives each gene's position from its perturbation-conditioned hidden state at every layer, allowing the attention genes exert on one another to reorganize without explicit supervision. Evaluated on genetic, pharmacological, and cytokine perturbation benchmarks, SPEAR demonstrates excellent recovery of differential gene-expression, distributional structure, and perturbation-specific identifiability. SPEAR also captures latent positional relationships that closely map to known transcription factor-target interactions. https://github.com/shouryaverma/SPEAR}{https://github.com/shouryaverma/SPEAR

title: scPCIP: cross-species annotation of plant cell types with conserved gene programs
authors: Yang, S., Si, C., Wu, Y., Sun, Z., Yao, C., Sun, X., Wang, L., Li, W., Zhong, Q.
abstract: Single-cell atlases now cover many plant species and organs, yet their cell types are still annotated with marker genes that often fail to transfer between species. Here we show that plant cell identities are captured by gene programs conserved across species. We learned programs for root, leaf, flower and seed cell types on ortholog groups from 112,905 author-labelled cells and implemented them in scPCIP, which annotates cells of species absent from training without a reference. Across 26 held-out datasets, scPCIP outperformed marker-based and plant deep-learning methods, matched supervised classifiers trained on the same atlas and transferred, at lower accuracy, to an independent study; its programs followed tissue position in spatial transcriptomes. The conserved core of each program separated cell types better than its periphery in all 11 held-out species, whereas most species-specific markers turned over. Across organs, leaf bundle-sheath cells carried a root endodermis program in 8 of 12 studies.

title: GeneFamHunter: annotation-independent recovery of divergent and tandemly arrayed gene-family members from genome assemblies
abstract: Motivation: Gene families expand by tandem duplication, diverge and decay, so their members are often missing, fragmented or fused in automated genome annotations, and divergent copies escape pairwise similarity searches. These challenges are particularly pronounced in non-model organisms, for which well-annotated genomes and reference proteomes are often unavailable, limiting the applicability of protein-based gene family recovery methods. Results: We developed GeneFamHunter to recover gene-family members directly from nucleotide assemblies. It searches continuous six-frame translations of overlapping genomic windows using four complementary domain- and profile-based methods, clusters hits while distinguishing tandem paralogs, predicts and validates gene models, and constructs gene trees. Across six Quest for Orthologs genomes, window-based HMMER searches recovered all 130 reference papain-like (C1A) loci, with 21 off-target hits, compared with 45 for stop-to-stop ORF searches; whole-contig HMMER searches recovered 108 (83.1%). With 11 distantly related queries, PSI-BLAST and DELTA-BLAST recovered all reference loci, whereas RPSTBLASTN recovered 98.5-99.2% and TBLASTN, as used by BITACORA, recovered 94.6-95.4%. Across six mite genomes, GeneFamHunter recovered all 209 previously reported C1 loci and identified 37 additional candidate loci. In a separate comparison, it recovered all 128 reference UniProt C1A proteins and identified five additional loci without annotated gene models; OrthoFinder included 35 non-C1A proteins, whereas OMA recovered 98 reference proteins. Availability and implementation: GeneFamHunter is implemented in Bash for Linux and SLURM clusters and is freely available at https://github.itap.purdue.edu/HeLab/GeneFamHunter (MIT license). Benchmark code and data: https://github.itap.purdue.edu/HeLab/GeneFamHunter_benchmarks and Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23744704).

title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of an endangered large carnivore, the wolverine, Gulo gulo gulo (Linnaeus, 1758)
authors: Torresen, O. K., Flagstad, O., Kleven, O., Strand, M. A., Skage, M., Ferrari, G., Tooming-Klunderud, A., Jakobsen, K. S.
abstract: We describe a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from a male wolverine (Gulo gulo gulo). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 2,523.2 Mb and 2,288.4 Mb, with 95.8% and 97.8% scaffolded into 20 autosomal chromosomes and sex chromosomes (placed in haplotype one). Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 98.2% and 88.9%), with 20,337 and 17,692 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. Compared to existing wolverine genomes, the current genome is more complete and contains both sex chromosomes. This reference genome will be an important resource for population studies and conservation biology of this large carnivore.

title: vafSOMA: Detecting cell-layer-fixed somatic mutations in plants
abstract: Somatic mutations are a source of heritable genetic variation in plants and have long been exploited by breeders through selection and vegetative propagation of bud sports. They often arise in specific meristem layers and can become fixed as descendant cell lineages expand during development. Bulk sequencing of plant organs mixes DNA from these layers, so the expected variant allele frequency of a layer-fixed mutation depends on that layer's tissue contribution, which complicates their detection. Here we present vafSOMA, a statistical model that uses tissue composition to detect fixed somatic mutations, assign them to layers and obtain counts for mutation-rate estimation. It accommodates bulk and layer-enriched samples, including those that retain DNA from other layers after enrichment. In simulations, vafSOMA performed close to the best variant allele frequency cutoff chosen in hindsight, without requiring a user-selected cutoff. Its diagnostics flagged layers for which the data did not support separate mutation counts or rates. Analysing replicate organs substantially improved detection of mutations fixed in the branch meristem and yielded estimates close to the simulated stem-cell mutation rate. Application to apricot sequencing data showed that most reference mutations fixed in the dominant layer were recovered from fruit mixtures at high depth, whereas epidermal mutations remained unresolvable in fruit and leaves. These findings suggest that published bulk somatic sequencing studies mainly capture mutations fixed in the dominant tissue layer and may therefore underestimate the combined input of fixed mutations by roughly two- to threefold when layer-specific rates are similar. vafSOMA is available at https://github.com/jlab-code/vafSOMA.

title: Omics-scale decoding of protein N-glycosylation using protein language model embeddings
authors: Zhou, X., Guan, X., Zhou, Y., Wang, J., Peng, Z., Ren, W., Wang, W., Xie, R., Li, W.
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N-glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape. Applied across proteomes, it reveals that canonical N-X-S/T motifs gain higher glycosylation propensities with increasing organismal complexity and that glycosylation preferentially occurs at structured, solvent-exposed regions. Mutations altering high-scoring motifs are more frequently disease-associated. The framework also captures signatures of glycosylation-mediated protein allostery. These results establish an interpretable and scalable route to study glycobiology from pLM-embeddings.

title: BioTrajX: evaluating biological plausibility in single-cell trajectory inference
authors: Li, T. Y., Chang, Y.-M., Chen, S.-Y.
abstract: Trajectory inference (TI) methods reconstruct cellular progression from single-cell RNA sequencing data, typically by ordering cells along a pseudotime axis. However, different TI methods and analytical choices can produce divergent trajectories from the same dataset, making it difficult to determine which inferred trajectory best reflects the underlying biological process. Existing evaluation strategies often rely on computational benchmarks or qualitative biological assessment, with limited standardized approaches for incorporating a priori biological knowledge. Here, we present BioTrajX, an R package for biologically informed evaluation of pseudotime trajectories using three complementary metrics: Directionality (D), which measures agreement between pseudotime and expected biological progression; Order Consistency (O), which quantifies the coherence of marker-program changes along the trajectory; and Endpoint Validity (E), which assesses enrichment of expected cell states at trajectory endpoints. Together, the DOE metrics provide an interpretable framework for comparing alternative trajectory inference results and evaluating root-cell choices prior to downstream analyses.

title: Context, not contradiction: a pan-cancer framework for conforming and nonconforming co-expression programmes
authors: Khan, S. U. U., Storgard, A., Mendez Tenorio, A., Stupack, D. G.
abstract: Reports of a gene's role in cancer frequently conflict: the same transcript is described as an adverse prognostic marker in one tumour type and a favourable one in another, and such discordance is usually attributed to cohort differences or to irreproducibility. An alternative explanation is that the transcriptional company a gene keeps genuinely differs between lineages. That claim is testable, but testing it requires separating real lineage-dependence from three artefacts that pervade pan-cancer co-expression analysis: public summaries report only coefficients above a fixed threshold, a gene in a recurrently gained region acquires correlates through dosage alone, and conservation across cancer types is assumed rather than measured. We present a framework that addresses all three for any index gene. Correlations are recomputed threshold-free from each cohort's expression matrix; transcripts are partitioned into cis and trans sets relative to the index gene after retired symbols are resolved; a recurrence rule freezes the gene set before any downstream analysis; cohorts are scored against expression-decile-matched permutation nulls; and copy number is residualised out using the cis set as a built-in positive control, so the adjustment is shown to work before the trans result is read. Applied to PTK2, encoding focal adhesion kinase, across 17 TCGA cohorts, expression was associated with poor outcome in several cancers and better outcome in others, independently of tumour purity. The framework shows this is not noise: cohorts separate into conforming and nonconforming groups enriched for different biology. The 44-transcript trans programme is unchanged by copy-number adjustment while the cis control collapses by 38%, and co-expression is recoverable within individual tumours in 133 of 243 single-cell cases.

title: Roost: Avian Influenza Host Genomics Resource
authors: Guhlin, J. G., Dearden, P. K.
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) causes mass mortality in poultry and wildlife, and puts already threatened species at further risk. Understanding differences in host susceptibility requires evidence currently scattered across publications, surveillance reports and genomic resources. We present Roost, a web resource that brings together more than 1,300 publications and reports, surveillance detections, and a catalogue of over 2,000 avian genome assemblies. Large language model-assisted literature analysis and comparative genomics link species, genes and molecular mechanisms to their supporting evidence. Around 51% of species with HPAI detections are not represented in the analysed corpus. Research concentrates on poultry, model organisms, and a small set of immune pathways. Research tracks neither mortality magnitude nor extinction risk; species with the largest recorded die-offs and threatened hosts alike remain largely unstudied.
