T cells additionally exhibited reduced cytotoxicity-associated and enhanced Th17-associated transcriptional programs, whereas B cells showed reduced antigen-processing and presentation programs. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested aging-associated differences in immune cell interactions following LPS challenge and potential features of cardiac inflammaging at baseline. Together, these findings demonstrate that aging bidirectionally reshapes the cardiac immune response to systemic inflammation, characterized by shared remodeling of mitochondrial-associated programs and cell type-specific changes in inflammatory, metabolic, cytoskeletal, and effector-associated programs. These aging-dependent transcriptional changes occurred in the context of the greater severity of illness observed in aged mice following LPS-induced endotoxemia.

title: Synthetic MPRA perturbation supervision improves variant-effect prediction in sequence-to-function models
authors: Wang, L., Galvin, J., Vaz, E., Keener, R., Battle, A.
abstract: Deep learning sequence-to-function (S2F) models learn to predict functional readouts, such as gene expression, from genetic sequence. However, these models are trained predominantly on the reference genome and struggle to accurately predict the effect of genetic variation on gene expression. Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) explore the direct impact of genetic variation on gene expression, but saturation-mutagenesis MPRAs that measure variant effects directly remain limited, thereby restricting their use for fine-tuning S2F models. In this work, we investigate fine-tuning Borzoi, a state-of-the-art S2F model, on model-generated synthetic MPRA variant-effect data as a scalable alternative to overcome limits on the availability of supervised training data for genetic variation. First, we trained an ensemble of 16 models on 110,359 K562 MPRA measurements. Then, we distilled their predictions into a single student model using MPRA elements associated with 1,000 genes. The distilled model was subsequently used to generate synthetic variant-effect labels across increasing numbers of genes (50 to 1,000), with 600 variants per gene, to fine-tune Borzoi. Performance improved as we included more genes in training. In data-limited settings, training on more genes with fewer variants per gene performed better than training on fewer genes with more variants per gene, given the same number of total variants. Compared to pre-trained Borzoi, Borzoi fine-tuned on 600,000 synthetic samples across 1,000 genes increased Pearson correlation from 0.28 to 0.54 on CAGI5 promoter variants and from 0.39 to 0.46 on 903 GTEx fine-mapped whole-blood expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs). Importantly, these improvements were achieved while preserving the pre-trained performance across all 7,611 output tracks. Furthermore, fine-tuned Borzoi recovered regulatory motifs identified by the MPRA model in genes unseen during training, suggesting that learned regulatory features can generalize across loci. Together, these results provide a proof of concept that model-generated synthetic supervision can improve variant effect prediction in S2F models while preserving their original pre-trained capabilities, offering a scalable strategy toward capturing the impact of genetic variation on gene regulation.

title: Continuous Topological Accessibility (RFA) as a 3D-Aware GRN Filter: Anticorrelation with eQTL and No Prediction of ΔRNA
authors: Andrey, T., Bratishchikov, A., Anufriev, A.
abstract: We formalize Relative Forest Accessibility (RFA), a topological accessibility index computed as the solution of (I - {gamma}P )x = v0, where P is a Markov transition matrix built from Hi-C contacts and v0 is a vector of TF peaks (or ATAC peaks). RFA yields a continuous accessibility profile across all genomic bins. We test RFA on three targets. First, on promoter TF counts (GM12878 chr1, 10 kb, 811 genes), RFA loses to 1D distance (AUC 0.836 vs 0.976); this is an artifact because the target and the 1D distance look at the same window. Second, on eQTL (GTEx v10 LCL, chr1+17+19, 10 kb, 1625 genes), RFA anticorrelates with eQTL: {rho}(RFA, - log10 pmin) = -0.09, AUC(RFA) = 0.386 (below chance), AUC(-RFA) = 0.614. High RFA corresponds to fewer eQTL, and dose-response analysis confirms that AUC(RFA) decreases with eQTL strength (mean trend -0.056, 19/20 TFs). A distance-preserving shuffle of the Hi-C matrix reproduces this anticorrelation ({triangleup}AUC vs real: [-0.074, +0.076] across 5 TFs, all CIs include 0), whereas a degree-preserving rewiring destroys it ({triangleup}AUC [isin] [-0.261, -0.003], CIs exclude 0 for 5/5 TFs); the anticorrelation therefore reflects distance-decay of Hi-C contacts (local 3D accessibility), not higher-order topology. The anticorrelation replicates on chr17 ({triangleup}{rho} = -0.13 for rewired, 0/5 for shuffled) and on chr19 with an inverted control pattern, consistent with local within-diagonal heterogeneity as the carrier on short gene-dense chromosomes. Third, on {triangleup}RNA (MCF10A vs MCF7, 40 kb, ATAC peaks), RFA does not predict {triangleup}RNA ({rho} = +0.005, permutation p = 0.87, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.040, +0.053], n = 1730); the CI includes zero and does not exclude the practical boundary |{rho}| = 0.05. Within-line sanity checks are also null. We conclude that RFA anticorrelates with eQTL via local distance-decay and does not predict {triangleup}RNA. The anticorrelation is carried by distance-decay, not by loops or TADs, and may reflect expression buffering: genes with strong eQTL are less dependent on local 3D accessibility. RFA is not a universal predictor but a filter with an inverted sign on eQTL and no signal on {triangleup}RNA.

title: Shared and divergent features of the immune response to acute and chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection in mice revealed by cardiac transcriptomics
authors: Olmo, F., Jayawardhana, S., Taylor, M. C., Kelly, J. M., Francisco, A. F.
abstract: Chagas disease is caused by infection with Trypanosoma cruzi and can result in chronic cardiomyopathy. However, the molecular programmes that define infected cardiac tissue, and how they change as the host-parasite relationship moves from acute pathogenic infection to long-term persistence, remain incompletely understood. Here, we used RNA sequencing to characterise host transcriptional responses in cardiac tissue during both acute and chronic infection in a mouse model. Cardiac parasite distribution was defined using bioluminescence imaging and histology, and RNA sequencing was performed on anatomically standardised cardiac tissue samples collected at both stages. Acute infection was associated with a broad interferon-driven immune activation, whereas during chronic infection this network contracted, with preservation of a tightly connected antigen presentation core centred on major histocompatibility complex genes and immunoproteasome components. Genes associated with extracellular matrix remodelling and fibrosis were not broadly activated. These findings indicate that reduced, but sustained immune activation, rather than widespread fibrotic transcriptional remodelling, represents a prominent feature of cardiac tissue in chronically infected mice. They identify a transition from an overtly inflammatory, pathogen-driven acute response to a more restricted chronic host-parasite equilibrium in which immune surveillance remains transcriptionally active despite very low and spatially intermittent cardiac infection. We identified a conserved 20-gene signature shared between acute and chronic stages. This overlap is consistent with continued or episodic parasite-derived stimulation and/or intrinsic host mechanisms that maintain cardiac immune surveillance. Thus, chronic T. cruzi infection can be viewed as a persistent host-parasite association in which biological coexistence does not imply benignity: immune containment and parasite persistence can occur alongside cumulative cardiac injury.

title: A validation approach for RNA structures based on deep-learning 3D-structure predictions
authors: Voorspoels, A., Simpkin, A. J., Keegan, R., Chojnowski, G., Rigden, D. J.
abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of life depends on accurate macromolecular structures. RNA, in particular, poses a particular challenge for structural biology due to its inherent flexibility and dynamic nature. The challenging nature of structure determination experiments and their interpretation have led to the development of validation approaches to prevent or fix errors in solved structures. Existing methods for RNA structure validation can, as with proteins, be broadly split into two types. Map-based validation tools seek to detect discrepancies between the experimental data and the determined structure. They are excellent for fixing all types of errors, but only when high-resolution experimental data are available.Model-only validation methods, which usually focus on molecular geometry, are excellent for fixing short-length-scale issues even when experimental resolution is low. Conkit-validate is a mapless method for protein validation, which is not based on chemical plausibility, but rather on the similarity between experimental models and structure predictions for the same protein. By comparing contact patterns, this tool leverages evolutionary covariance information, learned by state-of-the-art structural prediction models, into a mapless validation method capable of detecting sequence assignment issues, with notable success in detecting register errors. Here, we extend the conkit-validate method to work on RNA.The results show performance similar to that previously achieved for proteins. %We also show how this new method can detect errors missed by map-based approaches when the experimental data is of low resolution. In a scan of the PDB, its detection rate does not depend on the local resolution of the density, so it remains applicable where map-based approaches are not, and case studies show it can identify register errors where the density alone cannot decide between models.Together, this highlights the complementary value of a contact-prediction based validation approach using information orthogonal to map- and geometry-based approaches to ensure the quality of deposited RNA structures against varying criteria.The performance of the method can be expected to track ongoing improvements in RNA structure prediction methods.

title: Res ipSAE adhuc loquuntur: What the directionality of predicted aligned error in cofolding models can tell us about scoring diverse molecular complexes
abstract: AlphaFold 3 (AF3) and Boltz-2 estimate confidence in predicted biomolecular complexes using the interface predicted template modeling (ipTM) score, which is derived from probability distributions of predicted aligned errors (PAEs) between molecular tokens. These errors are directional: the predicted position of tokens in one molecule is evaluated relative to coordinate frames defined by tokens in another. The PAE matrix is therefore asymmetric, but AF3 reports the maximum of the two directional pairwise ipTM scores, whereas Boltz-2 reports them separately. In both programs, the TM-score scaling parameter, d0, depends on molecular system size rather than solely on the component being scored. In protein-protein complexes, including disordered regions and domains unrelated to the interface can further lower ipTM. I previously introduced the interaction predicted score from aligned errors (ipSAE) to address these limitations for protein-protein complexes. Here, I extend ipSAE to interactions involving proteins, nucleic acids, small-molecule ligands, and atomic ions. The framework makes three explicit choices for each molecular pair: which component supplies the alignment frames, which tokens are scored, and how d0 is defined. For different molecular types, I propose aligning on the more complex molecule and scoring the simpler one. For protein-ligand complexes, this entails aligning on protein residues, scoring all ligand heavy atoms without a PAE cutoff, and using a fixed d0 of 2 [A]. In benchmarks of 102 protein-ligand complexes predicted by AF3 and Boltz-2, this ipSAE formulation yields a substantially wider range of confidence scores than native ipTM. On a held-out set of 82 complexes, ipSAE thresholds of 0.5 for AF3 and 0.8 for Boltz-2 classified ligand placements with balanced accuracies of 0.938 and 0.862, respectively, using a ligand RMSD threshold of 5 [A]. Protein-DNA benchmarks support the same directional scoring scheme, while smaller protein-RNA benchmarks provide a preliminary assessment. These results establish a framework for interpreting predicted structural confidence across different classes of biomolecular interactions and suggest that directional scoring may also be useful for computationally designed protein binders. The new freely available ipSAE code is available from: https://github.com/DunbrackLab/IPSAE2.

title: irAEGIS: Pathway-guided interpretable prediction of immune-related adverse events
authors: Budhkar, A., Guo, S., Zhang, X., Su, J., Song, Q.
abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are major complications of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy and remain difficult to predict prior to treatment initiation. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides a unique opportunity to characterize immune states associated with future irAE development. However, translating single-cell measurements into accurate and biologically interpretable patient-level risk predictions remains challenging. Existing approaches typically aggregate cellular profiles into patient-level summaries, thereby obscuring cell type specific signals, or rely on complex deep-learning architectures that offer limited insight into the biological pathways and mechanisms underlying their predictions. Here, we present irAEGIS, a pathway-guided interpretable model for predicting irAE risk from pre-treatment scRNA-seq data. irAEGIS incorporates prior biological knowledge through gene set constrained representation learning, aggregates pathway activities within individual cell types, and integrates cell type specific risk signals through a hierarchical prediction framework. This design enables predictions to be decomposed into contributions from individual cell types, pathways, and genes, providing interpretable explanations across multiple biological resolutions. Across simulated datasets and independent pre-treatment ICI cohorts, irAEGIS consistently outperformed seven existing methods. Beyond predictive performance, irAEGIS identified biologically coherent immune programs associated with irAE risk. In non-small cell lung cancer, irAEGIS highlighted neutrophil-associated inflammatory pathways linked to future irAE development, whereas in melanoma, it identified apoptotic and immune activation pathways in CD8+ NKT-like cells associated with severe irAEs. These findings were independently supported by pathway enrichment, cell-cell communication, and trajectory analyses. Together, irAEGIS provides a biologically informed and interpretable model for linking single-cell immune states to patient outcomes, enabling both accurate risk prediction and mechanistic insight into immune-related adverse events. More broadly, irAEGIS establishes a general strategy for interpretable phenotype prediction and biological discovery from single-cell transcriptomic data.

title: FoXSight: Facilitating Computational Hit Identification in Crystallographic Fragment Screening Experiments
authors: Schulze, T., Meents, A., Rarey, M., Falke, S., Guenther, S.
abstract: X-ray crystallographic fragment screening reveals how small molecules bind to proteins, providing important starting points for drug design. Identifying these weak binding events remains difficult when electron density signals are noisy, partially occupied or obscured by solvent, and campaigns may comprise thousands of datasets. Here, we present FoXSight, a computational method for hit identification in crystallographic compound screening. FoXSight applies Difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) filtering to multi-reference subtraction maps to detect recurring, target-specific density features associated with bound ligands. Its output maps remain visually interpretable and support subsequent ligand modeling. We evaluated FoXSight on in-house and public datasets spanning seven protein targets, comparing its maps with PanDDA where suitable comparison data were available. FoXSight was successfully used as the primary hit identification tool in a challenging crystallographic fragment screening campaign for human Cathepsin L, where the output of established methods was impractical to inspect systematically.

title: FedEpitope: Parameter-Efficient Federated Protein Language Models for Linear B-Cell Epitope Prediction
authors: Joshi, D., Priyadarsinee, L., Chatterjee, B., Natarajan, A. M., Sastry, G. N.
abstract: Linear B-cell epitopes are antigenic regions recognised by antibodies that play crucial roles in vaccine development, antibody production, and other therapeutic applications.Their prediction can support peptide-based vaccine candidate screening and diagnostic assay development, but the experimental data required for model development may be distributed across institutions that cannot freely pool their records. We present FedEpitope, a federated framework that adapts the ESM-2 protein language model for peptide-level linear B-cell epitope prediction using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), keeping client-partitioned data local and restricting the communicated trainable model state to approximately 1.11 MB. Simulated benchmarks of FedAvg and FedProx algorithms, evaluated using homology-aware data splits of five biologically heterogeneous, organism-partitioned clients, achieve promising global test performance without centralising training data, with FedAvg outperforming all single-client models in mean AP, F1, and MCC. Additional experiments characterise post-federation personalisation, record-level differential privacy, sensitivity to controlled client heterogeneity, LoRA rank, and generalisation to the independent BCPreds and NetBCE benchmarks, demonstrating the feasibility of parameter-efficient federated protein language model adaptation for data-localised B-cell epitope prediction and the associated trade-offs among predictive performance, personalisation, privacy, communication efficiency, and distribution shift.

title: Ancient U/V sex chromosomes reveal slow expansion of recombination suppression in Polytrichaceae mosses.
authors: Rey-Giraud, F., Muskaan, M., Oort, S., Vanderpoorten, A., Cronberg, N., Blassiau, C., Charissou, I., Fraisse, C., Vekemans, X.
abstract: Sex chromosomes evolving in haploid versus diploid life cycles provide complementary systems for testing theories of sex chromosome evolution, yet haploid sex chromosomes remain poorly studied. In dioicous bryophytes, females and males carry non-recombining U and V chromosomes, respectively, providing a unique opportunity to examine the consequences of long-term recombination suppression independently of diploid heterogamety. Here, we characterize the U/V sex chromosomes of Polytrichaceae using chromosome-scale genomes from ten species. We identify homologous U/V chromosomes across the family and show that their non-recombining sex-determining regions (SDRs) originated early in Polytrichaceae evolution, approximately 124 million years ago. Despitetheir ancient origin, however, the SDRs have undergone limited expansion and are consistently flanked by large pseudoautosomal regions (PARs). The SDRs nevertheless show strong genomic signatures of recombination suppression, including reduced gene density, transposable-element accumulation, reduced diversity, high synonymous divergence, and altered codon usage. Yet they retain hundreds of genes and show limited evidence of functional degeneration. Their gene content is dynamic, with frequent lineage-specific gains and losses, while a conserved core of 60 orthogroups has persisted across all ten species for more than 100 million years. Comparisons across sex chromosome systems suggest that haploid U/V chromosomes retain more genes than similarly old diploid X/Y or Z/W chromosomes, consistent with a role for haploid selection in limiting degeneration. However, haploid selection alone cannot explain the limited SDR expansion observed in Polytrichaceae, suggesting that other factors also shape SDR evolution. Together, these results reveal an ancient U/V system in which recombination suppression has strong genomic consequences but has not driven extensive SDR expansion or functional degeneration. By decoupling recombination suppression from diploid heterogamety, U/V chromosomes provide a powerful framework for distinguishing the consequences of recombination arrest from those of ploidy in sex chromosome evolution.

title: Urban enrichment of molestus ancestry and opposing temperature clines in a metropolitan Culex pipiens hybrid zone
authors: Gregory, B. P., Arsenault-Benoit, A., Bell, K. L., Fritz, M. L.
abstract: Hybridization between ecologically distinct lineages can fuel rapid adaptation when introgressed alleles are locally favored. The North American Culex pipiens assemblage, a principal West Nile virus vector east of the Mississippi, comprises three lineages---temperate Cx. pipiens f. pipiens, urban-specialist Cx. pipiens f. molestus, and subtropical Cx. quinquefasciatus---that meet in a mid-Atlantic hybrid zone where temperature and urbanization gradients intersect. Using whole-genome Pool-seq of 24 field populations and three lineage-reference pools across the Baltimore--Washington corridor, we find a weakly differentiated, Cx. pipiens f. pipiens-like background, richer in molestus- and quinquefasciatus-like ancestry toward the warmer end of the corridor. Urbanization impacts allele frequencies across the genome: molestus-like ancestry rises with impervious surface, independently of temperature and position, while Cx. quinquefasciatus-like ancestry does not. An 11.6 Mb chromosome 3 inversion is molestus-like in every population, most of all in urban ones, and tracks genome-wide molestus-like ancestry. Temperature acts locus by locus. On chromosome 1, a cluster of six CYP6 paralogs, a family implicated in insecticide resistance and thermal-stress response, shows rising Cx. quinquefasciatus-like ancestry and read depth with temperature. A chromosome 2 interval centered on a Yan ortholog, a repressor of cell differentiation, shows non-quinquefasciatus ancestry increasing with temperature, consistent with selection against Cx. quinquefasciatus-like introgression. Urban populations therefore carry more ancestry from the human-commensal lineage, while temperature moves ancestry both ways at individual loci. Both molestus and Cx. quinquefasciatus donors carry human-contact traits, so these patterns bear on how warming and urbanization will reshape arboviral risk.

title: Bridging Bibliometrics and Biology: A Framework for the Relevance Scoring and Biological Stratification of Scalable MeSH Co-occurrence Networks
abstract: Systematic literature review is often limited by the rigidity of search strings, which often miss non-obvious but highly relevant topics. Controlled vocabularies such as Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) facilitate the review process, but relationships between terms, and their relevance to a hypothesis of interest, are rarely stated explicitly. Presented here is a MeSH term extraction and networking technique, seeded by a single query for Allergic Contact Dermatitis, forming a "themed" network of terms. The resulting co-occurrence network is pruned by an unsupervised consensus of Metropolis-criterion likelihood search strategies, isolating a significant core subgraph and filtering out incidental co-indexing. Symmetrically normalized Article Relevancy Scores (ARS) then evaluate each article against the network's weighted terms across the annotated MEDLINE corpus, correcting for publication volume bias; Mean Relevancy Scoring (MRS) inverts these scores back onto the terms, scoring each MeSH term by the mean ARS of the articles carrying it to measure its specificity to the query. Benchmarked against the expert-curated Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) for Allergic Contact Dermatitis, the network recovered key event terminology and identified highly specific literature that standard retrieval methods overlooked. This data-driven approach quantitatively assesses associated MeSH terminology, extracting biologically relevant concepts and key relationships directly from the underlying structure of the literature. By automating the discovery of these latent connections, the framework provides a reproducible, scalable foundation for understanding the biomedical literary space surrounding a given search string, assisting systematic review creation, mechanistic pathway mapping, and hypothesis generation across biomedical disciplines.

title: PhenoMe: An interactive AI framework for interpretable, microscopy-driven phenotyping
authors: Gonzalez-Marfil, A., Backova, L., Bernatchez, R., Hidalgo-Cenalmor, I., Dufour, A., Jacquemet, G., Lavoie-Cardinal, F., Arganda-Carreras, I., Gomez-de-Mariscal, E.
abstract: Extracting meaningful biological patterns from microscopy image datasets requires tools that quantitatively connect visual similarities and experimental context. Deep learning models, and in particular novel foundation models, have the capacity to translate images into high-dimensional embeddings that can better represent complex visual patterns. Using these complex representations analytically and linking them to experimental information, it is possible to build advanced exploratory and phenotyping capabilities. Here, we present PhenoMe, an open-source, model-agnostic framework to handle pretrained foundation model-derived image representations alongside quantitative image properties and experimental metadata. PhenoMe integrates multiple scriptable and interactive workflows for embedding space visualisation, dimensionality reduction and clustering, similarity-based comparison and retrieval of representative images for each phenotype, among others. It also supports correlation analyses that link the embedding structure to interpretable image properties. We demonstrate PhenoMe's capabilities on seven public microscopy datasets, ranging from cell painting assays, nanoscale synaptic images, drug-response analyses and dynamic cell-phenotyping. These case studies show how readily available image representations can support data contextualisation, curation and analysis. Through guided notebooks, reproducible configurations, extensible model wrappers and a napari plugin, PhenoMe makes representation-based microscopy exploration accessible to researchers without dedicated technical expertise. PhenoMe lays the groundwork for applying foundation models and representation learning to microscopy data analysis.

title: Integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of human cartilage reveals coordinated changes in fibronectin expression, splicing, and receptor signaling during osteoarthritis progression
authors: Lotz, M., Swahn, H., Sakamoto, T., Kenvisay, C., Olmer, M., Uchida, Y., Asahara, H., Miller, R. E., Malfait, A.-M., Orange, D. E., Mehta, B., Otero, M., Bugbee, W. D.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is defined by progressive loss of articular cartilage, but how chondrocytes change as the disease advances is unclear because most studies have focused on end-stage tissue. We profiled human knee articular cartilage across the full range of macroscopic OA grade, from young healthy to aged severe OA donors, by bulk RNA sequencing of 92 knees, single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 108,600 chondrocyte nuclei from 30 donors and single-nucleus multiome sequencing of 24 of these donors, treating grade as a continuous variable. With increasing grade, cartilage increased extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis and remodeling genes, lost glucocorticoid-responsive, lipid-metabolic and antioxidant programs, and changed the splicing of a small set of ECM transcripts, led by the extra domain B (EDB) exon of fibronectin (FN1). Nine chondrocyte clusters were present in every disease stage and formed a continuum ordered by cartilage zone and hypertrophic differentiation, with PRG4+ superficial and COL10A1+ hypertrophic chondrocytes as the only distinct cell types at its ends and a pre-hypertrophic state between them. With grade, all clusters shared a response in which ECM production rose and homeostatic programs fell, and they differed in which of its components was strongest: ECM production in the superficial cells, the secretory pathway in the hypertrophic and CYTL1+ cells, and inflammatory signaling in the ANXA1+ and CRISPLD2+ cells. Inferred communication between chondrocytes was remodeled with stage. FN1 was induced in every cluster in excess of its fibril-assembly machinery, together with the fibronectin-cleaving protease HTRA1, and FN1 signaling shifted in receptor use from integrin 5{beta}1 toward CD44 and, less robustly, v{beta}8, accompanied by a rise in TGF-{beta}/SMAD response genes. In four early-OA donors, tenascin-C was already largely induced and the FN1 receptor shift from 5{beta}1 toward CD44 was partly present, whereas the rise of FN1 outside superficial chondrocytes, of FGF1 and of developmental and ossification programs came with progression. Chromatin accessibility changed in the same direction across clusters, with regions linked to FN1 opening and regions linked to ITGA5 closing. OA progression in human cartilage therefore appears to be a change of chondrocyte state that differs in emphasis along a zonal and hypertrophic continuum and includes changes in fibronectin regulation, production, processing, and receptor engagement.

title: PHATE-Derived Ancestry Coordinates Capture Continuous Population Structure in Human Genomic Data
authors: Scicluna, M. C., Ni, S., Valdez Cordova, C. M., Grenier, J.-C., Poujol, R., Kanoun, M. E., Rocha, J. F., Moon, K. R., Lemieux, S., Wolf, G., Krishnaswamy, S., Hussin, J.
abstract: Population genetic data are increasingly visualized using low-dimensional embeddings as ancestry coordinates, yet how these methods represent population structure can depend strongly on sampling and construction choices. Principal component analysis (PCA), when visualized using only leading components, can obscure fine-scale structure, while nonlinear neighbor-based methods such as uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) often fragment geographic and admixture gradients into discrete clusters. Here, we introduce a framework for constructing ancestry coordinates using potential of heat-diffusion for affinity-based trajectory embedding (PHATE), a diffusion-based method that preserves relationships across scales. Across synthetic benchmarks and large genomic datasets, we show that appropriate scale tuning and population balancing allow PHATE to recover geographic organization and admixture gradients. We show that incorrectly tuned neighborhood scale and population imbalance can distort the resulting representations of population structure. These results therefore provide a methodological framework and practical guidance for constructing ancestry visualizations that better reflect continuous human genetic diversity.

title: DoAggregate: a pipeline for aggregation testing for rare-variant on a gene and pathway level
authors: Boutry, S., Van Marcke, C., Limaye, N., Smits, G., Pascal Brouillard, P., De Bortoli, M., Pairet, E., Saadat, A., Helaers, R., Fellay, J., Lenaerts, T., Vikkula, M.
abstract: Motivation Aggregation tests overcome the classical limitation of rare variant analysis in cohort study design. Choosing the right statistical test remains one of the biggest challenges. Existing tools fall short in offering a comprehensive solution that includes automatic data processing, testing across all genes, as well as exploration of broader genetic regions such as pathways and Gene Ontology (GO) terms. Most aggregation tests only report p-values and basic statistics, lacking in the presentation of cohort level statistics and comparison of results across whole genome or exome scales. Results We introduce DoAggregate, an innovative, scalable pipeline designed to address these challenges. DoAggregate enables users to perform aggregation tests across genes, pathways, and GO terms. It leverages Excalibur, an ensemble approach combining 36 distinct aggregation methods. The pipeline enhances data analysis by presenting over-representation analysis and aggregation results in detailed Excel sheets, complete with annotations and plots to facilitate nuanced interpretation and comparison. Applied to public exome data from the 1000 Genomes Project, DoAggregate tested 10,447 genes, 49 over-represented pathways and 36 over-represented GO terms in a single run, returning annotated, cohort-level results for each region. Availability and implementation DoAggregate source code, documentation and installation instructions as well as test data sets and results are freely available at https://github.com/boutrys/DoAggregate and released under the MIT license. The repository contains the serial implementation (R package), the parallel implementation for Slurm-based computer clusters and the web application.

title: Unsupervised prioritization of gene-regulatory variants with isolation forests
authors: Schmidt, A. W., Rosendahl, J., Laumen, H., Ossowski, S.
abstract: Most common variants occur in non-coding genomic regions. Numerous expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) can influence nearby gene expression. Across diverse traits and diseases, many genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci have been shown to colocalize with eQTLs, supporting gene-regulatory causal mechanisms. However, linkage disequilibrium (LD) obscures the identification of the causal variant(s), necessitating prioritization by functional annotations. Previously published variant prioritization tools relied on the machine-learning-based combination of diverse feature types like evolutionary conservation and chromatin information, whereas more recent deep learning tools learn and describe gene-regulatory DNA sequence grammar. However, the latter approaches often generate a large number of scores per variant. We designed a novel unsupervised machine-learning approach based on isolation forests to integrate the predictions from the broadly used Enformer deep learning model into a single gene-regulatory predictive score for each common variant. Our novel approach eQTL prediction with isolation forests (eQIF) demonstrates strong performance in predicting eQTLs and gene-regulatory GWAS variants. We show that top eQIF variants are located in evolutionarily conserved transcription factor binding site (TFBS) footprints, and that the frequency of top eQIF variants within overrepresented TFBS motifs recapitulates the motif information content. eQIF predictions are precomputed for 9,431,969 common variants and publicly available.

title: ARCADE disentangles cell abundance from continuous transcriptional state in spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics is widely used to infer both cell-type abundance and within-type transcriptional variation, but these signals are difficult to separate in mixed spot-level measurements. Here, we present ARCADE, a computational framework that addresses two major sources of uncertainty in spatial analysis: unstable single-cell references and entanglement between abundance and cell state. ARCADE first builds a robust reference through hyperparameter optimization and consensus filtering, then performs spatial inference in two stages by estimating cell-type composition before modeling continuous intratype transcriptional programs around this compositional anchor. Across simulated and semi-synthetic benchmarks, ARCADE improves deconvolution accuracy and yields more stable state inference than existing approaches. In matched human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex datasets with spatial proteogenomic readouts, ARCADE distinguishes localized cell enrichment from astrocyte and microglial activation programs. These results show that decoupled modeling can improve the interpretability of spatial transcriptomic signals in complex tissues.

title: scSTEC: Annotating Chromatin Subcompartments from Individual Single-Cell Hi-C Data via Direct Two-Dimensional Embedding and Chromosome-wise Consensus
authors: Peng, Y., Yang, L., Ge, H.
abstract: textbf{Motivation: }Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) technologies enable the study of three-dimensional (3D) genome organization at individual-cell resolution. Many computational methods have been developed to infer hierarchical structures from scHi-C data. However, annotating chromatin subcompartments from sparse scHi-C data remains a challenge. The recently developed scGHOST provides a framework for single-cell subcompartment annotation, but relies on a deep learning-based architecture, a multi-step upstream pipeline involving cell embedding and matrix imputation, and cross-cell information sharing. These features complicate algorithmic interpretation and make the annotation of an individual cell dependent on information from other cells in the dataset. Hence, methods are needed that annotate subcompartments directly from an individual cell's own contact matrix, without complex upstream processing or cross-cell information sharing. textbf{Results: }We developed scSTEC, a computational framework that annotates subcompartments directly from an individual scHi-C matrix without data imputation, complex upstream processing, or cross-cell data sharing. We show that the estimated inter-chromosomal matrix constructed by scGHOST is intrinsically of rank 2, revealing that the geometry relevant to clustering can be represented in two dimensions. Leveraging this low-dimensional structure, scSTEC performs direct subcompartment annotation through 2D genomic embedding and chromosome-wise consensus. Across bulk Hi-C, downsampled simulations, and real scHi-C datasets (four human cell lines, adult mouse cortex, developing mouse embryos, and developing olfactory sensory neurons), scSTEC achieves subcompartment annotations comparable to scGHOST despite operating on each cell independently, while providing greater algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, subcompartments identified by scSTEC effectively resolve cell types, capture developmental dynamics, and show consistent associations with gene expression and epigenetic profiles. \textbf{Availability: }scSTEC is freely available at url{https://github.com/Ge-lab-pku/scSTEC}.

title: CNVision: a computational framework for functional interpretation of intragenic copy number variants
abstract: Background Intragenic copy number variants (CNVs), including exon-level deletions and duplications within a single gene, represent an important class of pathogenic genomic variation. Their functional consequences depend on the precise relationship between the CNV breakpoints, exon structure, coding sequence boundaries, transcript orientation, and reading frame. Although intragenic CNVs contribute substantially to Mendelian disease, their interpretation remains difficult because many existing workflows rely on manual transcript review or annotation pipelines that do not consistently resolve exon-level and base-pair-level consequences. Results We developed CNVision, a containerized computational framework for standardized interpretation of intragenic CNVs. CNVision accepts multiple input formats, including exon-based entries, genomic coordinates, and HGVS genomic notation, and converts each into a unified internal representation for transcript-aware analysis. The system maps CNVs to coding sequence regions, calculates affected coding sequence length at base-pair resolution, and classifies predicted reading-frame consequence. CNVision was evaluated using a dataset including 200 curated intragenic CNVs spanning multiple genes, genome builds, variant structures, and input types. Across the dataset, CNVision produced predictions concordant with manual transcript-level analysis and correctly processed exon-based, coordinate-based, and HGVS-formatted inputs. Beyond basic evaluation, CNVision also identified discrepancies in previously published CNVs. Of 131 reported CNVs evaluated, 15 yielded classifications that differed from the original published interpretation; independent manual transcript-level analysis using the UCSC Genome Browser supported CNVision's classification in all 15 variants, indicating the discrepancies were attributable to differences in transcript interpretation or coordinate calculation rather than computational error. In terms of processing speed, CNVision was tested by two board-certified laboratory geneticists who compared the runtime of CNVision versus manual analysis across 18 CNVs, 6 of each input type. CNVision consistently outperformed manual analysis by both geneticists across all variants by a significant margin. Conclusion CNVision provides a reproducible framework for functional interpretation of intragenic CNVs by automating input parsing, transcript mapping, coding sequence overlap calculation, and reading-frame classification. The framework reduces manual burden, improves consistency, and provides a foundation for future expansion into batch CNV processing and graphical variant interpretation.

title: LabWeaver: reliable agentic data analysis grounded in laboratory knowled
authors: Li, L., Fort, G., Xu, J., Tan, A. C., Guo, B.
abstract: Agentic systems powered by large language models are rapidly automating biological data analysis. However, their reliability remains questionable because they often overlook experimental context, such as disease domain and experimental protocol. Existing agentic systems organize context around individual users and projects, whereas research is organized around laboratories whose projects share experimental context. As a result, experimental context learned in one project remains unavailable to related projects. We introduce LabWeaver, an agentic data analysis framework with a laboratory-organized architecture of three tiers: laboratory, user and project. Further, LabWeaver distills experimental context into laboratory memory and skills, which are shared across users and projects after human-gated review. To isolate the contribution of experimental context, we analyzed a synovial sarcoma single-cell RNA-seq dataset in two sessions that differed only in whether laboratory memory and skills were available. The context-free session lost the fusion reporter at read alignment and misannotated the tumor cells. In contrast, the context-enabled session recovered reporter expression and resolved five fusion-anchored tumor cell states.

title: AI-based structural modelling and pathogenic variant mapping across the human protein interactome
authors: Ille, A. M., Ille, A. L., Lamont, H. H., Holyoak, T.
abstract: Spanning the complex landscape of the human proteome, physical interactions between proteins coordinate cellular organization, signaling, regulation, and homeostasis. Yet the three-dimensional structures of most of these interactions remain unresolved. Here, we performed AI-based modelling of 109,282 human protein interaction structures, generating a structural resource for large-scale analysis. The predicted structures were systematically characterized through analysis of interface residue involvement, buried surface area, intermolecular bonding, and energetic properties. Additionally, we mapped pathogenic variant data onto the predicted structures, identifying interface-localized mutations for over 4,000 annotated disease categories. Acute myeloid leukemia, Alzheimer's disease, and cardiomyopathy were examined as representative disease contexts for exploring the distribution of interface mutations within disease-associated protein interaction networks. Strengths and limitations of predictive capabilities were also assessed, including through experimental structure comparisons. Collectively, this structural resource and accompanying analyses offer a basis for developing novel hypotheses and informing experimental studies involving human protein interactions in physiological and disease contexts.

title: Protein Pocket Coengagement Prioritizes Drug-Drug Interactions
abstract: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are largely catalogued empirically, with limited structural explanation of why two drugs interact. We asked whether a purely structural mechanism - competing or cooperating engagement of the same protein pocket - is sufficient to recover documented DDIs without any training on clinical interaction labels. Using composite protein multiple-ligand (COLIG) assignments, which classify co-bound ligand pairs as attractive or repulsive, we scored 21,945 pairs of 210 drugs by predicted engagement of each proteins top-ranked pocket. Confidence-summed COLIG ranking achieved top-5% precision of 49.3% against DDInter and 25.1% against KEGG, versus background prevalences of 29.6% and 14.7%, respectively; pooled top-pocket engagement reached 50.3% DDInter precision. These results support pocket-based DDI screening and class-dependent hypotheses about direct and noncontact ligand engagement, while leaving causal mechanisms to be established.

title: Phylogeny-Guided Global-Local Shrinkage for Microbiome Feature Selection
authors: Zhu, Z., Zhang, S., Tang, X., Zhang, L.
abstract: Microbiome feature selection is challenging because sequencing counts are sparseand compositional, while evolutionarily related taxa may exhibit similar associations with an exposure. We propose phylogeny-guided global--local shrinkage (PGL), a Bayesian regression method for identifying exposure-associated differences in the relative abundances of individual amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). A multinomial logit-normal working model analyzes relative abundance among ASVs detected in each sample. A zero-sum constraint gives the regression coefficients a log-ratio interpretation relative to the mean across retained ASVs. Global--local shrinkage accommodates weak and large associations, while an estimated weight controls information sharing along a supplied phylogenetic tree. Simulation ablation studies showed that phylogenetic borrowing improved detection power and estimation of nonzero coefficients when associations aligned with the tree, with little change under a tree-independent generator. Estimated borrowing decreased as the supplied tree was corrupted. Comparisons with benchmark methods revealed different trade-offs between detection power and false discovery rates across simulation settings. In an HIV oral microbiome application, ablation analysis showed that phylogenetic borrowing preserved the overall pattern of estimated associations while changing posterior uncertainty and selecting three additional ASVs. PGL provides ASV-level inference with adaptive information sharing across evolutionarily related features.

title: DEEPNET-LLM: Highly accurate structure prediction of unknown metabolites from mass spectra via their molecular neighborhoods
authors: Melnik, A. V., Roberts, A. M. P., Semenov, A., Moradi, D., Coler, E. A., Goldstein, J., Ojha, B., Swift, N. J., Demirovic, S., Peczuh, M. W., Horvath, T. D., Engevik, M. A., Boginski, V., Aksenov, A. A.
abstract: Most molecular features detected by untargeted mass spectrometry-based metabolomics remain unannotated. This so-called 'dark matter' currently comprises more than 90% and likely holds uncharacterized bioactive chemistry. Structure prediction from fragmentation spectra remains an outstanding challenge, because a spectrum does not uniquely determine a structure and the space of candidate structures is mostly unbounded; correspondingly, existing methods rarely return the correct de novo structure as their top prediction. Here we describe De novo Ego network-Enabled Propagation and Neighborhood Extrapolation of Topology using Large Language Models (DEEPNET-LLM) reasoning approach, which uses Molecular Community Networking (MCN) to restrict the search of a query spectrum to its local neighborhood within the global metabolome, and applies AI reasoning to propagate structural information from neighbors to the query. For a collection of 900 authentic standards (2,249 spectra) that have never been publicly released to exclude possibility of data leakage, DEEPNET-LLM returned the correct structure as its top prediction for 84.7% of spectra. Accuracy was independent of precursor mass across a range over which the number of candidate structures grows by 30 orders of magnitude, and was comparable across ion polarity, adducts and in-source fragmentation. On a random subset of the public MassSpecGym benchmark, DEEPNET-LLM reached 85.9% top-1 accuracy excluding stereochemistry. We showcase the use of DEEPNET-LLM with an example of a discovery of tryptamine amidate of a bile acid in mouse gut, confirmed against a synthetic standard. The DEEPNET-LLM approach is orthogonal to existing in silico methods and can be combined with them.

title: ssGSEA3.0: Feature-Level Bootstrap Resampling for Robust Assessment of Statistical Significance
authors: Clark, N. M., Mani, D. R.
abstract: Motivation Single-sample Gene/Post-Translational Modification Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA/PTM-SEA) methods assess pathway or signature activity per sample using permutation-based significance testing. ssGSEA2.0's weighted scoring (ssGSEA2.0-orig) uses a correlation-vector reordering that inflates false positives at nonzero weight; directly fixing this (ssGSEA2.0-fixed) restores null-distribution calibration but sacrifices detection power at nonzero weight. Results ssGSEA3.0 replaces feature-label (gene- or site-level) permutation with feature-level bootstrap resampling, which remains calibrated across weighting schemes. On published lung adenocarcinoma and phosphoproteomic perturbation datasets, ssGSEA3.0 shows greater detection power than ssGSEA2.0-fixed, with an additional gain for directional (PTM-SEA) scoring. Previously published findings remain robust across methods, including at nonzero weight. Bootstrapping adds a ~1.5- to 2-fold computational cost. Availability and Implementation ssGSEA3.0 is implemented as an open-source R package (github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA3.0, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23734262) and includes the worked examples on biological data presented here.

title: Ark-ADMET: endpoint-specific selection of molecular representations and hyperparameters for gradient-boosted ADMET models under the Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark protocol
authors: Shi, Y., Luo, H., Liu, F., Zhao, S.
abstract: Typical submissions to the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) benchmark leaderboard apply a single architecture and a single feature representation across all 22 endpoints, despite substantial heterogeneity in evaluation metric, training-set size, and class balance. Rather than proposing a new architecture, we show that endpoint-specific selection of molecular representations and CatBoost hyperparameters, carried out under the official TDC ADMET benchmark protocol, is a competitive alternative to that uniform recipe. For each endpoint, a fixed CatBoost backbone was paired with configurations chosen from a common candidate set comprising published fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors, truncated three-dimensional PaDEL descriptors, frozen graph isomorphism network (GIN) and MiniMol embeddings, and a convex combination with a shallow network trained on the MiniMol embedding alone. All feature and hyperparameter choices were made on an internal scaffold validation split under a prespecified strict-improvement rule. Against a frozen snapshot of the public leaderboard, the resulting Ark-ADMET family of 22 endpoint-specific models matched or exceeded the best previously listed score on 7 of 21 rankable endpoints and strictly exceeded it on 3. All selected configurations retain the baseline fingerprint-and-descriptor block; optional components differ across endpoints. Taken together, these results show that competitive performance on this benchmark can be achieved without a new architecture or a single optional representation shared across all endpoints.

title: LOTUS: lineage-aware optimal transport reconstructs continuous clonal fate dynamics
authors: Lu, J., Hou, H., Zhang, Z., Lin, Y., Lin, Y., Zhou, P.
abstract: Destructive sampling in single-cell sequencing obscures ancestor-descendant relationships, limiting the continuous reconstruction of cell-fate dynamics. Here we present Lineage-aware optimal transport for unbalanced single-cell dynamics (LOTUS), a framework that integrates time-resolved transcriptomic snapshots with clonal lineage information from engineered barcodes or endogenous T cell receptor clonotypes. LOTUS couples clone-level optimal transport with neural unbalanced transport to model continuous cellular state change, population growth and clonal propagation under lineage-consistent constraints. In branching simulations, LOTUS reduced lineage-inconsistent transport relative to benchmark methods, lowering off-target routing from 4.94-14.84% to 1.10%. On LARRY lineage-barcode scRNA-seq of hematopoiesis, LOTUS reconstructed branching trajectories, improved early neutrophil-monocyte fate-boundary prediction, and inferred multi-fate progenitors and fate-biased meta-clones, linking their distinct fate potentials to inferred epigenetic priming. On CellTagging scRNA-seq of fibroblast reprogramming, it distinguished reprogrammed from failed trajectories and prioritized fate-associated perturbation genes. In longitudinal scRNA-seq and TCR-seq of malaria-responsive memory (CD45RA-) CD4+ T cells, it preserved endogenous clonotype structure and reconstructed TR1 dynamics and regulatory networks. LOTUS thus converts lineage-resolved single-cell snapshots into interpretable, continuous models of fate dynamics and their regulatory programs.

title: BioResearchBench: 50 Long Horizon Biological Research Tasks
authors: Abedrabbo, S., Pryhoda, A., Goodman, K., Taavola, J., Milam, E., Albright, A., Jabal, R., Yang, M., Burrese, C., Tubby, J., Villagomez, J., Kim, J.
abstract: AI models are used in biology research to study disease mechanisms, discover potential treatments, analyze experimental data, troubleshoot problems, and plan next steps. Useful assistance depends on working with data in various scientific formats, interpreting results, and deciding what to test next. We present BioResearchBench, a benchmark of 50 research questions developed by PhD biologists drawing on their deep research expertise to reflect realistic problems encountered in their fields. Questions were refined through expert review and iterative model testing. The collection spans 10 diverse biology subdomains and includes sequencing data, proteomic measurements, microscopy images, assay readouts, and clinical datasets. We compared recorded outcomes and examined model responses in depth across the 50 tasks on OpenAI GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, Meta Muse Wonder, and SpaceXSI Grok 4.7. Success across our benchmark was 18% for Claude Opus 5.5, 13% for Gemini 4 Argon, 11% for Meta Muse Wonder, 4% for GPT-6 Astra, and 4% for Grok 4.7. These results describe a deliberately challenging collection selected through expert review and model testing. Despite low whole task success, the selected responses met most rubric requirements on average: the average fraction of criteria missed ranged from 18% to 32% across models. Across models, the proportion of eligible tasks with at least one category failure was highest in computation and data handling (66.9% failure), followed by uncertainty and identification (55.3% failure), reporting and completeness (54.7% failure), biological interpretation (39.0% failure), controls and causal claims (37.2% failure), and choosing the next experiment or decision (31.0% failure). Gemini 4 Argon had the highest proportion of reviewed tasks without a recorded category failure in computation and data handling (45% success) and biological interpretation (69% success). Claude Opus 5.5 led in controls and causal claims (72% success) and choosing the next experiment or decision (75% success). GPT-6 Astra led in uncertainty and identification (56% success) which included judging the precision of estimates and recognizing when measurements could not distinguish between biological explanations. GPT-6 Astra and Meta Muse Wonder tied for the highest proportion of answers with no recorded omissions or reporting failures (51% success). Five case studies presented here show how top AI models can perform many analytical steps correctly yet misinterpret what results signify. For example, some answers described cells as fully recovered when oxygen consumption improved even though mitochondrial membrane potential and cell number remained below control levels. These model answers therefore overstated the extent of cell recovery. Other answers incorrectly called a protein a direct microRNA target, although the experiment had not tested whether the microRNA acted directly on its mRNA or affected it through another process. In a protein turnover task, some model answers misestimated protein half-lives because they did not account for the gradual labeling of amino acids used to make new proteins. These model errors can lead researchers to pursue the wrong explanation even when individual analytical steps are completed correctly. This matters for major scientific goals such as drug discovery, where progress depends on choosing useful experiments and tools, interpreting unexpected results, troubleshooting failed approaches, and deciding which direction is most worth pursuing. Evaluating AI research assistance therefore requires checking whether its explanations, conclusions, and proposed experiments follow from the data and experimental design. These cases highlight continuing challenges in scientific reasoning for frontier AI models: bringing together different types of biological data, analyzing them with appropriate tools and databases, and using the results to draw appropriate conclusions and guide the next steps in research. The observed errors suggest training priorities in data analysis, biological interpretation, and experimental judgment and motivate evaluations that follow researchers and models through iterative scientific work.

title: A generative network model reveals hierarchical structural memory guiding post-mitotic 3D genome inheritance
authors: Morelli, L., Cretti, S., Michelatti, D., Bressan, D., Scandino, R., Chiacchiera, F., Cittaro, D., Peixoto, T. P., Zippo, A.
abstract: How three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is reestablished after mitosis to preserve gene regulatory programs and cell identity remains unresolved. We asked whether mitotic chromosome architecture contributes to cellular memory by preserving structural information while maintaining the flexibility required for cellular adaptation. Here we introduce HiCONA, a generative Bayesian framework that infers hierarchical genome organization and quantifies the structural contribution of individual interactions through an Entropy Impact Score. HiCONA resolves genome organization across multiple scales, revealing structure-defining interaction patterns underlying chromatin architecture, independently of experimental modality. We identify structurally impactful chromatin interactions retained during mitosis delineating distinct trajectories of post-mitotic genome reassembly. These mitotically preserved interactions are enriched for active, transcriptionally competent regulatory elements, consistent with a cis-encoded architectural memory subsequently remodeled by trans-acting regulators. Together, our findings suggest that molecular information retained on mitotic chromosomes guides structural trajectories, providing an architectural basis for epigenetic memory and post-mitotic genome inheritance.

title: A comparison of two culture and three sequencing methods for detection of the urobiome
authors: Khemmani, M., Noronha, M. F., Pham, T., Ferneyhough, B., Roddis, M., Parkinson, N. J., Wolfe, A. J.
abstract: Standard urine culture (SUC), the clinical reference method, is optimized for fast-growing aerobes and misses much of the urinary microbiota. Enhanced culture and sequencing methods have rarely been compared on the same specimens. We compared five methods (SUC, expanded quantitative urine culture [EQUC], short-read V4 16S rRNA gene sequencing, long-read near full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and PCR-free long-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing) on parallel aliquots of urine from pregnant participants screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria. Of 98 cultured samples, 98 (100.0%) were EQUC-positive while 85 (86.7%) SUC-positive. EQUC detected 102 species, but SUC only detected 41. Short-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing, long-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and shotgun sequencing were positive for 188/188, 186/188 and 139/139 samples, detecting 195, 69 and 528 species, respectively. In the 79 samples positive by EQUC and all three sequencing methods, sequencing profiles resembled each other more than culture profiles, and SUC captured only a subset of taxa detected by every other method. Shotgun sequencing gave the broadest taxonomic coverage and was the only sequencing method to identify Escherichia coli to the species level. With EQUC, it outperformed both 16S sequencing methods in detecting Gardnerella vaginalis and distinguishing Lactobacillus species, and it resolved six Gardnerella species, three detected by no other method. Long-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing gave the most confident amplicon-based species assignments, whereas culture better recovered Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus species. No single method was best across all endpoints, but long-read shotgun metagenomics provided the broadest species-level view. Method choice should match the research or clinical question; outcome-based studies are needed to establish clinical utility.

title: Follow-up availability and the robustness of immune transcriptomic recovery after myocardial infarction
authors: You, L., Zhang, G., Peng, Z., Guo, Y., Shen, L., Ge, J.
abstract: Background: Longitudinal blood transcriptomes describe immune changes after myocardial infarction, but later assays do not necessarily represent the population sampled at admission. We examined whether recovery summaries depend on observable selection and assumptions about unavailable assays. Methods: We reanalyzed official processed data from GSE59867, linking 111 patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction across admission, discharge, one month, and six months. Seven fixed Hallmark programs were scored on a common 17,590-gene vocabulary using a bounded within-sample rank statistic. The primary endpoint was the six-month inflammatory-response score. We separated paired-completer change from the observed follow-up mean minus the entire baseline mean; fitted cross-fitted availability and outcome models; and evaluated full-support completion bounds and prespecified missing-mean scenarios. Artificial deletion tested estimators in the 83 observed six-month participants. GSE123342 provided unlinked marginal comparisons and explicitly conditional completion scenarios. Results: GSE59867 contained 101, 95, and 83 follow-up assays. At six months, inflammatory-response change was -0.00893 among paired completers and -0.00999 for the marginal contrast (95% participant-bootstrap interval -0.01217 to -0.00783). Augmented inverse-probability weighting gave -0.01004 (-0.01556 to -0.00727). The full-support completion interval was [-0.16460,0.08765], but eliminating the negative change required an unavailable-assay mean 4.42 observed-follow-up standard deviations above the observed mean. The primary direction remained negative throughout the prespecified {+/-}2-SD scenarios; interferon and coagulation directions were less stable. Under artificial outcome-dependent deletion, all evaluated estimators retained bias. The unlinked external cohort had 65 admission, 64 day-30, and 37 year-one MI assays; the year-one inflammatory contrast was -0.00459, with a conditional tipping shift of 1.70 SD. Conclusions: The observed inflammatory-response rank-score decline was stable to baseline-score adjustment and the prespecified {+/-}2-observed-SD missing-mean scenarios, while unrestricted completion did not identify its direction. Robustness varied across programs and data settings. These findings concern relative transcriptomic scores and assay availability, not clinical recovery, survival, or intervention efficacy.

title: FastaGuard: FASTA preflight QC for modern bioinformatics pipelines
abstract: Summary: FastaGuard is a streaming, explainable FASTA preflight QC tool that validates assembly FASTA files, detects structural and composition red flags, and emits a versioned multi-format report with an explicit pipeline gate before expensive downstream analysis. We evaluated v1.1.0 in four analyses whose design was fixed before data collection. On 700 public NCBI assemblies the pipeline gate stopped 19.7% (1.9% weighted to the population), always on its high-N rule and mostly in scaffold-level genomes; the NCBI submission gate stopped 2.0%, and an independent recount confirmed every stop. Among 1,040 faults injected into real assemblies, the NCBI gate flagged 520 of 520 in 13 error classes (table2asn: 280 at error level) and blocked none of 120 benign changes. Across seven downstream tools, 46 of 182 defect cells failed and 12 altered the records without a warning, all in classes the pipeline gate blocks. Stopping a mismatched reference at the gate avoided about 54-62 s of mapping and sorting at a cost of 0.05-0.06 s. Availability and Implementation: Source code and documentation are freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/ehsanestaji/FastaGuard (release tag v1.1.0: https://github.com/ehsanestaji/FastaGuard/releases/tag/v1.1.0; archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23728753). Install via Bioconda (mamba install -c conda-forge -c bioconda fastaguard=1.1.0), BioContainers, or GitHub release binaries. Implemented in Rust; supported on Linux and macOS, including Bioconda builds for linux-64, linux-aarch64, osx-64, and osx-arm64. Contact: ehsan.estaji@umu.se; jianfeng.mao@umu.se Supplementary information: Supplementary Note (designs, all results, deviations from the pre-registered protocol); scripts, manifests and result tables at Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23729530.

title: Improving real-time search through deep learning-enhanced fragment ion indexing
authors: Eng, J., Hoopmann, M., Schweppe, D. K., MacCoss, M. J., Noble, W. S., Wen, B.
abstract: The fragment ion indexed database searching approach enables highly efficient tandem mass spectrometry database searches, including real-time search workflows. However, the index can require tens of gigabytes of memory, often exceeding the free memory available on instrument acquisition computers running the search. This restricts the size of the searchable database, the variable modification space, and the number of searches that can run concurrently. To address this problem, we developed an index-pruning pipeline within the Comet database search tool using Carafe, a deep learning tool that predicts fragment ion intensities based on peptide sequences. In our approach, only fragment ion positions that are predicted to be observable are written in the index, eliminating entries that are unlikely to contribute to spectrum detection. We evaluated this approach on two search spaces in three index configurations to demonstrate that masking significantly reduced the number of fragment ion index entries and, consequently, peak search memory use. Masked searches were also faster than unmasked searches and identified a comparable number of peptide-spectrum matches. Because all prediction and masking steps are performed before searching, their cost is amortized across repeated, future searches of the same database and modification configuration, introducing no per-spectrum search overhead. The complete implementation is open source with an Apache license.

title: VIGAT: VLM-guided gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq
abstract: Summary: Gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq is challenging because genomic regions informative of cell identity can vary across genes and tissues, while broadly accessible regions may provide limited cell-type-discriminative information. We developed VIGAT, a vision-language model (VLM)-guided tool that automates visual interpretation of ATAC coverage plots for adaptive gene activity quantification. VIGAT jointly examines accessibility patterns across multiple marker genes, integrating genomic annotations and biological context to select gene-specific regions enriched for cluster-discriminative signals. Selected regions are used to generate a gene-by-cell activity matrix. Across 196 paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq datasets, VIGAT outperformed five existing methods in recovering marker-associated accessibility enriched in the corresponding cell populations, demonstrating the utility of VLM-guided visual reasoning for scalable gene activity quantification. Availability and implementation: VIGAT is implemented as an open-source R package and is freely available at https://github.com/beijie02/VIGAT.

title: Folding without glutamine: Proteome-scale removal of a canonical amino acid
abstract:
by Alejandro Garciarrubio, Blanca Ramos-Cerrillo, Enrique Morett, Lorenzo Segovia 

All known life uses a canonical alphabet of 20 amino acids, yet which residues are structurally essential remains untested at proteome scale. Isoleucine was recently eliminated from ribosomal proteins in  Escherichia coli , establishing that amino acid alphabet reduction is feasible. Here we ask whether an entire amino acid can be eliminated from a proteome, and develop a computational framework to identify the best target. Using two independent approaches — ProteinMPNN structure-based probabilities and multiple sequence alignment conservation — we define “keep-score” as the fraction of positions where the native residue is optimal. Both methods converge on an unexpected candidate: glutamine has the lowest keep-score, with proline and glycine the highest — counter to substitution-matrix intuition. Glutamine’s low keep-score is not explained by a single obvious substitute; glutamate is preferred in only 14% of replacements. Removing this target proteome-wide, we replaced every glutamine across 4,148 proteins with ProteinMPNN-optimal alternatives and modeled the resulting sequences with AlphaFold2. The recoded proteome maintained native-like structures: 85.5% of models exceeded a TMscore of 0.8, indistinguishable from the 85.9% baseline for rebuilt native sequences. Orthogonal validation — ESMFold predictions, Rosetta energy calculations, and conformational ensemble comparisons — revealed no evidence of systematic misfolding attributable to glutamine removal. As a consistency check, a glutamine-free TEM-1 β-lactamase designed with ProteinMPNN conferred ampicillin resistance in  E. coli , indicating fold preservation can extend to biological function. Evolutionary evidence further supports these findings: 24% of  E. coli  proteins have glutamine-free orthologs in prokaryotic genomes, and glutamine ranks lowest in keep-score in  Saccharomyces cerevisiae . These results show that an entire amino acid can be removed from a proteome with folds broadly preserved, establishing keep-score as a general framework and glutamine as the primary candidate for recoding. Crucially, this reflects a computational analysis of structural replaceability, not a demonstration of biological dispensability.

title: The influence of ensemble size and composition on the performance of combined real-time COVID-19 forecasts
abstract:
by Friederike Becker, Katharine Sherratt, Nikos I. Bosse, Sebastian Funk 

During infectious disease outbreaks, short-term forecasts can play an important role for both decision makers and the general public. While previous research has shown that combining individual forecasts into an ensemble improves accuracy and consistency, practical guidance for organisers of multi-model prediction platforms on how to construct an ensemble has been scarce. In particular, it is not entirely clear how ensemble performance relates to the size of the underlying model pool, a relevant question when relying on voluntary contributions from modelling teams that face competing priorities. Furthermore, the exact composition of an ensemble forecast may influence its performance. Ensembles can either include all models equally or, alternatively, discriminate based on past performance or other characteristics. Using data from the European COVID-19 Forecast Hub we investigated these questions, with the aim of offering practical guidance to organisers of multi-model prediction platforms during infectious disease outbreaks. We found that including more models both improved and stabilised aggregate ensemble performance, while selecting for better component models did not yield any particular advantage. Diversity among models, whether measured numerically or qualitatively, did not have a clear impact on ensemble performance. These results suggest that for those soliciting contributions to collaborative ensembles there are more obvious gains to be made from increasing participation to moderate levels than from optimising component models.

title: Global sensitivity analysis for stochastic models of infectious diseases: Re-emergence of yellow fever virus in the Americas as a case study
abstract:
by Nate Kornetzke, Helen J. Wearing 

Emerging infectious diseases are a persistent public health threat that challenge deterministic, mechanistic modeling approaches. Because outbreaks initially start with a low number of infected hosts, their dynamics are highly stochastic, making traditional deterministic methods, e.g., ordinary differential equations, unable to qualitatively or quantitatively capture the transmission dynamics. In place, stochastic models are used, such as Markov chain models, but these models present their own challenges. Often, to infer a quantity of interest with stochastic models, we need to sample the model’s distribution many times over, introducing an additional source of noise to our analysis. This additional noise makes the inference of our quantity of interest more difficult and computationally expensive. Here, we show how novel tools from the field of uncertainty quantification can be used to efficiently separate these two channels of noise, allowing us to make rigorous statistical inferences about processes important for disease emergence. We illustrate these techniques with a model of yellow fever virus spillover in the Americas, a virus that has seen rapid re-emergence amongst multiple hosts and vectors in South America over the last decade. We show that only a handful of parameters’ uncertainties greatly affect variation in cumulative disease incidence. In particular, uncertainty in patch connectivity and non-human primate latency has the greatest impact on the variation of cumulative disease incidence of yellow fever virus across patches.

title: UniqSketch: sensitive and resource-efficient strain-level detection in metagenomes
abstract: Microbial communities contain diverse organisms, including multiple coexisting strains of the same species that display phenotypic differences influencing pathogenicity and host interactions. Detecting strains is challenging because of computational demands and their low abundance in metagenomes. We present UniqSketch, an open-source toolkit for identifying target strains across species within a single metagenome. It tracks specific microbial signatures or contaminants even in complex, multi-species samples. UniqSketch uses unique genomic fingerprints and a compact Bloom filter for efficient computation and accurate abundance estimation. Results show improved precision and accuracy over existing tools, with reliable performance at sequencing coverage as low as 0.1×.

title: EnzyREx: deep learning enables reaction-based comprehensive enzyme screening
abstract: Orphan enzymes for which the corresponding genes remain unidentified represent a major gap in functional annotation in genomic analysis. We present EnzyREx, an AI-based framework for comprehensive enzyme screening, to explore novel enzyme candidates. EnzyREx consists of two deep learning models to classify proteins as enzymes and non-enzymes and predict catalytic capability for enzyme‒reaction pairs. Both models achieved performance comparable to or better than that of existing software. When applied to 1,255 microbiome-related orphan reactions, EnzyREx identified candidate proteins for 897 reactions. EnzyREx provides a scalable approach for linking unannotated proteins to orphan reactions and extending functional annotation.

title: Predicting protein-RNA binding signals with a hybrid deep neural network
abstract:
Background
                      RNA-binding proteins play critical roles in post-transcriptional regulation by interacting with RNA to regulate various cellular processes. Inferring the binding signals and sequence patterns of these interactions is essential for elucidating the mechanisms underlying gene expression regulation. 
                  
                     Results
                      In this study, we present RBPSignal, a deep learning-based computational tool designed to predict RBP binding signals on RNAs and identify potential sequence motifs associated with these interactions. RBPSignal leverages the deep learning framework and trains on comprehensive eCLIP datasets, demonstrating an enhanced predictive accuracy. Furthermore, the integration of model interpretability through Integrated Gradients enables the detailed analysis of binding motif syntax. We validate the efficacy of RBPSignal on chromosome data and compare the discovered motifs with existing motif database, showcasing its ability not only to predict binding signals but also to uncover sequence patterns correlated with binding signals. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      Our findings provide insights into the sequence specificity of RBPs and explore the protein-protein motif-sharing network. RBPSignal serves as a valuable tool for exploring RBP-RNA interaction landscapes, facilitating further investigations into the regulatory networks underlying gene expression. The web server is freely available at  http://www.csbio.sjtu.edu.cn/bioinf/RBPSignal/ .

title: SHAKIRA: Scaled hierarchical ancestry K-population inference from RNA-seq alignments
abstract:
Background
                      Genetic ancestry estimation is an underutilized analytical approach that provides valuable biological context for studies investigating population-associated variation in gene expression, disease biology, and treatment response. Admixture-based ancestry estimates have historically relied on DNA microarray data, whole-genome sequencing, and whole-exome sequencing. However, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data contains informative markers suitable for broad ancestry estimates.
