Given the widespread availability of RNA-seq datasets, a standardized and accessible RNA-seq-based ancestry estimation pipeline would expand opportunities to incorporate genetic ancestry into transcriptomic analyses. 
                  
                     Results
                      Herein, we describe Superpopulation-level Haplotype Ancestry from K-population Inference of RNA Assays (SHAKIRA), a bioinformatic pipeline for estimating global genetic ancestry from cancer-derived RNA-seq data and evaluate its performance using both experimental tumor RNA-seq samples and an external reference dataset. First, we applied the pipeline to RNA-seq data from 86 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor samples and compared predominant ancestry coefficients to self-reported race. Using a 60% admixture proportion threshold to assign predominant ancestral superpopulation, 38 of 39 patients who self-reported as Black were assigned predominant African ancestry, and all 47 patients who self-reported as White were assigned predominant European ancestry. We then externally validated the pipeline using 144 Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) samples with published DNA microarray–based ancestry estimates. Ancestry estimates derived from RNA-seq data from CCLE samples demonstrated strong concordance with DNA-based estimates for African, American, and European ancestry components, with Pearson correlations of 0.995, 0.979, and 0.994, respectively. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      These findings support the feasibility of using RNA-seq-derived variants to estimate broad genetic ancestry, particularly for African and European superpopulation components. SHAKIRA provides a practical approach for incorporating genetic ancestry into RNA-seq-based studies when matched DNA sequencing or genotyping data are unavailable.

title: AMR GeoMapper: client-side geospatial and temporal visualization of user-provided antimicrobial resistance data
abstract:
Background
                      Geographic visualization is a key method for monitoring the profile of global antimicrobial resistance (AMR). While current mapping tools are capable, they lack the ability to visualize or compare to user-provided data. To address this gap, we have developed and deployed AMR GeoMapper (AMR-GM) to  https://camra.acegid.org/amr-geomapper/ . AMR-GM is a web-based tool that allows for client-side geographic and temporal analysis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) metadata. 
                  
                     Results
                      AMR-GM is a tool that enables users to produce interactive charts and maps of AMR genotypic/phenotypic and bacterial abundance data. Data can be easily formatted for AMR-GM by following the standards specified in the documentation. Additionally, AMR-GM natively loads data downloaded from amr.watch, allowing users to compare their data with publicly available datasets. The source code and documentation for AMR-GM is freely available at  https://github.com/JCVenterInstitute/AMR-GeoMapper-Public . 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      AMR-GM allows for private analysis of AMR data without reliance on public databases, giving researchers quicker access to high-quality visualizations. Because analysis of unpublished data is possible with AMR-GM, public health officials and researchers will have better software tools for analysis and surveillance of AMR and AMR pathogen spread in a geospatial framework.

title: Modality-aware external attention with explicit cross-omics interaction modelling for breast cancer subtype classification
abstract:
Background
                      Breast cancer is molecularly heterogeneous, and multi-omics measurements provide complementary information for molecular subtype classification. Their high dimensionality and modality-specific characteristics, however, make effective integration challenging. 
                  
                     Methods
                      We developed a modality-aware external attention (MAEA) framework for classifying five breast cancer subtypes using mRNA expression, DNA methylation, and miRNA expression data. Boruta feature selection is performed separately for each modality within each training fold. Modality-specific encoders generate latent representations, while pairwise Hadamard interaction tokens explicitly represent cross-omics relationships. These structured tokens query shared external key and value memories and are combined through a learned token gate. 
                  
                     Results
                      In stratified 10-fold cross-validation on TCGA-BRCA, MAEA achieved 86.78  ± 2.46% accuracy, 83.47  ± 4.38% macro-recall, 81.36  ± 3.48% macro-F1, and 0.9694  ± 0.0115 macro-AUC. A matched modality-aware self-attention model achieved 85.65  ± 3.76% accuracy and 81.26  ± 3.61% macro-F1, with no statistically significant fold-wise difference. MAEA improved accuracy by 3.40 percentage points and macro-F1 by 3.54 percentage points compared with a concatenation-based external-attention baseline. Ablation experiments further supported the contribution of feature selection, interaction modelling, and external-memory attention. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      MAEA provides a structured multi-omics fusion strategy that preserves modality identity while explicitly modelling pairwise cross-omics interactions. Independent external validation remains necessary before clinical application.

title: LEEN: local equivariant energy networks with evolution-guided structural reasoning for protein stability prediction
abstract:
Background
                      Accurate prediction of changes in protein thermodynamic stability ( Δ  Δ  G ) caused by single amino acid substitutions is important for protein engineering, therapeutic design, and interpretation of disease-associated variants. Recent approaches combine protein language models with structural neural networks via feature fusion, often yielding large, computationally expensive models that do not explicitly enforce thermodynamic consistency. We present LEEN (Local Equivariant Energy Network), a lightweight architecture that combines energy-based prediction with evolution-guided structural reasoning for protein stability prediction. 
                  
                     Results
                      LEEN is based on three complementary principles. First, mutation effects are predicted as the difference between mutant and wild-type energies evaluated in a shared local context, which guarantees fixed-context anti-symmetry algebraically; a symmetrized-context variant extends this to exact anti-symmetry when the same symmetrized context is applied to both mutation directions. Second, local protein geometry surrounding the mutation site is encoded using an E(n)-equivariant graph neural network, enabling rotation- and translation-equivariant structural representation learning. Third, evolutionary information extracted from a protein language model is incorporated via message gating, allowing sequence-derived context to modulate the flow of structural information rather than being concatenated with structural features. Despite using only approximately 2–3 million trainable parameters, LEEN achieves competitive performance on multiple low-sequence-similarity protein stability benchmarks. The full model obtains Spearman correlations of 0.657 on S461 and 0.470 on S669, while the best-performing variants reach 0.658 and 0.482, respectively. Ablation studies further show that incorporating evolutionary information contributes substantially more to predictive performance than the choice or complexity of the geometric encoder, while gating provides an additional, benchmark-dependent benefit. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      LEEN provides a compact framework for protein stability prediction that combines local equivariant structural reasoning with evolutionary information from frozen protein language model representations. The energy-difference formulation guarantees fixed-context anti-symmetry, and a symmetrized-context variant extends this to exact anti-symmetry for independently constructed mutation inputs when a shared symmetrized context is used, at a measurable accuracy cost. Across eleven benchmarks, LEEN achieves competitive predictive performance with a substantially smaller task-specific trainable component than larger multimodal predictors. These results highlight the importance of integrating evolutionary and structural information while making the trade-offs between predictive accuracy and thermodynamic consistency explicit.

title: Bringing seed barriers into focus: Optimized clearing and histological staining
authors:
Fabien Nirina Ramamonjy, 
Luca Piccinini, 
Vanessa Reyes Loaiza, 
Hongjun Meng, 
Robertas Ursache
abstract:
SUMMARY 
 Plant reproduction relies on tightly coordinated developmental programs that integrate environmental and endogenous signals. Within seeds, lipid-based extracellular polymers such as cutin and suberin are deposited at defined apoplastic interfaces, where they function as selectively permeable barriers. These structures are actively remodeled by hormonal and metabolic cues to regulate hydration, nutrient exchange, and stress responses. Although the genetic and biochemical pathways underlying these barriers are increasingly well understood, their spatial organization and developmental dynamics remain difficult to investigate because they are embedded within optically dense and multilayered tissues. Existing clearing approaches have substantially improved visualization of internal seed structures, yet systematic whole-mount imaging of multiple lipid-based barriers across development, particularly in combination with fluorescent reporters, remains challenging. To address this, we developed an optimized pipeline that enables rapid and efficient seed tissue clearing and selective visualization of polyaliphatic barriers across four key seed interfaces: the seed surface, seed coat suberin, cuticle at the endosperm/seed coat boundary, and embryo surface cuticle. The method preserves the spatial context of these barriers within intact seeds and enables their co-visualization with fluorescence-based marker lines. Using a common whole-mount imaging framework across successive developmental stages, we follow changes in the spatial organization of distinct barrier domains. The approach is also applicable to more complex seeds, such as those of  Camelina sativa,  and can be extended to other anatomically complex plant organs by combining the clearing and staining workflow with vibratome sectioning.

title: Root age structure governs long‐term architecture and hydraulic function in perennial plants: a modelling framework
authors:
Lukas Fichtl, 
Mona Giraud, 
Daniel Leitner, 
Andrea Schnepf, 
Katharina Steng, 
Matthias Friedel
abstract:
Conceptual overview of the perennial extensions implemented in CPlantBox, implemented for  Vitis vinifera .
 
 
 Summary 
 
Perennial root systems develop over decades and exhibit continuous turnover of structural and absorptive components, yet most root architecture models treat woody roots as permanent and neglect root age structure. We developed an empirically constrained modelling framework that explicitly represents age-structured demography, growth regulation and dormancy in perennial root systems ( Vitis vinifera ).
We extended the functional–structural plant model CPlantBox to simulate perennial root development over decades by integrating age-dependent survival, secondary radial growth and climate-driven dormancy. The model was parameterised using unique three-dimensional (3D) root system data from young and mature grapevines, together with dendrochronological root age measurements, and coupled to root hydraulic properties.
Empirical analyses revealed multicohort age distributions and substantial turnover of lignified structural roots, contradicting the assumption of a static woody scaffold. The model reproduced age distributions, order-specific survival probabilities and fine-to-structural root length ratios, and generated realistic, genotype-specific 3D architectures. Simulated uptake profiles and hydraulic scenarios showed strong age- and architecture-driven effects.
Explicitly representing woody root age distributions and age-dependent processes may fundamentally change predictions of perennial root system architecture and function. The framework advances root modelling beyond annual paradigms and provides a transferable tool for analysing long-term architectural and hydraulic consequences of genotype × climate interactions in perennial crops.

title: Identification of auxin response factor ARF27 as a regulator of maize root morphogenesis
authors:
Linkan Dash, 
Melissa A. Draves, 
Rajdeep S. Khangura, 
Maxwell R. McReynolds, 
Rebekah L. Muench, 
Craig L. Cowling, 
Gaoyuan Song, 
Brian P. Dilkes, 
Justin W. Walley, 
Dior R. Kelley
abstract:
Working model for  Zea mays  ARF27 mediated primary root growth in maize
 
 
 Summary 
 
Auxin is a central phytohormone that mediates root development. This study investigated the genetic basis of auxin-mediated primary root growth in  Zea mays  (maize) seedlings, which is not well-understood in this key cereal crop.
To address this knowledge gap, 618 accessions from the Wisconsin Diversity panel were leveraged for a genome wide association study (GWAS) followed by reverse genetics and  in silico  gene regulatory network reconstruction (GRN).
The GWAS identified several candidate genes associated with variation in root growth responses, including  RAMOSA2  and multiple members of the AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR (ARF) gene family. Maize  AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR27  ( ZmARF27 ), an ortholog of Arabidopsis  ARF7  and  ARF19 , was prioritized for functional characterization. A reduction in  ZmARF27  levels led to short primary roots, insensitivity to exogenous auxin, and altered transcriptional responses. Reconstruction of an ZmARF27 GRN included known maize classical root development genes, such as  ROOTLESS CONCERNING CROWN ROOTS , numerous auxin pathway genes, and genes associated with cell wall biogenesis.
Altogether, this study identifies  ZmARF27  as a novel genetic driver of auxin-mediated root growth and gene expression in maize.

title: PELOTA at the crossroads of tomato fertility and viral resistance
authors:
Zeenu Singh, 
Tali Sufrin Ringwald, 
Yardena Dahan, 
Dana Gelbart, 
Srinivas Kunta, 
Ben Avni, 
Haggai Wasserstrom, 
Vitaly Citovsky, 
Moshe Lapidot, 
Yogev Burko
abstract:
PELOTA (PELO) , a conserved ribosome surveillance factor underlying the tomato resistance allele  ty-5 , plays key roles in TYLCV susceptibility and reproductive development. Complete loss of  PELO  function ( pelo-1 CR 
 ) confers strong resistance to TYLCV but causes severe floral defects, impaired male and female fertility, and complete sterility. While  ty-5  reduces disease severity, it also decreases fruit size. CRISPR-mediated promoter editing generates novel  PELO  alleles, with reduced expression that confers resistance while maintaining normal fertility and fruit size ( PELO pro-31 
 ). Fine-tuning  PELO  expression therefore offers a promising strategy to improve tomato resistance without compromising reproductive development.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) is a major threat to tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum ) production, and durable resistance remains challenging to achieve.
We show that complete loss of function of  PELOTA  ( PELO ), a conserved ribosome surveillance factor underlying the resistance allele  ty-5 , confers near-immunity to TYLCV.
Unexpectedly, PELO is also required for reproductive development;  pelo  mutants display severe floral defects, impaired male and female fertility, and complete sterility, revealing a previously unknown role for PELO in tomato plant fertility.
Using CRISPR-mediated promoter editing, we generated novel  PELO  alleles with reduced expression that maintain fertility while conferring enhanced resistance to TYLCV, providing a new strategy.

title: Four universal modules and their combinations for decoding amplitude and frequency of Ca2+ signals in plants
authors:
Fernando Vergara‐Valladares, 
María E. Rubio‐Meléndez, 
Myriam Charpentier, 
Erwan Michard, 
Ingo Dreyer
abstract:
Modelling of Ca 2+  effects at the micro, macro, and cellular levels. (a) Ca 2+  binding to a calcium-binding protein (CBP) with two EF hands. (b) Four basic Ca 2+  sensor modules. (c) Combining Ca 2+  decoding modules with opposite properties can restrict the activity of the target protein (TP) to frequency islands.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Calcium signals are fundamental for plants and play crucial roles in developmental processes and in rapid responses to environmental stimuli and stress factors. Nevertheless, the mechanisms underlying the decoding of calcium signals in plants are still largely unclear.
We have addressed the question of Ca 2+  signal decoding in a bottom-up modelling approach starting with the thermodynamics of Ca 2+  binding to EF hands (EF: Glutamic acid–Phenylalanine) in Ca 2+ -binding proteins (CBPs). On this basis, we identified four universal, fundamental Ca 2+  decoding modules, in which a CBP modulates the activity of a target protein (TP).
Representatives of these basic modules are omnipresent in plant cells. Their Ca 2+  dependent properties are mainly determined by the interaction of the CBP with the TP rather than the Ca 2+ -binding properties of the EF hands. Combinations of the modules generated complexes that are also observed in plants, which decode not only the amplitude but also the frequency of Ca 2+  signals by setting specific ‘frequency islands’ in which a TP is active.
The modelling approach presented here addresses the decoding of Ca 2+  signals from the microscopic to the systemic level and could help to find the ‘Rosetta Stone’ for Ca 2+  signalling in plants.
 
 Resumen 
 
Las señales de calcio son fundamentales para las plantas y desempeñan funciones cruciales en los procesos de desarrollo, así como en las respuestas rápidas a los estímulos ambientales y los factores de estrés. Sin embargo, los mecanismos implicados en la decodificación de las señales de calcio en las plantas siguen sin estar claros en gran medida.
Hemos abordado el tema de la decodificación de las señales de calcio mediante un enfoque de modelado ascendente ( bottom-up ), partiendo de la termodinámica de la unión de Ca 2+  a los dominios  EF-hand  (EF: ácido glutámico–fenilalanina) en proteínas con unión de calcio (CBP, por sus siglas en inglés,  Ca 
 
    2+ 
 
 -binding proteins ). Sobre esta base, identificamos cuatro módulos universales y fundamentales de decodificación de Ca 2+ , en los cuales una CBP modula la actividad de una proteína diana (TP, del inglés  target protein ).
Los representantes de estos módulos básicos son omnipresentes en las células vegetales. Sus propiedades dependientes de Ca 2+  están determinadas principalmente por la interacción de la CBP con la TP, más que por las propiedades de unión de Ca 2+  de los dominios  EF-hand . Las combinaciones de estos módulos generaron complejos que también se observan en las plantas, lo que permitió decodificar no solo la amplitud, sino también la frecuencia de las señales de Ca 2+ , al establecer «islas de frecuencia» específicas en las cuales una TP está activa.
El enfoque de modelado presentado en este trabajo aborda la decodificación de las señales de Ca 2+  desde el nivel microscópico hasta el sistémico, y podría ayudar a encontrar la «piedra Rosetta» de la señalización por Ca 2+  en las plantas.

title: Engineering AP/Exo‐Cas12 as an efficient toolbox for rice genome editing via integrated repair and exonuclease modules
authors:
Nan Chai, 
Ruixiang Zhang, 
Guangzhou Li, 
Liying Su, 
Jun Wen, 
Shirui Huo, 
Xudong Yuan, 
Ruyue Chang, 
Xinglei Zheng, 
Zhiye Zheng, 
Taoli Liu, 
Dongchang Zeng, 
Qiupeng Lin, 
Yao‐Guang Liu, 
Xianrong Xie, 
Jiantao Tan, 
Qinlong Zhu
abstract: A modular apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP)/Exo‐Cas12 toolbox integrates cell selection enrichment with AP‐repair pathways or exonucleases for plant editing. It achieves efficient multiplex genome editing and easily detectable large DNA deletions in rice, providing a robust platform for multigene knockouts and crop improvement.

title: An alfalfa MYB71‐centered activation–attenuation module fine‐tunes redox homeostasis and drought tolerance in Medicago sativa
authors:
Bingcheng Han, 
Xueming Dong, 
Congcong Shi, 
Pei Mao, 
Yige Zhang, 
Qiang Zhou, 
Longfa Fang, 
Wenxian Liu, 
Chunxiang Fu, 
Jiangqi Wen, 
Zhipeng Liu
abstract:
In alfalfa, the transcription factor MsMYB71 activates the peroxiredoxin Q gene  MsPrxQ , which helps remove harmful reactive oxygen species and improves drought tolerance. The WD40-repeat protein MsPRL1 and the Cullin-family scaffold protein MsCUL4 interact with and limit MsMYB71 accumulation and activity in an activation-attenuation mechanism.

  
 ABSTRACT 
 Drought severely constrains alfalfa ( Medicago sativa  L.) productivity, yet dissecting drought–response mechanisms in this important perennial forage crop remains challenging because of its highly heterozygous autotetraploid genome, the extended cycle required for stable transformation and regeneration, and the time-consuming evaluation of drought responses in mature plants. Here, we identified  MsMYB71 , a drought-responsive R2R3-MYB transcription factor, as a positive regulator of drought tolerance in alfalfa. Mechanistically, MsMYB71 directly bound to the promoter of  MsPrxQ  (peroxiredoxin Q), encoding a chloroplast-associated peroxiredoxin Q, and activated its expression, thereby promoting redox homeostasis under drought stress. In contrast, MsPRL1 (PLEIOTROPIC REGULATORY LOCUS 1, a WD40-repeat protein) and MsCUL4 (Cullin4, a Cullin-family scaffold protein) interacted with MsMYB71 and attenuated its protein accumulation and transcriptional output. To establish the physiological relevance of this regulatory module directly in alfalfa, we generated stable overexpression and RNA interference lines for all four genes. Genetic and physiological analyses showed that MsMYB71 enhanced drought tolerance and restricted excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation. Stable manipulation of  MsPrxQ  further established its positive role in drought tolerance and antioxidant defense. In contrast, MsPRL1 and MsCUL4 negatively regulated drought tolerance and physically interacted with MsMYB71. Their co-expression reduced MsMYB71 protein accumulation in a proteasome-sensitive manner and attenuated MsMYB71-dependent activation of  MsPrxQ , consistent with an MsPRL1/MsCUL4-associated attenuation mechanism. Together, our findings define an MsPRL1/MsCUL4– MsMYB71 – MsPrxQ  module that couples transcriptional activation with protein-level attenuation to fine-tune redox homeostasis and drought adaptation in alfalfa.

Observation of a magneto-nonlinear Hall effect in an altermagnet candidate
abstract: Abstract Nonlinear Hall effects have emerged as defining probes of quantum geometry. Here we observe a Hall response that is nonlinear in the magnetic field rather than the electric field, in Mn 5 Si 3  thin films, an altermagnet candidate, in the canonical Hall geometry: a high-field Hall conductivity component that grows quadratically with an out-of-plane field. Opposite-sign Berry curvatures associated with opposite-spin bands nearly cancel at low fields, but Zeeman band shifts at high fields lift this cancellation and generate increasing net total Berry curvature. This magnetic-field-tuned Berry-curvature imbalance can generally produce a nonlinear Hall conductivity, and the observed quadratic dependence in Mn 5 Si 3  is consistent with chiral next-nearest-neighbor hopping involving magnetic exchange and Haldane-like flux phases. Moreover, reversal of magnetic order under opposite fields reverses the hopping chirality, making this quadratic contribution odd in field. Beyond fundamental advances, the nonlinear response remains unsaturated up to 57 T, suggesting possible opportunities for high-field Hall sensing.

title: Orbital magnetization from parallel transport of Bloch states
abstract: Abstract Quantum geometric formulations of linear and nonlinear responses can be constructed from a single building block in the form of a gauge-invariant interband transition operator. Here, we identify a second building block for quantum geometry: a band-resolved adiabatic connection operator that captures the noncommutativity between Bloch projectors and their momentum derivatives. The band-resolved adiabatic connection operator, first introduced in the theory of adiabatic driving, serves as a generalized angular momentum within the state manifold of single bands, and we employ it to reformulate expressions for the band-resolved orbital magnetic moment. This form provides a complementary geometric interpretation alongside the multiband separation between energetic- and quantum-state properties by the two-state Berry curvature. Our formalism allows us to present formulas valid for both nondegenerate and degenerate bands, thereby removing the limitations of the common Bloch-state formula. We illustrate our theory by calculating a large orbital magnetization emerging without spin-orbit coupling in a spin-compensated, noncoplanar anomalous Hall magnet with degenerate bands.

title: Miniaturization coincides with anatomical novelties during lissamphibian origins
abstract: Abstract Evolutionary miniaturization is often accompanied by phenotypic rearrangement, and may play an important role in occupying new adaptive zones. This process has hypothesised relevance to the origin of lissamphibians, which include the smallest living tetrapods. We test this by quantifying patterns of evolution of body size and other traits, using a dataset of 577 fossil and extant members of the lissamphibian total-group. We find that initial body size reduction occurred on the direct stem lineage leading to Lissamphibia and further miniaturization occurred in the crown group, giving rise to the down-shifted size distribution of living species. This coincides with rearrangements of skull morphology and the diversification of body shapes, indicating invasion of a fundamentally distinct adaptive zone. Our finding provides a compelling case of the potential contribution of miniaturization to ecological innovation at a macroevolutionary scale, facilitating the diversification and persistence of lissamphibians through ∼300 million years of evolutionary time.

title: Meta-state electrolytes with quasi-ordered clusters for stable lithium metal batteries
abstract: Abstract Ionic aggregation state in liquid electrolytes is generally constrained by the salt solubility limit of the solvent matrix, restricting the accessible coordination structures and limiting opportunities for electrolyte engineering. Here, we report a class of meta-state electrolytes (MSEs) that transcend this conventional solubility limit and access an atypical aggregation regime. Enabled by external-field regulation coupled with nonequilibrium kinetic access, the MSE reshapes the Li⁺ coordination landscape and stabilizes a previously inaccessible meta-state domain beyond the threshold region of the ternary phase diagram. Within this regime, the MSE remains macroscopically homogeneous while forming large anion-rich clusters with local coordination environments resembling those of solid lithium salt, yielding an inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) with high mechanical robustness and fast Li +  transport. Accordingly, the MSE effectively suppresses interfacial parasitic reactions, enabling Cu||LiNi 0.5 Co 0.2 Mn 0.3 O 2  pouch cells to retain 70% of their capacity after 136 cycles at 45°C. Our study establishes external-field regulation of the Li +  coordination environment as a new design principle for advanced electrolytes, with broad implications for solid/liquid interfacial chemistry.

abstract: Climate change is expanding the geographic distribution of infectious diseases into new areas and altering their seasonal transmission patterns. title: Leaving X: How scale insects repeatedly evolved alternatives to chromosomal sex determination
abstract: Abstract Reproduction is a core feature of life, yet it is still unclear why sex determination systems are conserved for hundreds of millions of years in some taxa but repeatedly turn over in others. A prime example is the true bugs; the vast majority of families employ a conserved X sex chromosomal system, but in scale insects (Coccomorpha), sex determination systems are more varied. Scale insects may retain X chromosomes, employ a form of haplodiploidy known as paternal genome elimination (PGE), or reproduce via selfing as simultaneous hermaphrodites. We sequenced 17 new scale insect species to study sex determination transitions. We recovered two independent losses of the X, once in the family Monophlebidae and a second time at the base of the PGE families. In the former, genomic rearrangements begin before the X is lost, leading to a pair of massive autosomes to which the X fuses in hermaphrodites. In the latter, the X chromosome has multiple fates, from being preserved intact, albeit without sex determination function, to being reshuffled as part of a massive whole genome rearrangement in mealybugs. We analyzed ortholog conservation across the transitions and found few genes lost, with only one orthogroup lost in both, and a number of orthogroups gained, suggesting these transitions did not require large changes to gene content. Finally, extreme sexual dimorphism of gene expression predates sex determination turnover and lingers on some formerly X-linked sequences. Together, these results illustrate the multiple routes to sex determination turnover, refine causal hypotheses, and provide a wealth of new resources for genomic study of scale insects.

title: On the limits of detection of higher-order epistatic interactions
abstract: Abstract The function of microbial communities is often dominated by additive and pairwise interactions, raising the question of whether this reflects intrinsic biological simplicity or fundamental limits of detection. Here, we leverage the theory of fitness landscapes to bridge microbial ecology and genetics, and show that this apparent simplicity is a generic consequence of structural and statistical constraints rather than evidence for intrinsically weak higher-order interactions. We separate the detectability of individual epistatic interactions from their contribution to functional variance, and demonstrate that local  k -order interactions suffer from exponential noise amplification while their contributions to total variance are intrinsically suppressed by order-dependent geometric dilution arising from the combinatorial structure of the landscape. Applying this framework to a fully sampled 210 experimental microbial landscape, we find that only first- and second-order interactions are distinguishable from experimental noise. Furthermore, generalized Lotka–Volterra landscapes reveal that experimental noise alone can generate the illusion of higher-order structure in communities where all direct mechanistic interactions are pairwise and indirect interactions are weak. Our findings identify universal, order-dependent limits on the quantification of epistasis that apply to high-dimensional landscapes across ecology and genetics, providing a principled foundation for rational community design.

title: Dynamic Supercooled Crystal–Gels for Ultrafast, Reversible Mechanical Adaptative Materials
authors:

abstract:
A dynamic supercooled crystal–gel mimics starfish tissue by storing non‐equilibrium energy in a metastable liquid. A gentle touch triggers templated crystallization, producing a 2596‐fold stiffness increase with negligible volume change. The lattice disintegrates reversibly under humidity or warmth. Developed Microneedles exploit this biomechanical logic for skin penetration and seconds‐scale drug release.








ABSTRACT
Endowing synthetic materials with adaptability and responsiveness to dynamically optimize their states represents a premier frontier in biomimetic science. However, achieving life‐like, rapid yet reversible adaptation under benign triggers remains hindered by high reconfiguration energy or delayed structural recovery. In this work, we present dynamic supercooled crystal‐gels that achieve ultrafast, reversible stiffening without requiring continuous energy input. Inspired by the tactile‐triggered stiffening of starfish tissues, it utilizes non‐equilibrium energy of internal supercooled liquid to realize templated crystallization upon a benign tactile stimulus trigger. Meanwhile, the crystalline structure is reversible under appropriate temperature and humidity perturbations. This synchronously achieves a 2596‐fold adjustment in compressive modulus, circumventing the conventional trade‐off between energy demands for mechanical reinforcement and structural stability. As a functional validation, microneedles based on supercooled crystal‐gels fulfill the divergent requirements for skin adaptation and seconds‐scale drug release through their mechanical adaptation, achieving rapid cumulative drug release of ≈37.76% at 10 s and 88.12% within 5 min. This work delineates a strategy for endowing materials with autonomous mechanical adaptation and opens new opportunities for life‐like functional evolution in soft robotics and bio‐integrated electronics.

Nitrogen-Fixing Microorganisms  
 On this cover, rainfall feeds the soil microhabitats where nitrogen-fixing microbes thrive. The artwork shows mean annual precipitation as the dominant driver of global nifH diversity: limited rainfall selects competitive larger-genome N-fixers, abundant rainfall favors smaller-genome species. abstract:
Cavity-Enhanced Eye-Readable Detection of 0.1% H 2 
  
 Featured on the cover is a cavity-structured eye-readable H 2  sensor operated via hydrogen-induced charge transfer mechanism. H 2  reduces the oxide shell of close-packed Au@Pd@oxide nanoparticles, which transitions plasmonic resonance from gap mode into charge-transfer mode, producing vivid color change.
